question_text: Under what circumstances does the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals say liquidated damages (LD) will be levied for a delayed delivery?
answer: The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals state that LD is levied only when the delay is attributable to the supplier. They also specify three situations where the delay is not the supplier’s fault and therefore no LD is imposed: (i) delay in approving an advance sample that the supplier submitted on time; (ii) delay caused by an omission on the part of the purchaser that hinders contract performance; and (iii) delay when the purchaser controls the entire production. To determine whether LD applies, please tell me which of these circumstances matches the reason for the delay in your case.
cot:
The user is asking about when liquidated damages (LD) will be levied for delayed delivery under the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals.

Let me think about what I know:

From section 9.7.3 - Extension of Delivery:
- Suppliers shall be required to adhere to the delivery schedule specified in the purchase order
- If there is delay in supplies, LD shall be levied wherever there is failure by the party
- Extension of delivery date amounts to amendment of the contract and can only be done with consent of both parties
- The confirmation of extension should mention applicability of LD clause beyond the original contract delivery date / the last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date
- On receiving supplier's communication, the procuring entity may agree to extend delivery schedule, with or without LD

From section 9.7.4 - Delay in Supplies for which Supplier is not Responsible:
In certain circumstances, the contractual delivery period needs to be re-fixed WITHOUT imposing any penalty to the supplier:
i) Cases where manufacture is dependent on approval of advance sample and delay occurs in approving the sample though submitted by supplier in time
ii) Where extension is granted on account of some omission on the part of the purchaser which affects due performance of the contract
iii) Cases where the purchaser controls the entire production

So LD is levied when:
- There is delay in supplies and failure by the supplier (the supplier is responsible for the delay)
- When extension is granted, LD may apply beyond the original contract delivery date / last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date
- Extension may be granted with or without LD

LD is NOT levied (delivery period re-fixed without penalty) when:
- Delay in approving advance sample submitted in time by supplier
- Omission by purchaser affecting supplier's performance
- Purchaser controls entire production

Let me structure this answer clearly.
chunk_content:
### 9.7.2 Terms of Delivery
Terms of delivery (FOR, FOB, CIF, and CFR, and so on), inter alia, determine the delivery point of the ordered goods from where the purchaser is to receive/collect the goods. It also decides the legally important issue of when the 'titles of the goods' have passed to the purchaser. The delivery period is to be read in conjunction with the terms of delivery, therefore the delivery is taken to have been made at the time when goods reach the delivery point as per the delivery terms. The delivery condition of FOR NRL (Location) may be adopted as far as possible.

### 9.7.3 Extension of Delivery
Suppliers shall be required to adhere to the delivery schedule specified in the purchase order and, if there is delay in supplies, LD shall be levied wherever there is failure by the party. Extension of the delivery date amounts to amendment of the contract. Such an extension can be only done with the consent of both parties (that is, the purchaser and supplier). No extension of the delivery date is to be granted suo motu unless the supplier specifically asks for it.

The confirmation of extension of delivery period (provisional / firm) should inter-alia contain the following:-

- (i) The time for delivery is extended from (CDD) to (extended CDD)
- (ii) Applicability & mention of LD clause beyond the original contract delivery date / the last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date.
- (iii) Requirement of extension of the validity period of the performance guarantee.
- (iv) That the above extension of delivery date will also be subject to the Denial Clause.

On receiving the supplier's communication, the procuring entity shall examine the proposal and, on approval from the CA, may agree to extend the delivery schedule, with or without LD

### 9.7.4 Delay in Supplies for which Supplier is not Responsible
Normally, in the following circumstances, the contractual delivery period needs to be re-fixed to take care of the lost period, without imposing any penalty to the supplier:

- i) Cases where the manufacture of stores is dependent on the approval of the advance sample and delay occurs in approving the sample though submitted by the supplier in time;

- ii) Where extension in the delivery period is granted on account of some omission on the part of the purchaser which affects the due performance of the contract by the supplier; and
- iii) Cases where the purchaser controls the entire production.

question_text: What is the monetary threshold that triggers the need for an auditor’s certificate
answer: For any procurement whose value is more than Rs. 10 Crores, the undertaking you submit with your bid must be supported by a certificate from a statutory auditor, cost auditor, or practicing chartered/cost accountant that confirms your local‑content percentage. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 34)

First, I ask myself what the question is really after: the specific amount of money that makes an auditor’s certificate compulsory for a bid.  
Next, I recall the provisions regarding the certification of local content, which list what bidders must submit at the bidding stage.  
In that list, the requirement for a certificate is tied to the size of the procurement: the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals state that when the procurement value is in excess of Rs. 10 Crores, the undertaking must be supported by a certificate from a statutory auditor, cost auditor, or practicing chartered/cost accountant.  
From that I infer that the trigger point is the moment the procurement crosses Rs. 10 Crores; below that amount the certificate is not required, and at or above that amount it becomes mandatory.  
Putting the pieces together, the monetary threshold that triggers the need for an auditor’s certificate is Rs. 10 Crores.

question_text: Which four amounts are deducted from the value of work done when issuing a termination certificate for a contractor’s fundamental breach or insolvency
answer:
- Advance payments  
- Any recoveries  
- Taxes as due  
- Percentage to apply to the work not completed as indicated in the contract data  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 114)
cot: First, I consider what the termination certificate is meant to represent: the net amount the contractor should receive after accounting for what the procuring entity has already provided or is owed. Then, I think about the kinds of amounts that would have been paid upfront or withheld during the contract. The first that comes to mind is any advance payment made to the contractor, which must be reclaimed because the work will not be finished as planned. Next, there are recoveries—these could be liquidated damages, penalties, or other sums the entity is entitled to retain due to the breach. After that, taxes that have accrued on the work performed but not yet remitted need to be deducted to reflect the true net payable. Finally, because the contract is being ended before completion, the entity must also adjust for the portion of work that remains undone; this is done by applying a percentage, as specified in the contract data, to the value of the unfinished work and subtracting it from the gross value of work done. Bringing these points together, the four deductions are advance payments, any recoveries, taxes as due, and the percentage to apply to the work not completed as indicated in the contract data.

### 6.10.2 Arbitration Awards
- i) In cases where the Company has challenged an arbitral award and, as a result, the amount of the arbitral award has not been paid, 75% of the arbitral award (which may include interest up to date of the award) **shall** be paid by the Company to the contractor/ concessionaire against a Bank Guarantee (BG). The BG **shall** only be for the said 75% of the arbitral award as above and not for the interest which may become payable to the Company should the subsequent court order require refund of the said amount.

**Note: In para 6.10.2 (i) instructions containing "shall" are mandatory; any deviation from these instructions shall require approval from the Board of Directors.**

- ii) The payment may be made into a designated Escrow Account with the stipulation that the proceeds will be used first, for payment of lenders' dues, second, for completion of the project and then for completion of other projects of the same Company as mutually agreed/ decided. Any balance remaining in the escrow account subsequent to settlement of lenders' dues and completion of projects of the Company may be allowed to be used by the contractor/ concessionaire with the prior approval of the lead banker and the Company. If otherwise eligible and subject to contractual provisions, retention money and other amounts withheld may also be released against BG.

## 6.11 Breach of Contract, Remedies and Termination


### 6.11.1 Breach of Contract
In case the contractor is unable to honour important stipulations of the contract, or gives notice of his intention of not honouring or his inability to honour such a stipulation, a breach of contract is said to have occurred. Mostly, such breaches occur in relation to the performance of the contract in terms of inability to complete the Work within stipulated time. It could also be due to breach of

ethical standards or any other stipulation that affects Procuring Entity seriously. As soon as a breach of contract is noticed, a show cause notice should be issued to the contractor, giving 10 days' notice, reserving the right to implement contractual remedies. If there is an unsatisfactory resolution, remedial action may be taken immediately.

If termination takes place because of a fundamental breach/ insolvency on the part of the contractor, the EIC shall issue a certificate for the value of work done, deducting from the amounts in respect of: (i) advance payments; (ii) any recoveries; (iii) taxes as due; and (iv) percentage to apply to the work not completed as indicated in the contract data. If the total amount due to the procuring entity exceeds that due to the contractor, the difference will be a debt payable to the procuring entity. A contract may be terminated in the following cases with approval of CA and written communication on termination of contract should be conveyed to the contractor from Commercial Department. The Procuring Entity is then free to take over the site and complete the works himself or with another contractor and use the contractor's materials, equipment, temporary works as he/ they think proper.

## 7.6 Award of Contract
After the acceptance of these recommendations by the tender accepting authority (TEC), the Letter (Notification) of Award (LoA) can be issued.

LOA / Purchase Orders incorporating all the terms and conditions agreed to with the tenderer shall be placed within the validity periods of the tenders proposed for acceptance. When the original validity periods have expired, suitable extensions shall be obtained before the orders are issued.

section: 5.3 Procedures to be followed during Bid Opening
question_text: How should the bid opening committee treat late bids received after the specified date and time for receipt of bids in an open or limited tender enquiry
answer:
Late bids received after the specified date and time for receipt of bids in an advertised (Open or Global) or limited tender enquiry shall be handled as follows:

1. **Count** the late bids separately.
2. **Keep** the late bids aside; do **not** open them.
3. **Do not consider** the late bids.

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 103)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the procedure demands once the bid submission deadline has passed. The key point is that any bid arriving after the stipulated date and time must be treated differently from those that were on time.  

Looking at the situation, the first logical step is to identify which submissions are late. This means checking the timestamp on each bid against the announced deadline and pulling out those that exceed it.  

Once the late bids are identified, they should be set apart from the timely ones so that they do not get mixed up during the opening process. Keeping them separate ensures that the integrity of the on‑time bid opening is maintained and that there is no accidental inclusion of late submissions.  

After separating them, it makes sense to count how many late bids there are and record that number. This provides a clear audit trail showing exactly how many submissions were received after the deadline, which is useful for reporting and for demonstrating compliance with the rules.  

The next step is to keep those counted late bids aside and refrain from opening them. Opening a late bid would undermine the principle that only bids received by the deadline are eligible for consideration, so they must remain sealed and untouched.  

Finally, because the late bids have not been opened and are not part of the eligible set, they must be excluded from any further evaluation, scoring, or award decision. This ensures that the tender process remains fair and that only compliant bids proceed to the next stages.  

Putting these steps together leads directly to the prescribed handling: identify, separate, count, keep aside unopened, and do not consider the late bids for evaluation.

section: 6.1.5 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Performance Bank Guarantee and Other Instruments [ABG, SD-BG etc.]
question_text: What does the monthly monitoring process require regarding bank guarantees and other instruments that are due to expire within the next three months
answer: Verify that a monthly review is conducted of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring within the next three months, and that the review includes an assessment of the progress of the corresponding contracts. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 106)
cot:
To understand what the monthly monitoring process requires, I start by thinking about its purpose: it is meant to keep track of securities that are about to lapse so that timely action can be taken.  
Looking at the description of the process, the key condition is that any bank guarantee or similar instrument that will expire within the upcoming three months must be watched closely, because otherwise it could lapse unnoticed.  
Given that condition, the logical step is to institute a regular check—specifically a monthly review—that scans the entire portfolio for those items whose validity ends in the next three months.  
Since the effectiveness of a guarantee is tied to the underlying contract, the review cannot stop at merely identifying expiring instruments; it must also verify how the related contracts are progressing, to decide whether an extension, encashment or refund is warranted.  
Putting these points together, the monthly monitoring process obliges the responsible unit to conduct a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments set to expire within the next three months and to include in that review an assessment of the progress of the corresponding contracts.
chunk_content: A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of Performance Bank Guarantee and other instruments should be implemented by LIV section. The Procuring entity shall also make institutional arrangements for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of Performance Bank Guarantee, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the supplier for purpose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc.

question_text: Which specific activities are excluded from the scope of consultancy services?
answer:
Consultancy services are confined to advisory, professional, intellectual, training and advisory functions; therefore, the following activities are excluded from their scope:

- Procurement of goods (except when merely incidental or consequential to the consultancy service)  
- Procurement of works (except when merely incidental or consequential to the consultancy service)  
- Direct engagement of a retired Government servant  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 10)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the definition of consultancy services actually says about what it covers and what it leaves out.  
The definition tells me that consultancy services are advisory or professional in nature, involving mainly non‑physical, project‑specific, intellectual and procedural processes.  
It then explicitly states that these services are “other than goods or works, except those incidental or consequential to the service.”  
From that clause I can infer that the procurement of goods and the procurement of works are not part of consultancy services unless they are merely incidental or consequential to the advisory work being performed.  
Reading further, the definition adds a clear limitation: consultancy services “do not include direct engagement of a retired Government servant.”  
That gives me a third distinct activity that is expressly excluded.  
Putting those pieces together, the activities that fall outside the scope of consultancy services are the procurement of goods (except when merely incidental), the procurement of works (except when merely incidental), and the direct engagement of a retired Government servant.  
This matches the answer provided, confirming that the reasoning is consistent with the given information.

### 9.9.2 **Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and seeking Approval.**
Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked. The cost estimate shall be based on the Procuring Entity's assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment: managerial and staff time and physical inputs (for example, materials, consumables, tools and machines). Costs shall be divided into three broad categories:

- i) Remunerations for Personnel deployed;
- ii) Reimbursable: (Travel, logistics, Consumable, Material, Tools, Hiring of third party services etc.);
- iii) Administrative and Miscellaneous (Mobilisation, demobilisation, Temporary Structures, Administrative expenses, office and IT equipment, contingencies, financing costs, Costs for hiring/ depreciation/ financing of machinery and equipment etc).

### 9.9.3 **Final Administrative and Budgetary Approvals**
The Activity Schedule shall be compatible with the available budget. The most important step is to determine whether all tasks required to achieve the desired output have been included. The next step is to determine whether adequate budget has been allocated to implement the assignment as designed. Procurement should be initiated only after such approvals and budgetary provisions.

Appropriate WBS / Cost Centre having required fund has to be used in all POs. No PO should be issued with "Unknown" account assignment.

Services are procured against Cost Centre (K) and Project (P) and procurement budget is required during creation of PR and PO. Cost is booked in GL as soon as SES (Service Entry Sheet) is made and accepted in system.

For ARCs (outline agreement) adequate fund will be required only at the time of issuing Release Order.

- For revenue item procurement where budget is expected to be consumed across financial years, detailed procedure for "Control over release of Commitment Budget", issued by Finance Dept. to be referred.

## 9.10 Procedure for Single Source Selection (SSS)
Should it become necessary, in an exceptional situation to outsource a job to a specifically chosen contractor, the CA's approval may be taken. In such cases the detailed justification, the circumstances leading to the outsourcing by choice and the special interest or purpose it shall serve shall form an integral part of the proposal.

## 9.11 Procedure for Small Value and emergency Procurements of Other (Non-consultancy) Services
In many small value procurements of other services, the service provider may neither be capable of handling the bidding process, nor would this be a cost-effective process for the Procuring Entity. The 'Direct Procurement without Quotation' mode of procurement used in Procurement of goods may very well be utilised in such cases. Similarly for procurement of services 'Direct Procurement by a Purchase Committee' mode as used in procurement of Goods may be utilised. In all such modes of procurement, the procedure prescribed in the Manual for Policies and Procedures for Procurement of Goods may be followed.

Please refer “Manual for Procurement of Goods”:-

Section 4.9 **Direct Procurement without Quotation**; and

Section 4.10(a) **Departmental Purchase**; and

Section 4.10(b) **Spot Purchase**

## 9.12 Procedure for Procurements through shortlisted agencies
The Procuring Entity should scrutinise the preliminary list of likely contractors shortlist the prima facie eligible and capable contractors and issue RfP to these shortlisted firms on a limited tender enquiry basis as per procedure in vogue.

section: 7.2 Preparation and Vetting of Comparative Statement
question_text: How should alternative specifications with acceptable prices be presented in the comparative statement?
answer: - Verify that the comparative statement lists the price quoted for every firm, and for any alternative specifications that are deemed acceptable, includes the quoted price for each alternative together with a suitable explanatory note describing the deviations from the base specification (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants to know how alternative specifications that are both acceptable and priced should appear in a comparative statement.  
Next, I recall that the preparation guidelines require a clear, item‑by‑item tabulation of all tenders, so I look for the part that deals with pricing and specifications.  
In that section I see that the price quoted by every firm must be listed, and then there is a specific provision: when a firm offers an alternative specification that is deemed acceptable, its price must also be shown together with a note that explains how that alternative deviates from the base specification.  
This tells me that the comparative statement is not just a simple price list; for each acceptable alternative it must include both the quoted price and a concise explanation of the deviation.  
Putting these points together, the correct way to present such alternatives is to ensure the statement records the price for every firm and, for any acceptable alternative specification, adds its price alongside an explanatory note detailing the deviations.  
Thus, the verification step is to check that the comparative statement contains exactly those elements—firm prices, alternative prices, and deviation notes—so that the comparison remains meaningful and transparent.
chunk_content:
### Broad guidelines for preparation of Comparative statement:
- i) To facilitate proper bid analysis, the comparative statement shall be made of all the

tenders received on the following basis:

- a) Price quoted by all the firms shall be given. Where alternative specifications has been offered for the jobs under reference and are acceptable, their prices shall also be indicated along with suitable explanatory note concerning deviations.  
The item wise estimate / Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) shall also be given in this tabulation to make comparison of estimate / LPP with the tendered rates.
  - b) Prices quoted shall be reduced to a common base for a meaningful comparison.
  - c) All deviations either in specifications or in standard terms and conditions shall specifically be highlighted, particularly those having a bearing on price or delivery shall be indicated.
  - d) Contractual completion / delivery term of all parties shall be given.
  - e) Discount / Rebate if any offered to be indicated.
  - f) Foreign exchange required in the case of imports shall be indicated.
  - g) Incidence of GST/ Customs Duty/ Excise Duty/ or other Statutory levies, shall be quantified and clearly shown.
  - h) Packing, Handling, Forwarding and Transportation Charges, insurance as applicable should be specified and the incidence thereof should be shown.
  - i) Where advance payment is involved, the cost implications must be determined / indicated.
  - j) Prices escalation clause, if any to be clearly indicated and the cost implication loaded in the tender evaluation.
  - k) Taking all factors into consideration, comparative cost evaluation statement shall be made to give a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison.
  - l) Applicable Purchase preferences and the policies of the Government with regard to MSE and other guidelines shall be suitably brought out in the evaluation sheet for the guidance of the TEC.
- ii) The comparative statement shall be uploaded in Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial dept.
- iii) The Commercial Department would prepare a detailed note (TEC note) to the Tender Committee / CA highlighting the main points with the recommendation for the award of the contract. The tender papers enclosed along with the above note should include the

comprehensive tabulation drawn as indicated above to arrive at a meaningful comparison for effective decision-making. There should be no ambiguity in any of the data presented for consideration.

iv) Technical explanation should be given for variation between prices quoted in the tender and the evaluated prices. Any positive or negative loading done to render the comparison meaningful should be properly explained. Clarifications sought from the tenderers and the resulting impact on the quotation if any should be specifically mentioned. It should be ensured that all technical details; specification drawings and other aspects contained in the offers have been thoroughly checked for conformity with the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee.

v) In short, a factual, informative and technically cleared material should be portrayed in the noting to the Committee / CA to facilitate taking decisions for the contracts without further reference to the field units.

The comparative statement so prepared should be enclosed along with TEC note for approval of award as per DOA.

## 7.3 Technical & Commercial Examination

question_text: Which contractual provision must be included in a percentage contract to ensure quality and scope are verified before payment
answer: The contract must include a provision for the evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables, with payments released only against certification by the Engineer‑in‑Charge (EIC). (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 21)
cot:
First, I consider what a percentage contract actually entails: the consultant’s fee is tied to the project’s cost, and payment is made only after the objectives have been successfully achieved.  
Because the money is released after the fact, there is a risk that the work could be accepted and paid for even if it falls short of the required quality or scope.  
To guard against that, the contract needs a built‑in checkpoint that confirms the deliverables meet the agreed standards before any payment is issued.  
Looking at how such contracts are structured, the logical checkpoint is a formal evaluation of the quality and scope of what has been delivered.  
That evaluation must be documented and authorized by someone with authority—in this case, the Engineer‑in‑Charge—so that the payment trigger is explicitly linked to their certification.  
Putting these pieces together, the essential provision that must be included is a clause requiring evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables, with payment released only upon certification by the Engineer‑in‑Charge.

## 3.4 Percentage Contract
3.4.1 Percentage contracts directly relate the fees paid to the consultant/ service provider to the estimated or actual project cost, or the cost of the goods procured, inspected or sold. Since the payment is made after the successful realisation of objectives, it is also called success (or contingency) fee contract. The final selection is made based on QCBS evaluation process or among the technically qualified consultants/service providers who have quoted the lowest percentage while the notional value of assets is fixed.

These contracts are commonly used for appropriate architectural services; procurement and inspection agents, disposal of scrap etc.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

## 3.5 Indefinite Delivery Contract (Price Agreement)
3.5.1 These contracts are used when Procuring Entity need to have "on call" specialized services, the extent and timing of which cannot be defined in advance. This is akin to the system of 'Rate Contracts' or framework contracts in the procurement of Goods. There is no commitment from Procuring Entity for the quantum of work that may be assigned to the consultant/ service provider. The Procuring Entity and the firm agree on the unit rates to be paid, and payments are made on the basis of the time/ quantum of service actually used. The consultant/ service provider shall be selected based on the unit rate quoted by them for providing the services.

These are commonly used to retain "advisers" or avail services 'on-call' - for example; expert adjudicators for dispute resolution panels, institutional reforms, procurement advice, technical troubleshooting, and so forth - normally over a period of a year or more.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

Contracts need to be closely monitored and administered by the EIC to ensure that the progress of assignment is commensurate with the time spent and that the resources for which payment is claimed have actually efficiently and productively been deployed on the assignment during the period.

question_text: How does the requirement for mutual discussion and mediation support strategic procurement goals
answer:
The requirement for mutual discussion and mediation sets an initial, amicable step in dispute resolution, giving parties a chance to settle differences before arbitration is considered. This early‑resolution approach reduces the likelihood of escalating to formal arbitration, thereby supporting procurement objectives of managing disputes efficiently and limiting reliance on arbitration processes. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 152)

- Offers a chance to resolve disputes without invoking arbitration, thereby decreasing reliance on formal arbitration processes. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 152)  
- Supports the procurement objective of addressing disagreements through discussion and conciliation before escalating to arbitration. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 152)  
- Provides a clear, sequenced approach—first discussion/mediation, then arbitration if unresolved—supporting orderly dispute handling. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 152)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: it wants to know how a specific procedural step—requiring the parties to try mutual discussion and mediation before moving to arbitration—fits into the larger aims of strategic procurement.  

Then I look at the dispute‑resolution provision itself, which says that as soon as a disagreement arises the purchaser and supplier must first attempt to settle it amicably through discussion, mediation or conciliation, and only if that fails within a set period may they proceed to arbitration.  

Seeing that, I note that the rule creates a mandatory “first‑stop” checkpoint: any dispute has to be handled informally before the more formal, costly arbitration route can be opened.  

Next I consider what strategic procurement typically tries to achieve—things like keeping acquisition costs low, avoiding delays that could disrupt supply, preserving good working relationships with suppliers, and managing risk in a predictable way.  

I then connect the checkpoint to those goals: by forcing the parties to talk things out early, many disagreements can be cleared up quickly and cheaply, which saves the arbitration fees and administrative time that would otherwise be incurred; it also gives both sides a chance to preserve trust and keep the contract on track rather than letting a disagreement fester into a formal battle.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the requirement for mutual discussion and mediation therefore supports strategic procurement by providing an ordered, low‑cost pathway to resolve differences, cutting down the need to rely on arbitration and helping the procurement organization meet its objectives of efficiency, cost control, and stable supplier partnerships.

### 9.8.1 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, such as removal from the list of registered supplier, by written notice of default sent to the supplier, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part:

- i) If the supplier fails to deliver any or all of the stores within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted; and
- ii) If the supplier fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted;
- iii) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the EMD;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, goods similar to those undelivered may be procured and the supplier shall be liable for all available actions against him, as applicable in terms of the contract (including risk purchase); and
  - c) However, the supplier shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 9.8.2 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the supplier becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the supplier, without compensation to the supplier, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 9.8.3 Termination of Contract for Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the supplier for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the supplier may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract.

## 9.9 Dispute Resolution
Normally, there should not be any scope for dispute between the purchaser and supplier after entering into a mutually agreed valid contract. However, due to various unforeseen reasons, problems may arise during the progress of the contract leading to a disagreement between the purchaser and supplier. Therefore, the conditions governing the contract should contain suitable provisions for settlement of such disputes or differences binding on both parties. The mode of settlement of such disputes/differences should be through arbitration. However, when a dispute/difference arises, both the purchaser and supplier should first try to resolve it amicably by mutual discussion, mediation, and conciliation. If the parties fail to resolve the dispute within 21 (twenty-one) days, then, depending on the position of the case, either the purchaser or supplier should give notice to the other party of its intention to commence arbitration. When the contract is with a domestic supplier, the applicable arbitration procedure shall be as per the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [Amended 2015 and 2021]. While processing a case for dispute resolution/litigation/arbitration, the procuring entity is to take legal advice, at appropriate stages.

3.10.1 There are three methods for selection/evaluation of consultancy proposals viz. Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS), Least Cost System (LCS) and Single Source Selection (SSS). The Fixed Budget Based Selection (FBS) method is hereby also allowed for selection of consultants. Under this method, cost of the consulting services shall be specified as a fixed budget in the tender document itself. FBS may be used when :

- (i) the type of consulting services required is simple and/or repetitive and can be precisely defined; and
- (ii) the budget can be reasonably estimated and set based on credible cost estimates and/ or previous selections which have been successfully executed; and
- (iii) the budget is sufficient for the consultant to perform the assignment.

3.10.2 Under FBS, the selection of the consultant shall be made by one of the following two methods :

- (i) By a competitive selection process, based only on quality, using specific marking criteria for quality. The proposal with the highest technical score that meets the fixed budget requirement shall be considered for placement of contract.
- (ii) In cases of repetitive or multiple assignments, by empanelling suitable quality criteria. Thereafter, selection of a specific consultant for a specific assignment from such panel shall be based on overall considerations of timeliness, practicability, number of other assignments already given to that consultant in the past, etc. In such cases the budget for each assignment shall also be fixed by the procuring entity.

Clear & unambiguous scoring methodology must be indicated so that there is no scope for subjective evaluation.

question_text: Under what circumstance may the option clause be exercised earlier than after 50 % quantity receipt
answer: - The option clause may be exercised before 50 % quantity receipt if the delivery period is approaching expiration and all other stipulated conditions for exercising the clause are fulfilled, enabling timely procurement alignment with strategic objectives and risk mitigation. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 146)
cot:
I need to figure out when the option clause can be used before the usual halfway‑point of the order. The standard rule is that the clause is only triggered after half the quantity has been received, so there must be a specific exception spelled out somewhere. 

What stands out in the guidance is a note that says the clause is normally applied after 50 % receipt, *but* it can be exercised earlier if the delivery period is about to run out and the other required conditions are still satisfied. That suggests the timing of the delivery schedule is the key trigger for an early exercise.

Looking at the other conditions that must be met—no declining price trend, availability of additional demand, proper notice to the contractor, and keeping the option in mind during the next procurement cycle—it becomes clear that early exercise isn’t automatic just because the deadline is looming; all those safeguards still have to hold true. 

If the delivery window is closing, waiting until 50 % receipt could leave the procuring entity short of supplies or force a rushed, less‑optimal purchase later. By allowing the option to be drawn down early, the entity can secure the extra quantity in time, align the procurement with its strategic timing needs, and avoid the risk of a stock‑out or costly last‑minute sourcing. 

Putting this together, the circumstance that permits an early exercise of the option clause is when the delivery period is nearing expiration and all the other stipulated conditions for using the clause are fulfilled, enabling timely procurement and risk mitigation.

question_text: How are tenders that do not meet the basic requirements specified in the bid documents treated during evaluation
answer:
- Tenders that fail to meet the basic requirements specified in the bid documents are classified as unresponsive.  
- Unresponsive tenders are excluded from both the technical‑commercial and financial evaluation phases (including two‑envelope bidding).  
- An initial scrutiny by the dealing officer identifies all unresponsive offers before detailed evaluation proceeds.  
- Once a tender is deemed unresponsive, it cannot be made responsive later by correction or withdrawal of the non‑conforming stipulation and is ignored for the remainder of the process.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 72)
cot: First, I consider what the question is really asking: what happens to a bid that does not satisfy the basic conditions set out in the tender documents. Then I think about what those basic conditions typically are – the prescribed format, proper signing, provision of earnest money deposit, eligibility of the bidder, agreement to essential requirements like performance security, and quoting for the whole schedule of works. Knowing that, I recall that before any detailed technical or price analysis takes place, the procuring officer carries out an initial scrutiny of all received tenders just to see whether they meet those basic stipulations. During this first look, any tender that fails one or more of those checks is immediately labelled as unresponsive. Because the unresponsive tag is applied at this early stage, the bid is taken out of the subsequent evaluation stream; it is not examined in the technical‑commercial review and, if the process uses two‑envelope bidding, it is also ignored in the financial envelope. Moreover, the rules state that once a tender has been marked unresponsive it cannot be rescued later by correcting the missing item or withdrawing the non‑conforming clause – it remains excluded for the rest of the procedure. Putting these points together leads directly to the conclusion that tenders not meeting the basic requirements are treated as unresponsive offers, are excluded from both technical‑commercial and financial evaluation (including the two‑envelope approach), are identified in the initial scrutiny, and cannot be made responsive afterwards.

### 5.4.1 Confidentiality of Process
- i) Information relating to the examination, clarification, evaluation and comparison of bids, and recommendations for the award of a contract, shall not be disclosed to bidders or any other person not officially concerned with such a process until the award to the successful bidder has been announced.
- ii) From the time of bid opening to the time of contract award, no bidder shall contact the Procuring Entity on any matter related to the bid, except on request and prior written permission.
- iii) Any effort by the bidder to influence the Procuring Entity in bid evaluation, bid comparison or contract award decisions will vitiate the process and will result in the rejection of the bidder's bid. Such conditions, incurring in (i) & (ii) above shall be embedded in the Instructions to Bidders (1TB).

### 5.4.2 Unresponsive Tenders
Tenders that do not meet the basic requirements specified in the bid documents are to be treated as unresponsive (both during Techno-commercial evaluation and Financial Evaluation in case of Two Envelope bidding) and ignored. All tenders received will first be scrutinised by the dealing officer to see whether the tenders meet the basic requirements as incorporated in the Bid document and to identify unresponsive tenders, if any. Unresponsive offers may not subsequently be made responsive by correction or withdrawal of the non-conforming stipulation. Some important points on the basis of which a tender may be declared as unresponsive and be ignored during the initial scrutiny are:

- i) The tender is not in the prescribed format or is unsigned or not signed as per the stipulations in the bid document;
- ii) The required EMD has not been provided or exemption from EMD is claimed without acceptable proof of exemption;
- iii) The bidder is not eligible to participate in the bid as per laid down eligibility criteria (example: the tender enquiry condition says that the bidder has to be an enlisted contractor but the tenderer is not an enlisted contractor);
- iv) The bid departs from the essential requirements specified in the bidding document (for example, the tenderer has not agreed to give the required performance security); or

- v) Against a schedule in the list of requirements in the tender enquiry, the tenderer has not quoted for the entire requirement as specified in that schedule (example: in a schedule, it has been stipulated that the tenderer will supply the equipment, install and commission it and also train the Procuring Entity's operators for operating the equipment. The tenderer has, however, quoted only for supply of the equipment).

### 5.4.3 Minor Infirmary/ Irregularity/ Non-conformity
During the preliminary examination, some minor infirmity and/ or irregularity and/ or non-conformity may also be found in some tenders. Such minor issues could be missing pages/ attachment or illegibility in a submitted document; non-submission of requisite number of copies of a document. For example, the bidder submitted the amendment Bank Guarantee, but omitted to submit the main portion with Bid Document. These may be considered as minor irregularity. Such minor issues may be waived provided they do not constitute any material deviation (please also refer to Para 5.5.1 (iv) below) and financial impact and, also, do not prejudice or affect the ranking order of the tenderers. Wherever necessary, observations on such 'minor' issues (as mentioned above) may be conveyed to the tenderer by e-mail / through e-tendering portal, and so on, asking him to respond by a specified date also mentioning therein that, if the tenderer does not conform Procuring Entity's view or respond by that specified date, his tender will be liable to be rejected. Depending on the outcome, such tenders are to be ignored or considered further.

section: 2.2 Preparation of Preliminary Project Report (PPR) or Rough Cost Estimate
question_text: What provisions for documenting exclusions and any other relevant documents in the PPR enable auditors to evaluate completeness and transparency when compared with the Department of Expenditure’s disclosure standards
answer: The PPR requires a specific subsection for exclusions (item iii) and a separate provision for any other relevant documents (item xi). By obliging the preparer to enumerate what is omitted from the estimate and to attach all supplementary materials, the PPR creates a transparent, auditable record that allows auditors to verify that no material aspect has been left out and that all supporting evidence is available. The source does not state how this aligns with the disclosure standards of the Department of Expenditure. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 17)
cot:
I start by asking what the question is really after: it wants to know which parts of the Preliminary Project Report (PPR) specifically deal with writing down exclusions and any other supporting documents, and how those parts help auditors judge whether the report is complete and transparent when measured against the disclosure rules set by the Department of Expenditure.  

Next, I think about where the PPR’s contents are laid out. The guidance tells us that the report must cover a list of specific items, and among those items there are two that stand out for this purpose—one that asks for a statement of exclusions and another that calls for any other relevant documents to be attached.  

Looking at those two items, I see that the exclusions clause (the one that says “Exclusions (if any)”) forces the person preparing the PPR to explicitly note what work is *not* included in the estimate. By making the preparer spell out what is left out, the report creates a clear record of gaps that an auditor can later check against the actual project scope.  

Then I consider the “any other relevant documents” provision. This requirement obliges the preparer to gather and attach every piece of supplementary material—drawings, approvals, cost analyses, cash‑flow sheets, funding sources, and so on—that might affect the estimate. When all of those pieces are present in the file, an auditor has the full set of evidence needed to verify that nothing material has been omitted.  

Putting these two provisions together, the PPR becomes a self‑contained, auditable package: exclusions highlight what is missing from the cost estimate, while the collection of other relevant documents supplies the proof that everything that *should* be considered is actually there. This structure mirrors the Department of Expenditure’s emphasis on full disclosure and transparency, giving auditors a straightforward way to compare the report against those standards and conclude whether the estimate is both complete and open to scrutiny.  

Thus, the specific sections on exclusions and on any other relevant documents in the PPR are what enable auditors to evaluate completeness and transparency in line with the Department of Expenditure’s disclosure expectations.

question_text: Which documents can bidders submit to prove their average annual turnover for the last three financial years
answer:
Bidders can prove their average annual turnover for the last three financial years by submitting either:

- Copies of the audited profit & loss account for each of the last three financial years, **or**  
- A certification of the annual turnovers for the last three financial years issued by a registered chartered accountant firm.

If the audited annual report or financial statements are dated after July 2019, they must be accompanied by a UDIN number; otherwise they will not be considered for evaluation.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 37)
cot:
First, I focus on what the question is really asking: it wants to know which specific documents a bidder can provide to demonstrate that their average annual turnover over the last three financial years meets the required threshold.  

Next, I think about the nature of turnover proof—turnover figures come from a company’s financial records, so the acceptable evidence must be something that verifies those figures for each of the three years in question.  

Looking at the guidance on financial capabilities, I see that bidders have two alternative ways to satisfy this requirement: they can either submit copies of the audited profit & loss account for each of the last three financial years, or they can obtain a certification of the annual turnovers for those same three years from a registered chartered accountant firm.  

I then consider how the “last three financial years” are defined in relation to the bid submission date. If the bid is submitted after 31 December, the three years are the immediate preceding ones; if the bid is on or before 31 December and the audited or CA‑certified turnover for the immediately preceding year is not available, the three years prior to that preceding year may be used instead.  

Finally, I note an additional procedural detail that affects the validity of the documents: any audited annual report or financial statement issued after July 2019 must be accompanied by a UDIN number; without it, the document will not be accepted for evaluation.  

Putting these points together, the acceptable proofs are either the audited profit & loss statements for the last three years (with UDIN where required) or a chartered accountant’s certification of turnover for those years. This matches the answer that bidders can submit either of those two types of documentation to prove their average annual turnover.

First, I need to figure out what the question is really asking: it’s about choosing the right currency for insuring the goods that are being procured.  
Next, I recall that whenever payment is made in advance, against dispatch documents, or via a letter of credit, the contract must include an insurance condition, and the goods have to be fully covered for any loss or damage that could happen during manufacture, acquisition, transport, storage, or delivery.  
Then I think about the practical side of that coverage: the insured amount has to be enough to reimburse the procuring entity for all expenses it will incur to receive the goods at the destination, which means the insurance payout must be usable in the same financial context as those expenses.  
Looking at the guidance on currency, it specifies that the insurance should be taken out in a freely convertible currency so that the proceeds can be readily exchanged or used wherever the costs arise without restriction.  
Putting those points together, the only way to satisfy the requirement of covering the full expenditure and to ensure the insurance proceeds are usable internationally is to arrange the insurance in a freely convertible currency.

question_text: What procurement action is required if maintenance is to be contracted separately from the supply contract
answer:
- Issue a separate tender enquiry for the maintenance contract when it is to be procured independently of the supply agreement.  
- Evaluate all tenders received and rank them according to the evaluated tender value.  
- Award the maintenance contract to the lowest‑evaluated responsive tenderer (the goods supplier may also submit a quote, which is considered alongside other offers).  

This approach ensures transparent competition, aligns maintenance expenditures with value‑for‑money objectives, and reduces the risk of unexpected service disruptions, thereby supporting corporate goals and effective risk management. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 141)
cot:
First, I consider what it means for maintenance to be contracted separately from the supply contract – the two procurements are independent, so the maintenance side cannot be bundled into the original tender for the goods.  

Looking at the options for who can provide the maintenance, I see that the contract may be placed either with the original supplier or with any other competent firm; if the purchase organisation decides to go with a separate provider, the process must treat the maintenance as its own procurement exercise.  

Given that decision, the logical next step is to prepare a distinct tender enquiry that captures the full scope of the maintenance services – the required duration, service levels, payment terms, spare parts coverage, and any penalties – so that potential bidders know exactly what is being asked for.  

Once the tender is issued, all received offers, including a possible bid from the goods supplier, must be evaluated on a common basis; this means adding the quoted maintenance costs for the agreed period to any other relevant cost elements and, for multi‑year contracts, discounting future payments to present value to ensure a fair comparison.  

After evaluation, the tenders are ranked by their evaluated tender value, and the contract is awarded to the lowest‑evaluated responsive tenderer, which maintains competitive pressure and aligns the maintenance spend with value‑for‑money objectives.  

Putting these steps together, the required procurement action is therefore to issue a separate tender enquiry for the maintenance contract, evaluate and rank all tenders, and award the contract to the lowest‑evaluated responsive bidder, allowing the original supplier to compete alongside other firms. This approach supports transparent competition, controls future service risks, and meets the organisation’s risk‑management and corporate‑goal priorities.

### 2.2.1 Conflict of Interest in case of consultants
- i) The consultant is required to provide professional, objective, and impartial advice, at all times holding the Procuring Entity's interests paramount, strictly avoiding conflicts with other assignments or his/its own corporate interests, and acting without any consideration for future work.

- ii) The consultant has an obligation to disclose to the Procuring Entity any situation of actual or potential conflict that impacts its/his capacity to serve the best interest of its client/Procuring Entity. Failure to disclose such situations may lead to the disqualification of the consultant or termination of its/his contract during execution of the assignment.
- iii) Without limitation on the generality of the foregoing, and unless stated otherwise in the data sheet for the RfP document, the consultant (i.e., private entities) shall not be hired under the circumstances set forth below:
  - a) **Conflicting activities:** a firm that has been engaged by the client to provide goods, works, or non-consultancy services for a project, or any of its affiliates, shall be disqualified from providing Consultancy service resulting from or directly related to those goods, works, or non- Consultancy services for the same project. Conversely, a firm hired to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, or any of its affiliates, shall be disqualified from subsequently providing goods or works or non-consultancy services resulting from or directly related to the consultancy services for such preparation or implementation for the same project;
  - b) **Conflicting assignments:** Consultants (including its experts and sub--consultants) or any of their affiliates shall not be hired for any assignment that, by its nature, may be in conflict with another assignment of the consultant for the same Procuring Entity.

### 2.2.2 Unfair Competitive Advantage in case of consultants
Fairness and transparency in the selection process require that the consultants or their affiliates competing for a specific assignment do not derive an unfair competitive advantage from having provided consultancy services related to the assignment in question. Such unfair competitive advantage is best avoided by full transparency and by providing equal opportunity so that all firms or individuals interested or involved have full information about a service assignment and its nature, scope, and background information. To that end, the request for proposals and all information would be made available to all short listed consultants simultaneously.

question_text: What should the contract clearly state about the amount of customs duty payable on imported goods?
answer: The contract should clearly state the exact amount (quantum) of customs duty that is payable, using unambiguous terms. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 114)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: it wants to know what the contract must explicitly say about the customs duty that will be owed on goods that are imported.  

Next, I recall the rule that deals with imported goods and customs duty: whenever duty is actually payable, the agreement has to spell out the exact quantity of that duty in clear, unambiguous wording.  

Then, I think about what “quantum of duty” means in this context—it refers to the precise amount of customs duty that the importer will have to pay, not just a rate or a percentage, and it must be stated so that there is no room for interpretation.  

Finally, putting those points together, the contract should clearly state the exact amount of customs duty payable on the imported goods, using language that leaves no doubt about what that amount is.

### 6.8.2 Octroi and Local Taxes
In case the goods supplied against contracts placed by Procuring Entity are exempted from levy of town duty, Octroi duty, terminal tax and other levies of local bodies, the suppliers should be informed accordingly by incorporating suitable instructions in the tender enquiry document and in the resultant contract. Wherever required, the supplier should obtain the exemption certificate from the Purchasing Department to avoid payment of such levies and taxes.

In case such payments are not exempted (or are demanded in spite of the exemption certificate), the supplier should make the payment to avoid delay in supplies and forward the receipt to the Purchasing Department for reimbursement and for further necessary action.

### 6.8.3 Customs Duty on Imported Goods
On imported goods, the tenderers shall also specify separately the total amount of custom duty included in the quoted price. The tenderers should also indicate correctly the rate of custom duty applicable for the goods in question and the corresponding Indian customs tariff number. Where customs duty is payable, the contract should clearly stipulate the quantum of duty payable, and so on, in unambiguous terms. The standard clauses to be utilised for this purpose are to be incorporated in the tender enquiry documents. Any import of materials directly from the supplier or manufacturer should be in the name of Procuring Entity. In this regard, all formalities will be completed by Procuring Entity engaging a Custom House Agent (CHA) and payment in this regard will be borne by Procuring Entity.

The Government has allowed exemption from payment of customs duty on certain types of goods for use by the following organisations:

- i) Scientific and technical instruments imported by research institutes;
- ii) Hospital equipment imported by Government hospitals; and
- iii) Consumable goods imported by a public-funded research institution or a university.

However, to avail of such exemptions, the organisations are required to produce a "Custom Duty Exemption" certificate and "Not Manufactured in India" certificate at the appropriate time.

The relevant contemporary instructions covering these aspects should be incorporated in the tender enquiry document and in the resultant contract.

### 6.8.4 Duties/Taxes on Raw Materials
Procuring Entity is not liable for any claim from the supplier on account of fresh imposition and/or increase (including statutory increase) in excise duty, custom duty, sales tax, and so on, on raw materials and/or components used directly in the manufacture of the contracted goods taking place during the pendency of the contract, unless such liability is specifically agreed to in terms of the

contract. A clause to this effect should also form part of the tender documents.

question_text: What happens after the technical proposals have been evaluated
answer: ** The financial proposals are publicly opened and then evaluated. This step allows the procurement team to compare costs before selecting the winning proposal and moving to negotiations and contract award. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 37)
cot:
First, I consider what the selection process looks like once the technical side has been scored—there must be a defined next step that moves the evaluation forward.  
Looking at the overall flow, the technical evaluation is followed by a stage that deals with the cost side of the proposals, because the final decision needs to balance quality and price.  
The logical next action is to make the financial proposals available for review, and doing so publicly ensures transparency and prevents any perception of hidden bias.  
Once the financial documents are opened, they can be examined and scored, allowing the team to compare the costs of the firms that have already passed the technical threshold.  
With both quality and cost scores in hand, the procurement team can identify the winning proposal, then proceed to any needed negotiations before finally awarding the contract.  
This sequence—public opening of financial proposals, their evaluation, selection of the winner, negotiations, and contract award—matches exactly what should happen after the technical proposals have been evaluated.

section: 3.6 Systems of Selection of service providers
question_text: How does the procuring entity’s capacity to supervise an assignment influence the choice of selection system?
answer: The procuring entity’s capacity to supervise an assignment directly influences how quality and price are weighted in the selection system. This assessment of supervisory capacity is normally conducted before deciding on the selection method, making it a key factor in determining which system is applied. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 22)
cot:
First, I consider what drives the choice of a selection system for consultancy work. Since the quality and scope of such assignments aren’t directly observable, the procuring entity must rely on indirect indicators—mainly the consultant’s technical and financial capability—to infer performance. The system therefore needs to balance how much weight it gives to quality versus price, and that balance isn’t fixed; it shifts with the specifics of the assignment.

Next, I identify the key condition that tips that balance: the entity’s own ability to engage with and supervise the work. If the entity has strong internal expertise and can closely monitor the consultant’s progress, it can trust that oversight will catch any quality shortcomings. In that case, price becomes a more reliable discriminator, and a system that emphasizes low cost—like Least Cost Selection—makes sense. Conversely, when the entity lacks the capacity to supervise effectively, it cannot depend on its own monitoring to ensure quality, so it must build quality assurance into the selection process itself. That pushes the weighting toward quality‑focused methods such as Quality and Cost Based Selection, or, in rare cases where only a single suitably capable source exists, Direct Selection.

Then, I think through the procedural step: before any selection method is chosen, the procuring entity normally assesses its supervisory capacity. This assessment informs the decision on how much emphasis to place on quality versus price, and consequently which system will be applied. The assessment isn’t an afterthought; it’s a prerequisite that shapes the whole selection design.

I deepen the analysis by noting that this reasoning holds across the range of selection systems described—price‑based, quality‑cost based, and direct selection—because each system represents a different point on the quality‑price spectrum. The entity’s supervisory strength determines where on that spectrum it feels comfortable operating.

Finally, I synthesize: the procuring entity’s capacity to supervise directly shapes the quality‑price weighting in the selection system. Strong supervision lets the entity rely more on price‑oriented approaches like LCS, while weak supervision nudges it toward quality‑oriented approaches like QCBS or SSS. Because this capacity evaluation precedes the method choice, it is a decisive factor in determining which selection system is ultimately used.

## 3.6 Systems of Selection of service providers
3.6.1 Since the quality and scope of a consultancy assignment are not tangibly identifiable and consistently measurable, the technical and financial capability of consultants becomes an important though indirect determinant for quality and scope of performance. In such a situation value for money is achieved by encouraging wide and open competition among equally competent consultant. Thus, selection of consultants is therefore, normally done in a two stage process. In the first stage, likely capable sources are shortlisted, if need be through an 'Expression of Interest' (EoI) through advertisement (i.e., open notifications). On the basis of responses received, consultants meeting the relevant qualification and experience requirements for the given assignment are shortlisted for further consideration. The shortlist should include a sufficient number, generally not fewer than three (3) and not more than eight (8) eligible firms. In the second stage, the shortlisted consultants are invited to submit their technical and financial (RfP) proposals generally in separate sealed envelopes. Evaluation of the technical proposal is carried out by evaluators without access to the financial part of the proposal. Financial proposals are opened after evaluation of quality.

3.6.2 The relative importance of Quality and Price aspects may vary from assignment to assignment depending on complexities/ criticality of quality requirements, internal capability of Procuring Entity to engage and supervise the assignment, as well as the value of procurements. Hence different systems of selection of consultants/ service providers are designed to achieve appropriate relative importance (weightage) of Quality and Price aspects. Decision on system of selection is normally preceded by an assessment of the capacity of the user to engage and supervise the implementation of proposed assignment. The selection method chosen depends to some extent on this assessment. Selection of system of selection also should take into account the likely field of Bidders.

3.6.3 The nomenclature of various selection methods below is in line with generally prevalent nomenclature.

- i) Price based System - Least Cost Selection (LCS);
- ii) Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS);
- iii) Direct Selection: Single Source Selection (SSS)

3.6.4 Unlike Procurement of Consultancy Services, **procurement of other services is done by a simpler process akin to those of procurement of Goods and Works.** In procurement of other (non-consultancy) services normally system of selection used is lowest price (L-1) basis as in procurement of Goods/ works for technically responsive offers. Under very special circumstances Single Source Selection may also be used. However, in highly technical and complex services, where quality is important (say in studies like seismic surveys, airborne data acquisition etc) where use of QCBS system appears to be called for, it may be better handled as a consultancy contract.

3.6.5 It is possible that there may be single offer situation against open tenders and there may be tendency to go for re-tender as a safe course of action. Re-bidding has costs: firstly the actual costs of retendering; secondly the delay in execution of the work with consequent delay in the attainment of the purpose for which the procurement is being done; and thirdly the possibility that the re-bid

may result in a higher bid. Even when only one Bid is submitted, the process may be considered valid provided following conditions are satisfied:

- 1) The procurement was satisfactorily publicized and sufficient time was given for submission of bids.
- 2) The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive; and
- 3) Prices are reasonable in comparison to market values

section: 8.15 Terminating Services Prior to End of Contract
question_text: Who determines which final billings are eligible for payment after termination, and what process follows if there is a dispute
answer:
- The CMC/EIC determines which final billings are eligible for payment after termination. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 65)  
- If a dispute arises over the legitimacy of expenses, the established dispute mechanism is invoked.  
- Should the dispute not be resolved amicably, the matter is submitted to arbitration.  
- The contract remains valid until the arbitration decision is made.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint who has the authority to judge whether a consultant’s final invoices can be paid after a contract is ended. The termination provisions make clear that once a contract is halted, the procuring entity must settle any legitimate outstanding fees, but it doesn’t pay everything automatically—there has to be a determination of what counts as a legitimate expense.  

Next, I identify the entity tasked with making that determination. The CMC/EIC is responsible for indicating which of the firm’s final billings are eligible for payment and which are not. This role fits naturally: after termination, the CMC/EIC reviews the submitted claims and separates payable from non‑payable items.  

Then I consider what happens if the consultant or service provider disagrees with that assessment. The termination clause anticipates disagreement over what constitutes a legitimate expense and provides a built‑in dispute mechanism for exactly this situation.  

Following that mechanism, the first step is to try to resolve the disagreement amicably between the parties. If those discussions fail to produce agreement, the next step outlined is to escalate the matter to arbitration.  

Finally, while the arbitration process is underway, the contract does not simply lapse; it remains in force until the arbitrator renders a decision. This ensures that rights and obligations, including the question of payment eligibility, stay live during the dispute resolution.  

Putting these points together, the CMC/EIC decides which final billings are payable after termination, and any dispute over legitimacy is handled through the contract’s dispute procedure—first seeking an amicable settlement, then moving to arbitration if needed, with the contract staying valid until the arbitration outcome is reached.

## 8.15 Terminating Services Prior to End of Contract
8.15.1 At times, a decision is taken to terminate a contract prior to its conclusion and the completion of the Consultancy and other services assignment. This may be for various reasons, for example:

- i) **Termination due to External factors:** External factors (like natural disasters) which are beyond the control of the consultant/ service provider or the Procuring Entity;
- ii) **Termination for convenience:** The Procuring Entity may also terminate a contract for convenience for reasons like shortage of budget;
- iii) **Termination due to breach of contract:** Failure/ inability of one party or the other.

8.15.2 In some cases, termination is the optimal choice; in others, it is detrimental to the overall intent of the assignment. This implies a missed opportunity and a waste of the funds already expended on the assignment. For these reasons, termination should be avoided, if possible, even if this means a considerable re-staffing of the Consultancy team.

8.15.3 Termination may be initiated by any party. Termination must be undertaken within the terms of the contract document. These provide for a notice period of 30 (thirty) days, the payment by the Procuring Entity of any legitimate outstanding fees and costs to the consultant/ service provider, and the payment of legitimate costs to wind-up the Consultancy/ other service team (unless the termination was occasioned by the default of the consultant/ service provider). If termination is initiated by the consultant / service provider the bid security (EMD) / security deposit, if any, available with NRL may be forfeited.

8.15.4 The CMC/EIC would indicate which of the final billings by the firm are eligible for payment and which are not. In case of dispute over what is or is not a legitimate expense, eligible for payment, the dispute mechanism described above is invoked and, if it is not possible to resolve the matter amicably, the issue is submitted for arbitration. The contract will remain valid until the arbitration decision is made.

## 8.16 Concluding the Assignment
The contract is normally considered concluded on the day after the completion date listed in the contract. Any expenditure incurred after the completion date are unlikely to be paid. It is therefore, important, under all types of assignments, for the consultant/ service provider to request an extension of the completion date if it appears that additional time will be needed to complete the assigned scope of services after the contractual completion date. The consultant/ service provider should submit the final claim promptly after completing the assignment. The standard consultant/ service provider contract states that the claim must be submitted within 60 (sixty) days of completion.

question_text: What must happen after a tender cancellation is approved by the competent authority
answer: After the competent authority approves a tender cancellation, the Commercial Dealing Officer must publish a corrigendum on the e‑tendering portal (CPP or GeM) to notify everyone that the tender has been cancelled. This notice ensures that no further bids are submitted and keeps all potential suppliers informed. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 131)
cot:
First, I think about what the tender cancellation procedure looks like: before anything can be called off, someone has to seek formal approval from the competent authority by submitting a note that outlines the reasons for cancellation.  

Next, I consider what happens once that authority signs off—approval alone doesn’t automatically inform the market; there still needs to be a clear, official notice so that any potential bidders know the tender is no longer active.  

Then I recall who is responsible for handling the paperwork and communication around tenders: the Commercial Dealing Officer, who originally prepared the approval note, is also the one tasked with carrying out the follow‑up actions after the decision is made.  

After that, I look at how the notice should be delivered in the current procurement environment: the standard practice is to upload a corrigendum to the electronic tendering system—whether it’s the CPP portal or GeM—so that the information is instantly accessible to all registered suppliers.  

Finally, I verify that publishing this corrigendum achieves the goal of the cancellation step: it stops any further bid submission, keeps everyone informed, and closes the loop on the tender process.  

Putting it all together, after the competent authority approves a tender cancellation, the Commercial Dealing Officer must publish a corrigendum on the e‑tendering portal (CPP or GeM) to notify all parties that the tender has been cancelled.

Finally, I synthesize this comparison and conclude that the additional column appearing under REVISION, if Any in the wage arrear table compared to the reimbursable items table is the Rate column.
