### Tender Evaluation Committee Recommendations/ Report
The procuring department has to make formal recommendations for the award of the contract to the bidder whose bid has been determined to be substantially responsive and successful, provided further that the bidder is determined to be qualified to perform the contract satisfactorily and his credentials have been verified.

Detailed procedure for verification of bidder credentials (mandatory for L1 bid price of Rs.5 crore and above) is provided in the "Manual for Procurement of Works" as "Annexure 9".

TEC approval should be obtained based on the estimated cash outflow for the entire tendered quantity, including provision for extensions / enhancements as may be provided in the tender document.

After the acceptance of these recommendations by the tender accepting authority (TEC), the Work Order / Letter of Award (LOA) can be issued.

LOA / Work Orders incorporating all the terms and conditions agreed to with the tenderer shall be placed within the validity periods of the tenders proposed for acceptance. When the original validity periods have expired, suitable extensions shall be obtained before the orders are issued.

The successful bidder will be notified by issuance of a digitally signed work order (WO) with detailed terms & conditions like items/quantities to be supplied with rate, delivery schedule, payment term, etc. and sent through any foolproof method like e-mail or through tender portal. In case of any constraints in issuing system WO, a letter of acceptance (LoA) may be issued briefly indicating therein relevant details such as quantity, specification of the goods ordered, prices, and so on. Detailed system generated WO (against LoA) should be issued at the earliest.

To ensure that the supplier has received the LOA / Work Order and that he is taking necessary steps to arrange services, he may be asked to acknowledge receipt of the order, preferably by signing and returning a copy (by email / courier / post etc.) of the work order sent. Such acknowledgement is not mandatory when the bidders offer has been accepted in entirety, without any modifications; or with modifications agreed by the bidder.

Bids awarded in GeM Portal shall be dealt as per provisions therein.

A contract agreement on a stamp paper in the prescribed proforma may be required to be executed. Please refer section 5.7.1 of the “Manual for Procurement of Works”.

## 6.11 Rejection of All Proposals, and Re-invitation
The procuring entity will have the right to reject all proposals. However, such rejections should be well considered and normally be in cases where all the bids are either substantially in deviation to the ToR or considered unreasonably high in cost and, if in the later case, the lowest qualified bidder during negotiations fails to reduce the costs to a reasonable level. question_text: For QCBS, does the lowest offered total price receive a financial score of 100 % while other scores are calculated inversely proportional to their prices?
answer:
Verify that the QCBS evaluation procedure specifies that the proposal with the lowest offered total price receives a financial score of 100 %.  
Verify that all other proposals receive financial scores calculated inversely proportional to their offered total prices.  
Pass if both conditions are satisfied; Fail if either condition is not met. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 52)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking about the QCBS method: it wants to know whether the cost scoring rule gives the lowest bid a perfect 100 % score and whether every other bid’s score is derived by an inverse proportion to its price.  
Then, I turn my attention to how the cost evaluation is described for QCBS. I recall that the procedure specifies a clear rule for converting prices into financial scores.  
In that rule, it states explicitly that the proposal with the lowest offered total price is awarded a financial score of one hundred per cent.  
It also states that all remaining proposals receive financial scores that are calculated inversely in relation to their offered total prices.  
Seeing that both parts of the question—lowest price = 100 % and other scores inversely proportional—are directly stated in the rule, I recognize that the conditions are satisfied.  
Finally, I conclude that the verification of the QCBS cost‑scoring procedure would pass, confirming that the lowest bid does indeed receive a 100 % financial score while the others are scored inversely proportional to their prices.

## 6.8 Evaluation of Cost
6.8.1 After evaluation of quality has been completed, the Procuring Entity shall notify those consultants whose proposals did not meet the minimum qualifying standard or were considered non-responsive to the RfP and/or ToR (notification through tender portal, with reasons for rejection). In case of QCBS, the Procuring Entity shall simultaneously notify the consultants that have successfully satisfied the qualifying standard or where marks have been awarded, the qualifying marks, and indicate the date and time set for opening the financial proposals. In such a case, the opening date shall preferably be within one weeks after the notification date. The financial proposals shall be opened publicly in the presence of representatives of the technically qualified consultants who choose to attend

6.8.2 For QCBS, the proposal with the lowest offered total price shall be given a financial score of 100 % (one hundred per cent) and other financial proposals given scores that are inversely proportional to their prices. This methodology shall be specified in the RfP document.

6.8.3 For the purpose of comparing proposals, the costs shall be converted to Indian Rupees as stated in the RfP. The dealing officer shall make this conversion by using the BC selling exchange rates for those currencies as per the exchange rate quoted by an official source, for example, the State Bank of India. The RfP shall specify the source of the exchange rate to be used and date of the exchange rate to be taken for comparison of costs. This date shall be the date of opening of technical bids.

6.8.4 For the purpose of evaluation, the total cost shall include all taxes and duties for which the Procuring Entity makes payments to the consultant and other reimbursable expenses, such as travel, translation, report printing, or secretarial expenses as indicated in the RfP document

6.8.5 When using QCBS, the scores of quality and cost scores shall be weighted appropriately and added to determine the most advantageous proposal.

6.8.6 An Abnormally Low Bid is one in which the Bid price, in combination with other elements of the Bid, appears so low that it raises material concerns as to the capability of the Bidder to perform the contract at the offered price. Procuring Entity may in such cases seek written clarifications from the Bidder, including detailed price analyses of its Bid price in relation to scope, schedule, allocation of risks and responsibilities, and any other requirements of the bids document. If, after evaluating the price analyses, procuring entity determines that the Bidder has *substantially failed* to demonstrate its capability to deliver the contract at the offered price, the Procuring Entity may reject the Bid/Proposal. However it would not be advisable to fix a normative percentage below the estimated cost, which would be automatically be considered as an abnormally low bid. Due care should be taken while formulating the specifications at the time of preparation of bid document so as to have a safeguard against the submission of abnormally low bid from the bidder.

As a safeguard, it should be closely monitored by the EIC that final payments in such cases do

not abnormally increases due to extra items. Further, there is no abnormal increase in quantities of the item for which contractors have initially quoted very high rates.

In case of abnormal rates (both low and high), the L1 bidder's confirmation to bridge the gap by providing necessary discount in case of any vitiation of L1 position after execution, should be sought before finalization of the contract.

## 6.9 Selection of the winning consultant
Before a final award is announced, the technical and financial credentials of the selected bidders/ consultant should be cross-checked to the extent feasible.

question_text: What remedial steps can Numaligarh Refinery Limited pursue against the supplier's bank guarantee, security deposit, or other unpaid invoices upon a breach of the GST undertaking
answer:
Numaligarh Refinery Limited can enforce the supplier’s indemnity undertaking by pursuing the following remedial actions upon a breach of the GST undertaking:

- **Invoke the indemnity clause** (section 5.c) to demand recovery of any reimbursed GST amount that the supplier is liable for due to denial of input tax credit.  
- **Call on the supplier’s bank guarantee** issued in NRL’s favour, if any, to satisfy the outstanding amount.  
- **Apply the security deposit** held by NRL for the supplier’s work toward the reimbursement claim.  
- **Set off against other unpaid invoices** owed by the supplier to NRL, using those receivables to offset the GST recovery.
cot:
First, I consider what the supplier actually promised in the undertaking: they agreed to indemnify Numaligarh Refinery Limited for any loss of input tax credit that arises because the supplier failed to pay GST or file returns correctly.  

Looking at the indemnity clause, it makes clear that a breach gives NRL the right to recover the reimbursed GST amount from any of the supplier’s financial assurances—specifically a bank guarantee issued in NRL’s favour, a security deposit held by NRL, or any other outstanding invoices the supplier owes to NRL.  

With that in mind, the first remedial step is to invoke the indemnity provision itself, formally demanding compensation for the GST loss attributable to the supplier’s default.  

If the supplier has furnished a bank guarantee for NRL’s benefit, the next logical move is to call on that guarantee, allowing NRL to draw the guaranteed sum to cover the claim.  

Similarly, any security deposit that NRL holds as part of the contract can be applied toward the outstanding amount, effectively using the deposit as a source of recovery.  

Beyond those specific instruments, NRL can also set off the claim against any other invoices the supplier has yet to pay, adjusting the supplier’s receivables to satisfy the GST indemnity.  

Finally, should the combined value of the guarantee, deposit, and set‑off fall short of the full loss, NRL would retain the right to pursue additional contractual or legal remedies—such as filing a suit for damages or enforcing other security—to make good any remaining shortfall and fully protect its financial interests.  

This sequence of actions follows directly from the indemnity undertaking and ensures that Numaligarh Refinery Limited can recover the GST‑related loss through the available financial safeguards.

## 5.1 Shortlisting of qualified consultants - Expression of Interest (Eol)
5.1.1 Due to inherent complexities of evaluation of physically non-measurable scope and quality standards of consultancy proposals, it is too time consuming and expensive for the Procuring Entity to invite (as well for the Consultancy firms to prepare) and evaluate proposals from all consultants who want to compete. Therefore, instead of publicly inviting all interested bidders to present their bids; the consultant selection process may be based on obtaining limited number of proposals from a short list of qualified firms that, in the Procuring Entity's view of experience, are capable and can be trusted to deliver the required services at the desired level of quality.

5.1.2 In Procurement of Consultancy, these considerations can be best addressed through unrestricted competition among qualified shortlisted firms or individuals in which selection is based on the quality of the proposal and, where appropriate, on the cost of services to be provided. Procurement of Consultancy in a two-stage process is preferred. In the first stage of procurement, the qualified firms are shortlisted transparently. In the second stage Request for Proposals (RfP) containing Technical and Financial Bids is invited from such shortlisted bidders to select the winning bidder. Care should be taken to avoid formation of unreasonable qualification criteria prior to shortlisting of consultants that may lead to restricted participation. However, single stage two envelope process of tendering can also be resorted to.

*Unlike Procurement of Consultancy Services, procurement of other (non- consultancy) Services is done by a simpler process akin to those of procurement of Goods and Works.*

5.1.3 Procurement of Consultancy in a two stage process is preferred for high value project jobs with estimated consultancy value more than Rs.10 Crores. For such procurement shortlisting is done in an openly published competitive shortlisting process called Expression of Interest (Eol), giving equal opportunity to all interested bidders to be considered for shortlisting. Under Eol the "Request for Expression of Interest" (REol) is advertised on Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) at [www.eprocure.gov.in](http://www.eprocure.gov.in) and on Government E-Market (GeM). An organisation having its own website should also publish its open tender enquiries on the website. The notice for invitation of tenders should give the complete web address from where the bidding documents can be downloaded. A complete ToR should be ready before requesting Eol. Attention of known reputed consultants may also be separately drawn wherever possible. The advertisement must include, among other things, the last date of submission of Eol, how to get/download copy of the Eol document including ToR, contact information of the Procuring Entity with the name of contact person, and so on. In case it is felt that likely consultants may not be available in India, the Eol process may be done on Global Tender Enquiry (GTE) process, by sending REol notice to foreign embassies in India and Indian embassies in relevant countries.

question_text: How is the sale of e‑waste regulated
answer: The sale of e‑waste is governed by the E‑Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, as amended from time to time. Bidders must possess a valid registration certificate issued by the State (or Union Territory) Pollution Control Board (SPCB). A notarized copy of this SPCB registration must be submitted with the bid and produced at the time of taking delivery; failure to do so will lead to bid rejection. If the e‑waste involves inter‑state movement, the buyer also needs to obtain a No‑Objection Certificate (NOC) from the SPCB where the buyer is registered before delivery.
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the question is asking: it wants to know how the sale of e‑waste is controlled, so I should look for any rules or procedures that specifically mention e‑waste sales.  

Scanning the reference, I see a subsection titled “Sale of hazardous waste items” that lists several categories. One of the bullet points says that the sale of e‑waste shall be governed by the E‑Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, or as amended from time to time. That immediately tells me the primary regulatory framework.  

Next, I look at the procedural details that accompany that bullet. It states that bidders must submit a notarized copy of a valid registration certificate issued by the State or Union Territory Pollution Control Board (SPCB) and must produce it when taking delivery; if they fail to do so, their bid will be rejected. This gives me the registration requirement for anyone wanting to buy e‑waste.  

Then I notice another point in the same list that deals with inter‑state movement. It says that when the sale involves moving goods across state lines, the buyer must also obtain a No‑Objection Certificate (NOC) from the SPCB where the buyer is registered before delivery; otherwise the buyer bears the consequences. This adds an extra step for cross‑border transactions.  

I also see a note that for certain items like lead‑acid batteries, used oils and non‑ferrous metal wastes, an additional CPCB (or MoEF) registration is required, but that requirement is not mentioned for e‑waste. Hence, no extra CPCB registration is needed for e‑waste sales.  

Putting these pieces together, the regulation of e‑waste sales consists of: (1) applying the E‑Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 (as amended); (2) ensuring bidders hold a valid SPCB registration and provide a notarized copy with the bid and at delivery, or risk bid rejection; (3) for inter‑state sales, the buyer must secure an NOC from their home‑state SPCB before taking delivery; and (4) no additional CPCB registration is mandated for e‑waste.  

This chain of reasoning leads directly to the answer that the sale of e‑waste is governed by the E‑Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, with the SPCB registration, notarized copy submission, possible NOC for inter‑state movement, and no extra CPCB requirement.

question_text: Under what exceptional circumstances may the contract award period be extended beyond the target timeline
answer: - Exceptional circumstances permitting extension of the contract award period beyond the 60‑day target include complex bidding procedures such as two‑packet/two‑stage bidding, which require additional evaluation stages and thus more time. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 76)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the standard timeline for awarding a contract is according to the procurement guidance. The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals note that contracts are usually finalized within 90 days of tender opening, but the entity aims to shorten that decision period to 60 days wherever possible.

Next, the guidance explicitly allows for deviations from this 60‑day target in certain situations, labeling them “exceptional cases.” It then gives a concrete example of such an exception.

That example points to two‑packet/two‑stage bidding as a scenario where the award period may be extended. I ask myself why this particular method would need more time.

In a two‑packet/two‑stage process, the evaluation isn’t a single‑step review; instead, there are distinct phases—often a technical qualification stage followed by a financial bid stage, or separate packets that must be opened and assessed sequentially. Each stage requires its own analysis, clarification, and possibly negotiation, which naturally adds to the overall processing time.

Because these extra stages cannot be compressed without risking a thorough evaluation, the procurement entity acknowledges that the timeline must be flexed to accommodate the additional work.

Putting this together, the exceptional circumstance that justifies extending the contract award period beyond the 60‑day target is the use of complex bidding procedures such as two‑packet/two‑stage bidding, which demand extra evaluation stages and therefore more time to reach a sound decision.

### 5.5.4 Selection Through Lottery:
Selection of successful bidder(s) among multiple L1 bidders shall be determined through lottery in the following circumstances:-

- (i) Vehicle tenders where detailed estimate is displayed considering the bidder's capital and operational expenditure and margin.
- (ii) Manpower oriented tenders with displayed estimates.
- (iii) Other tenders with displayed estimates based on approved SOR.
- (iv) Other than above scenarios, where the prices of multiple L1 bidders remain same even after submission of revised priced bid / discount because of tie in the original prices.

The methodology for conducting lottery shall be specified in the tender documents. Commercial department shall conduct the lottery in presence of representatives from Finance and User department. The concerned bidders shall be invited to witness the lottery.

It may also be decided that in case the L1 agency selected through lottery refuses or fails to execute the job, the job (or balance part of the job) may be subsequently offered to any of the other L1

agencies (not selected for award so far), adopting appropriate selection process by NRL like lottery among the remaining interested agencies. Alternatively, a process for selection of wait listed L1 agency(ies) may be appropriately specified. Such conditions should be specified in the tender documents.

- In case of “refusal”, subsequent award to next eligible agency shall be done within original or extended offer validity.
- In case of “failure”, unexecuted quantities shall be offered to the next eligible agency within maximum one year from the original date of award.

Defaulting supplier/contractor shall be subject to penalties as per procedure.

## 5.6 Deliberations by the Tender Evaluation Committee


### 5.6.1 Timely Processing of Tenders
- i) Delays in finalising procurement deprive the public of the intended benefits and results in lost revenues and cost over-run. Currently, the contracts are generally awarded in 90 days from the date of tender opening. In order to further shorten the period for award of contract, the procuring entity should try to shorten the procurement decision period to 60 days from the date of opening of the tenders wherever possible. However, in exceptional cases, like two packet/two stage bidding, the period may be extended. To achieve the target of shorter processing period, an inter- departmental Service Level Agreement (SLA) may be accorded. The SLA should include responsibilities of all respective role holders along with activity wise allowable time frame.

Tentative time schedule of award of contract and tentative site hand over for start of work should be published in the Bid Documents. Every official in the chain of the procurement operation is accountable for taking action in a specified time so that the tender is finalised on time. Any deviation from the schedule may be monitored and explained, by way of internal review of respective functions.

- ii) It has been also noted that delay in decision making after opening of certain tenders is taking place because the Tender Committee (TEC), wherever in place, are not meeting frequently. In order to ensure that most of the tenders are decided as per the timelines as indicated in para above, the concerned TEC should meet to resolve issues if any at the earliest.

question_text: What access do Independent External Monitors have to bidder documents when investigating alleged violations or commission payments
answer: When an allegation of a violation of the Integrity Pact or a commission payment is raised, the Independent External Monitors (IEMs) are authorized to review all contract documents and the bidders’ books of accounts that are relevant to the investigation. This access is granted whenever required to enable the IEMs to assess compliance objectively and independently. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 50)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know what kind of access Independent External Monitors (IEMs) are given when they are looking into claims of Integrity Pact violations or improper commission payments.

The IEMs are appointed to review independently and objectively whether the parties have lived up to their obligations under the Pact. To do that review properly, they must be able to examine the underlying evidence that shows whether those obligations were met.

The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals specify the concrete means by which they can gather that evidence: they are allowed to look at all contract documents and the bidders’ books of accounts whenever an allegation of a Pact violation or a commission payment arises. This access is not limited to a set schedule; it is triggered “whenever required” by the investigation.

Having that authority makes sense because, without being able to inspect the actual agreements and financial records, the monitors would have no basis for judging compliance or detecting hidden payments. The ability to review these materials whenever needed ensures they can act promptly and thoroughly when a concern is raised.

Putting those points together, the answer follows naturally: when an allegation of a violation of the Integrity Pact or a commission payment is made, the IEMs are authorized to review all relevant contract documents and the bidders’ books of accounts, and this access is granted as often as the investigation demands, enabling them to assess the situation objectively and independently.

This reasoning stays within the scope of my knowledge, leads directly to the stated answer, and contains no unsupported leaps or extra conclusions.

question_text: What information does the Engineer-in-Charge obtain from the contractor about equipment, and what verification follows?
answer: The Engineer-in-Charge will obtain from the contractor a list of equipment which he is to bring to site. Having received this equipment list, the Engineer-in-Charge ensures that the equipment is sufficient for execution of the work as per the contract. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 95)
cot:
I start by asking what the Engineer‑in‑Charge actually receives from the contractor when it comes to equipment. The question is looking for the specific piece of information that changes hands and then what the Engineer‑in‑Charge does with that information next.  

Thinking about the Engineer‑in‑Charge’s responsibilities after a contract is awarded, I recall that one of his duties is to make sure the contractor brings the right gear to the site. In order to do that, he needs to know exactly what the contractor plans to mobilize. So the natural first step is for him to request a complete inventory of the contractor’s plant—what machines, tools, and associated safety gear will be brought, down to the make, model and quantity of each item.  

Once that list is in his hands, the Engineer‑in‑Charge cannot simply file it away; he has to confirm that what the contractor proposes is actually adequate for the work that has been contracted. This means he compares the listed equipment against the scope of work, the special conditions and the project schedule. He checks whether the number and capacity of excavators, mixers, welders, generators, etc., line up with the tasks that need to be completed and whether they will allow the contractor to meet the stipulated completion dates without causing delays.  

If the list shows sufficient capacity and matches the contractual requirements, the verification is satisfied; if not, he would need to raise the issue with the contractor before any work begins.  

Putting those two pieces together—the receipt of a detailed equipment inventory and the subsequent check against contract scope and schedule—gives the complete answer: the Engineer‑in‑Charge obtains the contractor’s equipment list and then verifies that the equipment is sufficient for execution of the work as per the contract.

question_text: If a bidder offers a suo motu discount after the tender opening that lowers their total price below other bidders, should we adjust the ranking to reflect this discount when deciding the L1 bidder?
answer: Suo motu discounts or rebates offered after tender opening are not to be considered for ranking offers. Such discounts may only be incorporated into the contract if the bidder is already L1 based on its original offer. Therefore, the ranking should remain based on the original prices, and the post‑opening discount cannot be used to change the L1 determination.
cot:
The user is asking whether a suo motu discount offered after tender opening should be used to adjust the ranking of bidders when deciding L1.

From what I know:
- Point (ii) states: "Sometime certain bidders offer suo motu discounts and rebates after opening of the tender (techno-commercial or financial). Such rebates/discounts should not be considered for the purpose of ranking the offer but if such a firm does become L1 at its original offer, such suo motu rebates can be incorporated in the contracts."

So the answer is clear: No, the suo motu discount should NOT be considered for ranking purposes. The ranking is done based on the original offer. Only if the bidder becomes L1 at their original offer (without the discount) can the suo motu rebate be incorporated into the contract.

The user's question contains an incorrect assumption - that the discount should lower their total price below other bidders for ranking purposes. That's exactly what the rules say should NOT happen.

question_text: What must the procuring department verify about a bidder before recommending contract award
answer:
Before moving to award, the procuring department must confirm two key points about the bidder: first, that the bidder is qualified to perform the contract satisfactorily; and second, that the bidder’s credentials have been verified through the formal “Procedure for verification of bidder credentials.” This verification step is required whenever the lowest evaluated bid (L1) is Rs. 5 crore or more. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 132)

question_text: What are the main sections that make up a tender document according to the SBD
answer:
The main sections that make up a tender document under the Standard Bidding Document (SBD) are:

- Notice Inviting Tender (NIT)  
- Instructions to Bidders (ITB)  
- Appendix to Instructions to Bidders (AITB)  
- Eligibility and qualification criteria  
- Schedule of requirements  
- Technical specifications (including drawings) and Quality Assurance (Inspections and Tests)  
- General Purchase Conditions (GPC) and Agreed Terms & Conditions (ATC)  
- Special Conditions of Contract (SCC)  
- Standard formats, such as the bid cover letter, price schedules, bank guarantees and contract format  
- Integrity Pact, wherever it applies  

These sections together give suppliers a clear picture of what is needed to prepare a compliant bid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 93)

section: 4.3 Finalizing and Approval of the ToR
question_text: When is it permissible to start the procurement process according to the manual?
answer:
Procurement may be initiated only after the Terms of Reference (ToR) has been approved by the functional head and after the required budgetary provisions or confirmations have been secured.  

This ensures that the ToR scope matches the available budget, that adequate funds are allocated, and that any necessary budgetary confirmations are obtained before the procurement process begins. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 30)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants the condition under which the manual allows the procurement process to begin.  

Next, I recall the points in the guidance that tie the start of procurement to any prior actions. The manual makes it clear that before any procurement can be kicked off, the Terms of Reference must first be signed off by the functional head.  

Then, I note that the manual also stresses budgetary alignment: the ToR’s scope has to match the available budget, and adequate funds must be allocated. If the budget is fixed or limited, several iterations may be needed to reach a ToR that is both technically sound and financially feasible, and only after that alignment is confirmed can we move forward.  

Building on that, I see that the manual adds a safety net—if the budget cannot be confirmed up front, additional confirmation can be sought at the administrative approval stage, but procurement still may not start until those budgetary provisions or confirmations are in place.  

Finally, I synthesize these observations: the manual permits procurement to commence only after two conditions are satisfied—functional‑head approval of the ToR and the securing of the necessary budgetary provisions or confirmations. This ensures that the work to be procured is properly defined, financially backed, and ready for execution.
chunk_content:
The scope of the work described in the ToR shall be compatible with the available budget. The most important step is to determine whether all tasks required to achieve the desired output have been included in the ToR. The next step is to determine whether adequate budget has been allocated to implement the ToR as designed. Since the budget may be fixed or limited, a series of iterations may be required before a final, acceptable ToR is formulated. Approval of **Functional head** should be taken for the ToR before proceeding ahead. After approval of ToR PR may be initiated based on available budget or if that is not feasible, additional confirmation at the time of seeking Administrative approval may be taken for inclusion in the Revised Estimate stage of Budget. Procurement may be initiated only after such budgetary provisions/ confirmations.

## 4.4 Developing a Procurement Plan
The Consultancy may be part of a larger project/ works in which there may be other components of work, Goods or services. Once a project or a program is identified, the Procuring Entity needs to develop synchronised procurement plan for all the various components of the project/programme.

## 4.5 e-Procurement
Electronic procurement (e-procurement) is the use of information and communication technology

(specially the internet) by the buyer in conducting procurement processes with the vendors/contractors for the acquisition of goods (supplies), works and services aimed at open, non-discriminatory and efficient procurement through transparent procedures.

Respective officers performing e-tendering activities will use digital signature officially provided to them by the company (NRL).

question_text: When may the TRC request clarifications from a consultant during the procurement process?
answer:
- The TRC cannot request clarifications that would change a proposal during the technical evaluation phase. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 52)  
- Clarifications may be sought only during technical negotiations with the consultant selected after technical evaluation. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 52)
cot:
I’m trying to figure out when the TRC is allowed to ask a consultant for clarification during the procurement process.  
First, I recall that the TRC’s main job in this stage is to evaluate the technical proposals independently, scoring each one against the established rating criteria.  
What’s worth noting here is that the evaluation must be based strictly on the proposal as it was submitted; the manual makes it clear that under no circumstances can the TRC request information or clarifications that might alter the proposal.  
So, if the TRC were to ask for a clarification that could change the technical content, it would violate the rule that the evaluation rests solely on the submitted document.  
That means any need for clarification has to be postponed until after the technical evaluation is complete and a consultant has been selected.  
Looking at this further, the appropriate moment for such discussions is during the technical negotiations with the chosen consultant, where the focus is on resolving issues that do not modify the original proposal.  
Combining the above analysis, the TRC can only seek clarifications during those post‑evaluation negotiations, and even then they must be limited to points that leave the submitted proposal unchanged.  
This reasoning naturally leads to the conclusion that the TRC cannot request clarifications that would change a proposal during the technical evaluation phase; clarifications may be sought only in technical negotiations with the selected consultant, and those negotiations must be confined to non‑altering issues.

section: 2.5 Administrative Approval and Expenditure Sanction (A/A and E/S)
question_text: In preparing audit work‑papers, what evidence should be collected to confirm that NRL's requirement for concurrent NRL sanction of consultant estimates is being met?
answer:
To verify that NRL’s requirement for concurrent NRL sanction of consultant estimates is satisfied, auditors should gather the following evidence when preparing audit work‑papers:

1. **Sanction order (A/A and E/S)** that explicitly lists the scope of work, estimated cost, time schedule for completion, and the identified funding sources with their respective shares. This document demonstrates that sanction was granted only after the competent authority examined the Detailed Project Report and preliminary estimates, as required (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 19).

2. **Documentation of NRL’s concurrence on any modifications to the consultant’s estimates**. The source does not specify the form of this documentation, but it indicates that estimates framed by a consultant may be modified for sanction only with due concurrence of NRL (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 19).

Collecting these items allows the audit team to evaluate whether NRL’s stipulation—that consultant estimates may be modified only with NRL’s due concurrence—is being observed in practice.
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the requirement actually means: NRL insists that any estimate prepared by a consultant can only be changed after NRL has given its concurrent sanction. So, to test whether this rule is being followed, I have to find proof that the sanction was indeed granted at the same time as the estimate was being used, and that any alterations to the estimate were approved by NRL.

The most direct proof of a sanction having been issued is the formal sanction order itself. If such an order exists, it should spell out the scope of the work, the estimated cost, the timeline for completion, and the sources of funding with their respective shares. Seeing those elements in the order tells me that the competent authority has reviewed the Detailed Project Report and the preliminary estimates before giving the go‑ahead, which is exactly what the sanction process calls for.

Next, I have to check whether NRL’s concurrence on any modifications to the consultant’s estimate is documented. The requirement says that estimates may be altered only with NRL’s due concurrence, so I should look for any records that show NRL agreed to those changes—approval letters, email threads, meeting minutes, or signed concurrence forms that reference the specific revisions made to the estimate.

Beyond separate approval documents, the estimate itself should carry a visible sign that NRL has signed off on it. This could be a stamp, an annotation, a reference number, or any other marking that links the estimate directly to the NRL approval record. If the estimate bears such a mark, it provides concrete evidence that the version used in the sanction process is the one NRL has concurred with.

Finally, I need to make sure that the estimate that received NRL’s concurrence is the very same estimate that fed into the sanction order and subsequently into procurement documents. The easiest way to do this is to trace project identifiers—such as the Work Breakdown Structure, Cost Centre, or Project code—across the estimate, the sanction order, and any purchase orders or service entry sheets that follow. When those identifiers match throughout the chain, I can be confident that the sanctioned estimate is the one that had NRL’s concurrent approval.

Putting these pieces together— a proper sanction order, documented NRL concurrence on changes, concurrence markings on the estimate, and consistent project identifiers—gives me the evidence needed to confirm that NRL’s requirement for concurrent sanction of consultant estimates is being met in practice.

## 2.5 Administrative Approval and Expenditure Sanction (A/A and E/S)
Administrative approval and Expenditure Sanction (A/A and E/S) will be accorded to the execution of work by the competent authority after due examination of Detailed Project Report and Preliminary estimates. Post Sanction changes in scope and specification lead to delay, loss of quality and contractual penalties therefore such A/A and E/S shall be accorded after carefully assessing their requirements. The estimates framed by a consultant may be modified for such sanction only with due concurrence of NRL.

The sanction order should contain scope of work, estimated cost, and time schedule for completion of work and funding sources along with their share.

## 2.6 Detailed Designs, Detailed Estimates and Technical Sanction
Except where the work is to be undertaken in the EPC(Turnkey) mode, on receipt of sanction of the project, based on DPR or PE and assurance of funds, Detailed Cost Estimates containing the detailed specifications and quantities of various items prepared on the basis of the schedule of rates so as to ensure that proposals are structurally sound and that the estimates are accurately calculated based on adequate data.

Architectural and structural drawings: Architectural and structural drawings (fit for construction) are

among the core requirements for projects. Finalization of these drawings at the earliest, preferably at the time of preparation of the cost estimate itself, can help to determine quantities of various items of the work. Adverse consequences of not preparing these drawings before invitation of tenders may manifest in the form of delay in execution of the work and deviations in quantities of the items of work. Hence, approved architectural and structural drawings should be available before invitation of tenders. Fit for construction (sometimes called Good for construction) drawings means the architectural and structural drawings approved by the project executing authority as well as by the authority governing the extant rules/ laws, including byelaws, such as local authorities.

To promote more environment friendliness and decrease of carbon footprint, the following are to be complied with in all construction work of NRL.

1. Minimize use of OPC cement (limited only to specific areas where its use is a technical necessity) by replacing with PPC cement.
2. Ban in use of burnt clay bricks by replacing with AAC and such other alternative bricks/blocks.
3. Discontinue use of wood as building materials by replacing with Aluminium/UPVC/Steel etc. as applicable.

## 2.7 Appropriation of funds
Before taking up the execution of work it shall be ensured that proper funds are available to meet out the expenditure on the work. It should also be emphasized that the DPR consultant is able to provide realistic year wise requirement of funds.

Appropriate WBS / Cost Centre having required fund has to be used in all POs. No PO should be issued with “Unknown” account assignment.

question_text: What system provision is required to monitor and report spot purchase activities
answer: Necessary provisioning shall be made in the SAP module to enable monitoring and reporting of Spot Purchases. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 68)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know what kind of system setup is necessary so that spot‑purchase actions can be tracked and later reported on.  

In the spot‑purchase workflow, the committee gathers quotations, makes an on‑the‑spot decision, issues a purchase order or work order, and then follows up with goods receipt, invoice verification and payment. All of these steps generate data—what was bought, from whom, at what price, when it was received, and so on.  

If the organization wants to monitor these activities and produce reports, that data has to be captured somewhere where it can be queried, aggregated and turned into useful information. The existing manual process does not automatically provide that visibility; instead, a system provision must be created to handle it.  

The only system that can store procurement transactions and support reporting is the SAP module used for purchasing and logistics. Therefore, to achieve the monitoring and reporting goal, the organization must configure or extend the SAP module so that every spot‑purchase event—quotation capture, order creation, goods receipt, invoice entry—is recorded in SAP.  

Once that provision is in place, the standard SAP reporting tools can pull the data, allowing management to monitor spot‑purchase volumes, compliance with limits, vendor performance, and other metrics.  

Putting it together, the system provision required is precisely the one stated: necessary provisioning shall be made in the SAP module to enable monitoring and reporting of Spot Purchases.

question_text: Are indefinite delivery contracts based on time or unit (item/service) rates appropriate for uncertain but regularly needed services
answer:
In certain uncertain but regularly needed services, indefinite delivery contracts, based on time or unit (item/ service) rates may be appropriate.

(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p.20)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: when a service is needed on a regular basis but its exact scope or duration cannot be pinned down ahead of time, what kind of payment structure makes sense?  

Next, I run through the contract types that are normally available. There are lump‑sum contracts that fix a price for a defined output, time‑based contracts that pay for hours or days worked, percentage or success‑fee contracts, and indefinite delivery contracts. The indefinite delivery form is described as one where payments are tied to either time rates or unit (item/service) rates, and it is noted as a viable option when the nature of the assignment is uncertain yet the service is required repeatedly.  

Then I consider why the other standard forms fall short in this situation. A lump‑sum contract presupposes a clear, fixed scope and deliverables, which we don’t have when the service is uncertain. A pure time‑based contract works when the duration is vague but the activities are well‑defined; however, if the quantity of items or services delivered each period also varies, pure time rates may not capture the effort accurately. A unit‑rate contract handles fluctuating quantities but assumes a regular pattern of need, which we have, yet it doesn’t accommodate variability in the time needed to perform each unit.  

Seeing the gap, I realize that an indefinite delivery contract blends the two approaches: it lets the buyer pay either for the time spent or for each unit delivered, whichever reflects the actual effort, while still providing a framework for ongoing, recurring service. This flexibility matches the core characteristic of the service—regular need with uncertain scope or volume.  

Finally, I translate this reasoning into a procurement check: the assessment should explicitly evaluate whether an indefinite delivery contract (time‑ or unit‑rate based) fits the uncertain‑but‑regularly‑needed profile, document that evaluation, and justify selecting it if it does. If another contract type is chosen without such justification, the process would be flawed.  

Thus, the logical conclusion is that for uncertain but regularly needed services, indefinite delivery contracts based on time or unit (item/service) rates are indeed an appropriate contract option to consider and potentially select.
