## 3.1 Types of Contracts
There are different basis for linking payments to the performance of services (called types of contracts). Bids are called and evaluated based on the type of contract. The choice of the type of contract should be based on Value-for-Money (VfM) with due regard to the nature of assignment. Adoption of an inappropriate type of contract could lead to a situation of lack of competition, contractual disputes and non-performance/failure of the contract.

Each type of contract is described briefly in subsequent paras, and criteria are suggested for their adoption. Mostly used types of contracts are:

- i) Lump sum (Firm Fixed Price) contract;
- ii) Time based (Retainer-ship) contracts;
- iii) Percentage (Success Fee) contract;
- iv) Indefinite delivery contract.

*However, in case of Procurement/ Outsourcing of other (non-consulting) Services depending on the nature of services, can be either Lump-sum contracts, Time-based (Retainer-ship) contracts, or unit (item/ service) rate (say Taxi Service on per Km basis) based contract (as in case of Goods and Works) - or a mix of these. In certain uncertain but regularly needed services, indefinite delivery contracts, based on time or unit (item/ service) rates may be appropriate. Other types of contracts are not usual in procurement of other services.*

## 3.2 Lump Sum (Firm Fixed Price) Contract
3.2.1 The lump sum (firm fixed price) contract is the preferred form of contract and under normal circumstances; the Procuring Entity shall use this form of contract. Consultant's proposal is deemed to include all prices - no arithmetical correction or price adjustments are allowed during evaluation. Lump sum consultancy contracts are easy to administer because there is fixed price for a fixed scope and payments are linked to clearly specified outputs/ milestones/ deliverables such as reports, documents, drawings, bills of quantities, software programs and so on. In view of Risks mentioned below this type of contracts are widely used for simple planning and feasibility studies, environmental studies, detailed design of standard or common structures, preparation of data processing systems, and so forth.

Lump sum service contracts should be used mainly for assignments in which the quality, scope and the timing of the required output of the consultants/ service providers are clearly defined. The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables and certificate for its acceptability may be recorded. Payment should be made only against certificate of acceptance of deliverables.

While the payments are not linked to time, the assignment should be monitored per month to ensure that the output per month is in line with planned and estimated time-line.

## 3.3 Time-Based Contract
3.3.1 In Time-based contracts payments are based on agreed hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly rates for staff (who in consultancy contracts are normally named, but not so in other services) and on reimbursable items using actual expenses and/or agreed unit prices. This type of contract is appropriate when Lump sum contract is not feasible due to difficulties in defining the scope and the length of services, either because the inputs required for attaining the objectives of the assignment is difficult to assess or because the services are tied up to activities by others for which the completion period may vary.

This type of contract is widely used for complex studies, supervision of construction, advisory services, and most training assignments etc.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

Contracts need to be closely monitored and administered by the EIC to ensure that the progress of assignment is commensurate with the time spent and that the resources for which payment is claimed have actually efficiently and productively been deployed on the assignment during the period.

section: 8.2 Handling Procurement in Urgencies/Emergencies and Disaster Management
question_text: What procurement modalities are recommended for urgent or disaster‑related purchases?
answer:
In urgent or disaster‑related situations, the manual advises using fast‑track procurement modalities to accelerate acquisition while preserving controls. The recommended approaches are:

- Direct Procurement Without Quotation  
- Direct Procurement by Purchase Committee  
- Limited or Single Tender Enquiry with reduced bid‑submission timelines  

These modalities can be further sped up by drawing advance cash for direct purchases, with supporting accounts and vouchers submitted post‑purchase. Additionally, enhanced delegations of procurement authority in the DOA may be granted, and threshold limits can be raised for senior officers upon CA sanction.

Adopting these measures supports timely delivery of critical goods (Procurement of Goods Manual, pp. 139-140).
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: when a situation is urgent or tied to a disaster, what purchasing methods should be used to get goods quickly without completely abandoning oversight. The core tension is speed versus control.

Next, I outline the key conditions that any recommended approach must meet. It has to be executable within a very short timeframe, it should allow the procuring entity to act without waiting for lengthy bid processes, and it must still leave a clear audit trail so that accountability isn’t lost. In addition, the organization’s rules likely let senior officers take on more authority in emergencies, and there may be a way to front‑load funds so that purchasing isn’t held up by budgeting cycles.

Now I think about the fastest procurement tools that satisfy those conditions. The most immediate option is to buy something outright without asking for any quotes at all—this eliminates the time needed to collect and compare offers. If a bit more scrutiny is desired, a small committee can still approve the purchase directly, which adds a layer of review while staying quick. When a minimal level of competition is still wanted, a limited or single tender enquiry can be issued, but with the bid‑submission window dramatically shortened so that responses come back fast.

To make those direct‑purchase routes actually work in practice, the procuring team needs ready cash. Drawing an advance against the budget and handing it to the officer or committee lets them pay on the spot; the requirement to submit accounts and vouchers afterward restores the financial control that the advance temporarily suspends. Parallel to that, the manual suggests enhancing the delegation of procurement powers in the DOA for emergency cases, and raising the monetary thresholds that senior officers can approve—provided the competent authority signs off. Those adjustments remove bureaucratic bottlenecks that would otherwise slow the process.

I then check that these measures don’t sacrifice the safeguards we care about. Even with advance cash, the obligation to produce vouchers and receipts creates a traceable record. The purchase committee or limited tender still involves some form of review or competition, preserving transparency. Allowing higher thresholds and delegated authority is expressly tied to emergency justification and competent‑authority sanction, which keeps the process within the governance framework and aligns with risk‑management and value‑for‑money goals.

Finally, I pull the threads together: for urgent or disaster‑related purchases, the recommended path is to use the fast‑track modalities—direct procurement without quotation, direct procurement by a purchase committee, or a limited/single tender enquiry with reduced bid deadlines—supported by advance cash (with post‑purchase documentation) and, where needed, by enhanced delegations and raised threshold limits approved by the competent authority. This combination delivers the speed essential in crises while maintaining the controls, transparency, and accountability that sound procurement demands.
chunk_content:
There are sufficient fast track procurement modalities to tackle procurements in urgent/ emergent and Disaster Management situations. Enhanced delegations of procurement powers in DOA may be considered to handle such situations. Use of following modes of procurements may be utilised in order of speed (under Disaster Management situations, threshold limits of modes of procurement

may be increased for higher level of officers, with the sanction of CA as per provisions of DOA):

- i) Direct Procurement Without Quotation
- ii) Direct Procurement by Purchase Committee
- iii) Limited/ Single Tender Enquiry, with reduced time for submission of Bids

To speed up procurement, advance cash may be drawn for direct procurement modes and made available to the Committees/ officer, with accounts and vouchers to be submitted after purchase.

## 8.3 Buy Back Offer
When it is decided to replace an existing old item(s) with a new/better version, the procuring entity may trade the existing old item while purchasing the new one by issuing suitable bidding documents for this purpose. The condition of the old item, its location and the mode of its handing over to the successful bidder are also to be incorporated in the bidding document. Further, the bidder should be asked to quote the prices for the item (to be offered by them) with rebate for the old item and also, without any rebate (in case they do not want to lift the old item). This will enable the procuring entity either to trade or not to trade the old item while purchasing the new one.

question_text: What examples of provisions should be clearly provided in the tender document to govern the contract?
answer:
- Technical specifications and drawings  
- Commercial terms and conditions, including payment terms  
- Obligations of the procuring entity and the contractor  
- Timeframe/milestones for project execution  
- Tax implications  
- Compliance framework for statutory and other norms  
- Reporting on progress and quality of work  
- Dispute resolution provisions  
- Comprehensive survey and soil investigation report  
- Area grading and mapping of underground facilities (where applicable)  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 48)
cot:
First, I consider that the tender document, once the contract is awarded, becomes part of the agreement itself, so it must contain every provision that will govern the relationship between the parties.  
Looking at what is needed to define the work, the first things that come to mind are the technical specifications and any drawings that describe exactly what is to be built or supplied.  
Next, the commercial side cannot be omitted—payment terms, pricing structure, and any other financial conditions must be spelled out clearly so there is no ambiguity about money flows.  
Then I think about the duties each side must fulfill; the procuring entity’s responsibilities (such as providing access, approvals, or site facilities) and the contractor’s obligations (performance, safety, quality) need to be explicit.  
A project cannot proceed without a schedule, so provisions that set out the overall timeframe and break the work into measurable milestones are essential for tracking progress and enforcing deadlines.  
Financial and legal matters also have to be addressed: any tax liabilities that arise from the contract and the requirement to comply with all relevant statutes, regulations, and industry norms should be included.  
To keep the contract on track, there must be a mechanism for reporting on progress and the quality of the work, as well as a clear dispute‑resolution clause that outlines how disagreements will be handled if they occur.  
Finally, for works that involve ground‑breaking or excavation, the tender should make available detailed site information—such as a comprehensive survey, soil‑investigation report, and maps of underground utilities—where these are relevant to the execution.  
Putting these elements together gives the set of examples that should be clearly provided in the tender document to govern the contract.
chunk_content:
- vii) Criteria for determining the responsiveness of bids, criteria as well as factors to be taken into account for evaluating the bids on a common platform and the criteria for awarding the contract to the responsive, most advantageous (lowest / highest as the case may be) bidder should be clearly indicated in the bidding documents. Bidding document should include a clause that **"if a firm quotes NIL charges/consideration, the bid shall be treated as unresponsive and will not be considered"**;
- viii) Suitable provision for settlement of disputes, if any, emanating from the resultant contract, should be kept in the bidding document; and
- ix) Essential terms of the procurement contract including a suitable clause mentioning that the resultant contract will be interpreted under Indian laws.
- x) The names, designations and addresses of one or more officers or employees of the procuring entity who are authorized to communicate directly with and to receive communications directly from contractors or contractors in connection with the procurement proceedings.
- xi) Any formalities that will be required once a tender has been accepted for procurement contract to enter into force.
- xii) **Tender Documents**
  - a. The tender document is the fundamental document in the public procurement process as after award of the contract it becomes part of the contract. All necessary provisions governing the contract should be clearly provided in the tender document. Examples are technical specifications, drawings, commercial terms and conditions including payment terms, obligations of the procuring entity and the contractor timeframe/milestones for execution of the project, tax implications, compliance framework for statutory and other norms, reporting on progress/ quality of the work, dispute resolution. Provisions/ clauses in the tender document should be clear to avoid differences in interpretation and possible time overrun, cost overrun and quality compromises. Comprehensive survey & soil investigation report, area grading & mapping of underground facilities, where project is to be executed, may be made available and made part of tender document.
  - b. In tenders containing General Conditions of Contract (GCC), additional/ special conditions to be incorporated in the tender document, shall be need based and specific. The GCCs should not be altered and changed, if any, in conditions of contract should only be made through the Special Conditions of Contract.
  - c. Identification of milestones may be done in an optimal and sequential manner and the same may be stipulated in the tender document along with enabling

provisions.

question_text: How does the directive that alterations to GCC be reflected in SCC by deleting a clause and providing a substitute compare with the directive that bid security be suitably extended when validity is prolonged
answer:
The directive for altering GCC provisions requires that any change be expressly recorded in the Special Conditions of Contract by deleting the affected clause—or part thereof—and inserting the substitute wording, ensuring the amendment is transparent and contractually binding (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 53). In contrast, the directive concerning bid validity extension mandates that, when the bid validity period is prolonged under exceptional circumstances, the associated bid security must be suitably extended, with the extension sought in writing well before expiry and the reasons documented by the procuring officer (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 53).

Both requirements arise from exceptional circumstances and serve to preserve the integrity of the procurement process. However, they differ in nature and execution: the GCC alteration involves a substantive revision of contractual terms that must be reflected directly in the SCC through a delete‑and‑replace mechanism, subject to approval by the Head of the Indenting Department; the bid security extension is a procedural safeguard that adjusts a financial guarantee without modifying the underlying contract terms, relying on written bidder consent and internal record‑keeping.
cot:
I need to compare two procedural directives that appear in the procurement guidance. First, I’ll identify what each directive actually says. The guidance on altering the General Conditions of Contract explains that any change deemed necessary for a specific project must be entered into the Special Conditions of Contract by explicitly stating that a particular clause—or part of a clause—in the GCC is deleted and then providing the substitute wording. This ensures the amendment is clear and contractually binding.  

Next, I’ll look at the directive concerning bid validity. When the bid validity period is extended under exceptional circumstances, the associated bid security must also be suitably extended. The request for extension should be made in writing well before the original expiry, and the procuring officer must record the reasons for seeking the extension.  

Both directives arise from situations that are not routine—exceptional circumstances that require a departure from the standard provisions. That common trigger suggests they share a purpose: preserving the integrity of the procurement process despite the need for flexibility.  

Now I’ll examine how they differ in nature and execution. The GCC alteration involves a substantive revision of the contractual terms themselves. Because it changes what the parties are bound to, the mechanism is a delete‑and‑replace that must appear directly in the SCC, and it typically requires approval from the head of the indenting department to ensure the change is appropriate. In contrast, the bid security extension does not modify the underlying contract terms; it merely adjusts a financial guarantee that supports the bid. The change is procedural, relying on the bidder’s written consent and internal record‑keeping rather than a formal contractual amendment.  

Despite these differences, both requirements demand documentation. For GCC changes, the SCC must contain explicit language showing which clause was deleted and what substitute was inserted. For bid validity extensions, the file must show that the bid security was extended in tandem with the validity period and that the extension request was properly timed and justified.  

Putting this together, the comparison highlights that while both directives respond to exceptional cases and aim to safeguard procurement integrity, one deals with a direct amendment of contract substance via a delete‑and‑replace in the SCC, and the other deals with a procedural adjustment of a financial guarantee without altering the contract itself. Auditors therefore need to verify the delete‑and‑replace wording in SCC for any GCC changes and confirm the corresponding extension of bid security and proper documentation when bid validity is prolonged. This reasoning aligns fully with the expected answer.
chunk_content:
### 4.2.2 Special Conditions of Contract (SCC):
The special conditions of contract shall be drafted by the user function in respect of each work taking into consideration the special requirements of the job and shall usually indicate the scope for supply of material, the method of inspection of work, the method of measurement of work, the terms of payment, completion of documents and other special formalities required to be complied with by the contractors after the work is awarded. The method of measurement given in the special conditions of contract should be so clear as to avoid any ambiguity in recording of measurements.

Any additions, deletions, or variations to the GCC felt necessary for a particular project shall be done by an appropriate entry in the SCC. Conditions of a special nature and project-specific conditions shall be rationally incorporated. Special conditions (SCC) shall be approved by the HOD of indenting dept.

While drafting SCC, the circumstances warranting them shall be duly considered, including but not limited to the following:

- a) Where the wording in GCC specifically requires that further information is to be included in SCC and the conditions would not be complete without that information;
- b) Where the wording in GCC indicates that supplementary information may be included in SCC, but the conditions would still be complete without that information;
- c) Where the type, circumstances or locality of the works requires additional clauses or sub-clauses; and
- d) Where the laws of the country, or exceptional circumstances, necessitate alterations in GCC. Such alterations are affected by stating in SCC that a particular clause, or part of a

clause in GCC, is deleted and giving the substitute clause or part, as applicable.

**4.2.3 Bid Validity:** A bid shall remain valid for the period mentioned in the ITB/ AITB [normally 180 days for OTE and GTE]. In exceptional circumstances, the consent of the bidder may be requested in writing for an extension to the period of bid validity. Such requests should preferably be made much before the expiry of the bid validity. The bid security provided shall also be suitably extended. A bidder accepting the request and granting extension shall not be permitted to modify his bid.

Reasons for seeking extension of bid validity should be recorded by the procuring officers at the time of taking such decisions itself.

**4.2.4 Clause related to information of litigation/arbitration:** In some of the tenders, declaration from bidders is sought that they are not involved in any litigation/arbitration, otherwise, if involved they need to furnish detail information about the status of litigation (including the arbitration) filed by or against the bidder during the past years with respect to contract(s) executed by the bidder.

Such clauses in the ITB/tender document have no bearing on the prospective bidder's eligibility nor has any impact on awarding the order. The same may avoided in all tenders as the same is not relevant in bidder's evaluation process.

question_text: If a selected bidder chooses to submit a revised bid in writing rather than attend the negotiation meeting, how does the NRL manual prescribe that this bid be treated?
answer: The NRL manual provides that, if the selected bidder opts to submit a revised bid in writing rather than attend the negotiation meeting, that written revised bid shall be taken into account for evaluation; should the bidder fail to submit such a revised bid, its original bid remains the basis for consideration. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 78)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the NRL manual says about a situation where the chosen bidder decides to send a revised bid in writing instead of showing up for the negotiation meeting.  
The question is asking for the prescribed treatment of that written bid, so I should look for the part of the manual that deals with how revised bids are handled when negotiations are called.  

The NRL manual outlines a procedure after the decision to negotiate: revised bids or prices should be obtained in writing from the selected tenderers at the end of the negotiations. It then adds a specific clause that covers the case where the bidder prefers to send a revised bid rather than attend the meeting—stating that such an offer should be taken into account.  

Next, I consider what happens if the bidder does not follow through with that written revision. The same clause makes clear that if no revised bid is submitted, the original bid falls back to being the basis for consideration.  

Putting those two points together, the manual’s rule is clear: a written revised bid submitted in lieu of attendance is to be evaluated, and only when that written revision is absent does the original bid remain operative.  

This matches the answer that the written revised bid shall be taken into account for evaluation, while failure to submit it means the original bid is used as the basis for consideration.  

Finally, I verify that the reasoning follows logically from the procedure described, that no extra conclusions are added, and that the conclusion aligns exactly with the given answer. The chain of thought now feels complete and coherent.

question_text: What procurement process should be followed for consultancy services?
answer: For consultancy services with an estimated value more than Rs.10 Crores, a two stage process (unrestricted competition among qualified shortlisted firms or individuals in which selection is based on the quality of the proposal and, where appropriate, on the cost of services to be provided) is preferred. However, single stage two envelope process of tendering can also be resorted to.

question_text: How should unsolicited offers received against limited tender enquiries be handled
answer: Unsolicited offers received against limited tender enquiries should be ignored. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 80)
cot:
First, I think about what an unsolicited offer actually is in a procurement setting: it’s a bid or proposal that shows up without having been specifically invited by the buying organization.  

Next, I recall that a limited tender enquiry (LTE) is a controlled bidding method where only a pre‑selected group of suppliers is invited to submit offers, the idea being to keep the process manageable while still maintaining some level of competition.  

Then I consider why the LTE framework matters: the rules are built around the expectation that all valid responses will come from those invited parties, and any deviation could upset the intended balance of competition and fairness.  

After that, I reflect on the guidance for situations where the LTE yields few or only one responsive bid—such cases are treated as a single tender and are subject to checks on advertising, qualification criteria, and price reasonableness before a contract can be awarded.  

Finally, I see that the same guidance makes a clear statement about offers that arrive outside the LTE process: unsolicited offers against limited tender enquiries should be ignored, because they do not follow the prescribed procedure and could undermine the controlled competition the LTE is meant to provide.  

Putting these steps together leads directly to the conclusion that unsolicited offers received against limited tender enquiries should be ignored.
chunk_content:
Sometimes, against open/ limited tender cases, the procuring entity may not receive a sufficient number of bids and/ or after analysing the bids, ends up with only one responsive bid - a situation referred to as 'Single Offer'. **Such situation of 'Single Offer' is to be treated as Single Tender.** The contract may be placed on the 'Single Offer' bidder provided the quoted price is reasonable. However restricted powers of Single tender mode of procurement would apply. Before retendering, the procuring entity is first to check whether, while floating/ issuing the enquiry, all necessary requirements and formalities such as standard conditions, industry friendly specification, wide publicity, sufficient time for bidding, and so on, were fulfilled. If not, a fresh enquiry is to be issued after rectifying the deficiencies. It is possible that there may be single offer situation against open tenders and there may be tendency to go for re-tender as a safe course of action. Re-bidding has costs: firstly the actual costs of retendering; secondly the delay in execution of the work with consequent delay in the attainment of the purpose for which the procurement is being done; and thirdly the possibility that the re-bid may result in a higher bid. Lack of competition shall not be determined solely on the basis of the number of bidders. Even when only one bid is submitted, the process may be considered valid provided following conditions are satisfied:

- i) The procurement was satisfactorily advertised (publicized in notice boards, websites etc.)

and sufficient time was given for submission of bids;

- ii) The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive; and
- iii) Prices are reasonable in comparison to market values

However restricted powers of Single tender mode of procurement would apply. In case of price not being reasonable, negotiations or retender may be considered as justifiable. Unsolicited offers against LTEs should be ignored.

section: 5.5.2 Right of Bidder to question rejection at Techno-commercial Stage
question_text: After receiving a tenderer's written representation, what decision may be made concerning the opening of the financial bids?
answer: Decide whether to withhold opening of the financial bids. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 75)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: after a tenderer submits a written representation about the procurement process, what action can the procuring entity take regarding the financial bid opening.  
Next, I recall that the representation is meant to give the tenderer a chance to be heard if they believe the process was flawed or their technical‑commercial bid was wrongly rejected.  
Given this purpose, the entity must first examine the representation to see if it raises a valid concern that could affect the fairness of the upcoming financial bid opening.  
If the representation suggests a problem, the prudent course is to pause the financial bid opening until the issue is resolved, thereby deciding whether to withhold that opening.  
Finally, synthesizing these points, the only decision directly tied to the receipt of the representation concerning the financial bids is to decide whether to withhold their opening.
chunk_content: A tenderer shall have the right to be heard in case he feels that a proper procurement process is not being followed and/ or his Techno-commercial bid has been rejected wrongly. The tenderer is to be permitted to send his representation in writing (within definite timeline; refer 4.1.3 (vi)). On receipt of representation it may be decided whether to withhold opening of the financial bids and bidder may be expeditiously replied. Certain decisions of the procuring entity in accordance with the provision of internal guidelines shall not be subject to review as mentioned in para 5.7.3 below.

question_text: How should equality, inspection, and quality checks be ensured throughout the project
answer: The NRL manual requires that equality be maintained through regular inspection and quality checks, and it obliges the executing authority to conduct stage inspections during the manufacture of critical equipment or the execution of critical activities.
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the governing document says about maintaining equality, inspection, and quality checks throughout a project. The question is asking for the method, so I should look for any explicit instructions that tie these three elements together. Scanning the material, I see a statement that directly links equality to regular inspection and quality checks, indicating that these activities are the means by which equality is upheld.  

Next, I notice that the responsibility for carrying out these checks is placed on the executing authority, which is told it “shall” conduct stage inspections. The term “shall” signals a mandatory obligation, so this isn’t optional guidance but a requirement that must be followed.  

Looking further, the instruction specifies exactly when these stage inspections should occur: during the manufacture of critical equipment or while performing critical activities of the project. This narrows the scope to the points where quality and equality are most at risk, ensuring that oversight is focused where it matters most.  

Then I come across a note that clarifies the status of any “shall” provisions: they are mandatory, and any deviation from them must be approved by the Board of Directors. This tells me that while the inspection regime is strict, there is a formal process for exceptions, but such exceptions cannot be made unilaterally; they require higher‑level sanction.  

Putting these pieces together, the logical conclusion is that equality is ensured by instituting a system of regular inspections and quality checks, with the executing authority performing stage inspections at critical junctures. Because the directive is framed as a mandatory “shall,” any departure from this inspection regime must be sanctioned by the Board of Directors, which matches the description that the NRL manual imposes this requirement and allows deviations only with Board approval. This reasoning naturally leads to the answer provided.

- ix) The EIC (Consultant) has to have good experience in design, project supervision and works management.
- x) In EPC contracts, since primary responsibility to execute the work lies with the EPC contractor, success of the project also depends upon the quality of the tender document wherein enough clarity on the broad framework for execution of the work and the obligations of the contractor needs to be built in.
- xi) Milestones for payment to the contractor should be fixed in a manner that facilitates smooth cash flow for the contractor as well as for progress of the work. Milestones fixed should avoid excessive front loading or back loading, i.e., amount of payment should be commensurate with stage-wise quantum of work/ cost incurred. Milestones for payment to the contractor should also be linked with the deliverables.
- xii) In case of EPC contracts, only general arrangement drawings and architectural control parameters should be part of the tender document. In case of EPC contracts, timelines for submission of drawings by the contractors and approval thereof by the competent authority should be clearly prescribed in the tender document, wherein, damages for non-adherence of such timelines in this regard may also be incorporated.
- xiii) EPC contracts **shall** specify broad technical specification and key output parameters. Over-specification of design may lead to increase in cost. Technical specifications **shall** be framed in such a manner to allow sufficient freedom to the contractor to optimize design. Provisions on the following should be included in commercial conditions :
  - a) Limitation of liability for procuring entity as well as contractor.
  - b) Deviation limits and procedure for change of scope.
  - c) Contract closing timelines and procedure to ensure timely closing of contract.
  - d) Performance parameters and liquidated damages for shortfall in performance
  - e) Risk matrix and responsibilities of the contractor and the procuring entity.
- xiv) To mitigate the risk involved in the methodology proposed by the contractor, the project executive authority **shall** either have an in-house engineering, quality assurance and project management expert or alternatively hire an experienced engineer to intensively examine the proposal submitted by the contractor.
- xv) To ensure equality, regular inspection and quality checks must be carried out. The Project, executing authority **shall** carry out stage inspections in manufacturing of critical equipment/critical activities of the project.

question_text: What does the 'as-is-where-is' basis indicate about the seller's guarantees concerning the description, quality, or quantity of auctioned items
answer:
- The seller provides no assurance or guarantee that the advertised description, quality, or quantity of the auctioned items will be accurate; the indication is only approximate.  
- Items are accepted with any faults or errors in description, and the buyer assumes all risk for discrepancies in description, quality, or quantity.  
- Procurement must therefore treat the lot as approximate and rely on pre‑bid inspection to verify condition, safeguarding corporate value and limiting exposure to post‑award claims.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 169)
cot:
First, I think about what the expression “as‑is‑where‑is” usually conveys in a sale setting—it tells the buyer that the item is being transferred exactly as it sits, with no promise that it will match any prior description or specification.  

In the auction terms, the clause makes this explicit: the description, quality, and quantity indicated are only approximate, and the seller does not give any assurance or guarantee that the material will strictly adhere to what was advertised or shown in the e‑auction.  

From that wording I deduce that the seller is deliberately disclaiming any warranty or guarantee concerning those three attributes; the buyer cannot later claim that the lot fell short of the advertised description, quality, or quantity.  

The provision goes on to say that the buyer must take delivery of the item with any faults or errors in description, and that neither the sale can be invalidated nor can the buyer seek compensation for such discrepancies.  

That leads me to consider the practical implication for a procurement officer: if the seller offers no guarantees, the officer cannot rely solely on the catalogue details and must verify the lot’s condition, quantity and quality personally before placing a bid.  

Putting it all together, the “as‑is‑where‑is” basis indicates that the seller provides no assurance or guarantee that the advertised description, quality, or quantity of the auctioned items will be accurate; the indications are merely approximate, the buyer accepts the item with any faults or errors, and therefore must rely on pre‑bid inspection to protect against post‑award claims.
chunk_content:
### 10.6.1 'As-Is-Where-Is' and 'No Complaint' basis
Notwithstanding anything contained in the e-auction or advertisement issued on the description and particulars of material for sale, the sale is on 'as-is-where-is' basis only and the principle of caveat emptor (let the buyer be aware) will apply. As is where is means that the description/quality/quantity indicated are approximate and the seller does not give any assurance or guarantee that the material will strictly adhere to the advertisement or e-auction. All items shall be taken delivery of from the site by the successful bidders, with its faults and

errors in description, if any. Neither can the sale be invalidated nor the bidder make any claim/compensation, whatsoever, on account of any defect in description or deficiency in the quantity and quality. No plea of misunderstanding or ignorance of conditions put forth subsequent to a confirmation of sale shall be accepted.

No complaint regarding the quality or description of the materials sold will be entertained once the bid has been accepted.

### 10.6.2 Inspection by Bidders
In view of the 'as-is-where-is' condition, bidders are advised to quote rates only after inspection of items regarding quantity, quality, conditions of the items at the site, prior to his submission of bid. The bidder or his authorised representative may inspect the materials at their own cost, as per the inspection schedule mentioned in the auction details, in the specified time (excluding lunch hours) at the location specified against each lot on any working day with the prior entry permission from the contact person, as given in the auction details. The detailed description of all lots, including the list of spare parts, if any, is available at the site.

### 10.6.3 Right to Reject all Bids
The seller reserves the right to accept/reject and cancel any bid, amend the quantity under any lot or withdraw any lot at any stage before or after acceptance of bid/issue of acceptance letter/sale order/delivery order/deposit of the full sale value by the bidder, without assigning any reason thereof and the value of such material, if paid for, shall be refundable. The seller shall not be responsible for damage/loss to bidders on account of such withdrawal at any stage from the sale.

### 10.6.4 Duties and Taxes
Any applicable statutory taxes/duties are to be borne by the purchaser, including any variations in the rate of taxes/duties during the pendency of the contract. In order to avoid the imposition of penalty, the amount deposited by the successful bidder towards taxes and duties will be deposited with the concerned tax authorities on time.

## 10.7 Disposal through Tender
Disposal through tender could take place through the public e-Auction through service provider or normal tendering. In the bidding documents, Business Rule Document (BRD) / Auction Catalogue covering all applicable terms & conditions for the particular tender may be laid out.

question_text: Ensure that delays or failure of performance caused by Force Majeure do not constitute default nor give rise to claims for damages.
answer:

## 8.13 Disputes and Conflicts
8.13.1 Disputes between the consultant/ service provider and the client may arise for a number of reasons. This could relate to technical and administrative matters such as interpretation of contract, payment for services or substitution of key experts - all of which should be dealt with promptly and amicably between the contracting parties in terms of contract provisions. These may be the result of delays prompted by weaknesses on the part of the consultant/ service provider or the Procuring Entity; by a lack of funds; by delays in getting key approvals, data, or information; or by causes beyond anyone's control such as natural disasters. These may be the result of deviations from the Scope of Work or work plan by the consultant/ service provider or out-of-course requests for deviations by the Procuring Entity.

8.13.2 All reasonable efforts should be made to avoid disputes in the first place; both parties should attempt to deal with problems as they arise, on a mutually constructive basis. (This may include the repatriation of consultant/ service provider staff if necessary or a change in the personnel of the Procuring Entity's CMC/EIC) If this is not possible, GCC sets clear procedures for dealing with disputes. This entails provision of a notification of dispute by one party to the other, and provision for a mutual resolution at higher levels of authority within the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity. Finally, if the dispute cannot be amicably settled between the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity, then provision is made for arbitration under the Arbitration Clause. The award decreed by arbitration tribunal is binding.

For further details please refer section 6.10.1 and 6.10.2 of the “Manual for Procurement of Works”

## 8.14 Force Majeure
8.14.1 A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is

prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

8.14.2 Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

question_text: What is a single tender enquiry (STE) according to the SOP
answer:
A single tender enquiry (STE) is a procurement method in which an invitation to submit a tender is issued to only one firm.  

- **Definition** – A tender invitation to one firm only is called a single tender (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65).  
- **Categories of STE** – The SOP distinguishes three types:  
  1. **Nomination basis tender** – a single tender issued without a PAC certificate (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65).  
  2. **Standardization** – purchasing from a selected firm to maintain compatibility with existing machinery/equipment, as advised by a competent technical expert and approved by the competent authority (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65).  
  3. **Trial order** – a smaller‑quantity order issued before a large‑quantity contract to assess a firm’s capabilities when they are not fully known (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65).  

- **Permissible circumstances** – STE may be used only when:  
  i. The goods/services are of a specialized or proprietary nature.  
  ii. Technical/professional advice requires specialized parties/individuals (e.g., soil investigation, land valuation, arbitration, HR/Finance/IT interventions, technical investigation).  
  iii. Immediate or urgent action is warranted.  
  iv. Indigenous development for import substitution involves inviting a single party specializing in the field/commodity and negotiating with them (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65).  

- **Approval and documentation** – The reasons for choosing STE and the selection of the particular firm must be recorded and approved by the Competent Authority (CA) in accordance with the delegation of powers laid down in the DOA before the tender is issued (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 66).  

- **Applicable terms and conditions** – All other terms and conditions that apply to PAC procurement also apply to STE (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 66).  

- **Reporting and audit** – All works/purchase/consultancy contracts awarded on a nomination basis must be brought to the notice of the Board of Directors by the Commercial Department through the Company Secretary on a quarterly basis. For reporting, two lists are required: (i) contracts up to Rs 5 lakhs and (ii) contracts above Rs 5 lakhs. The Audit Committee is required to examine at least 10% of such cases (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 66).  

Thus, an STE is a tightly controlled, single‑firm tender process permitted only under the specified conditions, requiring prior approval, proper documentation, quarterly Board reporting, and periodic audit review.
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants the meaning of a single tender enquiry (STE) as laid out in the SOP, so I need to pull out the core definition and the surrounding rules that shape how an STE is used.  

The SOP opens by stating plainly that a tender invitation sent to just one firm is termed a single tender. That gives me the basic idea—STE is a procurement method where only one supplier is approached.  

Next, I notice the SOP breaks this single‑tender concept into three recognizable situations. One is a nomination‑basis tender, which occurs when the invitation goes to a single firm without a PAC certificate. Another is standardization, where a particular firm is chosen to keep machinery, components or spare parts compatible with existing equipment, based on a technical expert’s recommendation and authority approval. The third is a trial order, a small‑quantity purchase made before a larger contract to test a firm’s capabilities when they are not yet fully known.  

After identifying these categories, I look at the conditions that justify using an STE in the first place. The SOP limits it to cases where the goods or services are specialized or proprietary, where technical or professional advice calls for a specialist (such as soil investigation, land valuation, arbitration, HR/Finance/IT work, or technical studies), where immediate or urgent action is required, or where an item is being developed indigenously for import substitution and only a single specialist exists to negotiate with.  

Then I turn to the procedural safeguards. Before any STE can be issued, the reasons for choosing this route and the specific firm selected must be documented and signed off by the Competent Authority, in line with the delegation of powers in the DOA. This approval step ensures the decision isn’t made arbitrarily.  

The SOP also tells me that, aside from the special approval, all the usual terms and conditions that govern PAC procurements apply to an STE as well. So the same contractual clauses, delivery schedules, payment terms, and so on remain in force.  

Finally, I consider the oversight and reporting requirements. Every contract awarded on a nomination basis must be reported to the Board of Directors each quarter through the Commercial Department and the Company Secretary. The reporting is split into two groups—contracts up to Rs 5 lakhs and those above Rs 5 lakhs—and the Audit Committee is required to review at least ten percent of these cases, paying particular attention to the higher‑value ones.  

Putting all of this together, I see that an STE is not just a simple “one‑supplier” tender; it is a tightly controlled, single‑firm procurement process permitted only under narrowly defined circumstances, requiring prior authority approval, full documentation, adherence to standard PAC terms, quarterly Board disclosure, and periodic audit scrutiny. This matches the description given in the answer.

## 4.7 Single Tender Enquiry (STE)
4.7.1 A tender invitation to one firm only is called a single tender.

**A) Nomination Basis Tenders:** A tender invitation to one firm only without a PAC certificate is called a single tender nomination basis tender.

Procurements and Contracts will be permitted on a single tender basis in the following circumstances only:

- i. Where the material to be manufactured / fabricated or services to be obtained are of a specialized / proprietary nature.
- ii. Where under Technical / Professional Advice, works are to be obtained from specialized parties / individuals, such as cases of soil investigation, land valuation, arbitration, HR / Finance / IT interventions, technical investigation etc.
- iii. Where situation warrants immediate / urgent action.
- iv. In case of indigenous development of items for import substitution, invitation of offer from a single party specializing in the field / commodity and subsequent negotiations with them will be permissible.

Scrutiny of contracts & purchase orders awarded on nomination should continue as per prevailing practice for highlighting lapses observed for corrective action. The data on such contracts & purchase orders above Rs 5 lakhs in value should be checked by Internal Audit to the extent of at least 10%. Internal Audit shall put up to the Audit Committee of the Board their findings on such verifications.

**B) Standardization:** For standardization of machinery or components or spare parts to be compatible to the existing sets of machinery/equipment (on the advice of a competent technical expert and approved by the competent authority), the required goods are to be purchased only from a selected firm.

Standardization shall refer to instances where the User Function specifies a proprietary brand even though materials of equivalent specifications are available in order to maintain limited inventory / assist in speedier execution of job during RTA etc.

The items categorized as Standard items shall be valid for 2 years from date of approval.

**C) Trial Order:** Before an order for large quantity to any firm, the capabilities of which are not fully known, if considered necessary and feasible, Trial Order for smaller quantity can be issued.

The indenting department would be responsible for assessment of the performance of the party in case of extension / confirmation of the trial order.

### 4.7.2 Terms and Conditions
- i) The reasons for a STE and selection of a particular firm must be recorded and approved by the CA as per the delegation of powers laid down at in DOA, prior to single tendering. Unlike in PAC, powers of procurement of STE are more restricted; and
- ii) Other terms and conditions of PAC procurement mentioned above would also apply in this case.
- iii) All works / purchase / consultancy contracts awarded on nomination basis should be brought to the notice of the Board of Directors by Commercial department through Company Secretary for information on quarterly basis. For reporting, 02 lists (i) upto Rs.5 lakhs, and (ii) above Rs.5 lakhs shall be submitted.

The audit committee in the organisation may be required to check at least 10% of such cases.

question_text: What body can be established to oversee joint‑venture partners in a QCBS project?
answer: An Implementation Board that includes all joint‑venture partners (and allows the procuring entity’s Project Manager to attend when needed) can be set up to oversee JV partners in a QCBS project. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 60)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: in a QCBS (Quality‑and‑Cost‑Based Selection) procurement, how can we keep an eye on the partners that form a joint venture so that the venture actually works as intended throughout the contract.  

Next, I recall the special features of QCBS: quality carries significant weight in the evaluation, and the method is meant to discourage superficial or “name‑borrowing” joint ventures that would undermine accountability. Because the quality score can make or break the award, any joint‑venture arrangement must be monitored closely to ensure every partner is truly contributing and delivering the promised performance.  

Then I think about what kind of oversight mechanism would satisfy that need. The mechanism has to involve all joint‑venture partners directly, so that no partner can hide behind another’s effort, and it should also give the procuring entity a way to stay informed without dominating the board—otherwise the joint venture’s autonomy would be lost.  

Looking at the safeguards suggested for joint ventures in QCBS, the idea that emerges is to create an Implementation Board whose membership consists of every joint‑venture partner. This board would be the forum where progress, issues, and compliance are reviewed. To keep the procuring entity in the loop, the Project Manager from the purchasing agency is allowed to attend the board’s meetings when needed, but does not have a voting role unless specified.  

Finally, I see that the board’s work can be tied to concrete contract milestones—such as quarterly progress reviews linked to key dates or payment triggers—so that oversight is not just advisory but has real contractual teeth. Putting these pieces together, the body that can be established to oversee joint‑venture partners in a QCBS project is an Implementation Board that includes all joint‑venture partners and permits the procuring entity’s Project Manager to attend when required.

question_text: Through which mechanism should release of payment and settlement of the final bill be processed?
answer: - Release of payment and settlement of the final bill must be processed through the Associated/integrated Finance function, in accordance with the contract’s terms and conditions. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 107)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know the proper channel or mechanism for releasing payment and closing out the final bill in a procurement or supply contract.  

Next, I think about what typically governs payment actions in such contracts. Payment isn’t just a matter of sending money; it has to align with the agreed terms, verify that the supplier has fulfilled all obligations, and be recorded correctly in the organization’s financial systems.  

Then I consider who within an organization is responsible for ensuring that payments follow those contractual terms and that the financial records are accurate. That role usually falls to the finance function, especially when it is integrated or associated with the procurement unit, because finance handles the actual disbursement, checks against invoices, and ensures compliance with the contract’s payment schedule and conditions.  

Looking further, the process must also involve a final settlement step where any outstanding amounts, adjustments, or deductions are resolved before the bill is closed. This settlement still needs to be routed through the same finance channel to maintain a single, auditable trail of the transaction from invoice to payment.  

Finally, synthesizing these points, the only mechanism that satisfies both the requirement to adhere strictly to the contract’s terms and to provide proper financial oversight is to process the release of payment and the settlement of the final bill through the associated or integrated finance function, exactly as stipulated in the contract’s payment provisions. This ensures timely, accurate, and contract‑compliant closure of the financial obligation.

question_text: What should technical and financial eligibility criteria for bidders look like
answer:
** They should be clear, fair, and tailored to the specific procurement, prescribing appropriate parameters that balance quality, time, and cost to select the right bidders in the public interest.  

**Rationale:** Clear and fair criteria ensure bidders understand what is required, while well‑chosen parameters reflect the procurement’s unique circumstances and help achieve the desired balance among quality, schedule, and expense. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 46)
cot:
First, I think about what technical and financial eligibility criteria are meant to do in a procurement: they act as the initial filter that separates bidders who have the necessary capability and stability from those who do not, so the rest of the evaluation can focus on the actual offer.  

Then, I consider what makes such a filter work well. It has to be understandable to everyone involved—clear wording avoids confusion and disputes—and it has to be applied without bias, so fairness is essential to maintain confidence in the process.  

Next, I reason that the filter cannot be one‑size‑fits‑all. Each procurement has its own technical scope, risk profile, budget constraints and schedule demands, so the criteria must reflect those specific circumstances; otherwise we risk either excluding competent firms or letting in unsuitable ones.  

Further, I dig into what “reflecting the specific circumstances” looks like in practice. The criteria should prescribe measurable parameters—such as minimum years of relevant experience, financial turnover thresholds, or specific certifications—that directly relate to the quality of work needed, the time required to deliver, and the cost implications of the contract. By tying the parameters to these three dimensions, we create a balance that encourages bidders who can meet quality expectations within the desired timeframe and budget.  

Finally, I synthesize these thoughts: the eligibility criteria ought to be clear, fair, and tailored to the particular procurement, prescribing appropriate parameters that balance quality, time, and cost, thereby enabling the selection of the right bidders in the public interest. This lines up exactly with the answer that the criteria should be clear, fair, and suited to the specific procurement, with parameters that balance quality, time and cost to pick the right bidders for the public good.

question_text: What key element must facilitators emphasize must be present in tender documents when a contract is concluded with a variable price?
answer:
When a contract is to be awarded with a variable price, facilitators should stress that the tender documents must include an appropriate clause that incorporates a suitable price‑variation formula to calculate the adjustment between the base price level and the scheduled delivery date. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 110).  

To make this point interactive, the source does not cover how to conduct a hands-on check or apply it to real-world e-procurement scenarios.
cot:
First, I consider why a contract might be awarded with a variable price in the first place – it is usually because the goods involve inputs whose costs can swing sharply over the delivery period, such as raw materials, labor or energy prices. If the price were left fixed, the purchaser could end up paying far more than market value when costs drop, or the supplier could suffer losses when costs rise, jeopardizing contract performance.  

Next, I think about what safeguard is needed to keep the agreement fair for both sides when those underlying costs fluctuate. The safeguard must be built into the tender itself so that every bidder works from the same rule‑book; otherwise, each bidder might propose its own adjustment method, making comparison impossible and opening the door to disputes later on.  

From there, I focus on the concrete form that safeguard should take. The reference material points to a price‑variation clause that contains a suitable formula. This formula needs a baseline – the price level at the time the tender is issued – and a point in the future, the scheduled delivery date, at which the adjustment is applied. It also has to rely on neutral, published indices for the relevant cost elements and assign appropriate weights to things like material, labour and fixed overheads.  

Putting those pieces together, I see that the essential requirement facilitators must stress is that the tender documents contain an appropriate clause that incorporates such a price‑variation formula. The clause’s purpose is to calculate the adjustment between the base price level and the price at the scheduled delivery date, thereby protecting the purchaser’s interests when input costs are volatile.  

Finally, I verify that this conclusion captures exactly what the answer states: when a contract is to be awarded with a variable price, facilitators should emphasize that the tender documents must include an appropriate clause incorporating a suitable price‑variation formula to calculate the adjustment between the base price level and the scheduled delivery date. The reasoning flows naturally from the problem’s context to the required contractual provision, with no leaps or extra claims.

question_text: Under what circumstances can the procuring entity split the order quantity among multiple bidders if the bidding documents did not originally allow for splitting
answer: The procuring entity can split the order when it discovers that the total quantity required is much larger than what the bidder who offered the lowest price can actually supply, and the bidding documents did not already provide for splitting the contract. In that situation the entity may share the work among other bidders by offering them the same lowest price, using objective information from the bids—such as each bidder’s eligibility, the quantity they can deliver, and their delivery schedule—to decide a fair and equitable split. The split must be carried out transparently, and the lowest price must first be verified as reasonable; if it is not reasonable, the entity may negotiate with the lowest‑price bidder (with the competent authority’s approval) before proceeding. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p.126)
cot:
I’m trying to figure out when a procuring entity can go ahead and divide an order among several bidders even though the original bidding documents said nothing about splitting the contract.  

First, I need to pinpoint the trigger that would make splitting necessary. The only sensible reason is that the total quantity the entity wants to buy turns out to be far beyond what the bidder who submitted the lowest price—let’s call them L1—can actually deliver on its own. If L1 could handle the whole lot, there would be no need to look elsewhere.  

Next, I have to check whether the bidding documents already anticipated this situation. If they had included a clause allowing the contract to be split, the entity could simply follow that provision. But the premise of the question is that no such clause exists, so the entity must rely on a post‑hoc decision rather than a pre‑written rule.  

Now I consider what the entity can do once it recognizes the capacity shortfall. The Procurement of Goods Manual suggests that, after confirming the shortfall, the entity may turn to the other bidders and offer them the same L1 price. This counter‑offer is only permissible if it can be done in a way that is fair, transparent and equitable, and the fairness must be grounded in objective data that already exists in the bids—things like each bidder’s eligibility, the quantity they are capable of supplying, and their delivery timelines.  

Before distributing the work, however, the entity must verify that the L1 price itself is reasonable. If the lowest bid looks suspiciously low or otherwise unreasonable, jumping straight to splitting could undermine value for money. In that case, the proper step is to first negotiate with L1—perhaps adjusting the price or clarifying scope—subject to the approval of the competent authority. Only after the L1 rate is deemed reasonable does the entity proceed to allocate the remaining quantity to L2, L3, and so on, using the same counter‑offer approach and respecting each bidder’s spare capacity.  

Finally, the whole process must be carried out transparently, with clear documentation of how the shares were determined, so that the split remains defensible and free of favoritism.  

Putting these pieces together, the circumstances under which the procuring entity can split the order despite the absence of an original splitting clause are: (1) discovering that the required quantity greatly exceeds L1’s supply capacity, (2) confirming that no prior split provision exists in the bidding documents, (3) ensuring the L1 price is reasonable (or negotiating it to be so with competent‑authority approval), and (4) allocating the excess quantity among other bidders by offering them the L1 rate, using objective bid data to achieve a fair, transparent and equitable distribution. This matches the answer’s description of when and how the split may be effected.

### 7.5.5 Splitting of Contracts/ Parallel Contracts
After due processing, if it is discovered that the quantity to be ordered is far more than what L1 alone is capable of supplying and there was no prior decision/ declaration in the bidding documents to split the quantities, then the quantity being finally ordered may be distributed among the other bidders by counter offering the L1 rate in a manner that is fair, transparent and equitable based on objective data available in the bids e.g. eligibility data, Quantity/ Delivery etc. A suitable clause covering the above may be kept as tender condition.

However, in case of critical/ vital/ safety/ security nature of the item, large quantity under procurement, urgent delivery requirements and inadequate vendor capacity it may be advantageous to decide in advance to have more than one source of supply. In such cases a parallel contract clause should be added to the bid documents, clearly stating that Procuring Entity reserves the right to split the contract quantity between suppliers. The manner of deciding the relative share of lowest bidder (L1) contractor and the rest of the contractors/tenderers should be clearly defined, along with the minimum number of suppliers sought for the contract. In case of splitting in two and three, the ratio of 70:30; 50:30:20, respectively, may be used - a different ratio may also be justified.

Before splitting the quantity, it should be ensured that the L1 price is reasonable. If it is not reasonable, negotiation with the L1 party may be carried out, if justifiable, with the approval of the CA. The following guidelines are to be considered while opting for parallel contracts:

- i) L1 should be awarded at least the percentage mentioned above or his spare supply capacity, whichever is lower; and
- ii) For the rest of the contract quantity, the lowest rate accepted will be counter offered to the L2 party. On acceptance of the counter offer, the order will be placed on L2 for the respective percentage or the spare supply capacity of the L2 bidder, whichever is lower, and so on, to other tenderers. In case of non- acceptance of the counter offer by the L2 party, a similar offer shall be made to L3 and L4, and so on.
- iii) A suitable clause covering the above may be kept in the NIT.

section: 1.2 Amendments and Revision of this Manual
question_text: What activities are included in the definition of Original Works?
answer: Original works encompass all new constructions, site preparation, additions and alterations to existing works, as well as special repairs to newly purchased or previously abandoned buildings or structures, including remodelling or replacement (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 11).
cot:
I start by asking what the term “Original Works” is meant to capture within the broader classification of works. Since works are split into original, minor, and repair categories, original works must involve something that goes beyond routine upkeep or minor enhancements—it should create new value or substantially change an asset.  

I think about what actions actually bring a new asset into existence or give an existing asset a fundamentally different character. Building something from the ground up clearly qualifies, as does preparing a site so that construction can begin. Likewise, adding onto a structure or altering its layout changes the asset in a way that adds capital value, which feels more like creation than simple maintenance.  

Next, I consider buildings that are newly acquired or have been sitting vacant. Restoring such properties to usable condition often requires work that is more intensive than ordinary repairs; if the effort is substantial enough to be termed a “special repair,” it effectively gives the building a new lease on life or even replaces major components. This kind of work, including remodeling or replacing parts of the building, also results in a renewed or upgraded asset, aligning it with the idea of original creation rather than mere upkeep.  

Putting these observations together, the activities that fit the notion of original works are those that involve new construction, site preparation, additions or alterations to existing works, and special repairs—including remodeling or replacement—applied to newly purchased or previously abandoned buildings or structures. This collection of activities matches the definition of Original Works.
