## 7.1 Single Source Selection (SSS / STE)
7.1.1 Selection of consultants/ service providers through direct negotiations does not provide the benefits of competition in regard to quality and cost, lacks transparency in selection, and could encourage unacceptable practices. The reasons for SSS and selection of a particular consultant must be recorded and approved by the CA as per the delegation of authorities, prior to single tendering. Therefore, single-source selection shall be used only in exceptional circumstance, where it is inescapable over competitive selections as discussed in sub-paras below.

7.1.2 When in a Project, continuity for downstream work is essential, the initial RfP shall outline this prospect, and, if practical, the factors used for the selection of the consultant/ service provider should take the likelihood of continuation into account. Continuity in the technical approach, experience acquired, and continued professional liability of the same consultant/ service provider may make continuation with the initial consultant/ service provider preferable to a new competition subject to satisfactory performance in the initial assignment. For such downstream assignments, the Procuring Entity shall ask the initially selected consultant/ service provider to prepare technical and financial proposals on the basis of ToR furnished by the Procuring Entity, which shall then be negotiated (technical discussion).

7.1.3 If the initial assignment was not awarded on a competitive basis or if the downstream assignment is substantially larger in value, a competitive process shall normally be followed in which the consultant/ service provider carrying out the initial work is not excluded from consideration if it expresses interest.

7.1.4 For selecting a consultant/ service provider under this method, the Procuring Entity should prepare a full justification and take the approval of the competent authority as per the DOA.

7.1.5 While selecting the consultant/ service provider under this method, the Procuring Entity shall ensure that the consultant/ service provider has the requisite qualification and experience to undertake the assignment. Normally the Procuring Entity shall adopt the same short listing criteria as applied to similar assignments while evaluating the EoI.

question_text: Who takes part in the joint investigation when I file a written complaint about a rejection
answer: When you file a written complaint about a rejection, the joint investigation is carried out by a team of three people: an authorized representative from the Procuring Entity, a senior representative from the inspecting agency who knows the goods well, and an authorized representative from your own company. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 159)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know who is involved in the joint investigation that occurs after a supplier submits a written complaint about a rejection of goods.  

Next, I recall the part of the reference that deals with complaints and inspections. It explains that when a written complaint is received disputing a rejection, the matter should be handled jointly.  

From that description, I can pull out the three specific roles that must be present: an authorized representative from the procuring entity, a senior representative from the inspecting agency who is familiar with the goods, and an authorized representative from the supplier’s side.  

I then think about why each of these roles is necessary. The procuring entity’s rep ensures the investigation reflects the buyer’s position and authority, the senior inspecting agency rep brings the technical expertise needed to evaluate the grounds for rejection, and the supplier’s rep guarantees that the supplier’s perspective is heard and that the process remains fair.  

Putting these points together, the joint investigation team is precisely made up of those three parties, which matches the answer that the investigation is carried out by an authorized representative of the Procuring Entity, a senior representative of the inspecting agency conversant with the goods, and an authorized representative of the supplier.
chunk_content:
#### ii) **External Inspecting Authorities**
In case Procuring Entity does not have technical expertise or for other relevant reasons, inspection may also be entrusted to a third-party inspection authority. The procuring entity, however, retains the right to reject the consignment, even if it is cleared by third party inspection authorities.

Sometimes, it becomes necessary to conduct a type test, acceptance test or special test at external laboratories, when facilities for these tests are not available in-house with the supplier or carrying out of confirmatory tests is considered desirable before accepting the goods. The Procuring Entity should draw up a list of approved laboratories for this purpose, to which the samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier can be sent for tests. The list should also contain approved laboratories, which can be used as referral/appellate laboratories for retest, when samples tested at one laboratory are decided to be re-tested. The following guidelines should apply to such cases:

- a) External testing may invariably be done by national accredited or reliable laboratories, preference being given to National Test House (NTH). For testing the

samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier, an inspection agent qualified to conduct random sampling in accordance with Quality Assurance requirements should do the selection of samples;

- b) Test reports must contain the values obtained in the tests besides fail/pass results. The laboratory must preserve the sample and test records for a period of three years;
- c) The Department should lay down a liability statement for costs expended on tests, dispatch of samples, transportation costs, test charges, and so on., in respect of samples tested at outside laboratories as may be applicable; and
- d) In cases where the samples are to be tested at the supplier's cost because of non-availability of his own testing arrangements, the responsibility of depositing the testing fees would rest with the supplier.
- e) Normally unless otherwise intended in the contract, charges of routine testing prior to dispatch of materials are to be borne by the supplier and charges of testing of materials after receipt by consignee are to be borne by the procuring agency. Contract should be clear about responsibility of cost of materials expended in tests and charges of special tests e.g. type test or tests at external labs. **Even where procuring entity is responsible for testing charges, if the material fails in the test, the charges would become the responsibility of the seller.**

#### iii) **Joint Inspection on Complaint**
In case a written complaint is received from the supplier disputing the rejection of goods by the Procuring Entity's inspecting officer, it should be jointly investigated by a team consisting of an authorised representative of the Procuring Entity, a senior representative of the inspecting agency who is conversant with the goods and an authorised representative of the supplier.

section: 7.5.12 Handling Dissent among Tender Evaluation Committee
question_text: What steps are taken to keep the information in my bid private during the evaluation
answer:
During the evaluation of your bid, the Tender Evaluation Committee takes several straightforward steps to keep your information private:

- All discussions are held face‑to‑face across the table, so notes, comments or e‑mails are not passed around.
- If members disagree, they talk it out personally instead of writing back‑and‑forth; any remaining dissent is recorded in a balanced note together with the majority view.
- Every committee member must keep the bid details confidential and make sure the information does not reach anyone who is not authorised.
- At the end of their report each member signs a declaration saying they have no conflict of interest with any bidder, which reinforces their duty to protect your data.
- Members may ask subordinate officers for help with reports or evaluations, but the responsibility for safeguarding the information stays with the nominated TEC member.

These practices help ensure that your bid information remains private throughout the evaluation process. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 132)
cot:
First, I consider what it means to keep bid information private during an evaluation: the core goal is to prevent any unauthorized disclosure while the committee works on the technical, commercial and financial aspects of the tenders.  

Next, I identify the conditions that must be satisfied to achieve that goal. The evaluation must be conducted in a way that limits the creation of written records that could be intercepted, ensures that any disagreements are handled without leaving a trace, obliges every participant to treat the data as confidential, and reinforces that obligation through a formal statement of impartiality.  

Then I think about how those conditions translate into concrete practices. Holding deliberations face‑to‑face across the table eliminates the circulation of notes, comments or e‑mails that could be seen by outsiders. When members disagree, they resolve the difference through personal discussion instead of exchanging written comments; if a consensus still cannot be reached, any dissent is recorded only in a balanced note that accompanies the majority view, keeping the written record minimal and controlled.  

After that, I consider the personal responsibility of each committee member. Every member is required to keep the bid details confidential and to make sure the information does not reach anyone who is not authorised, which directly addresses the risk of leakage. To strengthen this duty, each member signs a declaration at the end of their report stating they have no conflict of interest with any bidder; this declaration serves as a reminder of their obligation to protect the data and to act impartially.  

Finally, I recognize that members may seek assistance from subordinate officers for preparing reports or evaluations, but the ultimate responsibility for safeguarding the information remains with the nominated TEC member who asked for help. This ensures that even when support is used, the confidentiality obligation does not shift away from the accountable official.  

Putting these points together, the steps—face‑to‑face discussions, personal resolution of disagreements, strict confidentiality, conflict‑of‑interest declarations, and retained responsibility despite subordinate assistance—form a coherent set of measures that keep the bid information private throughout the evaluation process.
chunk_content:
Tender Evaluation Committee duties are to be discharged personally by the nominated officers. They may take help of their subordinate officers by way of reports/ evaluations, but they would still be answerable for such decisions. TEC members cannot co-opt or nominate others to attend deliberations on their behalf. TEC deliberations are best held across the table and not through circulation of notes/comments/e-mails etc.

All members of the TEC should resolve their differences through personal discussions instead of making to and fro references in writing. In cases where it is not possible to come to a consensus and differences persist amongst TEC members, the reasons for dissent of a member should be recorded in a balanced manner along with the majority's views on the dissent note. The final recommendations should be that of the majority view. However, such situations should be rare.

### 7.5.13 Independence, Impartiality, Confidentiality and 'No Conflict of Interest' at all Stages of Evaluation of Bids
All technical, commercial and finance officials who have contributed to the techno- commercial or financial evaluation of bids, should deal with the procurement in an independent, impartial manner and should have no conflict of interest with any of the bidder involved in the procurement. They should also maintain confidentiality of the information processed during the evaluation process and not allow it to reach any unauthorised person. All TEC members should sign a declaration at the end of their reports/ noting stating that, "I declare that I have no conflict of interest with any of the bidder in this tender". TEC members may make such a declaration at the end of their reports.

section: 2.4 Preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) /Preliminary Estimates (PE)
question_text: Why is it important to verify a consultant's relevant experience and allocate sufficient time when outsourcing DPR preparation?
answer:
**Step‑by‑Step Operational Checklist: Verifying Consultant Experience and Time Allocation for DPR Preparation**

1. Confirm successful project design and supervision experience while selecting consultants, especially for large works contracts such as roads, highways, ports, runways, and dams. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 18)  
2. Ensure the Consultant is directed to exercise due diligence and that the DPR is based on proper ground investigation. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 18)  
3. Allocate sufficient time for the consultant to prepare the Detailed Project Report. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 18)
cot: First, I think about what a Detailed Project Report must deliver—clear scope, reliable cost estimates with escalation, land and environmental plans, and the systems needed for monitoring and quality—because any weakness here directly affects how competitive the bidding process can be. Then I recall the reference’s observation that many contract problems stem from consultants who are either inexperienced or pressed for time, which tells me that the root risk lies in the consultant’s ability to carry out thorough ground investigations, exercise due diligence, and produce all the required sections without cutting corners. This leads me to conclude that, before entrusting the work, I need to verify that the consultant has a proven record of successful design and supervision on similar projects, especially those involving the type of works contract at hand, so that I can be confident they understand the nuances of scope definition, cost estimation, and the preparation of environmental and social assessments. Next, I consider the time dimension: a proper DPR requires gathering field data, analyzing alternatives, preparing year‑wise cash‑flow projections, factoring in expected escalation, and drafting monitoring, quality assurance, and bidding system details—all activities that cannot be rushed without risking omissions or inaccurate estimates. Consequently, I allocate a realistic schedule that includes sufficient buffers for data collection, analysis, and iterative review, ensuring the timeline explicitly accommodates the preparation of escalation‑adjusted cost forecasts and cash‑flow statements. I then realize that simply setting a deadline is not enough; I must check that the allocated period genuinely covers the specific deliverables outlined for the DPR, such as the detailed land‑acquisition plan, the social‑impact and resettlement strategy, and the list of statutory approvals, so that the consultant is not forced to sacrifice any component to meet the date. To make sure this verification and the time agreement are not lost, I document the findings about the consultant’s experience and the agreed schedule in the selection record, creating a clear, traceable basis for accountability and future audits. Finally, I plan to monitor the consultant’s progress against that schedule, stepping in early if any delays appear, because a slip could jeopardize the ground‑investigation or due‑diligence work and ultimately undermine the usefulness of the DPR for competitive bidding. This chain of reasoning shows why confirming relevant experience and providing adequate time are essential steps when outsourcing the preparation of a Detailed Project Report.

section: 9.5 Payments to the Contractor and Handling of Securities
question_text: What mandatory features must the online system for monitoring contractor bills include, as stated in clause 9.5.2?
answer:
The online system for monitoring contractor bills must include the following mandatory features:

1. Monitor delays in payments and identify any unwarranted delays. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 147)  
2. Provide contractors with the facility to track the status of their submitted bills. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 147)  
3. Require that all contractor bills be entered into the system, recording both the date of submission and the date of payment. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 147)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what clause 9.5.2 actually says about the online system for monitoring contractor bills, because the question asks for the mandatory features that such a system must include.  

Looking at the passage, clause 9.5.2 discusses delayed payments and then adds that there should be a system to monitor delays in payments and to spot any unwarranted delays. It goes on to specify that this system should be an online system for monitoring the bills submitted by contractors.  

From that description I can see the first requirement: the system must be able to monitor payment delays and identify those that are unwarranted.  

Next, the text states that the online system shall have the facility for contractors to track the status of their bills. That gives me the second mandatory feature – a tracking interface for contractors.  

Finally, the clause makes it explicit that it shall be mandatory for all contractor bills to be entered into the system, recording both the date of submission and the date of payment. This tells me the third required feature: compulsory entry of every bill with submission and payment timestamps.  

Putting these together, the online system must (1) monitor and flag unwarranted payment delays, (2) let contractors view the status of their submitted bills, and (3) enforce entry of every bill with its submission and payment dates. These points match exactly the answer provided.
chunk_content:
## 9.5 Payments to the Contractor and Handling of Securities
**9.5.1** It should be ensured that all payments due to the firm, including release of the PBG, are made on a priority basis without avoidable delay as per the tender/contract conditions. Before the payment is made, the invoice should be cross-checked with the actual receipt of material to ensure that the payment matches the actual performance.

**9.5.2 Delay in payment to the contractors:** If claimed by the supplier/contractor, payment of interest shall be made in case of delayed payment of bills by more than 30 working days (or as per PO terms, whichever is later) after submission of eligible bill by the contractor. Where interest is to be paid, the rate of interest should be the rate of interest of SBI's Repo Rate plus Spread or SBI's MCLR plus Spread. Provision for payment of interest against delayed payments may be suitably framed for necessary compliance. In case of unwarranted discretionary delays in payments, as prescribed above, responsibility shall be fixed on the concerned officers. There should be a system to monitor delays in payments and to identify such unwarranted delays including an online system for monitoring of the bills submitted by contractors. Such system shall have the facility for contractors to track the status of their bills. It shall be mandatory for all contractors bills to be entered into the system with date of submission and date of payment.

## 9.6 Monitoring of Supplier Performance
As soon as the order is issued, information on the progress of supply along with the name of the supplier, items, rate, quantity, amount, delivery schedule, and so on should be available for monitoring purpose. Monitoring should ensure that suppliers adhere to contract terms, performance expectations are achieved (such as timely deliveries, quality of goods supplied, and adherence to proper procedure for submitting invoices, and so on) and any problems are identified and resolved in a timely manner. Without a sound monitoring process, there can be no assurance that the buyer has received what was contracted. A sound system for monitoring the performance of the suppliers in a contract would also be useful in selecting a good supplier in future procurement of the same or similar materials. Purchase order-wise data will be maintained regarding execution by and performance of the supplier.

## 9.7 Delays in Performance of Contract


### 9.7.1 Delivery Period
The period for delivery of the ordered goods and completion of any allied service(s) thereof (such as installation and commissioning of the equipment, operators' training, and so on) are to be properly specified in the contract with definite dates and these shall be deemed to be the essence of the contract. The delivery period stipulated in contracts should be specific and practical. Vague and ambiguous terms such as 1,000/5,000 (one to five thousand) numbers per month, 2 to 16 (two to sixteen) weeks from the date of receipt of order, 'immediate', 'ex-stock', 'as

early as possible', 'off the shelf', 'approximately' and the like should be scrupulously avoided as these will not be legally binding.

In case of items such as raw material which is delivered throughout the year, a defined delivery schedule should be specified. It is usual in such cases that there is a slight deviation from such monthly rate of supply. It should be clarified in such cases that the variation in the periodic rate of supply beyond agreed variation in any given period would be considered as delay in delivery attracting imposition of LD.

Unless otherwise agreed, the buyer of goods is not bound to accept the delivery thereof in instalments.

## 4.4 **Limited Tender Enquiry (LTE)**
4.4.1 LTE is a restricted competition procurement, where a preselected list of vendors is directly approached for bidding; bids from uninvited bidders are treated as unsolicited and are not entertained- The bidding documents should be simple

Limited tenders can be issued to foreign shortlisted parties also subject to adherence to relevant import regulations.

### 4.4.2 **Terms and Conditions**
- i) Information of the limited tenders will be published in NRL website by publishing a copy of the NIT. This will be in addition to the tender document published in the tender portal (CPP/GeM etc.) or notice board (manual tenders). The NIT may be uploaded on NRL website with a note saying:  
"This notice is being published for information only and is not an open invitation to quote in this limited tender. Participation in this tender is by invitation only and is limited to the selected agencies. Unsolicited offers are liable to be ignored."
- ii) A simplified Bid Document should be used, instead of a detailed Bid Document. The minimum number of bidders to whom LTE should be sent is three. In case less than

- three approved vendors/contractors are available, LTE may be sent to the available approved vendors/contractors with approval of the CA, duly recording the reasons.
- iii) The selection of bidders should be with due diligence, to ensure that bidders who do not meet eligibility criteria or whose past performance was poor do not get shortlisted.
  - iv) Administrative approval for floating of the limited tender shall duly record & justify the reasons for adopting the LTE route of tendering.

### 4.5 Selection of successful bidder among multiple L1 bidders:
In case of tie between two or more parties (even after consideration of applicable preferences for MSE / Local content, discount etc.), it shall be resolved through:-

- (i) The quantities be divided equally among the L1 bidders (provided that the quantity is divisible / economically viable).
- (ii) Lottery among the L1 bidders to select one successful bidder.

Methodology of evaluation should be clearly specified in the tender/RFQ.

It may also be decided that in case the successful agency as selected above refuses or fails to execute the supply/service after award, the quantities or unexecuted quantities may be subsequently offered to any of the other L1 agencies (not awarded any qty. so far), adopting appropriate selection process by NRL like lottery among the remaining interested agencies [in case of (i) above] or wait listed agencies determined in the original lottery [(ii) above].

- In case of “refusal”, subsequent award to next eligible agency shall be done within original or extended offer validity.
- In case of “failure”, unexecuted quantities shall be offered to the next eligible agency within maximum one year from the original date of award.

Defaulting supplier/contractor shall be subject to penalties as per procedure.

## 4.6 Proprietary / OEM
4.6.1 In procurement of goods, certain items are procured only from Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) or manufacturers having proprietary rights (or their authorised dealers/stockists) against a PAC / OEM certificate (Annexure 4) signed by the appropriate authority. Once a PAC is signed at the designated level as per DOA, the powers of procurement are the same as in normal conditions as per the delegation of powers.

question_text: How may the Earnest Money Deposit of a successful bidder be treated under the NRL manual if it falls short of the required Initial Security Deposit?
answer: The Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of a successful bidder that is insufficient to meet the required Initial Security Deposit (ISD) can be addressed in two ways under the NRL manual. First, the EMD may be converted to the ISD by the bidder making good the shortfall amount between the EMD and the ISD stipulated for the contract. Second, the bidder has the option to withdraw the EMD and, instead, submit a separate Bank Guarantee (BG) in lieu of the ISD/SD, prepared according to the proforma in Annexure 17. The BG must remain valid for three months beyond the later of contract completion or the end of the defect liability period. When a BG is accepted, the sponsoring function must ensure that the BG conforms to the prescribed proforma, that online systems are available for its monitoring and handling, that timely renewal is effected when required, and that prompt action is taken to realize the EMD from the bank upon any contractor breach. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 64)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know how the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of a bidder who wins the contract should be handled when that deposit does not reach the amount required for the Initial Security Deposit (ISD).  

Under the NRL manual, the key point is that on award of contract the EMD can either be turned into the ISD or be taken back and replaced by another form of security.  

If the EMD is to become the ISD, the bidder must cover any difference between what they have already deposited and what the ISD calls for; in other words, they make good the shortfall so that the total equals the required ISD.  

Alternatively, the bidder may choose to withdraw the EMD entirely and instead provide a Bank Guarantee that stands in lieu of the ISD/SD. The guarantee has to follow the proforma given in Annexure 17 and stay valid for three months beyond the later of contract completion or the end of the defect liability period.  

When a Bank Guarantee is accepted, the sponsoring function has to verify that the guarantee matches the prescribed format, set up online tracking for it, renew it promptly when needed, and be ready to call on the guarantee if the contractor breaches any term of the tender or contract.  

Putting these two pathways together, the EMD of a successful bidder that falls short of the ISD can either be supplemented to reach the ISD amount or be withdrawn and replaced by a compliant Bank Guarantee with the stated safeguards. This matches the description of the treatment under the NRL manual.
chunk_content:
On the award of contract, this is to be refunded to unsuccessful bidders or converted as initial security deposit for the successful bidder.

No interest will be allowed on EMD / Security Deposit.

On completion of Tender Procedure, the EMD will be returned to the unsuccessful bidders.

The EMD of the successful bidder may be converted to Initial Security Deposit, by making good the shortfall amount, if any, between EMD and the ISD required

Alternatively the successful bidder may call back his EMD amount and submit a separate Bank Guarantee in lieu of ISD/SD to cover all contracts as per the proforma enclosed in **Annexure 17**. The validity period for these Bank Guarantees should be 03 months beyond completion of execution of the contract or 03 months beyond end of defect liability period, whichever is later as per the terms and conditions of the particular contract.

question_text: What key information should a user include when preparing a Procurement Proposal for services
answer:
** The user should state the requirement, the purpose or objectives, the scope and expected outcomes, and provide a justification for the assignment. They should also indicate the staffing needed and the estimated budget. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 15)  

**Rationale:** Including these details ensures the proposal clearly defines what is needed, why it is needed, how it will be delivered, and that it is properly resourced and funded, which is required before seeking in‑principle approval.
cot:
I’m trying to figure out what a user must put into a Procurement Proposal when they’re looking to acquire services. First, I think about the purpose of such a proposal: it’s meant to convince the competent authority that the service is needed and that the organization is ready to move forward, much like an indent for goods. So the proposal has to make clear why the service is being sought in the first place. That leads me to consider the basic description of what is required—what exactly the user wants the service provider to do. Without stating the requirement, the approvers wouldn’t know what they’re approving.

Next, I ask myself why the requirement exists. The proposal should explain the purpose or objectives behind the assignment, linking the service to broader goals or problems the organization faces. This justification is crucial because it shows the need and helps the authority see the value. Alongside the purpose, I realize the proposal must also outline what the service will actually deliver—its scope and the expected outcomes. Defining the scope prevents misunderstandings later, and spelling out the outcomes gives a basis for measuring success.

At this point I have the “what,” “why,” and “what will be achieved.” But the reference also mentions that the proposal should be “appropriately staffed and budgeted.” That tells me the approvers need to see that the user has thought about who will carry out the work and how much it will cost. So I need to include an indication of the staffing required—perhaps the level of expertise or number of personnel—and an estimate of the budget needed to procure the service. Without these, the proposal would lack the practical details necessary for administrative and budgetary approval.

Putting it all together, the user must clearly state the requirement, articulate the purpose or objectives, describe the scope and expected outcomes, provide a justification for undertaking the assignment, and also indicate the staffing needs and the estimated budget. Only with those elements does the proposal give the competent authority a complete picture to grant in‑principle approval and move to the next steps in the procurement cycle.

question_text: In the narrative, what institutional arrangement should the procuring entity establish to manage the timely extension, encashment, or refund of EMDs and performance securities
answer:
A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of EMDs, performance securities and other instruments should be evolved and implemented by the procuring entity. Institutional arrangements shall be made for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of EMDs and performance securities, as the case may be.

Monitoring should include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period, with the rule that the Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the contractor for propose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc. For release of BGs, the proposal shall be forwarded by the executing agency with its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions.
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants the specific institutional setup that a procuring entity should put in place to make sure that earnest money deposits and performance securities are handled on time—whether that means extending them, cashing them in, or returning them when appropriate.  

Looking at the answer, it talks about a “suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring” that the procurement team created, turning that mechanism into clear institutional arrangements that designate who is responsible for acting on each guarantee. So the core idea is to assign responsibility and create a structured process for watching over these instruments.  

From that, I reason that the first step for the procuring entity is to establish a dedicated custodial function—some unit or officer tasked with keeping the guarantees safe and tracking their status. Without a clear owner, actions could be missed or delayed.  

Next, the entity must define what that custodial function actually does: it should monitor all guarantees, note when they are approaching expiry, and decide whether an extension, encashment, or refund is needed. The answer highlights a monthly review of every guarantee that will expire within the next three months, paired with a quick check on the related contract’s progress. This shows that monitoring isn’t just about dates; it’s tied to contract performance to determine if an extension is warranted.  

Building on that, the monitoring process needs to trigger action well before a guarantee lapses. The answer says that when an extension is warranted, the request is raised immediately and processed within the existing validity period, and crucially, the guarantee is never handed over to the contractor for the purpose of extending its life. This tells me the institutional arrangement must include a rule that prevents the contractor from holding the guarantee during extension procedures, ensuring the procuring entity retains control.  

To make the monthly review and timely alerts reliable, the answer suggests computerizing the monitoring system so it generates automatic alerts as expiry dates approach. This means the institutional arrangement should incorporate a technological platform that flags upcoming deadlines, prompting the responsible officer to act without needing manual reminders.  

Finally, when a guarantee is no longer needed—say, the contract is completed satisfactorily—the answer notes that the executing agency forwards a release proposal, complete with recommendations, in line with the contract conditions. Therefore, the institutional arrangement must also prescribe how release proposals are prepared, reviewed, and authorized, ensuring that the release follows the contractual terms.  

Putting these pieces together, the procuring entity should establish a formal custodial and monitoring unit, assign clear responsibility for each guarantee, institute a monthly review of guarantees expiring in the next three months linked to contract progress, enforce a rule that guarantees are not given to contractors for extension, implement a computerized alert system to prompt timely action, and define a contract‑based procedure for executing agencies to submit release proposals. This institutional setup directly enables the timely extension, encashment, or refund of EMDs and performance securities as described.

## 4.13 Sources and Verification of Bank Guarantees
Bank Guarantee for Bid Security (EMD) or Performance Guarantee (Security Deposit) should be irrevocable and operative Bank Guarantee (BG) as per format enclosed in the Bid Document and should be issued by a Scheduled Commercial (i.e. Indian or Foreign Banks included in the Second Schedule of Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 excluding Co-operative banks or Regional Rural Banks). In case of foreign bidders or in case of GTE, if Bank Guarantee is from a foreign bank branch situated outside India, the Bank Guarantee must be issued through any of the Scheduled Commercial Bank. In case BG is issued directly by a bank outside India, it should be executed on Letter Head of the Bank and should be advised and made payable through their Indian Branch/Corresponding Bank in India. The Issuing Bank should also state the name and designation of the next Higher Authority of the Officials who have issued the Bank Guarantee.

Bank guarantees submitted by the tenderers/ contractors as EMD/ performance securities need to be immediately verified from the issuing bank before acceptance. There may not be any need to get the Bank Guarantee vetted from legal/ finance authority if it is in the specified format. Guidelines for verification of BGs submitted by the bidders/ contractors against EMD/ performance security/ advance payments and for various other purposes are as follows:

- i) BG shall be as per the prescribed formats
- ii) The BG contains the name, designation and code number of the Bank officer(s) signing the guarantee(s);
- iii) The address and other details (including telephone no.) of the controlling officer of the bank are obtained from the branch of the bank issuing the BG (this should be included in all BGs);

The confirmation from the issuing branch of the bank is obtained in writing through registered post/ speed post/ courier /direct e-mail/ SFMS. The bank should be advised to confirm the issuance of the BGs specifically quoting the letter of Procurement Entity on the printed official letterhead of the bank indicating address and other details (including telephone nos.) of the bank and the name, designation and code number of the officer(s) confirming the issuance of the BG;

As far as possible organizations should follow e-verification of bank guarantees as per the procedure prescribed by Reserve Bank of India. Bank guarantee should be routed through SFMS platform.

Bank guarantees, either received in physical form or electronic form, should be verified for its genuineness following prescribed method for the same and the Organisations should do due diligence on genuineness of the Bank Guarantees before acceptance of the same.

## 4.14 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Securities
A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of EMDs and performance securities and other instruments should be evolved and implemented by procuring entity. Institutional arrangements shall be made for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of EMDs and performance securities, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the contractor for propose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc. For release of BGs, the proposal shall be forwarded by the executing agency with its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions.

section: 1.9 Public Procurement Infrastructure at the Centre
question_text: How do product reservation policies align with strategic goals of promoting locally manufactured goods
answer:
- Product reservation policies require that specific goods be sourced exclusively from designated local agencies, such as Khadi goods from the Khadi & Village Industries Commission and handloom textiles from approved clusters. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 25)  
- A minimum of 20% of all textile requirements must be procured from handloom‑origin items, guaranteeing a baseline share for locally manufactured products. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 25)  
- The government can institute mandatory procurement or give preference to bidders on the grounds of promoting locally manufactured goods or services, directly linking reservation to strategic objectives. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 25)  
- By directing spend through these reserved channels, procurement supports domestic industry development, aligns with national value‑for‑money goals, and maintains transparency via mandatory publication on the Central Public Procurement Portal and GeM. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 26)  
- This approach mitigates supply‑chain risk by diversifying sources with verified domestic suppliers while satisfying compliance obligations. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 26)
cot:
To understand how product reservation policies serve the goal of promoting locally made goods, I first think about what the policies actually require. They specify that certain categories of products must be bought only from particular domestic entities, such as Khadi goods from the Khadi & Village Industries Commission and handloom textiles from approved clusters. This immediately ties procurement to local producers.  

Next, I note that the rules also set a floor for local content: at least twenty percent of all textile needs must come from handloom‑origin items. That guarantees a baseline share for domestic manufacturers regardless of market fluctuations.  

Then I consider the broader authority given to the government: it can issue notifications that make procurement mandatory from certain sources or give preference to bidders who promote locally manufactured goods or services. This flexibility lets the state steer spending toward domestic industry whenever it deems necessary.  

After that, I reflect on the effects of directing spend through these reserved channels. By channeling purchases to verified local suppliers, the government supports domestic industry development, helps achieve national value‑for‑money objectives, and maintains transparency because all such procurements have to be published on the Central Public Procurement Portal and the Government e‑Marketplace.  

Finally, I see that this approach also reduces supply‑chain risk. Relying on a diversified base of vetted domestic suppliers lessens dependence on foreign sources while still meeting compliance obligations, thereby aligning reservation policies with the strategic aim of promoting locally manufactured goods.

### ii) Central Public Procurement Portal
Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) has been designed, developed and hosted by National Informatics Centre (NIC, Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology) in association with Dept. of Expenditure to ensure transparency in the public procurement process. The primary objective of the Central Public Procurement portal is to provide a single point access to the information on procurements made across various Ministries and the Departments. The CPPP has e-publishing and e-procurement modules. It is mandatory for all Ministries / Departments of the Central Government, Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and Autonomous and Statutory Bodies to publish on the CPPP all their tender enquiries and information about the resulting contracts. CPPP provides access to information such as documents relating to pre-qualification, Bidders' registration, Bidding documents; details of bidders, their pre-qualification, registration, exclusions/ debarments; decisions taken regarding prequalification and selection of successful bid.

iii) **Government e Marketplace (GeM):** The Government e Marketplace (GeM) platform was launched on 9th August, 2016 as an online, end to end solution for procurement of commonly used goods and services for all Central Government and State Government Ministries, Departments, Public Sector Units (PSUs) and affiliated bodies. Common use Goods and Services available on GeM are required to be procured mandatorily through GeM. Since, inception GeM has been continually evolving with new features & functionalities to facilitate the buyers & sellers to overcome technical & functional hurdles in public procurement process enabling them to maximize procurement through GeM.

The GeM portal shall be utilized by the Government buyers for direct on-line purchases as under within the allowed value limits:-

- (i) Through any of the available suppliers on the GeM, meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period.
- (ii) Through the GeM Seller having lowest price amongst the available sellers, of at least three different manufacturers, on GeM, meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period.

- (iii) Through the supplier having lowest price meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period after mandatorily obtaining bids, using online bidding or reverse auction tool provided on GeM.

The tools for online bidding and online reverse auction available on GeM can be used by the Buyer. Procurements through GeM will be governed by the built-in/set rules & procedures of GeM.

## 1.10 Product Reservation and Preferential/Mandatory Purchase from certain sources
The Central Government may, by notification, provide for mandatory procurement of any goods or services from any category of bidders, or provide for preference to bidders on the grounds of promotion of locally manufactured goods or locally provided services.

**Note:** Before considering any Purchase Preference/ product reservation mentioned below, the Procuring Entity should check the latest directives in this regard for necessary action. Product Reservation/ Purchase Preference provision shall invariably be part of the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) and Instructions to Bidders (ITB).

### 1.10.1 Reservation of Procurement of certain class of Products from certain agencies-Khadi Goods/Handloom Textiles
The Central Government has reserved all items of hand-spun and hand-woven textiles (Khadi goods) for exclusive purchase from Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC). Of all items of textiles required by the Central Government departments, it shall be mandatory to make procurement of at least 20% from amongst items of handloom origin, for exclusive purchase from KVIC and/ or Handloom Clusters such as Co-Operative Societies, Self Help Group (SHG) Federations, Joint Liability Group (JLG), Producer Companies (PC), Corporations etc. including Weavers having Pehchan Cards.

question_text: What are the consequences of withdrawing or revising my bid upward after becoming the lowest bidder?
answer: If you withdraw your bid or revise it upward after you have become the lowest (L1) bidder, NRL may place your agency on the Holiday List. Being holiday‑listed means you could be barred from participating in NRL’s future procurements until the listing is removed. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 53)
cot:
First, I think about what it means to be the lowest, or L1, bidder in a tender process – it signals that the agency has offered the most competitive price and, under normal circumstances, would be expected to stand by that offer.  
Next, I consider how the procurement rules view any change to that bid after the L1 status has been established; altering the bid upward or pulling it back is seen as undermining the fairness of the competition and is treated as a breach of integrity.  
Looking at the specific grounds that can lead to an agency being placed on the Holiday List, I see that one of the explicit conditions is “withdraws/revises the bid upwards after becoming the L1 bidder.” This matches exactly the action described in the question.  
If that condition is met, the consequence is that the agency is added to the Holiday List, which is a register used by NRL to track entities that have violated procurement integrity.  
Being on that list means the agency is barred from participating in any future NRL procurements until the listing is formally removed, effectively restricting its ability to bid on new contracts.  
Putting these steps together, withdrawing or revising a bid upward after becoming the lowest bidder can trigger holiday listing, and the direct outcome is a potential debarment from NRL’s upcoming tender opportunities.

### 3.5.2 Reasons for Holiday Listing:
An agency may be placed in Holiday List for any one or more of the following circumstances:

#### 3.5.2.1 If the Agency, in the context of its dealings with the Corporation:
- a) Has breached the Code of Integrity for Public Procurement (CIPP)
- b) Has indulged in malpractices;
- c) Has submitted fake, false or forged documents / certificates;
- d) Has substituted materials in lieu of materials supplied by NRL or has not returned or has unauthorized disposed off materials / documents / drawings / tools or plants or equipment supplied by NRL.
- e) Has deliberately violated and circumvented the provisions of labour laws/ regulations / rules, safety norms, environmental norms or other 'statutory' requirements.
- f) Has deliberately indulged in construction and erection of defective works or supply of defective materials.
- g) Has not cleared previous dues to NRL if applicable.
- h) Has committed breach of contract or has abandoned the contract.
- i) Poor performance of the Agency in one or several contracts.
- j) Has not honoured the fax of award / letter of award / Contract / Purchase order after the same is issued by NRL.
- k) Withdraws/ revises the bid upwards after becoming the L1 bidder (downward revision by H1 in case of disposal).
- l) Has parted with, leaked or provided confidential / proprietary information of NRL to any third party without the prior consent of NRL.
- m) The L1 bidder (Lowest quoted price) quotes an abnormally low/ unworkable price and the bidder fails to provide proper price break up and reasonability of his quoted price, resulting in cancellation of tender.
- n) Bidder withdraws his quote after opening of techno-commercial bid.
- o) GST registration/ account of the contractor is cancelled/ revoked/ seized by Government authority during the pendency of the contract.

#### 3.5.2.2 The following additional grounds can also be reasons for Holiday listing of an agency:
- a) If a communication is received from the Administrative Ministry of the Corporation to ban Agency from dealing with the Corporation;
- b) If the Agency is or has become bankrupt, OR is being dissolved OR has resolved to be wound up OR if proceedings for winding up or dissolution has been instituted against the Agency;
- c) Any other ground, including transgression of Integrity Pact, which, in the opinion of

the Corporation makes it undesirable to deal with the Agency; In the case of transgression of Integrity Pact, the same should be substantiated by the verdict of the Independent External Monitor.

question_text: What steps must authorised officials take when receiving bulky or oversized bids that cannot be placed in the tender box
answer:
- Verify that authorised officials maintain proper records for the receipt of bulky or oversized bids that cannot be placed in the tender box.  
- Confirm that a signed receipt, indicating the date and time of receipt, is provided to the bearer of the bid.  
- Ensure that the officials sign the bid cover, clearly marking the date and time of receipt on the cover.  
- Check that the bid documents include the names and designations of at least two authorised officers responsible for receiving such bids.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 102)
cot:
First, I consider what the core issue is: when a bid is too large or awkward to fit into the standard tender box, the usual automatic drop‑off mechanism cannot be used, so a manual handling procedure must be put in place to preserve transparency and accountability.  

Next, I identify the conditions that any such procedure must satisfy. It needs to create a verifiable trail of who received the bid, when it was received, and that the receipt was acknowledged by the bidder. It also must ensure that the responsibility is not left to a single individual, reducing the risk of mishandling or tampering.  

From those conditions, I reason that the officials in charge should first document the receipt in a log or register—this creates the proper record that can be audited later. Simultaneously, they should give the person delivering the bid a signed receipt that clearly states the date and time the bid was taken into custody; this gives the bidder proof of submission and timestamps the transaction.  

I then think about how to link the receipt to the physical bid itself. The officials should mark the bid’s outer cover with their signature and the same date and time, so that the bid carries its own evidence of receipt and cannot be later disputed as having been received at a different moment.  

Finally, I consider who is authorised to perform these actions. To avoid reliance on a single person, the tender documents should specify at least two named officers—along with their designations—who are permitted to receive such bulky bids. This ensures that the procedure is known in advance, that there is always a qualified official available, and that the responsibility is shared.  

Putting these steps together—maintaining a record, issuing a signed receipt with date/time, signing the bid cover with that information, and pre‑naming at least two authorised officers in the bid documents—provides a complete, transparent process for handling oversized bids that cannot go into the tender box. This matches the required actions for authorised officials in such situations.

### 5.2.3 Extension of Tender Opening Date
Sometimes, situations may arise necessitating modification of the tender documents already issued (LTE/OTE case). Also, after receiving the documents, a tenderer may point out some genuine mistakes necessitating amendment in the tender documents. In such situations, it is necessary to amend/modify the tender documents suitably prior to the date of submission of bids. Copies of such amendment / modification should be uploaded in the tender portal as well as NRL website.

When the amendment/ modification changes the requirement significantly and/or when there is not much time left for the tenderers to respond to such amendments, and prepare revised tender, the time and date of submission of tenders are also to be extended suitably, along with suitable changes in the corresponding time-frames for receipt of tender, tender validity period etc and validity period of the corresponding EMD /bid security. Depending on the situation, such an amendment may also need fresh publication adopting the same procedure as for publication of the original tender enquiry.

### 5.2.4 Sealing, and Marking of Bids by Bidders
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (e.g., in duplicate or in triplicate etc.) required to be submitted. In case of two envelop bidding system, the techno-commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked these with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before..... (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed covers are to be put in a bigger cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. In case bids are asked in a number of copies, the tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate" and so on and also marking these as mentioned above. The inner envelopes are then to be put in a bigger outer envelope, which will also be duly sealed marked etc. as above. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the purchaser will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening etc.

These details regarding the submission of bids should also form a part of the ITB and AITB in the tender documents; all the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

### 5.2.5 Submission, Receipt and Custody of Tenders
In e-procurement, all tenders uploaded by tenderers are received, safeguarded and opened online on the portal. In offline tenders, receipt and custody of bids shall be done in a transparent manner to maintain the credibility of the process. The following guidelines should be adhered to for receipt and custody of bids:

- 1) Bids received by courier or direct submission shall be deposited in the tender box by the Dispatch Section till the date and time of bid submission. Bids sent by telex, cable, e-mail or facsimile are to be ignored and rejected, unless otherwise specifically allowed.; and
- 2) For bulky/oversized bids which cannot be dropped into tender boxes, the officials authorised to receive such bids shall maintain proper records and provide a signed receipt with date and time to the bearer of the bid. He will also sign on the cover, duly indicating the date and time of receipt of the tender(s). Names and designations of at

question_text: Is the contractor entitled to any compensation when the contract is ended due to insolvency
answer: No, the contractor is not entitled to any compensation when the contract is terminated for insolvency; the termination is carried out without compensation to the contractor (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 115).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: whether a contractor has any right to receive payment or other compensation when the contract is brought to an end because the contractor becomes insolvent.  

Next, I consider how contracts typically handle termination. There are usually distinct grounds for ending an agreement—such as breach by the contractor, insolvency of the contractor, or convenience of the procuring entity—and each ground comes with its own set of consequences.  

Turning my attention to the insolvency scenario, I recall that the provision governing termination for insolvency specifies that the procuring entity may end the contract by giving a written notice to the contractor. Importantly, the wording states that this termination is carried out “without compensation to the contractor.”  

I then note that the clause does mention that the procuring entity’s existing rights of action or remedies are preserved, but it does not create any corresponding obligation to pay the contractor for work already done or for any losses arising from the termination itself.  

Putting these points together, the logical conclusion is that when a contract is terminated on the basis of the contractor’s insolvency, the contractor is not entitled to any compensation; the termination is expressly without compensation.

### 6.11.2 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, by written notice of default sent to the Contractor, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part, if the contractor:

- i) has seriously or repeatedly breached the contract, including
  - a) failure to complete the work within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted;
  - b) failure to obey instructions in relation to his progress or defective work, material or plant;
  - c) breach of the prohibition against sub-contracting
  - d) Failure to supply sufficient and suitable constructional plant, temporary works, labour and material as proposed in the work programme;
  - e) Substantial suspension of work for more than the specified days without authority from the engineer and failure to proceed with the work within the specified days of receipt of notice from the engineer
  - f) Failure to comply with the requirements regarding JVs
- ii) committed fraud
- iii) If the contractor fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted.
- iv) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the security deposit;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, taking over the site and to complete the works himself or with another contractor (risk Purchase) and use the contractor's materials, equipment, temporary works as he/ they think proper; and
  - c) However, the contractor shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 6.11.3 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the contractor becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses

substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the contractor, without compensation to the contractor, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 6.11.4 Termination of Contract for Procuring Entity's Failure or Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the contractor for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the contractor may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract. If termination occurs because of Procuring Entity's convenience or a fundamental breach on his part, the engineer will certify the value of works executed, value of any materials lying at site, reasonable cost of removal of equipment, repatriation of project staff, cost of protecting and securing the works and deducting from it: (i) pending advances; (ii) other recoveries; and (iii) taxes as due.

### 2.1.3 Individual consultants/ service providers
Individual consultants or service providers are recruited for similar activities as Consultancy/ Service providing firms when a full team is not considered necessary. They may be independent experts not permanently associated with any particular firm, or they may be employees of a firm recruited on an individual basis. They may also be employees of an agency, institution, or university. They are normally recruited for project implementation supervision, training, provision of specific expert advice on a highly technical subject, policy guidance, special studies, compliance supervision, or implementation monitoring. Individual consultants/ service providers are not normally recruited for project preparation unless the proposed project is simple and, generally, a repeat of an already established and successful project. If more than three experts are required, then the assignment should normally be undertaken by a team from a firm. As with firms, individual consultants/ service providers are classed as either international or national, depending on their level of expertise and their international experience and exposure.

### 2.1.4 Specialized Agencies and Institutions
Specialized agencies or institutions (including Government/ Semi-Government agencies, universities and professional institutions) may also from time to time be recruited to provide Consultancy/ other services. These services may be provided by individuals (as discussed above) or by teams. Nonetheless, there are at times distinct advantages to using such agencies. Experts and teams from such agencies and institutions may undertake a variety of roles across the whole field of possible Consultancy and other services. These may range from project preparation through project supervision and policy advice to project benefit monitoring and evaluation.

### 2.1.5 Non-governmental Organizations (NGO)
There may be distinct advantage in use of Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in Projects which emphasize experience in community participation and in-depth local knowledge - for example, Projects related to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

The consulting services do not include direct engagement of retired Government servants. They should not be engaged against regular vacant posts as consultant under this rule. question_text: If a bidder’s offer is under consideration and a breach of integrity is found, what immediate actions may the procuring entity take concerning bid security and negotiations?
answer:
When a breach of integrity is discovered while a bid is under consideration, the procuring entity can act swiftly to protect corporate value and manage risk by securing financial redress and terminating further discussions.

- Forfeit or encash the bidder’s bid security. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 48)  
- Call off any pre‑contract negotiations with the bidder. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 48)  

These immediate steps uphold transparency, deter misconduct, and reinforce the procurement function’s role in safeguarding the organization’s financial interests.
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: when a bid is still being evaluated and the procuring entity discovers that the bidder has violated the integrity code, what can the entity do right away to protect its interests?  

Next, I look at the situation described in the rules: the bid is “under consideration,” which triggers a specific set of remedial measures meant to address the breach before any contract is formed.  

Then, I identify the measures that are explicitly tied to this stage. The rules state that, if the breach is found while bids are under consideration, the entity may forfeit or encash the bidder’s bid security, and it may also call off any pre‑contract negotiations that have begun.  

After that, I think about why these two actions are the immediate ones. Forfeiting the bid security provides a financial remedy that compensates the entity for the risk and potential loss caused by the bidder’s misconduct, while calling off negotiations stops any further commitment or discussion that could legitimize the breach.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the procuring entity’s prompt response to an integrity breach during bid evaluation is to secure the bidder’s financial guarantee and halt any ongoing talks, thereby safeguarding its financial position and upholding the procurement process’s integrity. This matches the answer’s two immediate actions.

### 3.2.3 Obligations for Proactive Disclosures

question_text: How should technical and financial proposals be submitted to safeguard the integrity of the procurement process
answer:
**How to Submit Technical and Financial Proposals to Safeguard the Procurement Process**  

**Step 1: Prepare each proposal separately**  
- Complete the technical proposal in accordance with the RfP requirements.  
- Complete the financial proposal in accordance with the RfP requirements.  

**Step 2: Place each proposal in its own sealed envelope**  
- Insert the technical proposal into an envelope, seal it, and label it clearly as “Technical Proposal”.  
- Insert the financial proposal into a second envelope, seal it, and label it clearly as “Financial Proposal”.  

**Step 3: Combine the two sealed envelopes into an outer sealed envelope**  
- Put the sealed technical envelope and the sealed financial envelope together inside a third envelope.  
- Seal the outer envelope and label it (e.g., “Bid Submission – [Project Name]”).  

**Step 4: Submit the outer envelope by the stipulated deadline**  
- Deliver the outer sealed envelope to the designated submission point (e.g., the e‑Procurement portal or the physical bid box) **before** the closing time for receipt of proposals.  
- If the procurement is conducted through e‑Procurement, upload the scanned copies of the three envelopes as a single package in accordance with the portal’s instructions.  

**Step 5: Verify that no late bids are accepted**  
- Confirm that the submission timestamp (or physical receipt log) shows receipt **on or before** the closing time.  
- Any proposal received after the closing time must be rejected outright.  

**Step 6: Understand the opening procedure**  
- After the closing time, the technical envelopes are opened immediately by the Consultancy Evaluation Committee (CEC) or Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC).  
- The financial envelopes remain sealed and are opened publicly **only** for those bidders whose technical proposals have been deemed qualified.  

### Practical Example  
A bidder for a consultancy assignment prepares a 25‑page technical proposal and a 5‑page financial proposal.  
1. The technical proposal is placed in Envelope A, sealed, and marked “Technical Proposal”.  
2. The financial proposal is placed in Envelope B, sealed, and marked “Financial Proposal”.  
3. Both Envelope A and Envelope B are inserted into Envelope C, which is sealed and labeled “Bid Submission – Road‑Design Consultancy”.  
4. Envelope C is uploaded to the e‑Procurement system at 09:45 AM on the deadline day (the closing time is 10:00 AM).  
5. At 10:05 AM, the CEC opens Envelope C, extracts Envelope A and Envelope B, opens Envelope A immediately, and keeps Envelope B sealed until the technical evaluation is complete.  

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid  
- **Mixing proposals**: placing technical and financial documents in the same envelope violates the requirement for separate sealed envelopes.  
- **Missing outer seal**: submitting only the two inner envelopes without an outer sealed envelope exposes the financial proposal to premature viewing.  
- **Late submission**: any delay, even a few minutes, results in automatic disqualification.  
- **Incorrect submission channel**: using email or courier when the RfP mandates e‑Procurement can lead to rejection.  
- **Inadequate labeling**: unclear or missing labels can cause confusion during the opening process and may be treated as a procedural error.  

By following these numbered steps—preparing separate proposals, sealing them individually, combining them in an outer sealed envelope, submitting before the deadline via the prescribed method, and observing the prescribed opening procedure—you safeguard the integrity of the procurement process as required.  

(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 46)
cot:
First, I think about what could undermine the fairness of a procurement process—mainly the risk that financial details influence the technical evaluation or that late submissions give some bidders an unfair advantage. To prevent that, the two parts of a bid must be kept completely separate until the technical merit has been judged on its own merits.  

That leads me to the idea of sealing each proposal in its own envelope so that the contents cannot be seen or altered before the designated opening time. If the technical and financial documents were placed together, an evaluator might inadvertently glimpse cost information while reviewing the technical response, which would bias the assessment.  

Next, I consider how to handle the two sealed envelopes together without breaking that separation. Placing both inner envelopes inside a third, outer sealed envelope keeps them united for submission while preserving the inner seals. The outer envelope can be labeled clearly so that the receiving office knows it contains a complete bid, yet the inner seals remain intact until the opening stage.  

Now I turn to the timing of submission. To avoid any perception of favoritism, all bidders must deliver their bids at the same moment, and any bid arriving after the stipulated deadline must be rejected outright. This rule eliminates the possibility of a bidder gaining extra time to improve their proposal after seeing others’ submissions.  

Because many organizations now use electronic procurement, the physical envelopes can be represented by scanned copies uploaded as a single package through the e‑procurement portal. The electronic system must enforce the same deadline check and preserve the integrity of the sealed‑envelope concept by treating the uploaded file as a locked unit that can only be opened after the closing time.  

After the deadline passes, the opening procedure itself must protect the financial information. The outer envelope is opened, the inner technical envelope is extracted and opened immediately by the evaluation committee, while the financial envelope stays sealed. Only after the technical evaluation concludes and a bidder is deemed technically qualified does the financial envelope get opened in a public setting. This staged opening guarantees that financial scores are never seen before technical merit is established.  

Finally, I run through a quick mental checklist to catch common mistakes: ensuring each proposal is sealed separately, not forgetting the outer seal, submitting before the cutoff, using the correct submission channel, and labeling everything clearly. If any of those steps are missed, the bid could be disqualified or the process could be compromised.  

Putting all of these considerations together yields the prescribed method: prepare technical and financial proposals separately, seal each in its own envelope, place the two sealed envelopes inside a third sealed envelope, submit the outer package before the deadline via the stipulated (often electronic) channel, verify that no late bids are accepted, and then follow the opening sequence where technical bids are opened first and financial bids remain sealed until technical qualification is confirmed. This approach safeguards the integrity of the procurement process by keeping financial information hidden until the technical evaluation is complete and by enforcing equal, timely submission for all bidders.

## 6.3 Pre-proposal (Pre-Bid) Meeting
- i) In case of large value or complex assignments, a pre-proposal meeting may be prescribed in the RfP. The date and time for such a meeting should normally be after 07 (seven) days of issue of the RfP and should be specified in the RfP itself. During this meeting, the scope of assignment, responsibilities of either parties or other details should be clearly explained to the prospective bidders so that there is no ambiguity later at the time of submission of

technical/financial bids. Where some significant changes are made in the terms/scope of the RfP as a result of the pre-bid meeting or otherwise considered necessary by the Procuring Entity, a formal corrigendum to the RfP may be issued, to all bidders. In such cases, it should be ensured that, after issue of the corrigendum, reasonable time is available to the bidders to prepare/submit their bids. If required, the time for preparation and submission of bids may be extended, suitably.

- ii) **Pre-Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) Conference:** In complex and innovative procurement cases or where the procuring entity may not have the required knowledge to formulate tender provisions, a pre-NIT conference may help the procuring entity in obtaining inputs from the industry. Such conferences should be widely publicised so that different potential bidders can attend.

## 6.4 Receipt of Proposal
The technical and financial proposals shall be submitted at the same time. To safeguard the integrity of the process, the technical and financial proposals shall be submitted in separate sealed envelopes, kept in an outer sealed envelope. The technical bids will be opened immediately after closing of receipt of technical bids by the Consultancy Evaluation Committee (CEC) / TEC. Guidelines regarding constitution of bid opening committee are provided in the DOA. The financial proposals shall remain sealed and shall be opened publicly only for those firms that have qualified technically. Any proposal received after the closing time for submission of proposals (Late Bids) shall not be considered. It may be noted that as per guidelines, now all procurement are to be done through e-Procurement.

question_text: What preliminary steps does NRL recommend parties take before resorting to arbitration or litigation for contract disputes
answer: NRL advises that, prior to initiating arbitration or litigation, the contracting parties should first seek to resolve the dispute through mutual discussion, and if unsuccessful, pursue mediation and conciliation (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 113).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants the preliminary actions that NRL suggests parties should take before they move to arbitration or litigation when a contract dispute arises.  

Next, I scan the provided material for any guidance that talks about steps to be taken prior to formal dispute resolution. In the section on arbitration and dispute resolution, the first point explicitly states that, before resorting to arbitration or litigation, parties may choose mutual discussion, mediation, and conciliation to settle their differences.  

Seeing that, I recognize that the recommendation is sequential: start with informal talks between the parties, and if those do not resolve the issue, move to structured but still non‑binding processes like mediation and conciliation.  

Finally, I combine this insight with the understanding that this guidance is captured in NRL’s Procurement of Works Manual, leading to the conclusion that NRL advises parties to first seek mutual discussion, and if unsuccessful, to pursue mediation and conciliation before considering arbitration or litigation.
