## 4.13 Sources and Verification of Bank Guarantees
Bank Guarantee for Bid Security (EMD) or Performance Guarantee (Security Deposit) should be irrevocable and operative Bank Guarantee (BG) as per format enclosed in the Bid Document and should be issued by a Scheduled Commercial (i.e. Indian or Foreign Banks included in the Second Schedule of Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 excluding Co-operative banks or Regional Rural Banks). In case of foreign bidders or in case of GTE, if Bank Guarantee is from a foreign bank branch situated outside India, the Bank Guarantee must be issued through any of the Scheduled Commercial Bank. In case BG is issued directly by a bank outside India, it should be executed on Letter Head of the Bank and should be advised and made payable through their Indian Branch/Corresponding Bank in India. The Issuing Bank should also state the name and designation of the next Higher Authority of the Officials who have issued the Bank Guarantee.

Bank guarantees submitted by the tenderers/ contractors as EMD/ performance securities need to be immediately verified from the issuing bank before acceptance. There may not be any need to get the Bank Guarantee vetted from legal/ finance authority if it is in the specified format. Guidelines for verification of BGs submitted by the bidders/ contractors against EMD/ performance security/ advance payments and for various other purposes are as follows:

- i) BG shall be as per the prescribed formats
- ii) The BG contains the name, designation and code number of the Bank officer(s) signing the guarantee(s);
- iii) The address and other details (including telephone no.) of the controlling officer of the bank are obtained from the branch of the bank issuing the BG (this should be included in all BGs);

The confirmation from the issuing branch of the bank is obtained in writing through registered post/ speed post/ courier /direct e-mail/ SFMS. The bank should be advised to confirm the issuance of the BGs specifically quoting the letter of Procurement Entity on the printed official letterhead of the bank indicating address and other details (including telephone nos.) of the bank and the name, designation and code number of the officer(s) confirming the issuance of the BG;

As far as possible organizations should follow e-verification of bank guarantees as per the procedure prescribed by Reserve Bank of India. Bank guarantee should be routed through SFMS platform.

Bank guarantees, either received in physical form or electronic form, should be verified for its genuineness following prescribed method for the same and the Organisations should do due diligence on genuineness of the Bank Guarantees before acceptance of the same.

## 4.14 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Securities
A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of EMDs and performance securities and other instruments should be evolved and implemented by procuring entity. Institutional arrangements shall be made for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of EMDs and performance securities, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the contractor for propose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc. For release of BGs, the proposal shall be forwarded by the executing agency with its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions.

### ii) Central Public Procurement Portal
Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) has been designed, developed and hosted by National Informatics Centre (NIC, Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology) in association with Dept. of Expenditure to ensure transparency in the public procurement process. The primary objective of the Central Public Procurement portal is to provide a single point access to the information on procurements made across various Ministries and the Departments. The CPPP has e-publishing and e-procurement modules. It is mandatory for all Ministries / Departments of the Central Government, Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and Autonomous and Statutory Bodies to publish on the CPPP all their tender enquiries and information about the resulting contracts. CPPP provides access to information such as documents relating to pre-qualification, Bidders' registration, Bidding documents; details of bidders, their pre-qualification, registration, exclusions/ debarments; decisions taken regarding prequalification and selection of successful bid.

iii) **Government e Marketplace (GeM):** The Government e Marketplace (GeM) platform was launched on 9th August, 2016 as an online, end to end solution for procurement of commonly used goods and services for all Central Government and State Government Ministries, Departments, Public Sector Units (PSUs) and affiliated bodies. Common use Goods and Services available on GeM are required to be procured mandatorily through GeM. Since, inception GeM has been continually evolving with new features & functionalities to facilitate the buyers & sellers to overcome technical & functional hurdles in public procurement process enabling them to maximize procurement through GeM.

The GeM portal shall be utilized by the Government buyers for direct on-line purchases as under within the allowed value limits:-

- (i) Through any of the available suppliers on the GeM, meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period.
- (ii) Through the GeM Seller having lowest price amongst the available sellers, of at least three different manufacturers, on GeM, meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period.

- (iii) Through the supplier having lowest price meeting the requisite quality, specification and delivery period after mandatorily obtaining bids, using online bidding or reverse auction tool provided on GeM.

The tools for online bidding and online reverse auction available on GeM can be used by the Buyer. Procurements through GeM will be governed by the built-in/set rules & procedures of GeM.

## 1.10 Product Reservation and Preferential/Mandatory Purchase from certain sources
The Central Government may, by notification, provide for mandatory procurement of any goods or services from any category of bidders, or provide for preference to bidders on the grounds of promotion of locally manufactured goods or locally provided services.

**Note:** Before considering any Purchase Preference/ product reservation mentioned below, the Procuring Entity should check the latest directives in this regard for necessary action. Product Reservation/ Purchase Preference provision shall invariably be part of the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) and Instructions to Bidders (ITB).

### 1.10.1 Reservation of Procurement of certain class of Products from certain agencies-Khadi Goods/Handloom Textiles
The Central Government has reserved all items of hand-spun and hand-woven textiles (Khadi goods) for exclusive purchase from Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC). Of all items of textiles required by the Central Government departments, it shall be mandatory to make procurement of at least 20% from amongst items of handloom origin, for exclusive purchase from KVIC and/ or Handloom Clusters such as Co-Operative Societies, Self Help Group (SHG) Federations, Joint Liability Group (JLG), Producer Companies (PC), Corporations etc. including Weavers having Pehchan Cards.

question_text: What circumstances lead to an agency being placed on the Holiday List?
answer: The NRL procurement manuals distinguish between two sets of grounds for holiday listing. First, they list specific breach‑related reasons such as violation of the Code of Integrity for Public Procurement, malpractice, submission of fake documents, unauthorized disposal of NRL‑supplied materials, labour/ safety/ environmental violations, defective work, unpaid dues, contract breach or abandonment, poor performance, non‑honouring of award letters, upward bid revision after becoming L1, leakage of confidential information, abnormally low bids without justification, bid withdrawal after techno‑commercial opening, and GST registration cancellation. Second, they note additional grounds including a ban communicated by the Administrative Ministry, bankruptcy or winding‑up proceedings, and any other ground (including Integrity Pact transgression) deemed undesirable by the Corporation, which must be substantiated by the Independent External Monitor where applicable. Please clarify whether you are interested in the breach‑related grounds or the additional grounds (or any other specific condition) so I can give the precise answer.

### 3.5.2 Reasons for Holiday Listing:
An agency may be placed in Holiday List for any one or more of the following circumstances:

#### 3.5.2.1 If the Agency, in the context of its dealings with the Corporation:
- a) Has breached the Code of Integrity for Public Procurement (CIPP)
- b) Has indulged in malpractices;
- c) Has submitted fake, false or forged documents / certificates;
- d) Has substituted materials in lieu of materials supplied by NRL or has not returned or has unauthorized disposed off materials / documents / drawings / tools or plants or equipment supplied by NRL.
- e) Has deliberately violated and circumvented the provisions of labour laws/ regulations / rules, safety norms, environmental norms or other 'statutory' requirements.
- f) Has deliberately indulged in construction and erection of defective works or supply of defective materials.
- g) Has not cleared previous dues to NRL if applicable.
- h) Has committed breach of contract or has abandoned the contract.
- i) Poor performance of the Agency in one or several contracts.
- j) Has not honoured the fax of award / letter of award / Contract / Purchase order after the same is issued by NRL.
- k) Withdraws/ revises the bid upwards after becoming the L1 bidder (downward revision by H1 in case of disposal).
- l) Has parted with, leaked or provided confidential / proprietary information of NRL to any third party without the prior consent of NRL.
- m) The L1 bidder (Lowest quoted price) quotes an abnormally low/ unworkable price and the bidder fails to provide proper price break up and reasonability of his quoted price, resulting in cancellation of tender.
- n) Bidder withdraws his quote after opening of techno-commercial bid.
- o) GST registration/ account of the contractor is cancelled/ revoked/ seized by Government authority during the pendency of the contract.

#### 3.5.2.2 The following additional grounds can also be reasons for Holiday listing of an agency:
- a) If a communication is received from the Administrative Ministry of the Corporation to ban Agency from dealing with the Corporation;
- b) If the Agency is or has become bankrupt, OR is being dissolved OR has resolved to be wound up OR if proceedings for winding up or dissolution has been instituted against the Agency;
- c) Any other ground, including transgression of Integrity Pact, which, in the opinion of

the Corporation makes it undesirable to deal with the Agency; In the case of transgression of Integrity Pact, the same should be substantiated by the verdict of the Independent External Monitor.

question_text: In an e‑procurement environment, how are tenders handled after they are uploaded by bidders?
answer: Facilitator: Let’s walk through what happens after a bidder uploads a tender in an e‑procurement setting. The portal first **receives** the submission, then it **safeguards** the bid—keeping it secure and unchanged—until the scheduled opening date and time. At that moment, the tender is **opened online**. This sequence ensures the tender’s integrity from receipt through opening. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 102)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: once a bidder has uploaded a tender in an e‑procurement setting, what does the system do with that submission before it is evaluated.  
Then I consider the essential capabilities the platform must have—it needs to accept the file, keep it protected from any alteration or premature viewing, and only make it available when the official opening time arrives.  
Next I picture the receipt stage: the portal logs the upload automatically, stores the bid in a secure repository, and enforces access controls so that only the system itself can handle the file.  
After that I focus on the safeguarding phase: while the bid sits in that repository, the system maintains its integrity by preventing any changes and shielding it from unauthorized access until the predefined deadline.  
Then I turn to the opening moment: at the scheduled date and time the portal releases the lock, presents the tender online, and makes it visible to the evaluation committee, guaranteeing that no one could have seen it earlier.  
Finally I put these pieces together: the portal first receives the upload, then safeguards the bid unchanged until the set opening, and at that point opens it online for review, which ensures the tender’s integrity from receipt through opening.

### 5.2.3 Extension of Tender Opening Date
Sometimes, situations may arise necessitating modification of the tender documents already issued (LTE/OTE case). Also, after receiving the documents, a tenderer may point out some genuine mistakes necessitating amendment in the tender documents. In such situations, it is necessary to amend/modify the tender documents suitably prior to the date of submission of bids. Copies of such amendment / modification should be uploaded in the tender portal as well as NRL website.

When the amendment/ modification changes the requirement significantly and/or when there is not much time left for the tenderers to respond to such amendments, and prepare revised tender, the time and date of submission of tenders are also to be extended suitably, along with suitable changes in the corresponding time-frames for receipt of tender, tender validity period etc and validity period of the corresponding EMD /bid security. Depending on the situation, such an amendment may also need fresh publication adopting the same procedure as for publication of the original tender enquiry.

### 5.2.4 Sealing, and Marking of Bids by Bidders
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (e.g., in duplicate or in triplicate etc.) required to be submitted. In case of two envelop bidding system, the techno-commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked these with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before..... (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed covers are to be put in a bigger cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. In case bids are asked in a number of copies, the tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate" and so on and also marking these as mentioned above. The inner envelopes are then to be put in a bigger outer envelope, which will also be duly sealed marked etc. as above. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the purchaser will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening etc.

These details regarding the submission of bids should also form a part of the ITB and AITB in the tender documents; all the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

### 5.2.5 Submission, Receipt and Custody of Tenders
In e-procurement, all tenders uploaded by tenderers are received, safeguarded and opened online on the portal. In offline tenders, receipt and custody of bids shall be done in a transparent manner to maintain the credibility of the process. The following guidelines should be adhered to for receipt and custody of bids:

- 1) Bids received by courier or direct submission shall be deposited in the tender box by the Dispatch Section till the date and time of bid submission. Bids sent by telex, cable, e-mail or facsimile are to be ignored and rejected, unless otherwise specifically allowed.; and
- 2) For bulky/oversized bids which cannot be dropped into tender boxes, the officials authorised to receive such bids shall maintain proper records and provide a signed receipt with date and time to the bearer of the bid. He will also sign on the cover, duly indicating the date and time of receipt of the tender(s). Names and designations of at

least two such authorised officers should be mentioned in the bid documents.

question_text: Explain how compensation for the contractor is determined when termination is due to the Procuring Entity's convenience.
answer:
1. Certify the value of the works already executed by the contractor.  
2. Certify the value of any materials lying at the site.  
3. Determine the reasonable cost of removing equipment from the site.  
4. Determine the cost of repatriating project staff.  
5. Determine the cost of protecting and securing the works.  
6. Add the amounts from steps 1‑5 to obtain a subtotal.  
7. Deduct any pending advances paid to the contractor.  
8. Deduct any other recoveries owed to the Procuring Entity.  
9. Deduct taxes as due.  
10. The resulting amount is the compensation payable to the contractor for termination due to the Procuring Entity’s convenience.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 115)
cot: First, I consider what the Procuring Entity must do when it decides to end the contract for its own convenience: it needs to ascertain what the contractor has already earned and what costs it will incur to wind down the work. Then, I think about the specific items that have to be quantified: the value of the work already completed, the value of any materials left on site, the reasonable expense for taking away the contractor’s equipment, the cost of sending the project staff home, and the expense of safeguarding the unfinished works until they can be handed over. Next, I add those five figures together to obtain a subtotal that represents the gross amount the contractor is entitled to before any adjustments. After that, I look at what must be subtracted from that subtotal: any advances that have already been paid to the contractor and have not yet been earned, any other recoveries the Procuring Entity is entitled to (such as liquidated damages or penalties), and the taxes that are due on the amount. Finally, I subtract those deductions from the subtotal; the remainder is the compensation that should be paid to the contractor for a termination carried out for the Procuring Entity’s convenience.

### 6.11.2 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, by written notice of default sent to the Contractor, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part, if the contractor:

- i) has seriously or repeatedly breached the contract, including
  - a) failure to complete the work within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted;
  - b) failure to obey instructions in relation to his progress or defective work, material or plant;
  - c) breach of the prohibition against sub-contracting
  - d) Failure to supply sufficient and suitable constructional plant, temporary works, labour and material as proposed in the work programme;
  - e) Substantial suspension of work for more than the specified days without authority from the engineer and failure to proceed with the work within the specified days of receipt of notice from the engineer
  - f) Failure to comply with the requirements regarding JVs
- ii) committed fraud
- iii) If the contractor fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted.
- iv) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the security deposit;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, taking over the site and to complete the works himself or with another contractor (risk Purchase) and use the contractor's materials, equipment, temporary works as he/ they think proper; and
  - c) However, the contractor shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 6.11.3 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the contractor becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses

substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the contractor, without compensation to the contractor, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 6.11.4 Termination of Contract for Procuring Entity's Failure or Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the contractor for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the contractor may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract. If termination occurs because of Procuring Entity's convenience or a fundamental breach on his part, the engineer will certify the value of works executed, value of any materials lying at site, reasonable cost of removal of equipment, repatriation of project staff, cost of protecting and securing the works and deducting from it: (i) pending advances; (ii) other recoveries; and (iii) taxes as due.

### 10.7.4 Shortfall
The measurement / counting shall be countersigned by the buyer or his representative.

NRL shall refund immediately to the buyer the equivalent amount arising out of shortfall in quantity of the auction lot than that as specified in the Delivery Order, without any interest. ### 2.1.3 Individual consultants/ service providers
Individual consultants or service providers are recruited for similar activities as Consultancy/ Service providing firms when a full team is not considered necessary. They may be independent experts not permanently associated with any particular firm, or they may be employees of a firm recruited on an individual basis. They may also be employees of an agency, institution, or university. They are normally recruited for project implementation supervision, training, provision of specific expert advice on a highly technical subject, policy guidance, special studies, compliance supervision, or implementation monitoring. Individual consultants/ service providers are not normally recruited for project preparation unless the proposed project is simple and, generally, a repeat of an already established and successful project. If more than three experts are required, then the assignment should normally be undertaken by a team from a firm. Specialized agencies or institutions (including Government/ Semi-Government agencies, universities and professional institutions) may also from time to time be recruited to provide Consultancy/ other services. Experts and teams from such agencies and institutions may undertake a variety of roles across the whole field of possible Consultancy and other services. These may range from project preparation through project supervision and policy advice to project benefit monitoring and evaluation.

question_text: Is it mandatory to use the CPPP for all government procurements, or can other portals be used
answer:
** End‑to‑end e‑procurement is mandatory for all procurements, but the requirement can be met either through the CPPP portal or any other suitable portal.  

**Rationale:** The CPPP must be used for publishing tender information, yet the current rule states that all procurements must be conducted via end‑to‑end e‑procurement either on the CPPP or on another appropriate portal. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 13)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: does the rule require every government purchase to be processed exclusively through the Central Public Procurement Portal, or are other platforms permissible?  
Then I recall that the CPPP serves two distinct purposes—it is the place where tender notices and contract details must be posted, and it also offers an e‑procurement module for conducting the purchase itself.  
Next, I consider the requirement for publishing information: the guidance states that all Ministries, Departments, CPSEs and statutory bodies must put their tender enquiries and resulting contract information on the CPPP, making that step compulsory.  
After that, I consider the rule covering the actual procurement transaction: end‑to‑end e‑procurement is mandatory for all procurements, but it can be carried out either through the CPPP portal or through any other suitable portal.  
This means that while the publishing obligation locks the CPPP in for notices, the transactional side of e‑procurement is flexible—entities may choose the CPPP or any other platform that meets the end‑to‑end e‑procurement standards.  
Finally, I synthesize these points: the CPPP is not universally mandatory for the procurement act itself; other portals can be used as long as they satisfy the mandatory end‑to‑end e‑procurement requirement, with the CPPP remaining compulsory only for publishing tender and contract data.  
Thus, the answer is that end‑to‑end e‑procurement is required for all purchases, but the requirement can be fulfilled via the CPPP or any other appropriate portal.

question_text: What is the primary objective of a pre‑Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) conference in complex or innovative procurements?
answer: - To obtain industry inputs for formulating tender provisions in complex or innovative procurement cases. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 46)
cot:
First, I think about why a procuring entity would hold a meeting before actually issuing a notice inviting tender, especially when the procurement is described as complex or innovative. In such cases the entity often finds itself without sufficient internal knowledge to draft precise technical specifications, eligibility criteria, or contract clauses that will attract capable bidders while protecting its own interests.  

Next, I consider what the entity could do to fill that knowledge gap. The most direct way is to turn to the market itself – the firms that regularly perform similar work and therefore understand the practical challenges, available technologies, and realistic cost structures. By bringing those potential bidders together in a forum, the entity can hear their concerns, suggestions, and constraints firsthand.  

Then I reason about what the entity would do with that information. The inputs gathered are not just for informal discussion; they are used to shape the actual tender documents. Adjustments to the scope of work, clarification of performance requirements, or refinement of qualification criteria can be made based on the industry feedback, ensuring that the eventual NIT is both realistic and competitive.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the core reason for convening a pre‑NIT conference in complex or innovative procurements is precisely to obtain those industry inputs so that the tender provisions can be formulated with a solid grounding in market reality. This matches the stated primary objective – to obtain industry inputs for formulating tender provisions in complex or innovative procurement cases.

### 6.10.1 Arbitration and dispute resolution
- i) During operation of the contracts, issues and disputes arising due to lack of clarity in the contract become the root cause of litigation. Litigation has adverse implications on the timelines and overall cost of the project. Before resorting to arbitration/litigation, the parties may opt for mutual discussion, mediation, and Conciliation for the resolution of disputes.
- ii) Arbitration /court awards should be critically reviewed. In cases where there is a decision against NRL, the decision to appeal should not be taken in a routine manner, but only when the case genuinely merits going for the appeal and there are high chances of winning in the court/ higher court. There is a perception that such appeals etc. are sometimes resorted to postpone the problem and defer personal accountability. Casual appealing in arbitration / court cases has resulted in payment of heavy damages / compensation / additional interest cost, thereby causing more harm to the exchequer, in addition to tarnishing the image of NRL.
- iii) The Organisation should monitor the success rate of appealing against arbitration awards. There should be a clear delegation to empower officials to accept arbitration / court orders. A special board / committee may be set up to review the case before an appeal is filed against an order. Arbitration /court awards should not be routinely appealed without due application of mind on all facts and circumstances including realistic probability of success. The board /

committee or other authority deciding on the matter shall clarify that it has considered both legal merits and the practical chances of success and after considering the cost of, and rising through, litigation / appeal / further litigation as the case may be, it is satisfied that such litigation / appeal / further litigation cost is likely to be financially beneficial compared to accepting the arbitration / court award.

- iv) In cases where the arbitration award is challenged, the case may be decided in favour of the contractor. In such cases, the amount may become payable with the interest, at a rate which is often far higher than the company's cost of funds. This results in huge financial losses to the company. Hence, in aggregate, it is in company's interest to take the risk of paying a substantial part of the award amount (against BG or through escrow account) subject to the result of the litigation, even if in some rare cases of insolvency etc. recovery of the amount in case of success may become difficult.
- v) The only circumstances in which such payment need not be made is where the contractor declines, or is unable, to provide the requisite bank guarantee and/or fails to open an escrow account as required. Persons responsible for not adhering to are liable to be held personally accountable for the additional interest arising, in the event of the final court order going against the procuring entity.

section: 3.5.7 Safeguarding Procuring Entity's Interests during debarment of suppliers
question_text: In cases of supplier shortage or less serious misdemeanours, what actions should auditors check were undertaken to reform the supplier and obtain a written commitment before considering temporary debarment
answer:
- Verify that a show cause notice was served to the defaulting supplier/contractor/consultant/service provider. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 57)  
- Confirm that the views of the concerned department were sought, including the recommendation of its functional head, and that the department considered the supplier’s past performance records and/or obtained a written commitment from the supplier to improve performance. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 57)  
- Ensure that a proposal for condonation or temporary debarment was prepared and submitted to the Appellate Authority (Managing Director) for consideration. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 57)
cot:
First, I consider what the auditor’s goal is: to make sure that, before any temporary debarment is even thought about, the procuring entity actually tried to reform the supplier and secured a written promise of better performance, especially when there is a shortage of suppliers or only a minor breach has occurred.  

Next, I look at the prescribed process for handling such situations. The first step that the rules lay out is to serve a show‑cause notice to the defaulting supplier, contractor, consultant or service provider. This gives the party a chance to explain why the alleged shortcoming should not lead to sanctions.  

Then, the procedure requires that the views of the department that actually uses the goods or services be obtained. That means the functional head of that department must be consulted, and their recommendation should be taken into account. At the same time, the department is expected to weigh the supplier’s historical performance record and, if possible, obtain a written commitment from the supplier that future performance will improve.  

After those two actions have been completed, the next logical step is to prepare a formal proposal. This proposal can either recommend condoning the shortfall (i.e., accepting the supplier’s commitment and allowing them to continue) or, if that fails, suggest a temporary debarment. The proposal must then be submitted to the Appellate Authority—in this case, the Managing Director—for their consideration and final decision.  

Putting these pieces together, the auditor’s checklist becomes clear: verify that a show‑cause notice was indeed issued, confirm that the concerned department’s opinion (with the functional head’s input) was sought and that past performance and/or a written improvement commitment were considered, and finally ensure that a proposal for either condonation or temporary debarment was forwarded to the Managing Director for review.  

If all three items are present, the auditor can conclude that the entity followed the required steps to reform the supplier and obtain a written commitment before even contemplating temporary debarment.

### 3.5.7 Safeguarding Procuring Entity's Interests during debarment of suppliers:
Suppliers/ contractors/ consultants/ service providers are important assets for the procuring entities and punishing delinquent suppliers should be the last resort. It takes lot of time and effort to develop, register and mature a new supplier. In case of shortage of suppliers in a particular group of materials/equipment, such punishment may also hurt the interest of Procuring Entity. Therefore, views of the concerned Department may always be sought about the repercussions of such punitive action on the continuity of procurements. Past records of performance of the supplier may also be given due weightage. In case of shortage of suppliers and in cases of less serious misdemeanours, the endeavour should be to pragmatically analyse the circumstances, reform the supplier and get a written commitment from the supplier that his performance will improve. If this fails, efforts should be to see if a temporary debarment can serve the purpose.

Such condoning to reform the supplier based on views of the concerned department and/or after consideration of past records of performance of the supplier and/or a written commitment from the supplier that his performance will improve will be done in the following manner:-

- (i) A show cause may be served to the defaulting party.
- (ii) Views of the concerned Department, with recommendation of their functional head, will be sought including consideration of past records of performance of the supplier and/or a written commitment from the supplier that his performance will improve.
- (iii) Submit the proposal of condoning or any temporary debarment for consideration of the "Appellate Authority" i.e., Managing Director.

question_text: Which documents are essential for validating the authenticity and conformity of imported goods prior to payment
answer:
To safeguard corporate value and mitigate risk, procurement must confirm the authenticity and conformity of imported goods before releasing payment. The essential documents that the supplier must provide—and that the paying authority must verify against contract stipulations—are:

- Supplier’s original invoice detailing quantity, value, and full description of the goods  
- Packing list  
- Certificate of country of origin issued by the seller, a recognised chamber of commerce, or a government‑designated agency  
- Certificate of pre‑dispatch inspection by the purchaser’s representative  
- Manufacturer’s test certificate and guarantee  
- Certificate of insurance  
- Bill of lading, airway bill, rail receipt, or any other dispatch document showing:  
  • Name of the vessel or carrier  
  • Bill of lading/airway bill number  
  • Port of loading  
  • Date of shipment  
  • Port of discharge and expected date of arrival  

Any additional documents stipulated in the contract must also be presented. Verification of these items ensures that imports comply with FEMA, RBI directions, and the export‑import policy, thereby supporting transparent, value‑for‑money procurement aligned with strategic objectives.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 109)
cot:
Before releasing payment for imported goods, I need to be certain that what is being paid for is genuine, matches the contract, and complies with all import regulations—otherwise I risk financial loss and regulatory penalties. The only reliable way to gain that confidence is to examine the documents the supplier provides and check them against what the contract requires.  

First, I consider the basic proof of what is being supplied: the supplier’s original invoice must show a clear description, quantity, and value of the goods, and a packing list should detail how those items are packed and marked. These two documents together confirm that the shipment matches the commercial agreement.  

Next, I think about where the goods come from, because import policy and FEMA rules demand proof of origin. A certificate of country of origin—issued by the seller, a recognised chamber of commerce, or a government‑designated agency—is essential to verify that the goods are allowed into the country and to calculate any applicable duties.  

Then I turn to quality and conformity. Even if the origin is correct, the goods must meet the technical specifications in the contract. A pre‑dispatch inspection certificate from our representative shows that the goods were examined before they left the supplier’s premises, and the manufacturer’s test certificate and guarantee provide evidence that the items perform as promised and are backed by a warranty.  

After that, I consider the risks during transport. Loss or damage in transit could leave me paying for goods that never arrive intact, so I need an insurance certificate that covers the shipment. I also need a transport document—such as a bill of lading, airway bill, or rail receipt—that names the vessel or carrier, gives the document number, shows the port of loading, the date of shipment, and the port of discharge with the expected arrival date. This confirms that the goods have actually been dispatched and are en route.  

Finally, I remember that the contract may call for additional paperwork—perhaps special test reports, certifications, or licenses. Any such stipulated documents must also be presented and verified.  

By running through each of these pieces—invoice, packing list, origin certificate, pre‑dispatch inspection, manufacturer’s test and guarantee, insurance certificate, and transport document (plus any contract‑specific items)—and checking them against the contract terms, I can be satisfied that the imported goods are authentic, conforming, and compliant with FEMA, RBI directions, and the export‑import policy. Only then is it appropriate to release payment.

question_text: If a tenderer has not agreed to provide the required PBG, how should the tender be treated?
answer:
**Standard Operating Procedure – Handling Tenders That Do Not Agree to Provide the Required PBG**

1. **Perform initial scrutiny** of each tender to verify that it meets the basic requirements stipulated in the bid document (see 7.3.1).  
2. **Check the tender against the unresponsiveness criteria** listed in paragraph 7.3.1:  
   - i) Format or signature deficiencies  
   - ii) Missing or inadequately justified EMD  
   - iii) Ineligible bidder  
   - iv) Lack of required manufacturer authority letter  
   - **v) Departure from essential requirements (e.g., tenderer has not agreed to give the required PBG)**  
   - vi) Incomplete quotation against a schedule  
3. **If the tenderer has not agreed to provide the required PBG**, the tender satisfies criterion v) of 7.3.1 and must be classified as **unresponsive**.  

*(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 119)*
cot: First, I think about what the question is really asking: how do we handle a tender that refuses to give the required performance bank guarantee? The evaluation process always starts by checking every submission against the basic requirements laid out in the bid documents. If a tender fails any of those basic checks, it is deemed unresponsive and removed from further consideration. The basic requirements cover a range of items—format and signatures, earnest money deposit, bidder eligibility, manufacturer authority letters, completeness of the quotation, and, importantly, agreement to provide the PBG. So when I see that a tenderer has not agreed to give the PBG, I recognize that it violates the “departure from essential requirements” condition. That violation makes the tender unresponsive. Consequently, I would note this finding, mark the tender as unresponsive because of the missing PBG agreement, set it aside so it does not enter the technical or financial evaluation stages, inform the procurement file keeper (and, if required, the tenderer) of the decision citing the specific unresponsiveness ground, and then move on to evaluate only the tenders that remain responsive. This sequence ensures that the non‑compliant tender is properly excluded while the evaluation of the compliant tenders proceeds unhindered.

section: 2.3 Obtaining Technical, Administrative and Budgetary Sanctions/ Approvals and signing of Indents
question_text: When managing regular consumable materials classified as stock items, at what point does the system deduct the cost from the budget
answer:
When you work with regular consumable materials that are classified as stock items, the system does **not** deduct the cost from the budget at the time you create the purchase requisition or purchase order. Instead, the budget impact occurs later—when Cost is booked in GL during issue of material in system. At that point the system charges the relevant cost centre (or project), thereby reducing the available budget.  

*(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 43)*  

**Facilitator prompt:** “Why do you think it’s useful to separate the procurement step from the budget‑consumption step for stock items? Share any experiences where this timing helped you monitor spending more effectively.”
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: it wants to know at which stage the system actually reduces the budget when we deal with regular consumable materials that are treated as stock items.  

I start by recalling how stock items differ from direct‑charge items. Stock items are materials we keep in inventory for repeated use, and their procurement is not tied to an immediate budget check because they are meant to sit in stores until they are needed.  

Next, I consider what happens when we create a purchase requisition or a purchase order for such a stock item. Since the material will sit in inventory, the system does not reserve or deduct any funds at that moment; the PO can be raised without verifying that the budget has enough available balance.  

Then I think about the moment the material actually leaves the store and is used. When a goods issue is posted, the system generates a material document that moves the quantity out of inventory and simultaneously creates a financial posting to the general ledger.  

At that GL posting, the cost of the consumed material is charged to the appropriate cost centre (or project, if it is a capital stock item). This charge is what reduces the available budget, because the budget is tracked against those cost centres/projects.  

Putting it together, the budget impact does not occur at procurement; it occurs later, when the material is issued from stores and the cost is posted to the GL, thereby charging the cost centre/project and lowering the remaining budget.

question_text: Who is responsible for approving mobilisation advances according to the DOA
answer:
- Mobilisation advances require approval by the competent authority as specified in the Delegation of Authority (DOA).  
- If the authority that approves the proposal lacks the power to approve the mobilisation advance, a separate approval must be obtained.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 102)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: it wants to know who holds the authority to approve mobilisation advances when we refer to the Delegation of Authority, or DOA.  

The Procurement of Works Manual states that every mobilisation advance must be approved by the competent authority as defined in the DOA. This tells me that the approval does not rest with just any officer; it must be the one who has been delegated the power under the DOA framework.  

The manual also adds a qualifier: if the person who normally sanctions the proposal does not themselves possess the power to sanction a mobilisation advance under the DOA, then an additional, separate approval is required. This means the responsibility can shift depending on the specific delegations in place.  

Putting these points together, the core answer is that the competent authority—i.e., the officer or body to whom the DOA has granted the approval power for mobilisation advances—is responsible. When that authority differs from the proposal‑approving authority, a separate sign‑off becomes necessary.  

Thus, the responsibility for approving mobilisation advances lies with the competent authority as per the DOA, with a separate approval needed only when the proposal‑approving authority lacks that specific DOA power.

Before commencement of the Services, the service provider shall submit to the Procuring Entity for approval a Program showing the general methods, arrangements, order and timing for all activities.

After studying time allowed for completion, the EIC should plan the work in consultation with the contractor, to complete the same within the stipulated time and make available the work front to the contractor in time to enable him to execute the work without delay. question_text: What is the maximum cumulative liquidated damages that can be recovered as a percentage of the value of delayed goods
answer:
- **Clause:** 9.7.8 Quantum of LD  
  **Requirement:** The cumulative liquidated damages recoverable for delayed supplies shall not exceed **5 % of the value of the delayed goods**.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants the highest percentage of the delayed goods’ value that can be claimed as liquidated damages when delivery is late.  
Then I look at the provisions that govern liquidated damages: they specify a weekly rate and an overall ceiling.  
Next, I note the weekly rate is half a percent for each week or part of a week of delay.  
From that, I see that damages accrue week by week, but there is a safeguard that prevents them from growing without limit.  
Further, the text states that the total damages shall not exceed five percent of the value of the delayed goods, establishing the upper bound.  
I also see a clause saying the liquidated damages cannot exceed any amount stipulated in the contract, which reinforces that the five percent cap is the governing limit unless the contract sets a lower figure.  
To verify this limit, I would first determine the contract‑specified value of the delayed goods, then calculate the damages using the half‑percent‑per‑week rule, and finally check that the summed amount does not surpass five percent of that value; if it does, the recoverable amount is reduced to the five percent ceiling.  
Combining these points, the maximum cumulative liquidated damages recoverable is therefore five percent of the value of the delayed goods.

### 9.7.8 Quantum of LD
While granting extension of the delivery period, where the delivery of stores or any instalment thereof is accepted after expiry of the original delivery period, the buyer may recover from the vendor, as agreed, the LD a sum equivalent to 0.5% (half percent) of the prices of any portion of stores delivered late, for each week or part thereof of delay. The total damages shall not exceed 5% (five percent) of the value of delayed goods. The LD cannot exceed the amount stipulated in the contract.

LR date will be considered as delivery completion date for calculation of price reduction in the case of delivery on ex works contract. Date of receipt of materials at owner's premises shall be considered for calculation of price reduction for F.O.R destination contract.

In contracts governed by any type of variation (PVC, ERV or statutory variations), LDs (if a percentage of the price) will be applicable on the price as varied by the operation of the PVC. LDs accrue only in case of delayed supplies. Where or in so far as no supplies have been made under a contract, upon cancellation, recovery of only the loss occasioned thereby can be made, notwithstanding the fact that prior to the cancellation one or more extensions of the delivery period with reservation of the right to LD are granted.

Government establishments/Departments, as distinct from PSUs, that execute contract work should not be dealt with as ordinary contractors and not generally be penalised for late delivery and claims for loss on risk-purchase should not be enforced against them. Serious cases of defaults should, however, be brought to the notice of the HOD or the Government Department concerned.

Relaxations allowed to Government establishments/Departments, as above, will not apply to PSUs as a matter of course. Each case should be decided on merits and the decision to waive the recovery of LDs or risk purchase expenditure should be taken on merit.

In the case of development/indigenisation contracts, LDs are not levied. However, the nature of such contracts should be declared at the time of placing them.

### 9.7.9 Waiver of LD
There should normally be no system of waiver of LDs for delayed supplies in supply contracts and it may be strictly be an exception rather than a rule. For an extension of the delivery date with waiver of LD, approval of the CA with consultation of associated Finance may be taken and justifications recorded.

question_text: What is done when there is no standard schedule of rates available for a percentage rate contract?
answer: - In the absence of a standard schedule of rates, a project‑specific schedule of items and their rates is drawn. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 27)
cot: When a percentage rate contract is used, the contractor’s bid is expressed as a single percentage above or below the total estimated cost of the work. That estimate is normally built by applying a schedule of rates to the quantities of each item in the bill of quantities. If a standard schedule of rates is not on hand, the estimator lacks a reliable way to turn those quantities into a cost figure. To move forward, the only practical option is to create a set of rates that reflects the specific items, materials, and conditions of the particular project. This project‑specific schedule then provides the necessary basis for calculating the estimated total cost, allowing the percentage rate contract to be prepared and administered as intended. Thus, in the absence of a standard schedule of rates, a project‑specific schedule of items and their rates is drawn.
chunk_content:
### 3.2.2 Item rate (Unit Rate) Contract
- i) For item rate tenders, contractors are required to quote rate for each individual items of work on the basis of Bill of quantities (BOQ) provided in the Bid Documents. Reasonable variations in quantities can be allowed during the execution in terms of the contract. This is the most commonly used contract type for civil works.
- ii) The payment is made at the rate set out in the contract for the measured quantity within prescribed range [usually+/- 15 (fifteen) percent per item] of the estimated quantity of the initial BOQ.
- iii) This type of contract is suitable for all types of major works such as buildings, bridges, culverts, roads, sewer lines, and carries the least risk of uncertainty for the parties.
- iv) Specifications, design, drawings and contract conditions (including availability of land, forest clearance, social and environmental impact assessment, where applicable) have to be critically appraised before the initiation of procurement process, in order to minimise the incidence of internal inconsistencies, variations, and situation of claims/ disputes or contract failure.

### 3.2.3 Percentage Rate Contract
- i) For percentage rate contract, the contractors are required to quote rate as overall percentage above or below the total estimated cost (i.e., against displayed estimates).
- ii) This type of contract works best when the work does not involve major design process and directions, and simple drawings are sufficient for execution. It saves on the time and effort of detailed design before the procurement process. This type of tender can be used in respect of small and routine types of original works for which estimates can be made based on available schedule of rates and all repair works e.g. levelling and development works including such works as storm water drainage, water supply and sewer lines etc.

As per prevailing practice of NRL, such schedule of rates, may be prepared/adopted based on available standards (like CPWD DSR, APWD SOR etc.), applying suitable factors/indices and with specified validity period of the rates.

*Please also refer section “9.4.6 Manpower Oriented Contracts” in the “Manual for Procurement of Consultancy & Other Services” on display of wage rates to obtain*

*percentage rates.*

- iii) Orders for percentage rate contracts shall be prepared at the estimated rates by adding or subtracting the percentage excess or less on individual items. The payment is made for the measured quantity. Contract provisions are made to determine the price of the items not included in SOR. In the absence of a standard schedule of rates, a project-specific schedule of items and their rates is drawn.

section: 2.11 Preparation of Estimates for works other than Mega Projects
question_text: Under what circumstance should the reason for not being able to prepare a meaningful estimate be recorded
answer: - When a meaningful estimate cannot be prepared for a particular job or case (i.e., estimates cannot be made meaningfully), the full reason for this inability must be recorded. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 22)
cot:
First, I consider why the Procurement of Works Manual talks about preparing estimates at all—it’s to check the reasonableness of tenders before they’re issued, so a solid cost baseline is normally expected.

Next, I recall that the manual acknowledges that this baseline isn’t always possible; it notes there are particular cases where an estimate simply can’t be made meaningfully.

Then I focus on the directive that follows that acknowledgement: when you run into such a case, you must record the full reason for the inability to prepare the estimate.

From that, I infer that the trigger for recording the reason is exactly the situation where a meaningful estimate cannot be prepared for a given job or case.

Finally, I check that this conclusion lines up with the answer statement and that no additional conditions are needed—the reasoning stops at the point where the estimate fails to be meaningful, and the reason is recorded.
chunk_content:
## 2.11 Preparation of Estimates for works other than Mega Projects
For ascertaining the reasonableness of the tender, detailed estimates of cost of each job to be carried out on contract will, as a rule, be made before the tender enquiries are floated. If, in particular cases, estimates cannot be made meaningfully, full reason should be recorded.

Estimates should be realistic and take into consideration all relevant factors viz. Soil / site condition for foundations etc. As far as possible estimates should be prepared using approved 'Schedules of Rates'. Where approved 'Schedule of Rates' is not in existence; estimates should be based on Market Price/Statutory requirements of the various Cost Elements such as labour, materials, and equipment prevailing at the concerned location.

In arriving at the Estimated Rates, the following should be considered:

- I. Labour: Approximate area / volume / quantity that can reasonably be covered by appropriate craftsman during normal working of 8 hours/shift wherever possible.
- II. Norms / parameters for consumption according to area / volume/unit as applicable to items like cement, steel, paint etc.
- III. While preparing the estimates where there are no drawings, the basis on which the material quantity / cost is estimated should be indicated clearly. The rate for costing

the material will normally be based on prevailing Market Rates obtained from Procurement Department if available. If it is from other sources e.g. CPWD Schedule of Rates and quantities, the same should be indicated.

- IV. The usage of company's resources should be taken in to account while preparing the estimate. Free materials issued to the contractor should be quantified.
- V. Estimate Rates should inter-alia consider specifically basic price, quantity, fabrication charges, third party inspection fees, customs/excise duty, packing, handling / forwarding and Transport charges, GST other Statutory levies, Installation / Erection, Testing and Commissioning Charges, Statutory Testing/License Fees, Contingencies etc. as appropriate. It should be comprehensive covering all the relative elements, so as to be meaningful and effective as a guideline.

Detailed estimates need not be made for jobs estimated to cost up to Rs.1,00,000/-

All estimates prepared by User function, including those prepared by Consultants / Architects shall be scrutinized as appropriate and approval of competent authority shall be obtained as per DOA.

All additional and supplementary information required shall be provided or attached as a separate annexure. All signature shall have the name, designation as well as the date of such signature.

Approved estimates are to be treated as strictly confidential and retained securely, without disclosing it to any third party. However, certain approved rates like NRL approved manpower rates, NRL approved SOR rates etc. are allowed to be displayed in tenders (wherever required), as per approval of CFD / policy in vogue at the time of issuance of tender.

To facilitate comparison and ascertaining reasonableness of quotes obtained, estimates prepared should be brought out in the TEC Note.

question_text: How can the Procuring Entity determine if a consultant firm has sufficient experience for a project?
answer:
** The Procuring Entity should examine the firm’s past work on similar types of projects, how long it has been in business, and its track record in the relevant field and geographic region. It should also consider whether the firm is a small specialised outfit or a larger firm with a broad pool of expertise, and verify that it holds appropriate in‑house quality‑control certifications (such as ISO) and maintains an ethics code. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 34)  

**Rationale:** These factors directly show whether the firm has the experience and capability needed to undertake the assignment, as outlined in the short‑listing evaluation criteria. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 34)
cot:
First, I consider what it means for a consultant firm to have sufficient experience: it must demonstrate that it has successfully handled work comparable to the project at hand and possesses the stability and capability to deliver it reliably.  
Then, I identify the concrete indicators that can reveal this experience—namely, the firm’s record of past projects similar in type and scope, how long it has been operating, and its proven track record in the relevant technical field and geographic region.  
Next, I think about how to assess those indicators: reviewing the firm’s portfolio to see if it has completed analogous assignments gives a direct measure of relevance, while the length of time in business suggests accumulated knowledge and resilience, and a consistent history of successful work in the specific sector or area signals sustained competence.  
Further, I reflect on the firm’s structure and qualifications: a small, specialized outfit may offer deep niche expertise, whereas a larger firm with a broad pool of specialists can bring complementary skills; checking for in‑house quality‑control certifications such as ISO shows that the firm follows recognized standards, and confirming the presence of an ethics code points to reliability and impartiality.  
Finally, I synthesize these lines of inquiry: by examining past similar work, duration and track record, firm size and expertise pool, and verifying certifications and ethical practices, the Procuring Entity can form a well‑rounded judgment on whether the consultant firm possesses the experience needed for the project. This comprehensive evaluation directly answers the question of how sufficient experience can be determined.

section: 6.8.1 Statutory Duties and Taxes on Domestic Goods
question_text: What consequence follows if a tenderer quotes a price inclusive of GST/excise duty but does not specify the rate or seek adjustment for statutory variations
answer: If a tenderer quotes a price that already includes GST or excise duty but does not specify the rate of those taxes or ask for an adjustment to cover any future statutory changes, the price is presumed to be firm. As a result, the procuring entity will not accept any later claim for the taxes, duties, or statutory variations; the quoted amount will be taken as the final contract price. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 113)
cot:
I begin by picturing exactly what the tenderer has done: they have presented a single figure that already bundles GST or excise duty into it, but they have not broken out the tax rate nor asked for any provision that would let the price move if those taxes change later.  

Looking at the tender rules, the default stance is that when a price is quoted as all‑inclusive, it is to be read as a firm offer unless the bidder explicitly signals that the tax component is separate or adjustable.  

Because the tenderer never disclosed the rate at which the tax was calculated, there is no way for the procuring entity to isolate the tax portion from the base cost or to apply a later statutory variation to it.  

In addition, the bidder did not insert any clause that would allow the price to be revised upward or downward in response to changes in GST or excise duty, so the contract contains no built‑in adjustment mechanism.  

With neither a disclosed tax rate nor an adjustment clause, the risk of any future tax movement stays with the party who offered the fixed, all‑inclusive sum – namely the supplier.  

Hence, the procuring entity must treat the quoted amount as the final, unalterable contract price and will not accept any later claim for taxes, duties or statutory variations. This matches the consequence that the price is presumed firm and no further tax‑related claims are entertained.
chunk_content:
### 6.8.1 Statutory Duties and Taxes on Domestic Goods
The duties and taxes including GST, excise duty and VAT levied by the Government on domestic goods vary from product to product. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, statutory variation in duties or taxes are to be borne by the buyer (procuring entity) as per the section 64A of the Sales of Goods Act, 1930. As a general policy, the statutory variations in such duties and taxes are to be allowed during the period from the date of the tender to the date of acceptance of the tender (that is, placement of the contract) and during the original/re-fixed delivery period of the contract so that both the supplier and purchaser are equally compensated for rise or fall in the price of the goods on account of such statutory variations.

*(Note: Re-fixed delivery period means the fresh delivery period which is arrived at by recasting the original contractual delivery period after taking care of the lost period, for which the supplier was not responsible.)*

In the tender enquiry conditions, the tenderers, wherever applicable, should be asked to specifically state in their offer whether they intend to ask for the duties and taxes as extra over and above the prices being *quoted*. In the absence of any indication to this effect by the tenderers, it is to be assumed that the prices quoted include these elements and no claim for the taxes or duties or statutory variations thereon should be entertained after opening of tenders and during the currency of the resultant contract. If a tenderer chooses to quote price inclusive of GST/excise duty/Sales Tax/ VAT, it should be presumed that the duties/ taxes so included is firm unless he has clearly indicated the rate of duties/ taxes included in his price and also sought adjustment on account of statutory variation thereon. If a tenderer is exempted from payment of GST / excise duty upto a certain value of turnover, he should clearly state that no GST / excise duty will be charged by him upto the limit of exemption enjoyed by him. If any concession is available in regard to rate/quantum of GST / Central Excise Duty, it should be brought out clearly. It should also be clearly indicated whether increase in rate of GST / excise duty due to increase in turn over will be borne by the tenderer. Stipulation like, "GST / excise duty is presently not applicable but the same will be charged if it becomes leviable later on", should not be accepted unless in such cases it is clearly stated by the tenderer that GST / excise duty will not be charged by him even if the same becomes applicable later on due to increase in turnover. If a tenderer fails to comply with this requirement, his quoted price shall be loaded with the quantum of maximum GST / excise duty which is normally applicable on the item in question for the purpose of comparison with the prices of other tenderers.

Note: Sales tax/ VAT are not levied on transactions of sale in the course of import. Categories of

cases constituting sale in course of import are:

- i) Where the movement of goods from the foreign country to India is occasioned directly as a result of the sale;
- ii) Where the Indian supplier acts as the agent of the foreign manufacturer in the agreement of the sale.

question_text: What is the main purpose of the bid evaluation stage in supporting corporate objectives
answer:
- Bid evaluation consists of assessing submitted bids and awarding the contract. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 36)  
- This stage ensures that procurement decisions are made on objective criteria, delivering value for money and supporting corporate financial goals. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 36)  
- By providing a transparent and auditable process, bid evaluation reduces risk and strengthens governance, aligning with senior management’s oversight responsibilities. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 36)
cot:
First, I think about where bid evaluation sits in the overall procurement flow – it comes after bids have been invited and opened, and before the contract is actually executed, so its core activity must be to look at what suppliers have offered and decide which one will get the award.  

Next, I ask what the organization hopes to achieve by picking a supplier in this way. It isn’t just about choosing the lowest price; the goal is to make sure the decision is based on clear, objective criteria so that the purchase delivers the best possible value for the money spent, which directly supports the company’s financial targets and bottom‑line performance.  

Then I consider how that objective decision‑making is carried out in practice. By establishing a structured evaluation process – scoring against predefined specifications, checking compliance, and documenting the rationale – the stage creates a record that can be reviewed later, making the choice transparent and auditable.  

Looking at transparency further, I see that an auditable trail reduces the chance of favoritism, errors, or corrupt practices, thereby lowering procurement risk. When risk is managed well, the organization avoids costly disputes or rework, which again protects its financial health and reputation.  

Finally, I connect risk reduction and transparency to broader corporate governance. Senior management relies on reliable, traceable procurement outcomes to fulfill oversight duties; a solid bid evaluation process gives them the confidence that contracts are awarded fairly and in line with policy, aligning the procurement function with the company’s governance objectives.  

Putting these pieces together, the main purpose of the bid evaluation stage is to assess submitted bids and award the contract through an objective, value‑driven, transparent process that supports corporate financial goals, reduces risk, and strengthens governance.

question_text: What are the terms and conditions regarding the availability of tender documents for open tenders?
answer:
Open tender documents must be made freely available to all eligible bidders to promote competition, transparency, and value for money. The specific terms and conditions are:

- All eligible bidders are free to participate in the open tender process.  
  (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 58)  
- Tender notices are published on the NRL website and the designated tender portal (CPP/GeM, etc.), with the complete web address provided for downloading documents; no cost may be charged for downloading the tender documents.  
  (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 58)  
- The sale or availability for downloading of tender documents against the NIT must not be restricted and must remain accessible up to the last submission date for tenders.  
  (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 58)  
- Tender documents are to be prepared based on the relevant Standard Bidding Document (SBD) for the procurement category; detailed preparation guidance is provided in Chapter 6 of the manual.  
  (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 58)  

These conditions ensure that procurement supports corporate goals of transparency, risk mitigation, and optimal financial outcomes.
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know the rules that govern how tender documents are made available when an open tender is issued.  

The section on Open Tender Enquiry in the Procurement of Goods Manual lays out a dedicated “Terms and Conditions” subsection, which is exactly where those rules are spelled out.  

I note that the first point there says that every eligible bidder is free to take part; this immediately tells me that there are no artificial barriers to entry based on who the bidder is.  

Next, the manual explains how the invitation is communicated: the notice inviting tenders is posted on the NRL website and also on the designated tender portal (CPP/GeM or similar), and the notice must include the full web address where the documents can be downloaded. It further stresses that no fee may be charged for downloading those documents, which reinforces the idea of unrestricted access.  

Then I see a clause about the availability window: the documents must remain accessible for download up to the final date for submitting bids, and the sale or availability must not be restricted in any way. This ensures that bidders have ample time to obtain the paperwork without encountering sudden cut‑offs.  

Another condition concerns the preparation of the documents themselves: they have to be drawn up according to the relevant Standard Bidding Document for the particular category of procurement, and the manual points to Chapter 6 for detailed guidance on how to do that correctly.  

Putting these pieces together, I can state the terms and conditions as follows: all eligible bidders may participate freely; tender notices are published on the NRL website and the official tender portal with the complete download link, and downloading the documents incurs no charge; the documents must stay available for download without restriction until the last submission date; and they must be prepared based on the appropriate SBD, with further preparation details found in Chapter 6.  

These points naturally satisfy the goal of promoting wide competition, transparency, and value for money in open tender processes.
chunk_content:
## 4.2 Open Tender Enquiry (OTE)
4.2.1 In OTE, an attempt is made to attract the widest possible competition by publishing the NIT simultaneously on the designated websites. This is the default mode of procurement and gives the best value for money but the procedure is relatively complex and prolonged. OTE procedures through e-procurement or through traditional tendering should be adopted: Exceptions to OTE route shall have be approved by competent authority as provided in the DOA in vogue.

4.2.2 All tenders should be floated through Open Tender route only.

4.2.3 Floating of tenders on Single Tender / Nomination basis shall be resorted to in exceptional cases only.

4.2.4 Floating of tender to limited vendors shall not be adhered to, except for any special

requirements. The procedure for such proposal requiring limited tender shall be as follows:

- a) The requesting (user) department shall forward to commercial department an approval with proper justification for requesting limited tender and why only the specific vendors / contractors are chosen to participate.
- b) The approval should contain the list of shortlisted agencies to whom the limited tender is intended to be floated.
- c) The approval note should be duly approved by competent authority.

### 4.2.5 Terms and Conditions
- i) All eligible bidders are free to participate;
- ii) Information of the open tenders will be published in NRL website by publishing a copy of the NIT. This will be in addition to the tender document published in the tender portal (CPP/GeM etc.) or notice board (manual tenders). Notice for invitation of tenders should give the complete web address from where the bidding documents can be downloaded. In order to promote wider participation and ease of bidding, no cost of tender document may be charged for the tender documents downloaded by the bidders.; and

question_text: Which element of a Purchase Requisition defines the work to be performed and is considered part of the Special Terms & Conditions of Contract
answer: - Scope of work – defines the work to be performed and is included as part of the Special Terms & Conditions of Contract (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 31)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants the specific item in a Purchase Requisition that both describes the work to be done and is classified under the Special Terms & Conditions of the contract.  

I recall that a Purchase Requisition is meant to capture all the details a buying department needs before issuing a tender or order, so I mentally run through the typical pieces of information it must contain. Among those pieces, there is a field that explicitly outlines what the contractor will actually do—this is the description of the work itself.  

Looking at the typical structure, besides the name of the work and justification, there is a distinct entry labeled “scope of work.” The description of this entry notes that it details the exact tasks, deliverables, and performance expectations that the contractor must fulfill.  

Importantly, the note attached to that entry indicates that the scope of work is treated as a component of the Special Terms & Conditions (often abbreviated as SCC). This means it isn’t just a generic description; it carries contractual weight and forms part of the special provisions that govern the agreement.  

Putting those observations together, the element that satisfies both criteria—defining the work to be performed and residing within the Special Terms & Conditions—is the scope of work.  

Thus, the answer is the scope of work.

## 4.6 Initiation of Procurement of Services
The concerned user departments such as, Operations, Maintenance, HR, Township & Estates etc. will do initiation for procurement which are to be executed, by creating the Purchase Requisitions (PRs) through Aarohan system and getting the same released by the Competent Authority after ascertaining that there is requirement of procurement of such services.

To the extent practicable, planning for procurement and contracts should be done on an integrated basis, should be adequate and effective, so as to keep the contracts to the minimum number.

Should Commercial Department feel that any of the PRs received by them could be executed by Company's own resources / skills and available ARCs, they may refer it back to User Department for review (with their reasons) before processing the said PR.
