### 7.3.4 Clarification of Bids/Shortfall Documents
During evaluation and comparison of bids, the purchaser may, at his discretion, ask the bidder for clarifications on the bid. The request for clarification shall be given in writing, asking the tenderer to respond by a specified date, and also mentioning therein that, if the tenderer does not comply or respond by the date, his tender will be liable to be rejected. Depending on the outcome, such tenders are to be ignored or considered further. No change in prices or substance of the bid shall be sought, offered or permitted. No post-bid clarification at the initiative of the bidder shall be entertained. The shortfall information/documents should be sought only in case of historical documents which pre-existed at the time of the tender opening and which have not undergone change since then. (Example: if the Permanent Account Number, registration with sales tax/ VAT has been asked to be submitted and the tenderer has not provided them, these documents may be asked for with a target date as above). So far as the submission of documents is concerned with regard to qualification criteria, after submission of the tender, only related shortfall documents should be asked for and considered. For example, if the bidder has submitted a supply order without its completion/performance certificate, the certificate can be asked for and

lakhs considered. However, no new supply order should be asked for so as to qualify the bidder.

If the bidder cites any reference of a job executed for NRL and the bidder is not able to furnish documentary evidence, the internal records of shall be considered.

## 7.4 Evaluation of Responsive Bids and Decision on Award of Contract
All responsive bids are evaluated with a view to select the lowest (L1) bidder who meets the qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects. In case of single stage single envelop bidding, the evaluation of qualification of bidders, technical, commercial and financial aspect is done simultaneously. In single stage multiple envelops, initially only the techno-commercial bids would be opened and evaluated for bids which successfully meet the qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects. Financial bids of such successful bidders only would be opened for selecting the L1 bidder. In two stage bids, the PQB/ Eol stage would have already been evaluated as detailed in Chapter 4 and this second stage is for evaluation of responses to the Second Stage multiple envelops from the shortlisted qualified bidders. Evaluation of techno-commercial and financial aspects are, however, discussed separately below.

Clause 3.4.2 deals with empanelment that is triggered by a need rather than a regular, ongoing requirement.

To double‑check, the clause does not mention any other authority or additional steps for need‑basis empanelment, so the administrative approval of CFD stands as the sole requirement.  
Putting it together, the answer is that empanelling vendors or contractors on a need basis requires the administrative approval of the Contract Finance Division.

question_text: How are incentives or bonuses structured for early completion of supplies
answer: Incentives or bonuses for completing supplies ahead of schedule are usually expressed as a set percentage of the contract value for each month you finish early. For example, the bonus might be 1 % of the contract value per month, with the total bonus capped at a maximum of 5 % of the contract value. The exact rate and any upper limit are clearly stated in the tender documents in plain monetary terms, and before a bonus clause can be included in a tender, it must receive prior administrative approval from the CFD (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 149).
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: how a contract might reward a supplier for finishing the supply ahead of the scheduled date.  
Then, I consider that such a reward is usually tied to the amount of time saved, so it makes sense to express it as a rate applied to the contract value for each unit of time the delivery is early.  
Next, I recall that the rate is often set as a fixed percentage of the contract value per month (or week) of early completion, and to protect the buyer from excessive payouts a ceiling is placed on the total bonus that can be earned.  
Further, I note that the exact percentage and any upper limit must be spelled out in plain monetary terms inside the tender documents so that bidders can see precisely what they stand to gain.  
Finally, I remember that before a bonus clause of this sort can be inserted into a tender, it has to receive prior administrative approval from the responsible authority—typically the CFD—to ensure it complies with procurement policy, as noted in the Procurement of Goods Manual (p. 149).  

Putting these points together, the incentive or bonus for early completion is structured as a set percentage of the contract value for each month finished early (for example, 1 % per month), with the total bonus capped at a maximum percentage of the contract value (such as 5 %), the rate and limit clearly stated in the tender documents in plain monetary terms, and the clause requiring prior administrative approval from the CFD.

### 9.7.5 Force Majeure Clause
A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

### 9.7.6 Denial Clause
Since delay in delivery is a default by the seller. In such a case, the buyer should protect himself against extra expenditure during the extended period by stipulating a denial clause (over and above levy of LD) in the letter informing the supplier of extension of the delivery period. In the denial clause, any increase in statutory duties and/or upward rise in prices due to the PVC clause and/or any adverse fluctuation in foreign exchange are to be borne by the seller during the extended delivery period, while the purchaser reserves his right to get any benefit of a downward revisions in statutory duties, PVC and foreign exchange rate. Thus, PVC, other variations and foreign exchange clauses operate only during the original delivery period.

### 9.7.7 Liquidated Damages and Incentives/ Bonus
Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of supplies. Provision of incentives for completion of supplies before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear

monetary terms.

Incentives/ Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

question_text: How should the members of a Tender Evaluation Committee be arranged to ensure no one reports directly to another member?
answer:
Facilitator: Let’s examine how to compose a Tender Evaluation Committee so that no member reports directly to another. The manual states that the TEC must consist of officers where **no member of the Committee should be reporting directly to any other member of such Committee** (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  

The source does not cover the specific practical steps for arranging the committee to achieve this.
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the rule really means: the Tender Evaluation Committee must be formed so that no sitting member is the direct supervisor of any other member.  

That immediately tells me that I cannot simply pick people who sit in the same chain of command; if I chose a manager and one of his subordinates, the condition would be violated.  

So the next step is to think about how to avoid that situation. I should look for officers whose reporting lines either run in completely different branches of the organization or who sit at the same hierarchical level but answer to different supervisors. In either case, each person’s direct boss lies outside the committee.  

To make sure I’ve actually achieved that, I need a concrete way to check the relationships. The most reliable tool is an up‑to‑date organizational chart: it shows who reports to whom at a glance.  

With the chart in hand, I can run a quick exercise: take any two names I’m considering for the TEC and trace their lines upward. If I find that one name appears as the immediate superior of the other, I know that pair would break the rule.  

When such a conflict shows up, the fix is straightforward—replace one of the two with someone whose supervisor is not on the list, preferably from a different department or a different tier of the same department.  

By repeating this check for every possible pairing, I can build a committee where every member’s direct manager sits outside the group, thereby satisfying the “no direct reporting” requirement.  

Putting it all together, the arrangement is achieved by selecting officers from separate reporting chains or equivalent levels and verifying the absence of supervisor‑subordinate links through an organizational chart, swapping out any conflicting members until the condition holds for the whole team.

answer: In a two‑envelope bidding system, the techno‑commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate inner covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed inner covers are to be put in a bigger outer cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. I cannot answer whether the bid validity period can be extended after a tender has been submitted from what I know.

### 4.9.2 Sealing and Marking of Tenders
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (e.g., in duplicate or in triplicate etc) required to be submitted. In case bids are asked in a number of copies, the tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate" and so on and also marking these as mentioned above. In case of two envelope bidding system, the techno- commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate inner covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed inner covers are to be put in a bigger outer cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the Procuring Entity will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening etc. These details regarding the submission of bids should also form a part of the ITB and AITB in the tender documents; all the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

### 4.9.3 Withdrawal, Substitution and Modification of Tenders
The tenderer, after submitting the tender, is permitted to withdraw, substitute or modify the tenders in writing without forfeiture of Bid Security/ EMD, provided these are received duly sealed and marked like the original tender, up to the date and time of receipt of the tender. Any such request received after the prescribed date and time of receipt of tenders will not be considered. No bid may be withdrawn in the interval between the deadline for submission of bids and expiration of the period of bid validity. Withdrawal of a bid during this period will result in forfeiture of the bidder's bid security (EMD) and other sanctions.

question_text: What actions can the EIC/CMC take if a consultant's performance does not meet contract requirements
answer:
The Engineer‑in‑Charge (EIC) or Contract Monitoring Committee (CMC) has a range of remedial measures available when a consultant’s performance falls short of contract requirements. These actions are intended to protect the Procuring Entity’s interests while giving the consultant an opportunity to correct deficiencies.

- **Assess and reject deliverables** – The EIC/CMC may review the quality of outputs and reject any part of the assignment that does not meet the stipulated standards.  
- **Impose liquidated damages or penalties** – If the work is not carried out as per the contract or the service quality is inferior, the EIC/CMC can levy appropriate liquidated damages or penalties in accordance with the Contract, Special Conditions of Contract (SCC) or General Conditions of Contract (GCC).  
- **Suspend or withhold payments** – Payments may be suspended until satisfactory progress is achieved, ensuring that financial outflow aligns with performance.  
- **Require corrective action** – The EIC/CMC can issue notices to proceed with modifications, request revisions to the work plan, or direct the consultant to address specific problems identified during monitoring.  
- **Manage disputes and arbitration** – The committee is responsible for resolving problems faced by the consultant, handling disputes, and initiating arbitration procedures when necessary.  
- **Terminate the contract** – In cases of persistent non‑performance, the EIC/CMC may terminate services prior to the contract’s end date.  
- **Conduct post‑contract evaluation** – After completion or termination, the EIC/CMC undertakes a post‑contract evaluation to document lessons learned and inform future procurements.  

These measures collectively enable the EIC/CMC to enforce contractual compliance, safeguard project objectives, and maintain accountability throughout the consultancy engagement. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 60‑61)
cot:
First, I think about the role of the Engineer‑in‑Charge or Contract Monitoring Committee: they are the nodal authority tasked with watching over a consultancy assignment, making sure it stays aligned with the procuring entity’s goals, and they have the power to intervene when things go off track.  

Looking at what the contract monitoring framework actually gives them, I see a toolbox of specific actions—reviewing and accepting or rejecting work, applying financial sanctions, pausing payments, directing changes, handling disputes, ending the contract early, and wrapping up with a review after the fact.  

When a consultant’s performance slips below what the contract requires, the first logical step is to examine the deliverables themselves. The EIC/CMC can therefore assess the quality of the outputs and reject any portion that fails to meet the agreed standards.  

If the shortcoming continues, the next recourse is to use the financial levers built into the contract. They can levy liquidated damages or penalties as prescribed in the General or Special Conditions of Contract, or simply suspend or withhold further payments until the consultant demonstrates satisfactory progress.  

Beyond money, the EIC/CMC also holds the authority to require corrective action. This might mean issuing a notice to proceed with a revised scope, asking for an updated work plan, or directly instructing the consultant to fix the problems identified during monitoring.  

When disagreements arise over what constitutes acceptable performance or how to remedy it, the EIC/CMC steps in to manage the dispute, facilitating negotiations and, if needed, initiating arbitration procedures as outlined in the contract.  

Should the consultant repeatedly fail to cure the breach despite these measures, the ultimate sanction available is to terminate the services before the contract’s scheduled end date, protecting the procuring entity from further loss.  

Finally, whether the contract runs its full course or ends early, the EIC/CMC conducts a post‑contract evaluation. This review captures what worked, what didn’t, and feeds lessons learned into future procurement processes, completing the cycle of oversight.  

Putting these steps together gives the full range of actions the EIC/CMC can take when a consultant’s performance does not meet contract requirements.

section: 5.2.6 Withdraw/ Amendments / Modifications to Bids by Bidders
question_text: Can I withdraw or change my tender after I have submitted it, and until when?
answer: Yes, you can withdraw or change your tender after you have submitted it, provided that your withdrawal, alteration or modification is received in a properly sealed and marked envelope—just like your original tender—on or before the date and time set for receipt of tenders. Any request that arrives after that deadline will not be considered. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 103)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question is really getting at: it wants to know whether a tender that has already been lodged can still be taken back or altered, and if there is a cut‑off point after which such actions are no longer allowed.  

Then I recall the rule that governs tender submissions: once a tenderer has submitted its tender, it retains the right to withdraw, alter or modify that tender, but only if the withdrawal or amendment is delivered in the same way as the original—properly sealed and marked—and it reaches the procuring entity no later than the prescribed date and time for receipt of tenders.  

From that rule I see two clear conditions: the formal condition (sealed and marked like the original tender) and the temporal condition (arrival on or before the tender receipt deadline). If either condition fails, the withdrawal or change will not be considered.  

Next I focus on the temporal condition because the question specifically asks “until when.” The deadline is exactly the date and time set for the receipt of tenders; any request that arrives after that moment is treated as if it were never submitted.  

Putting the formal and temporal requirements together, I conclude that a tenderer can indeed withdraw or change its tender after submission, provided the withdrawal or amendment is properly sealed and marked and is received on or before the tender receipt deadline; otherwise the request will be ignored.  

Finally I check that this conclusion mirrors the given answer: it affirms the possibility, stresses the sealing/marking requirement, and notes that any request after the deadline will not be considered. The reasoning flows naturally from the question to the answer without any gaps.
chunk_content: The tenderer, after submitting its tender, is permitted to withdraw/ alter/modify its tender so long such withdrawal/ alterations/ modifications are received duly sealed and marked like original tender, up to the date & time of receipt of tender. Any withdrawal/ amendment/ modification received after the prescribed date & time of receipt of tenders are not to be considered.

question_text: How should a procuring entity handle the Notice Inviting Tender for a limited tender
answer: For a limited tender, the procuring entity should upload the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) to the CPPP portal and its own website, adding a note that says the notice is for information only, that participation is by invitation limited to the entity’s registered suppliers, and that unsolicited offers will be ignored. The entity must keep a record of the publication, noting the exact dates the notice appeared on the website, as proof of publicity. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 94)
cot:
First, I think about what a limited tender actually means: it’s not an open call; only those who have been specifically invited may submit a bid. So the notice inviting tender isn’t meant to attract unsolicited offers, but it still needs to be made public for transparency and record‑keeping.

Next, I consider what the notice itself should look like. The procuring entity should use the standard model format for a Notice Inviting Tender, because that ensures all the essential details—description of the procurement, submission deadline, how to obtain documents, etc.—are present while keeping the notice brief enough for a quick scan.

Then I turn to where the notice should be placed. For limited tenders the guidelines say the notice must go on the Central Public Procurement Portal and also on the procuring entity’s own website. Publishing in both places satisfies the requirement for wider visibility while still signaling that the tender is not open to everyone.

After deciding the placement, I focus on the wording that must accompany the notice. Since the tender is limited, the notice needs a clear disclaimer: it is being published for information only, participation is by invitation restricted to the entity’s registered suppliers, and any unsolicited offers will be disregarded. This prevents confusion and protects the entity from having to evaluate bids that weren’t invited.

Finally, I think about proof of compliance. Simply uploading the notice isn’t enough; the entity should keep a record of exactly when the notice appeared on its website (dates, screenshots, or logs). Those records serve as evidence that the publicity requirement was met, which can be shown to higher authorities if needed.

Putting these steps together—using the model NIT format, publishing on the CPPP portal and the entity’s website with the appropriate limited‑tender note, and retaining dated proof of publication—gives the complete, correct way a procuring entity should handle the Notice Inviting Tender for a limited tender.

question_text: What action must the Warehouse take regarding balance surplus materials after considering requirements from group companies
answer: - Verify that, after circulating the balance surplus materials list to group companies and allowing one month for their responses, the Warehouse initiates disposal of any remaining surplus materials in accordance with the established disposal procedure. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 162)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the warehouse is supposed to do once it has heard back from the group companies about any possible reuse of the surplus items.  
The core of the question is the action that follows the consideration of those external requirements.  

Thinking about the workflow, the warehouse cannot simply discard the materials right away; it must first give the group companies a chance to claim what they might need.  
That means the warehouse has to issue a notice or list detailing all balance surplus materials and ask each group company to confirm whether they have a requirement for any of those items.  

After sending out that list, there has to be a defined window for responses so that no potential internal demand is overlooked; the stipulated period is one month, which allows enough time for the companies to review and reply.  

Once that month elapses and all replies are in, the warehouse can assess which items have been claimed and which remain unclaimed.  
Only the items that no group company has requested should be considered truly surplus and eligible for removal from inventory.  

Finally, with the surplus confirmed, the warehouse must act to dispose of those remaining materials, following the established disposal procedure that governs how such items are written off or scrapped.  

Putting it all together, the warehouse’s required action is to verify that, after circulating the balance surplus materials list to the group companies and allowing one month for their responses, it then initiates disposal of any remaining surplus materials in accordance with the set disposal procedure.

question_text: Why should a procuring entity avoid setting a fixed normative percentage below the estimated cost to automatically label a bid as abnormally low?
answer:
**Why a Procuring Entity Should Avoid a Fixed Normative Percentage for Automatically Labeling a Bid as Abnormally Low**

1. **Automatic application ignores other bid elements** – A set percentage below the estimated cost does not consider the full scope of the bid, such as schedule, risk allocation, responsibilities. Abnormality must be judged by examining the price in relation to all these factors, not by a single numeric threshold. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 127)

2. **Risk of erroneous rejection** – Without a case‑by‑case assessment, a bid that is genuinely capable of delivering the contract may be incorrectly deemed abnormal and rejected. The proper procedure requires seeking written clarifications from the bidder and conducting a detailed price analysis before any determination of incapability is made. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 127)

3. **Undermines due care in bid‑document preparation** – The manual emphasizes that care should be taken when preparing specifications to guard against abnormally low bids. Relying on a rigid percentage bypasses this safeguard and may discourage competitive bidding by creating an arbitrary barrier. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 127‑128)

4. **Inconsistent with the prescribed evaluation process** – The guidance states that a bid should only be rejected after evaluating price analyses and determining that the bidder has substantially failed to demonstrate capability. A fixed percentage skips this analytical step and therefore does not follow the mandated process. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 127)

**Conclusion:** To ensure fair, transparent, and compliant procurement, entities must avoid setting a fixed normative percentage below the estimated cost for automatically labeling bids as abnormally low. Instead, they should follow the outlined steps of seeking clarifications, performing price analyses, and evaluating the bidder’s capability before making any rejection decision. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 127)
cot:
First, I need to grasp why the question is focused on a fixed percentage rule: it’s asking whether a simple numerical cutoff can reliably flag a bid as abnormally low without further scrutiny. The core of the issue is that abnormality isn’t just about the price being low; it’s about whether the bidder can actually fulfill the contract at that price, which depends on many other aspects of the bid.

Next, I identify the key elements that should be examined when judging a bid’s legitimacy. Besides the offered price, one must look at the scope of work, the proposed schedule, how risks and responsibilities are allocated, and whether the bidder has demonstrated the technical and financial capacity to meet all requirements. A percentage‑based test ignores all of these dimensions, reducing a complex judgment to a single number.

From there, I reason about what happens if we apply that rigid cutoff automatically. Any bid that falls below the line would be dismissed outright, even if the bidder could provide a convincing explanation—perhaps they have innovative methods, lower overhead, or a different risk‑sharing arrangement that makes the low price feasible. Without seeking clarifications or conducting a detailed price analysis, we risk rejecting a capable bidder simply because their price looks low on paper.

I then consider the procedural guidance that the procurement framework provides. It specifies that a bid should only be labeled abnormal after the procuring entity has asked for written clarifications, reviewed the bidder’s price breakdown, and determined that the bidder has substantially failed to prove they can deliver the contract at the offered price. Skipping straight to a percentage threshold bypasses this mandated analytical step, meaning the process would no longer follow the prescribed evaluation route.

Finally, I reflect on the broader implications for bid‑document preparation. The manual emphasizes that care should be taken when drafting specifications to guard against abnormally low bids, not to rely on a mechanical shortcut. A fixed percentage undermines that safeguard, creates an arbitrary barrier that could deter genuine competition, and fails to ensure that decisions are based on a thorough, case‑by‑case assessment of capability.

Putting these thoughts together, it becomes clear that a procuring entity should avoid setting a fixed normative percentage below the estimated cost for automatically labeling a bid as abnormally low. Instead, they must follow the outlined steps of seeking clarifications, performing price analyses, and evaluating the bidder’s ability to perform before making any rejection decision, thereby ensuring a fair, transparent, and compliant procurement process.

### 7.5.7 Consideration of Abnormally Low Bids
An Abnormally Low Bid is one in which the Bid price, in combination with other elements of the Bid, appears so low that it raises material concerns as to the capability of the Bidder to perform the contract at the offered price. Procuring Entity may in such cases seek written clarifications from the Bidder, including detailed price analyses of its Bid price in relation to scope, schedule, allocation of risks and responsibilities, and any other requirements of the bids document. If, after evaluating the price analyses, procuring entity determines that the Bidder has *substantially failed* to demonstrate its capability to deliver the contract at the offered price, the Procuring Entity may reject the Bid/Proposal. However it would not be advisable to fix a normative percentage below the estimated cost, which would be automatically be considered as an abnormally low bid. Due care should be taken while formulating the specifications at the time of preparation of bid document so as to have a safeguard against the submission of abnormally low bid from the

bidder.

In the case of predatory pricing as well, procuring entities may refer to the above consideration of Abnormally Low Bids to assist themselves in finalization of tenders.

No provisions should be kept in the Bid Documents regarding the Additional Security Deposit/ Bank Guarantee (BG) in case of Abnormally Low Bids. Wherever, there are compelling circumstances to ask for Additional Security Deposit/ Bank Guarantee (BG) in case of ALBs, the same should be taken only with the approval of the next higher authority competent to finalise the particular tender.

### 7.5.8 Cartel Formation/Pool Rates
It is possible that sometimes a group of bidders quote the same rate against a tender, where they were at liberty to quote any competitive price. Such pool/cartel formation is against the basic principle of competitive bidding and defeats the very purpose of an open and competitive tendering system. A warning clause may also be included in the bid documents to discourage the bidders from indulging in such practices.

# Chapter 10: Identification and Disposal of Scrap, Condemned & Surplus Assets
Disposal of Scrap, Condemned Goods & Surplus Assets is desirable considering the following benefits:-

- Monetary returns to the organization.
- Reduce cost of maintaining idle inventories.
- Reduce security hazard, enhance safety.
- Make space available for other purpose.
- Recycling for cleaner environment.
- Improvement of housekeeping.

## 10.1 Identification of Scrap, Condemned & Surplus Assets:
A) Like any other organization, NRL also has a considerable quantity of stores and spares, equipment, plant and machinery, furniture etc. While every effort is made to prolong their life, they do become unserviceable after a long use and their further retention becomes uneconomical. In addition, changes occur constantly in design and specifications, their components and materials in the scenario of a fast moving technology thereby rendering the items at time as obsolete. Consequently, there accumulates, a large quantity of material which is neither usable for the purpose for which it was originally procured nor of any other operational value. Such material should be distinguished from other stores and component parts which can be utilised after repair or renovation.

B) In the day to day activities also, considerable quantities of scraps are accumulated for which there are no further use.

C) Prompt and proper identification of such material is essential. For a proper control over the assets of the Company, it is necessary that an effective system to identify all assets and material which have ceased to be useful to the organization, shall operate continuously, so that immediate action is possible for their timely discarding and disposal.

## 4.3 Publication of Bid Documents
It is mandatory to publish tender enquiries, corrigenda thereon and details of bid awards on the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) / GeM Portal and own website and dispense with advertisements in Newspapers. However, in exceptional circumstances, procuring entities may issue the advertisement in newspapers as deemed fit. Such advertisement should also consist of the link of website from where the detailed advertisement and bidding document can be seen and downloaded. Individual cases where confidentiality is required, for reasons of national security, would be exempted from the mandatory e-publishing requirement. The decision to exempt any case on the said grounds should be approved by CA. In order to promote wider participation and ease of bidding, no cost of tender document may be charged for the tender documents downloaded by the bidders. To ensure competition, attention of all likely tenderers, for example, enlisted vendors, past contractors and other known potential contractors, should be invited to the NIT through email/ SMSs/ letters. In e-procurement, the website may be programmed to generate these alerts automatically. In case of procurement through a limited tender, the NIT may be uploaded on CPPP Portal or Procuring Entity's website with a note saying:

*"This notice is being published for information only and is not an open invitation to quote in this limited tender. Participation in this tender is by invitation only and is limited to the selected Procuring Entity's enlisted contractors. Unsolicited offers shall be ignored."*

Soft copy of the tenders published on the website should be collected and kept on record as a proof of publicity. The complete details of the dates, on which NIT actually appeared on the website, should be indicated while sending cases to higher authorities.

## 4.4 Issue/ Availability of tender documents, Bidding Period, Minimum Response
The availability for downloading of tender documents against NIT should not be restricted. Tender documents should be available for download up to the last date of bid submission. The organization should also post the complete tender document in its web site and on CPPP to enable prospective tenderers to make use of the document downloaded from the web site. The advertisement for

invitation of tenders should give complete web-address from where bid documents can be downloaded.

All Proposals (Open or Limited), GeM Custom Bid , BOQ Based Bidding: 14 days.

GeM Bid where Item Category is available: 10 days

Global Tenders : 4-6 weeks

question_text: As per clause vii), what must be included in the tender document?
answer: Clause vii) – Verify that the tender document includes relevant INCOTERMS. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 60)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what clause vii) says about the tender document. Clause vii) is stated as: “Relevant INCOTERMS should be included in the tender.” This is a direct requirement rather than a suggestion.  

Next, I consider what it means for something to be “included in the tender.” In procurement practice, the tender document is the package of information given to bidders, so any item that must be included becomes part of that document. Therefore, the phrase “should be included in the tender” translates to a mandate that the tender document contain the relevant INCOTERMS.  

Then, I think about the purpose of INCOTERMS in a tender. They define the responsibilities, costs, and risk transfer points between buyer and seller for the delivery of goods. Including them ensures that bidders understand the delivery terms and can prepare their offers accordingly.  

Finally, I synthesize the above: the requirement from clause vii) is that the tender document must list the applicable INCOTERMS. This matches the answer that the tender document should include relevant INCOTERMS, which is what needs to be verified.  

Thus, the logical conclusion is that, as per clause vii), the tender document must contain the relevant INCOTERMS.

question_text: What evidence should auditors verify to confirm that the procurement was satisfactorily advertised and sufficient time was provided for bid submission?
answer:
- Verify that the procurement was advertised by obtaining copies of the advertisement posted on notice boards or websites.
- Confirm that sufficient time was allowed for bid submission; however, the source does not specify the evidence to be verified for this point.

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p.130)
cot:
First, I need to pin down exactly what the question is asking for: what concrete proof would show that a procurement was properly advertised and that bidders were given enough time to prepare their bids.  

The reference tells me that a single‑offer situation can still be valid only if two conditions are met – the procurement was satisfactorily advertised and sufficient time was allowed for bid submission. So my goal is to think about what evidence would satisfy each of those conditions.  

For the advertisement part, I reason that simply saying “we posted it” isn’t enough; I need something tangible that demonstrates the notice actually reached the public. That could be a photocopy of a notice‑board posting, a print‑out or screenshot of the website where the tender was published, or a clipping from a newspaper or official gazette. Any of those artifacts would show the advertisement existed and when it appeared.  

Moving to the time‑allowed condition, I realize the key is to compare two dates that must be present in the tender notice itself: the date the advertisement was first made public and the final date and time for bid submission. By extracting those dates from the notice, I can calculate the interval between them and judge whether it gives bidders a reasonable window to prepare their offers.  

Putting the two strands together, I see that obtaining the advertisement proof gives me the first piece of evidence, while examining the same tender notice (or a duplicate copy) for the publication and deadline dates gives me the second piece. If both pieces are present and the interval looks adequate, then I have verified that the procurement was satisfactorily advertised and sufficient time was provided for bid submission.  

Thus, the evidence auditors should verify consists of (1) copies or screenshots of the advertisement showing where and when it was posted, and (2) the tender notice itself to confirm the advertisement date and the bid submission deadline, ensuring the gap between them is sufficient.

Sometimes, against open/limited tender cases, the procuring entity may not receive a sufficient number of bids and/or after analysing the bids, ends up with only one responsive bid - a situation referred to as 'Single Offer'. **Such situation of 'Single Offer' is to be treated as Single Tender.** It is possible that there may be single offer situation against open tenders and there may be tendency to go for re-tender as a safe course of action. Re-bidding has costs: firstly the actual costs of retendering; secondly the delay in execution of the work with consequent delay in the attainment of the purpose for which the procurement is being done; and thirdly the possibility that the re-bid may result in a higher bid. Even when only one Bid is submitted, the process may be considered valid provided following conditions are satisfied:

- i) The procurement was satisfactorily advertised (publicized in notice boards, websites etc.) and sufficient time was given for submission of bids.
- ii) The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive; and
- iii) Prices are reasonable in comparison to market values

However restricted powers of approval of award on Single tender basis of procurement would apply. In case of price not being reasonable, negotiations (with L1) or retender may be considered as justifiable.

Unsolicited offers against LTEs should be ignored.

question_text: What must be extended alongside the delivery date when an extension is approved, according to the policy?
answer: - When an extension of the delivery date is approved, the validity period of the performance guarantee must also be extended. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 148)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the policy says about approving an extension of the delivery date. The question is asking what else must be extended at the same time when such an extension is granted.  

Looking at the section on extension of delivery, I see that granting an extension is treated as an amendment to the contract and requires mutual consent. The policy then lists what the confirmation of that extension should include.  

Among those items, one point stands out: the confirmation must mention the requirement to extend the validity period of the performance guarantee. This is presented as a necessary condition that accompanies any approved delivery date extension.  

Since the confirmation is what is issued after approval, and it explicitly states that the performance guarantee’s validity period must be extended, it follows that whenever an extension of the delivery date is approved, the performance guarantee’s validity period must also be extended.  

Thus, the item that must be extended alongside the delivery date is the validity period of the performance guarantee.

### 9.7.2 Terms of Delivery
Terms of delivery (FOR, FOB, CIF, and CFR, and so on), inter alia, determine the delivery point of the ordered goods from where the purchaser is to receive/collect the goods. It also decides the legally important issue of when the 'titles of the goods' have passed to the purchaser. The delivery period is to be read in conjunction with the terms of delivery, therefore the delivery is taken to have been made at the time when goods reach the delivery point as per the delivery terms. The delivery condition of FOR NRL (Location) may be adopted as far as possible.

### 9.7.3 Extension of Delivery
Suppliers shall be required to adhere to the delivery schedule specified in the purchase order and, if there is delay in supplies, LD shall be levied wherever there is failure by the party. Extension of the delivery date amounts to amendment of the contract. Such an extension can be only done with the consent of both parties (that is, the purchaser and supplier). No extension of the delivery date is to be granted suo motu unless the supplier specifically asks for it.

The confirmation of extension of delivery period (provisional / firm) should inter-alia contain the following:-

- (i) The time for delivery is extended from (CDD) to (extended CDD)
- (ii) Applicability & mention of LD clause beyond the original contract delivery date / the last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date.
- (iii) Requirement of extension of the validity period of the performance guarantee.
- (iv) That the above extension of delivery date will also be subject to the Denial Clause.

On receiving the supplier's communication, the procuring entity shall examine the proposal and, on approval from the CA, may agree to extend the delivery schedule, with or without LD

### 9.7.4 Delay in Supplies for which Supplier is not Responsible
Normally, in the following circumstances, the contractual delivery period needs to be re-fixed to take care of the lost period, without imposing any penalty to the supplier:

- i) Cases where the manufacture of stores is dependent on the approval of the advance sample and delay occurs in approving the sample though submitted by the supplier in time;

- ii) Where extension in the delivery period is granted on account of some omission on the part of the purchaser which affects the due performance of the contract by the supplier; and
- iii) Cases where the purchaser controls the entire production.

question_text: In cases where proposals have been sanctioned by the CFD, SCBT, or Board, which officials’ prior approval is required by the NRL manual before proceeding with the work
answer: In cases where proposals have been sanctioned by the CFD, SCBT, or Board, the NRL manual requires prior approval from both the Director (Finance) [D(F)] and the Director (Technical) [D(T)] before work may proceed.
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know which officials must give their prior approval before any work can start when a proposal has already been cleared by the CFD, the SCBT, or the Board.  

The key condition here is the involvement of those higher‑level sanctioning bodies—CFD, SCBT, or Board—because the manual treats their approvals differently from routine or lower‑level clearances.  

Next, I recall that the manual outlines a graded approval structure, where the level of authority that has already signed off determines who else needs to be consulted before moving forward.  

Looking at the provisions for approvals, I see that for ordinary tenders or scope changes, the Engineer‑in‑Charge or the Functional Head of the executing department can give the go‑ahead, sometimes with only post‑facto clearance.  

However, the manual makes an explicit exception for cases where the proposal has already received the sanction of the CFD, the SCBT, or the Board: it states that in such situations, prior approval must be obtained from both the Director (Finance) and the Director (Technical).  

This requirement makes sense because those bodies represent the financial and technical oversight arms of the organization, and their sign‑off ensures that any work stemming from a high‑level sanction aligns with both budgetary limits and technical specifications.  

Putting it together, when a proposal has been cleared by the CFD, SCBT, or Board, the NRL manual mandates that the Director (Finance) [D(F)] and the Director (Technical) [D(T)] must both approve the work before it can proceed, contrasting with the lower‑level approvals that might be handled by the Engineer‑in‑Charge or the Functional Head alone.  

Thus, the officials whose prior approval is required are the Director (Finance) and the Director (Technical).

### 6.4.5 Extension of Time (EOT)
- i) Extension of Time (EOT) / Provisional extension of time must not be left to the end; it should be dealt with promptly during the progress of the contract and for ongoing critical delay interim EOT may be awarded. The engineer shall, after due review with the contractor, determine the length of such extension and notify the contractor accordingly, with a copy to the procuring department. After the final stage of completion is reached (final taking-over certificate issued), EOT and LD may be reviewed, if required. Delay analysis should be supported by appropriate hindrance register / back-up records.
- ii) If a compensation event occurs during the execution of the contract, the same shall be dealt with in terms of the GCC. The Engineer will assess whether and by how much the intended completion date shall be extended.
- iii) Graded authority structure for extension of time for completion of contract as per DOA to be followed.
- iv) In case of contracts of regular nature (AMCs, ARCs etc.) where the works/services are required on continuous basis, action for renewal of such contracts or lining up of fresh contracts in its place must be taken by the user functions and PR should be forwarded to Commercial Dept. at least **four months** before the date of expiry/completion of contract.

As far as possible, extension of contract beyond provision of tender terms & conditions, should be avoided. Cases where action is not taken on time and extension of contract is necessary, prior approval from the competent authority must be taken before expiry of the contractual period.

## 6.5 Financial Monitoring
Besides administering the contract with regard to its quality and completion, the engineer will regularly assess the financial position and exercise financial control. He will update, on a monthly / quarterly basis, cash flow projections, cost estimates and yearly/ quarterly /monthly milestones, and submit them to the Procuring Entity. Variations should take place with a view to achieving economical completion of the work, and not to result in avoidable higher rates or costs. In case of a significant number of variation orders or unexpectedly rapid cost escalation, updation may be done more frequently. The financial statements should bring out comparisons of the initial estimated/ tendered cost with the actual cost -- component- and activity --wise -- both with respect of quantities and value. The Procuring Entity should examine these statements critically. If costs are likely to be exceeded, this should be anticipated, and a revised estimate of cost prepared, with complete explanations, for approval by the CA.

### (i) APPROVAL BY ENGINEER-in-CHARGE :
In circumstances where the situation warrants an immediate decision, the Engineer in charge can take a decision to go ahead with the extra work including increase in SOR quantities and seek post facto approval from the appropriate authority at the earliest possible time.

The detailed justification for not seeking prior approval duly approved by the HOD shall be forwarded along with the bill. Post facto approval shall be obtained immediately and in no case not more than three months from the date of the deviation. Further, in respect of tenders approved by Standing Committee/ Board, prior approval of functional director shall be obtained in such circumstances.

In case of change in the scope of work, prior approval should be obtained from Functional Head of executing department. However, in case of proposals approved by CFD/SCBT/Board, prior approval should be obtained from D(F) & D(T).

section: 1.10.4 Preference to Make in India (PP-LC (MII) POLICY)
question_text: What is the specific percentage margin of purchase preference that Class I local suppliers must fall within to be eligible to match the L1 price under the procurement policy?
answer: The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals do not specify the exact percentage margin of purchase preference; they only state that a Class I local supplier's quoted price must fall within that margin to be eligible to match the L1 price. The manuals describe the matching procedure but do not provide the numeric threshold. For the precise margin, one would need to refer to the relevant government notifications.
chunk_content:
The manufacturers/ service providers having the capability of meeting/ exceeding the local content targets shall be eligible for purchase preference under the policy, i.e., LC manufacturers/ LC service providers respectively as described below:

- a) In procurement of all items/ services/ works which are divisible in nature, the Class I local supplier shall get purchase preference over 'Class II local supplier' as well as 'Non Local Supplier' as per following procedure:
  - i. Among all qualified bids, the lowest bid will be termed as L1. If L1 is 'Class I local supplier', the contract for full quantity will be awarded to L1.
  - ii. If L1 bid is not a 'Class-I local supplier', the bidders shall be ranked in the ascending order of evaluated prices and the lowest bidder among the 'Class-I local supplier' will be invited to match the lowest bidder's evaluated price for the 50% quantity against the respective item(s) of MR subject to the Class-I local supplier's quoted prices falling within the margin of purchase preference, and contract for that quantity shall be awarded to such 'Class-I local supplier' subject to matching the lowest bidder's evaluated price. In case such lowest eligible Class-I local supplier fails to match the lowest bidder's evaluated price or accepts less than the offered quantity, the next higher Class-I local supplier with the margin of purchase preference shall be invited to match the L1 price for remaining quantity against the respective item(s) of MR and so on, and contract shall be awarded accordingly. question_text: Which stages of the procurement process qualify a bidder to exercise the right to be heard
answer:
- Pre‑qualification stage (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 86)  
- Bidder enlistment stage (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 86)  
- Bidding stage – technical bid evaluation (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 86)  
- Bidding stage – financial bid evaluation (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 86)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the reference says about when a bidder can actually be heard. It mentions that a tenderer has the right to be heard if they feel the procurement process wasn’t followed correctly or if their tender was wrongly rejected, but only a directly affected bidder can make such a representation.  

So the key is to understand what “directly affected bidder” means in this context. The reference clarifies that only a bidder who has taken part in the specific procurement process—whether that’s pre‑qualification, bidder enlistment, or the actual bidding—can raise a representation. In other words, you have to be involved at the stage where the decision you’re challenging is made.  

Next, I look at the sequential nature of the evaluation steps. If pre‑qualification is assessed before the technical and financial bids, then only those who have successfully passed pre‑qualification are in a position to question the later technical or financial bid evaluations. Likewise, if the technical bid is opened and evaluated before the financial bid, only bidders whose technical bids are deemed acceptable can later challenge the financial bid outcome.  

Putting these pieces together, the stages at which a bidder is both participating and potentially affected are: the pre‑qualification stage itself, the bidder enlistment stage (since enlistment is another form of participation), the technical bid evaluation stage (provided they’ve cleared any prior pre‑qualification), and the financial bid evaluation stage (provided their technical bid was acceptable).  

These four points line up exactly with the answer: pre‑qualification, bidder enlistment, technical bid evaluation, and financial bid evaluation. Each stage represents a point where a bidder who has participated can be directly affected by a decision and therefore exercise the right to be heard.

question_text: In the context of comparative policy analysis, what specific elements of the NRL manual's arbitration award payment procedure would an internal audit team need to verify against the Department of Expenditure guidelines?
answer:
The internal audit team should verify the following specific elements of the NRL manual’s arbitration award payment procedure when comparing them to the Department of Expenditure guidelines:

- Whether the manual requires payment of 75 % of the arbitral award (including interest accrued up to the date of the award) to the contractor/concessionaire against a Bank Guarantee, and whether the BG is limited strictly to that 75 % amount, excluding any interest that may later become payable to the Company (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 114).  
- Whether the directive using the term “shall” is treated as a mandatory requirement, such that any deviation from the 75 % payment/BG rule requires approval from the Board of Directors (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 114).  
- Whether the manual permits the payment to be deposited into a designated Escrow Account and prescribes the order of application of escrow proceeds: first to satisfy lenders’ dues, second to complete the project in question, third to complete other projects of the same Company as mutually agreed, and whether any residual balance after these uses may be released to the contractor/concessionaire only with the prior approval of the lead banker and the Company (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 115).  
- Whether the manual allows the release of retention money or other amounts withheld against BG, provided contractual provisions permit it (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 115).  

These elements constitute the procedural benchmarks against which the Department of Expenditure guidelines must be examined for convergence or divergence.
cot:
First, I consider what the audit team is actually being asked to do: they must compare the NRL manual’s arbitration award payment procedure with the Department of Expenditure guidelines, so I need to isolate the specific, verifiable steps that the manual lays out for handling an arbitral award when the company has challenged it and the award remains unpaid.  

Next, I recall the core payment rule that appears in the manual: when the award is contested and not yet paid, the company is required to pay 75 % of the arbitral award—this amount includes any interest that has accrued up to the date of the award—to the contractor or concessionaire, and the payment must be secured by a Bank Guarantee. Importantly, the guarantee is limited strictly to that 75 % figure; it does not cover any additional interest that might later become payable to the company if a court orders a refund.  

Then I notice the mandatory language used in that provision: the term “shall” signals a non‑negotiable requirement. Any departure from the 75 % payment/BG rule would therefore need prior approval from the Board of Directors, making this a control point the audit team must verify for compliance or for the existence of proper authorization.  

After that, I look at how the manual treats the actual disbursement of the funds. It allows the payment to be placed into a designated Escrow Account and prescribes a clear order of application for the escrow proceeds: first to satisfy lenders’ dues, second to complete the project in question, third to finish other projects of the same company as mutually agreed, and only after those uses can any remaining balance be released to the contractor or concessionaire, and even then only with the prior agreement of the lead banker and the company.  

Further, I see that the manual also contemplates the release of other amounts that might be withheld under the contract—such as retention money—against the same Bank Guarantee, provided the contract permits it and both the lead banker and the company concur. This adds another layer of verification concerning the conditions under which additional funds can be drawn.  

Finally, I synthesize these observations: the audit team needs to check whether the NRL manual contains (1) the 75 % payment with interest‑up‑to‑award‑date rule and the BG limitation, (2) the mandatory “shall” condition triggering board approval for any deviation, (3) the escrow account mechanism with its prescribed priority of uses and the conditional release of residual balances, and (4) the provision for releasing retention or other withheld amounts against the BG subject to contractual and dual‑approval conditions. Verifying each of these elements against the Department of Expenditure guidelines will reveal where the two sets of rules converge or diverge, which is exactly what the comparative policy analysis requires.

### 6.10.2 Arbitration Awards
- i) In cases where the Company has challenged an arbitral award and, as a result, the amount of the arbitral award has not been paid, 75% of the arbitral award (which may include interest up to date of the award) **shall** be paid by the Company to the contractor/ concessionaire against a Bank Guarantee (BG). The BG **shall** only be for the said 75% of the arbitral award as above and not for the interest which may become payable to the Company should the subsequent court order require refund of the said amount.

**Note: In para 6.10.2 (i) instructions containing "shall" are mandatory; any deviation from these instructions shall require approval from the Board of Directors.**

- ii) The payment may be made into a designated Escrow Account with the stipulation that the proceeds will be used first, for payment of lenders' dues, second, for completion of the project and then for completion of other projects of the same Company as mutually agreed/ decided. Any balance remaining in the escrow account subsequent to settlement of lenders' dues and completion of projects of the Company may be allowed to be used by the contractor/ concessionaire with the prior approval of the lead banker and the Company. If otherwise eligible and subject to contractual provisions, retention money and other amounts withheld may also be released against BG.

## 6.11 Breach of Contract, Remedies and Termination


### 6.11.1 Breach of Contract
In case the contractor is unable to honour important stipulations of the contract, or gives notice of his intention of not honouring or his inability to honour such a stipulation, a breach of contract is said to have occurred. Mostly, such breaches occur in relation to the performance of the contract in terms of inability to complete the Work within stipulated time. It could also be due to breach of

ethical standards or any other stipulation that affects Procuring Entity seriously. As soon as a breach of contract is noticed, a show cause notice should be issued to the contractor, giving 10 days' notice, reserving the right to implement contractual remedies. If there is an unsatisfactory resolution, remedial action may be taken immediately.

If termination takes place because of a fundamental breach/ insolvency on the part of the contractor, the EIC shall issue a certificate for the value of work done, deducting from the amounts in respect of: (i) advance payments; (ii) any recoveries; (iii) taxes as due; and (iv) percentage to apply to the work not completed as indicated in the contract data. If the total amount due to the procuring entity exceeds that due to the contractor, the difference will be a debt payable to the procuring entity. A contract may be terminated in the following cases with approval of CA and written communication on termination of contract should be conveyed to the contractor from Commercial Department. The Procuring Entity is then free to take over the site and complete the works himself or with another contractor and use the contractor's materials, equipment, temporary works as he/ they think proper.

question_text: When does the delivery liability period begin for a contract that results from a purchase order or Letter of Acceptance that includes GPC/GCC, SCC, and the schedule of requirements?
answer: When a purchase order (PO) or Letter of Acceptance (LoA) is issued and the tender documents contain the General Conditions of Contract (GPC/GCC), Special Conditions of Contract (SCC) and the schedule of requirements, the PO/LoA creates a binding contract. Consequently, the delivery liability period starts on the date of that PO/LoA, unless the contract itself specifies a different commencement date for delivery liabilities. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 134)
cot:
I need to figure out when the delivery liability period starts for a contract that comes from a purchase order or Letter of Acceptance which already incorporates the General Conditions of Contract (or GPC/GCC), the Special Conditions of Contract (SCC) and the schedule of requirements.  

First, I consider what makes a purchase order or LoA turn into a binding contract. The reference notes that when the tender documents already contain those contractual elements—GPC/GCC, SCC and the schedule of requirements—the issuance of the PO or LoA itself creates a binding agreement between the buyer and the supplier.  

Next, I look at what governs the timing of delivery liabilities once that contract is in place. The same passage states that, in such cases, all delivery liabilities are counted from the date of the PO/LoA, unless the contract itself specifies a different commencement date for those liabilities.  

So, the logical flow is: the presence of GPC/GCC, SCC and the schedule of requirements in the tender documents makes the PO/LoA a contract; because it is a contract, the delivery liability period is anchored to the date that contract is formed—that is, the date of the PO/LoA—unless the parties have agreed otherwise in the contract terms.  

Putting it together, the delivery liability period begins on the date the purchase order or Letter of Acceptance is issued, provided the tender documents include the GPC/GCC, SCC and schedule of requirements, unless the contract explicitly states a different start date for delivery liabilities.

section: 5.3 Procedures to be followed during Bid Opening
question_text: How should auditors verify that the BOC has ensured and demonstrated that the seal on the tender box has not been tampered with prior to opening?
answer: Auditors should verify that the BOC ensured and demonstrated that the seal on the tender box had not been tampered with prior to opening the box. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 103)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the auditor’s role is in this context: they are checking whether the bid opening committee (BOC) followed the prescribed procedure for handling the tender box before the bids are revealed.  
The core of the procedure, as described, is that the BOC must not only make sure the seal on the box is intact but also show, in a visible and verifiable way, that the seal has not been interfered with.  
So, the auditor’s task reduces to confirming two things: that the BOC carried out a check of the seal’s condition and that they provided some form of demonstration—such as letting observers see the seal, recording its state, or noting any anomalies—before the box was actually opened.  
To verify this, the auditor would look for evidence of that check and demonstration: perhaps a signed attendance sheet, a log entry, photographs, or witness statements that attest to the seal being examined and found untampered.  
If such evidence exists, it shows the BOC fulfilled the requirement to ensure and demonstrate the seal’s integrity; if it is missing or contradictory, the auditor would note a lapse in compliance.  
Putting these points together, the auditor should verify that the BOC ensured and demonstrated that the seal on the tender box had not been tampered with prior to opening the box.

section: 6.1.5 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Performance Bank Guarantee and Other Instruments [ABG, SD-BG etc.]
question_text: Is there a system that will alert me automatically if my bank guarantee is about to lapse?
answer: Yes. The procuring entity should put in place a computerised system that monitors performance bank guarantees and other instruments, and it will generate automatic alerts when a guarantee is approaching its lapse date (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 106). This helps ensure you are notified in time to take any needed action without having to track the expiry yourself.
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: I want to know whether there’s a way to get a heads‑up automatically when a bank guarantee is nearing its expiry, so I don’t have to keep track of it myself.  

Next, I consider what would be needed for such an alert to work. The system would have to know the guarantee’s validity date, monitor that date over time, and trigger a notification when the date gets close enough to require action.  

Looking at the information provided, it describes that the procuring entity should establish a mechanism for the safe custody and monitoring of performance bank guarantees, including a monthly review of all guarantees that are set to expire in the next three months. It goes on to say that this monitoring arrangement can be computerised and that the computerised system would generate automatic alerts about the lapse of validity.  

From that, I infer that if the procuring entity puts in place a computerised monitoring tool that checks the expiry dates each month and sends out a warning whenever a guarantee falls within the three‑month window (or any other chosen threshold), then the user will receive an automatic alert before the guarantee lapses.  

Putting the pieces together, the answer is yes: a computerised monitoring system, as outlined, will automatically alert the holder when a bank guarantee is approaching its lapse date, thereby removing the need for manual tracking and ensuring timely action.
chunk_content: A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of Performance Bank Guarantee and other instruments should be implemented by LIV section. The Procuring entity shall also make institutional arrangements for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of Performance Bank Guarantee, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the supplier for purpose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc.

section: 9.9.2 Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and seeking Approval.
question_text: For an outline agreement (ARC), at what point is adequate funding required
answer: For an outline agreement (ARC), adequate funding must be secured at the time the Release Order is issued. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 71)
cot:
First, I consider what an outline agreement (ARC) actually represents in procurement—it establishes the terms, prices, and conditions for future purchases but does not by itself commit any money or create a binding obligation to buy.  

Next, I think about how the procurement process moves from agreement to actual acquisition: the agreement sits dormant until a specific request for goods or services is made, and that request is formalized through a release order (sometimes called a call‑off or delivery order).  

Then I recall that budgetary controls are tied to the moment when a financial commitment is entered into the system; until that point, the organization can treat the funds as still available for other uses.  

Looking at the flow described for ARCs, the only step that triggers a financial posting is the issuance of the release order, at which point the service entry sheet is created, costs are booked to the general ledger, and the procurement budget is consumed.  

Therefore, to avoid overruns or unauthorized spending, the necessary funding must be secured exactly when the release order is issued—because that is the point at which the outline agreement turns into an actual, funded procurement action.  

Synthesizing these points leads to the conclusion that adequate funding for an outline agreement (ARC) is required at the time the Release Order is issued.

### 9.9.2 **Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and seeking Approval.**
Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked. The cost estimate shall be based on the Procuring Entity's assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment: managerial and staff time and physical inputs (for example, materials, consumables, tools and machines). Costs shall be divided into three broad categories:

- i) Remunerations for Personnel deployed;
- ii) Reimbursable: (Travel, logistics, Consumable, Material, Tools, Hiring of third party services etc.);
- iii) Administrative and Miscellaneous (Mobilisation, demobilisation, Temporary Structures, Administrative expenses, office and IT equipment, contingencies, financing costs, Costs for hiring/ depreciation/ financing of machinery and equipment etc).

### 9.9.3 **Final Administrative and Budgetary Approvals**
The Activity Schedule shall be compatible with the available budget. The most important step is to determine whether all tasks required to achieve the desired output have been included. The next step is to determine whether adequate budget has been allocated to implement the assignment as designed. Procurement should be initiated only after such approvals and budgetary provisions.

Appropriate WBS / Cost Centre having required fund has to be used in all POs. No PO should be issued with "Unknown" account assignment.

Services are procured against Cost Centre (K) and Project (P) and procurement budget is required during creation of PR and PO. Cost is booked in GL as soon as SES (Service Entry Sheet) is made and accepted in system.

For ARCs (outline agreement) adequate fund will be required only at the time of issuing Release Order.

- For revenue item procurement where budget is expected to be consumed across financial years, detailed procedure for "Control over release of Commitment Budget", issued by Finance Dept. to be referred.

## 9.10 Procedure for Single Source Selection (SSS)
Should it become necessary, in an exceptional situation to outsource a job to a specifically chosen contractor, the CA's approval may be taken. In such cases the detailed justification, the circumstances leading to the outsourcing by choice and the special interest or purpose it shall serve shall form an integral part of the proposal.

## 9.11 Procedure for Small Value and emergency Procurements of Other (Non-consultancy) Services
In many small value procurements of other services, the service provider may neither be capable of handling the bidding process, nor would this be a cost-effective process for the Procuring Entity. The 'Direct Procurement without Quotation' mode of procurement used in Procurement of goods may very well be utilised in such cases. Similarly for procurement of services 'Direct Procurement by a Purchase Committee' mode as used in procurement of Goods may be utilised. In all such modes of procurement, the procedure prescribed in the Manual for Policies and Procedures for Procurement of Goods may be followed.

Please refer “Manual for Procurement of Goods”:-

Section 4.9 **Direct Procurement without Quotation**; and

Section 4.10(a) **Departmental Purchase**; and
