section: 7.2 Preparation and Vetting of Comparative Statement
question_text: What procedure is required to enable a meaningful price comparison among tenders
answer:
- List the price quoted by each tenderer, including alternative specifications with explanatory notes (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Provide the item‑wise estimate or Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) for comparison with the tendered rates (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Reduce all quoted prices to a common base to enable a meaningful comparison (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Highlight every deviation in specifications or standard terms and conditions, especially those affecting price or delivery (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- State the contractual completion or delivery term offered by each tenderer (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Indicate any discount or rebate offered (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Show the foreign exchange requirement for imported items (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Quantify and clearly show the incidence of GST, Customs Duty, Excise Duty or other statutory levies (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Specify packing, handling, forwarding, transportation charges and insurance, and indicate their cost incidence (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Determine and indicate the cost implications of any advance payment provisions (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Clearly indicate any price escalation clause and load its cost implication into the tender evaluation (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Incorporate applicable purchase preferences and government policies (e.g., MSE) into the evaluation sheet for the Tender Evaluation Committee (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Taking all the above factors into account, prepare a comparative cost evaluation statement that gives a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Upload the comparative statement in the Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial Department (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Prepare a detailed TEC note to the Tender Committee/CA, highlighting main points and recommendation, and enclose the comprehensive tabulation for decision‑making (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Provide a technical explanation for any variation between tendered prices and evaluated prices, detailing any positive or negative loadings and clarifications sought from tenderers (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Verify that all technical details, specification drawings and other offer contents conform to the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).
cot:
First, I think about what it means to compare tenders meaningfully – the prices must be comparable on the same footing, so I need to gather every element that influences the final cost each bidder is offering.  

Next, I list the basic price each tenderer has quoted, making sure to note any alternative specifications they have proposed and adding a brief explanation of how those alternatives differ from the baseline requirement.  

Then, I bring in the item‑wise estimate or the last paid unit price for each line item; having this reference point lets me see whether a tendered rate is above, below, or in line with what has been paid before.  

After that, I adjust all quoted prices to a common base – stripping out any location‑specific factors, different currencies, or varying tax treatments – so that the numbers I am looking at truly reflect the same scope of work.  

With the prices normalized, I turn my attention to every deviation: changes in specifications, different delivery schedules, or special terms and conditions. I highlight those that could affect price or timing, because ignoring them would distort the comparison.  

I also record the contractual completion or delivery period each bidder is offering, any discounts or rebates they have mentioned, and the amount of foreign exchange required for imported components.  

Further, I quantify all statutory charges – GST, customs duty, excise duty, or other levies – and show how they add to the base price. I do the same for packing, handling, forwarding, transportation, and insurance, making sure their cost impact is visible.  

If a tender includes advance payment terms, I work out the financial implication of that and note it; similarly, I identify any price‑escalation clause, calculate its expected effect over the contract period, and load that amount into the evaluated price.  

I then incorporate any applicable purchase preferences or government policies – such as those for micro‑ and small‑enterprises – into the evaluation sheet so that the tender committee sees the full picture.  

Taking all of these adjusted elements together, I construct a comparative cost evaluation statement that presents a realistic, representative, and comprehensive view of each offer’s total cost.  

Finally, I make sure this statement is uploaded to the Aarohan system by the commercial department’s dealing officer, prepare a detailed TEC note that summarizes the key findings and recommendation, attach the comprehensive tabulation for the committee’s review, provide a technical explanation for any differences between the tendered and evaluated prices, and verify that every technical detail, drawing, and specification in the offers conforms to the original tender enquiry before the committee makes its decision.
chunk_content:
### Broad guidelines for preparation of Comparative statement:
- i) To facilitate proper bid analysis, the comparative statement shall be made of all the

tenders received on the following basis:

- a) Price quoted by all the firms shall be given. Where alternative specifications has been offered for the jobs under reference and are acceptable, their prices shall also be indicated along with suitable explanatory note concerning deviations.  
The item wise estimate / Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) shall also be given in this tabulation to make comparison of estimate / LPP with the tendered rates.
  - b) Prices quoted shall be reduced to a common base for a meaningful comparison.
  - c) All deviations either in specifications or in standard terms and conditions shall specifically be highlighted, particularly those having a bearing on price or delivery shall be indicated.
  - d) Contractual completion / delivery term of all parties shall be given.
  - e) Discount / Rebate if any offered to be indicated.
  - f) Foreign exchange required in the case of imports shall be indicated.
  - g) Incidence of GST/ Customs Duty/ Excise Duty/ or other Statutory levies, shall be quantified and clearly shown.
  - h) Packing, Handling, Forwarding and Transportation Charges, insurance as applicable should be specified and the incidence thereof should be shown.
  - i) Where advance payment is involved, the cost implications must be determined / indicated.
  - j) Prices escalation clause, if any to be clearly indicated and the cost implication loaded in the tender evaluation.
  - k) Taking all factors into consideration, comparative cost evaluation statement shall be made to give a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison.
  - l) Applicable Purchase preferences and the policies of the Government with regard to MSE and other guidelines shall be suitably brought out in the evaluation sheet for the guidance of the TEC.
- ii) The comparative statement shall be uploaded in Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial dept.
- iii) The Commercial Department would prepare a detailed note (TEC note) to the Tender Committee / CA highlighting the main points with the recommendation for the award of the contract. The tender papers enclosed along with the above note should include the

comprehensive tabulation drawn as indicated above to arrive at a meaningful comparison for effective decision-making. There should be no ambiguity in any of the data presented for consideration.

iv) Technical explanation should be given for variation between prices quoted in the tender and the evaluated prices. Any positive or negative loading done to render the comparison meaningful should be properly explained. Clarifications sought from the tenderers and the resulting impact on the quotation if any should be specifically mentioned. It should be ensured that all technical details; specification drawings and other aspects contained in the offers have been thoroughly checked for conformity with the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee.

v) In short, a factual, informative and technically cleared material should be portrayed in the noting to the Committee / CA to facilitate taking decisions for the contracts without further reference to the field units.

The comparative statement so prepared should be enclosed along with TEC note for approval of award as per DOA.

question_text: What selection method is recommended for awarding a percentage contract when using QCBS evaluation
answer:
**Step‑by‑Step Instructional Guide for Awarding a Percentage Contract Using QCBS Evaluation**  

**Purpose:** To provide procurement officers with a clear, actionable walk‑through of the selection method recommended for percentage contracts when a Quality‑and‑Cost‑Based Selection (QCBS) process is employed.  

---

### Step 1: Issue the Request for Proposals (RFP)  
- Prepare the RFP that specifies the scope of work, the requirement for a percentage‑based fee, and that the final selection will follow a QCBS evaluation.  
- *Example:* For architectural services, the RFP states that fees will be a percentage of the estimated project cost and that award will be based on QCBS.  

*(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 21)*  

### Step 2: Receive and Log Proposals  
- Record all submitted proposals, ensuring each includes both a technical proposal and a financial proposal quoting the percentage fee.  

### Step 3: Conduct Technical Evaluation  
- Evaluate the technical proposals against predefined criteria (experience, methodology, qualifications, etc.).  
- Identify consultants who meet the minimum technical threshold (“technically qualified”).  

### Step 4: Open Financial Proposals of Technically Qualified Consultants  
- Only the financial proposals of those consultants who passed the technical evaluation are opened.  
- Record the percentage fee quoted by each technically qualified consultant.  

### Step 5: Apply the QCBS Weighting Formula  
- Combine the technical score (e.g., 70 % weight) and the financial score (e.g., 30 % weight) for each technically qualified consultant.  
- The financial score is inversely related to the quoted percentage fee – the lower the percentage, the higher the financial score.  

### Step 6: Rank Consultants by Combined QCBS Score  
- Rank all technically qualified consultants from highest to lowest combined QCBS score.  

### Step 7: Award the Contract  
- Issue the award to the consultant with the highest combined QCBS score.  
- If multiple consultants have identical scores, the contract may be awarded to the one quoting the lowest percentage fee, as the content notes that selection can also be made “among the technically qualified consultants/service providers who have quoted the lowest percentage.”  

### Step 8: Ensure Payment Release Conditions  
- Stipulate in the contract that payments will be released only against certification by the Engineer‑in‑Charge (EIC) that the services have been satisfactorily delivered.  

*(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 21)*  

---

#### Practical Example  
A procuring entity needs architectural design services for a new office building. The RFP specifies a fee of X % of the construction cost and states that selection will follow QCBS. After technical evaluation, three firms are deemed qualified. Their quoted percentages are 6.5 %, 7.0 %, and 6.8 %. Applying a 70 % technical / 30 % financial weighting yields combined scores that rank Firm A (6.5 %) highest. The contract is awarded to Firm A, and invoices are paid only after EIC certification of completed design milestones.  

---

**Common Pitfalls to Avoid**  
- Opening financial proposals before technical evaluation – this violates the QCBS procedure and can lead to biased scoring.  
- Awarding to the lowest percentage fee without confirming technical qualification – the contract must be awarded only to consultants who have passed the technical evaluation.  
- Releasing payments without EIC certification – payments must be tied to verified performance as stipulated in the contract.  

By following these numbered steps, procurement officers can correctly apply the QCBS evaluation method to percentage contracts, ensuring compliance, transparency, and value for money.
cot: First, I consider what a percentage contract entails: the consultant’s fee is tied to a proportion of the project cost, making the payment contingent on successful delivery. This tells me that the selection process must ensure both technical capability and a reasonable fee proportion. Then I look at the guidance that says the final selection for such contracts is made through a QCBS evaluation, or alternatively among the technically qualified consultants who have quoted the lowest percentage when the notional value is fixed. This indicates that the recommended method is to apply QCBS after technical qualification. Next, I break down what a QCBS process involves: the request for proposals must state that fees will be percentage‑based and that award will follow QCBS; proposals are logged and then technical proposals are scored against predefined criteria. Only those consultants who meet the technical threshold move forward, so their financial proposals—containing the quoted percentage—are opened. After that, I combine the technical and financial scores using the agreed weighting (for example, 70 % technical, 30 % financial), noting that a lower quoted percentage yields a higher financial score. The combined scores are then ranked from highest to lowest, and the contract is awarded to the consultant at the top of the list. If a tie occurs, the guidance suggests breaking it by selecting the consultant with the lowest percentage fee, reinforcing the cost‑effectiveness aim. Finally, I recall that the contract must stipulate that payments are released only upon certification by the Engineer‑in‑Charge, linking fee disbursement to verified performance. This series of considerations reproduces the recommended step‑by‑step method for awarding a percentage contract under QCBS.

## 3.4 Percentage Contract
3.4.1 Percentage contracts directly relate the fees paid to the consultant/ service provider to the estimated or actual project cost, or the cost of the goods procured, inspected or sold. Since the payment is made after the successful realisation of objectives, it is also called success (or contingency) fee contract. The final selection is made based on QCBS evaluation process or among the technically qualified consultants/service providers who have quoted the lowest percentage while the notional value of assets is fixed.

These contracts are commonly used for appropriate architectural services; procurement and inspection agents, disposal of scrap etc.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

## 3.5 Indefinite Delivery Contract (Price Agreement)
3.5.1 These contracts are used when Procuring Entity need to have "on call" specialized services, the extent and timing of which cannot be defined in advance. This is akin to the system of 'Rate Contracts' or framework contracts in the procurement of Goods. There is no commitment from Procuring Entity for the quantum of work that may be assigned to the consultant/ service provider. The Procuring Entity and the firm agree on the unit rates to be paid, and payments are made on the basis of the time/ quantum of service actually used. The consultant/ service provider shall be selected based on the unit rate quoted by them for providing the services.

These are commonly used to retain "advisers" or avail services 'on-call' - for example; expert adjudicators for dispute resolution panels, institutional reforms, procurement advice, technical troubleshooting, and so forth - normally over a period of a year or more.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

Contracts need to be closely monitored and administered by the EIC to ensure that the progress of assignment is commensurate with the time spent and that the resources for which payment is claimed have actually efficiently and productively been deployed on the assignment during the period.

question_text: What are the two specific conditions under which a contract may be cancelled for supplier default according to section 9.8.1?
answer:
When reviewing a contract for possible cancellation due to supplier default, the trainer should point out that the contract may be terminated if:  

1. The supplier fails to deliver any or all of the stores within the delivery period specified in the contract – including any approved extension.  
2. The supplier fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the time frame stipulated – again, extensions apply.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 151)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants the two specific grounds for cancelling a contract when a supplier is in default, as laid out in section 9.8.1.  
Next, I turn my attention to that section and see that it opens with a statement that, without prejudice to other remedies, the contract may be terminated by written notice of default. Right after that, it enumerates the situations that trigger this right.  
The first situation listed concerns delivery: it says the contract may be ended if the supplier fails to deliver any or all of the stores within the time period(s) stipulated in the contract, or any extension thereof that has been granted. This clearly ties cancellation to a failure to meet the delivery schedule.  
Moving on, the second situation addresses any other contractual duty: it states that the contract may also be terminated if the supplier fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted. This captures defaults that are not about delivery but about any other promised performance.  
Finally, I note that the subsection goes on to describe possible recourse actions after termination, but those are consequences, not conditions for cancellation. Therefore, the two conditions that must be present for a supplier‑default cancellation are precisely the failure to deliver on time (including approved extensions) and the failure to perform any other contractual obligation on time (again, with extensions allowed). These match exactly what the answer expects.
chunk_content:
### 9.8.1 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, such as removal from the list of registered supplier, by written notice of default sent to the supplier, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part:

- i) If the supplier fails to deliver any or all of the stores within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted; and
- ii) If the supplier fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted;
- iii) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the EMD;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, goods similar to those undelivered may be procured and the supplier shall be liable for all available actions against him, as applicable in terms of the contract (including risk purchase); and
  - c) However, the supplier shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 9.8.2 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the supplier becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the supplier, without compensation to the supplier, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 9.8.3 Termination of Contract for Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the supplier for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the supplier may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract.

## 9.9 Dispute Resolution
Normally, there should not be any scope for dispute between the purchaser and supplier after entering into a mutually agreed valid contract. However, due to various unforeseen reasons, problems may arise during the progress of the contract leading to a disagreement between the purchaser and supplier. Therefore, the conditions governing the contract should contain suitable provisions for settlement of such disputes or differences binding on both parties. The mode of settlement of such disputes/differences should be through arbitration. However, when a dispute/difference arises, both the purchaser and supplier should first try to resolve it amicably by mutual discussion, mediation, and conciliation. If the parties fail to resolve the dispute within 21 (twenty-one) days, then, depending on the position of the case, either the purchaser or supplier should give notice to the other party of its intention to commence arbitration. When the contract is with a domestic supplier, the applicable arbitration procedure shall be as per the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [Amended 2015 and 2021]. While processing a case for dispute resolution/litigation/arbitration, the procuring entity is to take legal advice, at appropriate stages.

question_text: Why is it important to use material codes in SAP when raising a Purchase Requisition
answer:
?  

Using a material code in SAP ties your Purchase Requisition directly to the correct item in the system. The code tells SAP exactly what you need, so the requisition can move forward without unnecessary delays. When you include a material code, you also avoid creating duplicate entries for the same item—before raising the PR you check the SAP material master to see if a code already exists. If the material isn’t yet coded, you get it set up through the material master governor (the Warehouse‑based material master team). This keeps your purchasing data clean, lets the system track the item from requisition through receipt and payment, and supports accurate reporting and inventory control. In short, using the right material code makes the procurement process smoother, reduces errors, and helps ensure your bid or order is handled correctly.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 45)
cot:
When I think about raising a Purchase Requisition in SAP, the first thing that comes to mind is that the system needs a clear, unambiguous identifier for what is being requested. If I just write a free‑text description, there is always a risk that the buyer or the system interprets it slightly differently, which can lead to confusion, extra clarification steps, or even the wrong item being sourced.  

So I ask myself how SAP avoids that ambiguity. The answer lies in the material master: each unique item that the company procures is assigned a material code, and that code is the key that locks the requisition to a specific record in the master data. By entering the code, I tell SAP exactly which set of specifications, valuation class, storage conditions, and other attributes belong to the item I need.  

Before I even create the requisition, I should check whether a code already exists for the item. If I find one, I can use it right away, which prevents me from creating a duplicate entry for the same thing. Duplicate material codes would clutter the master data, make reporting messy, and could cause the same item to be tracked under two different numbers, leading to errors in inventory and valuation.  

If the material isn’t yet coded, the reference material tells me to get it set up through the material master governor—usually the warehouse‑based team that maintains the material master. Once the code is created, I can proceed with the requisition. After the goods are received and the invoice is processed, the material is then capitalized (if it’s an asset) and the code remains attached throughout the entire procure‑to‑pay cycle.  

Having that code attached means the system can automatically trace the item from the requisition, through the purchase order, goods receipt, and invoice verification, all the way to payment. This end‑to‑end visibility supports accurate reporting, reliable inventory control, and smooth settlement because every transaction posts to the correct material master record.  

Putting it all together, using a material code in SAP when raising a Purchase Requisition ensures that the request is tied to the precise item master record, avoids duplicate entries, enables seamless processing through the procurement cycle, and keeps the data clean for reporting and inventory management. That is why it is important to always include the material code.

section: 3.10 Fixed Budget - based Selection (FBS) for consultancy services
question_text: Under FBS, what are the two permissible methods for selecting a consultant
answer:
- Verify that the consultant selection under Fixed Budget Based Selection (FBS) is conducted using one of the two permissible methods:  
  1. A competitive selection process based solely on quality, applying specific marking criteria; the consultant with the highest technical score that meets the fixed budget requirement is selected for contract award.  
  2. For repetitive or multiple assignments, the establishment of a panel of consultants meeting agreed quality criteria, after which a specific consultant is chosen for each assignment based on timeliness, practicability, and the number of prior assignments given to that consultant, with the budget for each assignment fixed by the procuring entity.  

(Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 26)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants the two allowed ways to pick a consultant when the Fixed Budget Based Selection (FBS) approach is used.  
Next, I recall that FBS is defined by setting a fixed budget for the consulting services in the tender document, which means the cost side is predetermined and the selection must focus on other criteria.  
Looking at the guidance on FBS, it explicitly states that the selection of the consultant shall be made by one of two specific methods, so I should identify those two methods directly.  
The first method described is a competitive process that evaluates proposals solely on quality, using predefined marking criteria; the consultant with the highest technical score that still fits within the fixed budget is chosen for the contract.  
The second method applies when there are repetitive or multiple assignments: a panel of consultants is first created based on agreed quality standards, and then for each individual assignment a consultant is selected from that panel by considering practical factors such as timeliness, suitability, and how many previous assignments that consultant has already received, while the budget for each assignment remains fixed by the procuring entity.  
Putting these together, I see that the two permissible methods under FBS are exactly the quality‑only competitive selection and the panel‑based selection for repetitive work, each with its own detailed procedure as outlined.  
This reasoning naturally leads to the answer that under FBS, consultant selection can be done either by a quality‑focused competitive bid or by using an empanelled panel with selection based on timeliness, practicability and past assignment load, with the budget fixed in both cases.
chunk_content:
3.10.1 There are three methods for selection/evaluation of consultancy proposals viz. Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS), Least Cost System (LCS) and Single Source Selection (SSS). The Fixed Budget Based Selection (FBS) method is hereby also allowed for selection of consultants. Under this method, cost of the consulting services shall be specified as a fixed budget in the tender document itself. FBS may be used when :

- (i) the type of consulting services required is simple and/or repetitive and can be precisely defined; and
- (ii) the budget can be reasonably estimated and set based on credible cost estimates and/ or previous selections which have been successfully executed; and
- (iii) the budget is sufficient for the consultant to perform the assignment.

3.10.2 Under FBS, the selection of the consultant shall be made by one of the following two methods :

- (i) By a competitive selection process, based only on quality, using specific marking criteria for quality. The proposal with the highest technical score that meets the fixed budget requirement shall be considered for placement of contract.
- (ii) In cases of repetitive or multiple assignments, by empanelling suitable quality criteria. Thereafter, selection of a specific consultant for a specific assignment from such panel shall be based on overall considerations of timeliness, practicability, number of other assignments already given to that consultant in the past, etc. In such cases the budget for each assignment shall also be fixed by the procuring entity.

Clear & unambiguous scoring methodology must be indicated so that there is no scope for subjective evaluation.

section: 9.3.2 Conditions Governing Operation of Option Clause
question_text: What security instrument should be used when issuing stores or prototypes to a contractor for fabrication guidance?
answer: - Issue stores or prototypes to contractors for fabrication guidance against an appropriate bank guarantee; additional insurance may be required if deemed necessary. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 146)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: when a procuring entity hands over tangible items like stores, drawings or prototypes to a contractor so that the contractor can use them as a guide for fabrication, what kind of security should protect those items? The core concern is safeguarding the entity’s property while it is in the contractor’s possession.

Next, I think about the general practice for loaning government or procuring‑entity assets to contractors. Transparency is key – the possibility of providing such resources should have been flagged in the tender or at least requested by the contractor and written into the contract. This sets the contractual backdrop for any protective measure.

From there, I focus on the specific situation of issuing stores or prototypes for fabrication guidance. The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals make it clear that, in these cases, the items should not be handed over without some form of financial backing that ensures their return or compensates for loss. The instrument that fits this purpose is a bank guarantee, which serves as a enforceable promise from the contractor’s bank to cover the value of the loaned items if they are not returned in good condition.

I then weigh whether a bank guarantee alone is sufficient. The manuals note that, in addition to the guarantee, appropriate insurance may be asked for when it is considered necessary. This suggests that the bank guarantee is the primary security, but an insurance layer can be added on top of it when the risk profile warrants extra protection.

Finally, I synthesize these points: the appropriate security instrument for issuing stores or prototypes to a contractor for fabrication guidance is a bank guarantee, with the option to require additional insurance if the circumstances deem it prudent. This aligns with the need to protect the procuring entity’s assets while allowing the contractor to use them for guidance.

question_text: Can a tender that was initially deemed unresponsive later be made responsive by correcting the issue
answer: ** No. Once a tender is classified as unresponsive because it fails to meet the basic requirements set out in the bid documents, it cannot be made responsive by later correcting or withdrawing the non‑conforming stipulation. This rule is stated explicitly in the procurement manual (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 72). Minor irregularities that do not constitute a material deviation may be waived under section 5.4.3, but they do not apply to tenders that have already been deemed unresponsive.
cot:
I begin by asking what it means for a tender to be labeled unresponsive. The procurement rules state that a tender is unresponsive when it fails to satisfy any of the basic requirements set out in the bid documents—things like missing signatures, absent earnest money deposits, ineligibility of the bidder, departure from essential terms, or not quoting for the full schedule of requirements. Because these are fundamental conditions, the tender is set aside immediately and is not considered further in either the technical‑commercial or financial evaluation.

Next, I consider whether there is any provision that allows a bidder to remedy such a deficiency after the initial determination. The Procurement of Works Manual makes it clear that once a tender has been classified as unresponsive, it cannot be revived by later correcting or withdrawing the non‑conforming stipulation. This is an explicit prohibition: unresponsive offers may not subsequently be made responsive by correction or withdrawal.

I then contrast this with the treatment of minor irregularities. The manual distinguishes minor issues—such as missing pages, illegible copies, or omitted attachments—that do not amount to a material deviation. These can be waived or clarified through a request for clarification, provided they do not affect the ranking or introduce a financial impact. However, this leniency applies only to tenders that have not already been deemed unresponsive; it does not override the rule that an unresponsive tender remains ineligible.

Putting these points together, I see that the core of the question hinges on the distinction between fundamental non‑compliance and trivial shortcomings. Since the tender in question failed a basic requirement, it falls into the first category, and the rule that bars any later correction applies directly. Therefore, the only logical conclusion is that a tender initially deemed unresponsive cannot later be made responsive by fixing the issue.

Finally, I verify that this conclusion matches the given answer: it affirms that correction is not permissible, notes the explicit rule, and acknowledges that only minor, non‑material irregularities may be waived—exactly what the answer states. The reasoning flows naturally from the definition of unresponsiveness, through the prohibition on correction, to the limited scope for minor irregularities, and ends with the clear answer that no, the tender cannot be rescued.

### 5.4.1 Confidentiality of Process
- i) Information relating to the examination, clarification, evaluation and comparison of bids, and recommendations for the award of a contract, shall not be disclosed to bidders or any other person not officially concerned with such a process until the award to the successful bidder has been announced.
- ii) From the time of bid opening to the time of contract award, no bidder shall contact the Procuring Entity on any matter related to the bid, except on request and prior written permission.
- iii) Any effort by the bidder to influence the Procuring Entity in bid evaluation, bid comparison or contract award decisions will vitiate the process and will result in the rejection of the bidder's bid. Such conditions, incurring in (i) & (ii) above shall be embedded in the Instructions to Bidders (1TB).

### 5.4.2 Unresponsive Tenders
Tenders that do not meet the basic requirements specified in the bid documents are to be treated as unresponsive (both during Techno-commercial evaluation and Financial Evaluation in case of Two Envelope bidding) and ignored. All tenders received will first be scrutinised by the dealing officer to see whether the tenders meet the basic requirements as incorporated in the Bid document and to identify unresponsive tenders, if any. Unresponsive offers may not subsequently be made responsive by correction or withdrawal of the non-conforming stipulation. Some important points on the basis of which a tender may be declared as unresponsive and be ignored during the initial scrutiny are:

- i) The tender is not in the prescribed format or is unsigned or not signed as per the stipulations in the bid document;
- ii) The required EMD has not been provided or exemption from EMD is claimed without acceptable proof of exemption;
- iii) The bidder is not eligible to participate in the bid as per laid down eligibility criteria (example: the tender enquiry condition says that the bidder has to be an enlisted contractor but the tenderer is not an enlisted contractor);
- iv) The bid departs from the essential requirements specified in the bidding document (for example, the tenderer has not agreed to give the required performance security); or

- v) Against a schedule in the list of requirements in the tender enquiry, the tenderer has not quoted for the entire requirement as specified in that schedule (example: in a schedule, it has been stipulated that the tenderer will supply the equipment, install and commission it and also train the Procuring Entity's operators for operating the equipment. The tenderer has, however, quoted only for supply of the equipment).

### 5.4.3 Minor Infirmary/ Irregularity/ Non-conformity
During the preliminary examination, some minor infirmity and/ or irregularity and/ or non-conformity may also be found in some tenders. Such minor issues could be missing pages/ attachment or illegibility in a submitted document; non-submission of requisite number of copies of a document. For example, the bidder submitted the amendment Bank Guarantee, but omitted to submit the main portion with Bid Document. These may be considered as minor irregularity. Such minor issues may be waived provided they do not constitute any material deviation (please also refer to Para 5.5.1 (iv) below) and financial impact and, also, do not prejudice or affect the ranking order of the tenderers. Wherever necessary, observations on such 'minor' issues (as mentioned above) may be conveyed to the tenderer by e-mail / through e-tendering portal, and so on, asking him to respond by a specified date also mentioning therein that, if the tenderer does not conform Procuring Entity's view or respond by that specified date, his tender will be liable to be rejected. Depending on the outcome, such tenders are to be ignored or considered further.

section: 2.2 Preparation of Preliminary Project Report (PPR) or Rough Cost Estimate
question_text: What is the minimum project value that triggers the requirement to prepare a Preliminary Project Report (PPR)?
answer: The manuals outline the contents of a PPR, which include the background of the work, details of scope, exclusions, availability of land and auxiliary services, reference to concept plans, rough cost estimate, cost benefits analysis, cash flow, source and availability of funds, and other relevant documents. They also state that approval of the competent authority for accepting the necessity of works and its scope may be sought on the basis of the PPR or Rough Cost Estimate. ## 2.2 Preparation of Preliminary Project Report (PPR) or Rough Cost Estimate
2.2.1 A preliminary project report (PPR) or Rough Cost Estimate shall be prepared based on Land, Site Details, functional and space requirements (or Various Facilities, Special Requirements/ Features and Broad Specifications for specialised Equipment and Plants), Layout Plans etc, with the technical details/ documents.

2.2.2 The preliminary project report shall provide the following details:

- i) Background of the work/ project justifying the need for the work
- ii) Details of scope of the project / work.
- iii) Exclusions (if any) - This will cover part of the work, which is not included in this particular project estimate.
- iv) Availability of land - There should be a clear indication about the availability of land required for completion of whole project. The land shall be made available free of all encumbrances.
- v) Availability of auxiliary services - like roads, power, water, solid & liquid waste disposal system, street lighting and other civic services shall be ensured.
- vi) Reference to Concept Plans/ Preliminary Drawings, if any and their acceptance
  - This shall indicate the details of Concept Plans/ Preliminary Drawings prepared and their approval by the requisitioning authority.
- vii) Rough Cost Estimate: NRL may carefully assess alternative technological options, their area requirements and obtain Rough Cost on the basis of prevailing Plinth Area rates (or any other reliable basis) without preparation of drawings to enable the competent authority to accord in principle approval.
- viii) If relevant, Cost benefits analysis of the project, including evaluation of options for cost sharing/ recovery (user charges) for infrastructure/ services. Principles of Life Cycle Cost may also be considered, to the extent feasible.
- ix) Cash flow: This will show year-wise requirement.
- x) Source & availability of funds - The manner of transferring the fund to the executing agency to be spelt out.
- xi) Any other relevant documents.
- xii) A presentation on the findings of the feasibility study/ PPR may be made by a team

(which may include engineers/ consultants/ outside experts, finance officers etc.) before the competent authority.

Approval of competent authority for accepting the necessity of works and its Scope may be sought on the basis of PPR or Rough Cost Estimate.

question_text: Which elements must be included in the tender enquiry document to define the scope of a maintenance service?
answer:
To define the scope of a maintenance service in the tender enquiry document, the following elements must be included:

- A clear description of the services required for maintenance of the goods.  
- The required period of maintenance.  
- Other relevant terms and conditions, especially payment terms (e.g., half‑yearly or quarterly).  
- Service Level Agreement details where applicable, covering guaranteed uptime, performance output levels, channels for registering service requests, response times, escalation procedures, monitoring of service levels, help‑line/complaint registration, inventory of common spares, use of genuine spares, and any liquidated‑damage provisions for delays or performance degradation.  
- Specification of what the maintenance charges include or exclude, such as visiting charges, price of spares (noting that consumables like rubber gaskets, bulbs, etc., may be excluded), and price of consumables (fuel, lubricants, cartridges, etc.).  

These elements ensure that bidders understand the full maintenance obligation and allow the purchasing organisation to evaluate total cost of ownership. (Procurement of Goods Manual, pp. 141-142)
cot:
First, I consider what it means to “define the scope” of a maintenance service in a tender enquiry document – the purchaser must make it absolutely clear to bidders exactly what work is expected, for how long, and under what conditions, so that the offers can be compared on a common basis.  

A maintenance contract is only meaningful after the warranty period, and the purchaser can either bundle it with the supply tender or run a separate tender; in either case the enquiry must spell out the maintenance obligations.  

The first thing that jumps out is the need to describe the services required for maintaining the goods – without a clear statement of what tasks are to be performed (inspections, repairs, replacements, etc.), bidders cannot know what they are pricing.  

Next, the duration of that service is essential; the enquiry must state the required period of maintenance (e.g., three years, five years) because the length directly affects the total cost and the supplier’s resource planning.  

Beyond the basic description and period, the document has to contain other relevant terms and conditions, especially the payment terms – whether payments are half‑yearly, quarterly, or tied to milestones – since cash‑flow expectations are part of the scope definition.  

For more complex or large‑scale contracts, the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals indicate that a Service Level Agreement (SLA) should be woven into the enquiry. This means specifying guaranteed uptime percentages, required performance output levels, how service requests are to be logged, expected response times, escalation channels, monitoring procedures, help‑line or complaint registration processes, the need to keep an inventory of common spares, the obligation to use genuine spares, and any liquidated‑damage clauses for missed responses or performance degradation.  

Finally, to avoid disputes later, the enquiry must clarify what the maintenance charges actually cover or exclude – visiting charges, the price of spares (noting that consumables like rubber gaskets, bulbs, etc., may be left out), and the price of consumables such as fuel, lubricants, or cartridges.  

Putting these pieces together – a precise service description, the maintenance period, clear terms and conditions (especially payment), SLA details where appropriate, and an explicit statement of what is included or excluded in the charges – gives bidders a full picture of the maintenance obligation and lets the purchasing organisation evaluate the total cost of ownership. This collection of elements is exactly what must be included in the tender enquiry document to define the scope of a maintenance service.

### 2.2.1 Conflict of Interest in case of consultants
- i) The consultant is required to provide professional, objective, and impartial advice, at all times holding the Procuring Entity's interests paramount, strictly avoiding conflicts with other assignments or his/its own corporate interests, and acting without any consideration for future work.

- ii) The consultant has an obligation to disclose to the Procuring Entity any situation of actual or potential conflict that impacts its/his capacity to serve the best interest of its client/Procuring Entity. Failure to disclose such situations may lead to the disqualification of the consultant or termination of its/his contract during execution of the assignment.
- iii) Without limitation on the generality of the foregoing, and unless stated otherwise in the data sheet for the RfP document, the consultant (i.e., private entities) shall not be hired under the circumstances set forth below:
  - a) **Conflicting activities:** a firm that has been engaged by the client to provide goods, works, or non-consultancy services for a project, or any of its affiliates, shall be disqualified from providing Consultancy service resulting from or directly related to those goods, works, or non- Consultancy services for the same project. Conversely, a firm hired to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, or any of its affiliates, shall be disqualified from subsequently providing goods or works or non-consultancy services resulting from or directly related to the consultancy services for such preparation or implementation for the same project;
  - b) **Conflicting assignments:** Consultants (including its experts and sub--consultants) or any of their affiliates shall not be hired for any assignment that, by its nature, may be in conflict with another assignment of the consultant for the same Procuring Entity.

### 2.2.2 Unfair Competitive Advantage in case of consultants
Fairness and transparency in the selection process require that the consultants or their affiliates competing for a specific assignment do not derive an unfair competitive advantage from having provided consultancy services related to the assignment in question. Such unfair competitive advantage is best avoided by full transparency and by providing equal opportunity so that all firms or individuals interested or involved have full information about a service assignment and its nature, scope, and background information. To that end, the request for proposals and all information would be made available to all short listed consultants simultaneously.

question_text: What contractual clause should be included in tender documents to limit the Procuring Entity's liability for tax changes on raw materials
answer: - Include a clause stating that the Procuring Entity is not liable for any supplier claim arising from fresh imposition or increase (including statutory) in excise duty, customs duty, sales tax, or similar levies on raw materials/components used directly in the manufacture of the contracted goods during the contract period, unless such liability is expressly agreed in the contract. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 114)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants a contractual provision that shields the Procuring Entity from having to pay extra when taxes on the raw materials used to make the contracted goods go up during the life of the contract.  

Next, I consider why such a provision is necessary. Tax rates—excise, customs, sales, or similar levies—can be altered by statute or regulation while a contract is still being performed. If the supplier’s cost rises because of a new tax or an increase, they might seek reimbursement from the Procuring Entity unless the contract clearly says who bears that risk.  

Then, I think about risk allocation. In most procurement arrangements, the supplier is expected to absorb fluctuations in input costs unless the parties agree otherwise. To avoid disputes and unexpected liabilities, the Procuring Entity should make it explicit that it will not be responsible for any claim the supplier might make based on those tax changes.  

After that, I refine the wording of the clause. It must cover any fresh imposition or increase—including statutory increases—in excise duty, customs duty, sales tax, and any comparable levies that apply to the raw materials or components directly used in manufacturing the goods. The clause should also make clear that this non‑liability applies for the entire duration of the contract, unless the contract itself expressly states that the Procuring Entity will assume such liability.  

Finally, I verify that the clause, when placed in the tender documents, achieves the goal: it tells tenderers up front that they bear the risk of tax changes on raw materials, thereby limiting the Procuring Entity’s exposure to unexpected tax‑related claims. This matches the required answer.

### 6.8.2 Octroi and Local Taxes
In case the goods supplied against contracts placed by Procuring Entity are exempted from levy of town duty, Octroi duty, terminal tax and other levies of local bodies, the suppliers should be informed accordingly by incorporating suitable instructions in the tender enquiry document and in the resultant contract. Wherever required, the supplier should obtain the exemption certificate from the Purchasing Department to avoid payment of such levies and taxes.

In case such payments are not exempted (or are demanded in spite of the exemption certificate), the supplier should make the payment to avoid delay in supplies and forward the receipt to the Purchasing Department for reimbursement and for further necessary action.

### 6.8.3 Customs Duty on Imported Goods
On imported goods, the tenderers shall also specify separately the total amount of custom duty included in the quoted price. The tenderers should also indicate correctly the rate of custom duty applicable for the goods in question and the corresponding Indian customs tariff number. Where customs duty is payable, the contract should clearly stipulate the quantum of duty payable, and so on, in unambiguous terms. The standard clauses to be utilised for this purpose are to be incorporated in the tender enquiry documents. Any import of materials directly from the supplier or manufacturer should be in the name of Procuring Entity. In this regard, all formalities will be completed by Procuring Entity engaging a Custom House Agent (CHA) and payment in this regard will be borne by Procuring Entity.

The Government has allowed exemption from payment of customs duty on certain types of goods for use by the following organisations:

- i) Scientific and technical instruments imported by research institutes;
- ii) Hospital equipment imported by Government hospitals; and
- iii) Consumable goods imported by a public-funded research institution or a university.

However, to avail of such exemptions, the organisations are required to produce a "Custom Duty Exemption" certificate and "Not Manufactured in India" certificate at the appropriate time.

The relevant contemporary instructions covering these aspects should be incorporated in the tender enquiry document and in the resultant contract.

### 6.8.4 Duties/Taxes on Raw Materials
Procuring Entity is not liable for any claim from the supplier on account of fresh imposition and/or increase (including statutory increase) in excise duty, custom duty, sales tax, and so on, on raw materials and/or components used directly in the manufacture of the contracted goods taking place during the pendency of the contract, unless such liability is specifically agreed to in terms of the

contract. A clause to this effect should also form part of the tender documents.

** Consultants are shortlisted by issuing an Expression of Interest (EoI) through open advertisement; responses are reviewed and those meeting the required qualifications and experience are placed on a shortlist, which normally contains between three and eight eligible firms.  
**Rationale:** This approach encourages wide and open competition among capable consultants before proceeding to the technical and financial proposal stage. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 22)

First, I consider that the selection process for consultancy services is described as a two‑stage approach, where the initial stage is meant to narrow down the field to those consultants who appear capable of handling the assignment.

## 3.6 Systems of Selection of service providers
3.6.1 Since the quality and scope of a consultancy assignment are not tangibly identifiable and consistently measurable, the technical and financial capability of consultants becomes an important though indirect determinant for quality and scope of performance. In such a situation value for money is achieved by encouraging wide and open competition among equally competent consultant. Thus, selection of consultants is therefore, normally done in a two stage process. In the first stage, likely capable sources are shortlisted, if need be through an 'Expression of Interest' (EoI) through advertisement (i.e., open notifications). On the basis of responses received, consultants meeting the relevant qualification and experience requirements for the given assignment are shortlisted for further consideration. The shortlist should include a sufficient number, generally not fewer than three (3) and not more than eight (8) eligible firms. In the second stage, the shortlisted consultants are invited to submit their technical and financial (RfP) proposals generally in separate sealed envelopes. Evaluation of the technical proposal is carried out by evaluators without access to the financial part of the proposal. Financial proposals are opened after evaluation of quality.

3.6.2 The relative importance of Quality and Price aspects may vary from assignment to assignment depending on complexities/ criticality of quality requirements, internal capability of Procuring Entity to engage and supervise the assignment, as well as the value of procurements. Hence different systems of selection of consultants/ service providers are designed to achieve appropriate relative importance (weightage) of Quality and Price aspects. Decision on system of selection is normally preceded by an assessment of the capacity of the user to engage and supervise the implementation of proposed assignment. The selection method chosen depends to some extent on this assessment. Selection of system of selection also should take into account the likely field of Bidders.

3.6.3 The nomenclature of various selection methods below is in line with generally prevalent nomenclature.

- i) Price based System - Least Cost Selection (LCS);
- ii) Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS);
- iii) Direct Selection: Single Source Selection (SSS)

3.6.4 Unlike Procurement of Consultancy Services, **procurement of other services is done by a simpler process akin to those of procurement of Goods and Works.** In procurement of other (non-consultancy) services normally system of selection used is lowest price (L-1) basis as in procurement of Goods/ works for technically responsive offers. Under very special circumstances Single Source Selection may also be used. However, in highly technical and complex services, where quality is important (say in studies like seismic surveys, airborne data acquisition etc) where use of QCBS system appears to be called for, it may be better handled as a consultancy contract.

3.6.5 It is possible that there may be single offer situation against open tenders and there may be tendency to go for re-tender as a safe course of action. Re-bidding has costs: firstly the actual costs of retendering; secondly the delay in execution of the work with consequent delay in the attainment of the purpose for which the procurement is being done; and thirdly the possibility that the re-bid

may result in a higher bid. Even when only one Bid is submitted, the process may be considered valid provided following conditions are satisfied:

- 1) The procurement was satisfactorily publicized and sufficient time was given for submission of bids.
- 2) The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive; and
- 3) Prices are reasonable in comparison to market values

## 8.15 Terminating Services Prior to End of Contract
8.15.1 At times, a decision is taken to terminate a contract prior to its conclusion and the completion of the Consultancy and other services assignment. This may be for various reasons, for example:

- i) **Termination due to External factors:** External factors (like natural disasters) which are beyond the control of the consultant/ service provider or the Procuring Entity;
- ii) **Termination for convenience:** The Procuring Entity may also terminate a contract for convenience for reasons like shortage of budget;
- iii) **Termination due to breach of contract:** Failure/ inability of one party or the other.

8.15.2 In some cases, termination is the optimal choice; in others, it is detrimental to the overall intent of the assignment. This implies a missed opportunity and a waste of the funds already expended on the assignment. For these reasons, termination should be avoided, if possible, even if this means a considerable re-staffing of the Consultancy team.

8.15.3 Termination may be initiated by any party. Termination must be undertaken within the terms of the contract document. These provide for a notice period of 30 (thirty) days, the payment by the Procuring Entity of any legitimate outstanding fees and costs to the consultant/ service provider, and the payment of legitimate costs to wind-up the Consultancy/ other service team (unless the termination was occasioned by the default of the consultant/ service provider). If termination is initiated by the consultant / service provider the bid security (EMD) / security deposit, if any, available with NRL may be forfeited.

8.15.4 The CMC/EIC would indicate which of the final billings by the firm are eligible for payment and which are not. In case of dispute over what is or is not a legitimate expense, eligible for payment, the dispute mechanism described above is invoked and, if it is not possible to resolve the matter amicably, the issue is submitted for arbitration. The contract will remain valid until the arbitration decision is made.

## 8.16 Concluding the Assignment
The contract is normally considered concluded on the day after the completion date listed in the contract. Any expenditure incurred after the completion date are unlikely to be paid. It is therefore, important, under all types of assignments, for the consultant/ service provider to request an extension of the completion date if it appears that additional time will be needed to complete the assigned scope of services after the contractual completion date. The consultant/ service provider should submit the final claim promptly after completing the assignment. The standard consultant/ service provider contract states that the claim must be submitted within 60 (sixty) days of completion.

question_text: Who grants approval for a tender after the price bid has been opened and the award is made?
answer:
- After the price bid is opened and the award is made, the approving authority varies with the proposal’s estimated/order value and the body that originally sanctioned it.  
  - **If the proposal was (or would have been) approved by the Board, SCBT or CFD**, the same body (Board/SCBT/CFD) grants the post‑award approval.  
  - **For all other proposals**, approval is given by the committee one level above the committee that originally approved the Technical Evaluation Committee (TEC) based on the estimated/order value.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 131)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: after the price bid has been opened and an award has been made, which authority is responsible for giving the final approval to proceed with that tender?  

Then, I sort out the conditions that influence this decision. The reference material makes it clear that the approving authority is not fixed; it depends on two related factors—the estimated or order value of the proposal and which body originally sanctioned the proposal (or would have sanctioned it if it had reached that stage).  

Next, I break down the two distinct cases that emerge from those conditions. If the proposal was, or would have been, approved by the highest‑level bodies—namely the Board, the SCBT, or the CFD—then the same body retains the authority to approve the tender even after the price bid is opened and the award is made. This makes sense because those bodies already exercised oversight at the planning stage, so continuity of approval is logical.  

For all other proposals, the approving authority shifts to a different level. Specifically, it is the committee that sits one step above the committee that originally approved the Technical Evaluation Committee (TEC) for that proposal, again calibrated to the proposal’s estimated or order value. This ensures that proposals that did not initially require top‑level endorsement still receive appropriate scrutiny from a higher supervisory tier once the bidding process is complete.  

Further, I consider why the rule is structured this way. By tying post‑award approval to the original sanctioning body—or to the next higher committee when the original sanction was at a lower level—the process maintains a clear chain of accountability and prevents gaps in oversight that could arise after bids are opened.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: after the price bid is opened and the award is made, the approving authority is determined by whether the proposal was (or would have been) cleared by the Board, SCBT, or CFD; if so, that same body grants approval. Otherwise, approval falls to the committee one level above the TEC‑approving committee, with the exact level dictated by the proposal’s estimated/order value. This matches the description of the post‑award approval process.

question_text: What are the consequences of treating reimbursable items separately for compliance with statutory requirements
answer:
Statutory‑related costs such as PF, ESI, overtime, shift/height allowances, safety items, PPE, toll fees, travel expenses, accommodation and statutory charges are kept as “SOR items not to be quoted by the bidder” and are reimbursed only on submission of documentary evidence after the EIC verifies the rates for reasonableness.  

As a result, several consequences emerge that directly support compliance with statutory requirements:  

* The PR estimate includes the reimbursable amount but shows it separately, making it clear that these statutory contributions are not part of the competitive bid price.  
* When determining bidders’ PQC and the EMD limit, the total estimated cost—encompassing both the SOR items to be quoted and the reimbursable items—is used, ensuring that the financial capacity to meet statutory obligations is evaluated up front.  
* TEC approval is based on the total financial outgo, which incorporates the reimbursable items and all taxes, guaranteeing that the agency has funded the full scope of statutory payments before work began.  
* The final contract value excludes the reimbursable items, while the security deposit and performance guarantee are calculated on that same base, preventing any accidental under‑funding of statutory dues.  
* Upon completion, the job completion certificate itemises both the executed basic value and the executed reimbursable items, providing a transparent record that all statutory contributions had been actually paid.  
* Any contract variations are assessed on the final executed value that includes the reimbursable items, and liquidated damages are applied only to the contract value excluding those items, preserving the integrity of the statutory‑related funds throughout the project lifecycle.  

By keeping these items separate, it is ensured that statutory requirements are met uniformly, quality standards are upheld, and the same treatment can be replicated across other procurement initiatives, thereby fulfilling the manual’s goal of compliance, quality and uniformity. (Procurement of Works Manual, p.21)
cot:
First, I think about why certain costs—like PF, ESI, overtime, shift/height allowances, safety items, PPE, toll fees, travel expenses, accommodation and statutory charges—might be pulled out of the regular bid price and treated as reimbursable items.  

Looking at the manual’s guidance, these items are kept as “SOR items not to be quoted by the bidder” and are only paid back after the contractor submits documentary evidence and the EIC verifies the rates for reasonableness; this approach is meant to safeguard statutory compliance, maintain quality standards and achieve uniform treatment across projects.  

With that purpose in mind, I trace how the separation plays out at each stage of procurement. The PR estimate must include the reimbursable amount but show it separately, so the statutory contributions are visible even though they are not part of the competitive price.  

When evaluating bidders’ PQC and setting the EMD limit, the total estimated cost—combining the quoted SOR items and the reimbursable items—is used, ensuring that the agency checks up front whether the bidder has the financial capacity to meet those statutory obligations.  

TEC approval then hinges on confirming the total financial outgo, which adds the reimbursable items and all taxes; this guarantees that the full scope of statutory payments is funded before any work starts.  

The resulting contract value excludes the reimbursable items, and both the security deposit and performance guarantee are calculated on that same base, preventing any accidental under‑funding of the statutory dues that could arise from guarantees tied only to the quoted price.  

Upon job completion, the completion certificate itemises the executed basic value alongside the executed reimbursable items, giving a transparent record that all statutory contributions have actually been paid.  

If the contract varies, the variation amount is assessed on the final executed value that includes the reimbursable items (excluding any built‑in escalation), while liquidated damages for delay are applied only to the contract value excluding those items, preserving the integrity of the statutory‑related funds throughout changes and potential delays.  

Seeing how each step—clear separation in estimates, inclusion in qualification and approvals, exclusion from contract value and guarantees, itemised completion, and protected treatment in variations and LDs—directly supports the goal of meeting statutory requirements uniformly, I conclude that treating reimbursable items separately yields exactly the consequences described: it makes statutory costs visible, ensures financial capacity is vetted, guarantees full funding, safeguards against under‑funding via guarantees, provides auditable proof of payment, and shields those funds from being diluted by contract changes or delay penalties, thereby fulfilling the manual’s aim of compliance, quality and uniformity.

## 2.10 Estimation for Reimbursement Items
The PR comprise of the SOR of the activities against which the agency has to quote its bid price and perform them as per the terms and conditions of the contract. Normally bidder has to quote for all the items of the SOR.

But in certain contracts, items like PF, ESI, Overtime, Shift/Height Allowance, Safety Items, PPE, Toll Fee, Travel Expenses, Accommodation, Statutory Charges etc. are separately kept in the contracts as “reimbursable items”. These items are kept as ‘SOR items not to be quoted by the bidder’. Contractor has to perform these activities and get reimbursed as per terms & conditions of the contract.

Provision for reimbursement of actual outgo from the contractor is kept, and payment is released on submission of documentary evidence. The rates for reimbursement shall be duly verified for reasonableness by the EIC before certification for payment. This is done to keep such items outside the ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ as a measure to ensure compliance of statutory requirements, quality standards and uniformity.

For estimation of such “reimbursement items” a standard practice should be followed across all departments as far as possible, to ensure meeting the quality norms at uniform rate.

**Treatment of “REIMBURSEMENT ITEMS” in various stages of procurement, shall be as follows:-**

- a) **PR Estimate:** The PR estimate should be inclusive of the reimbursable amount, which is to be shown separately.
- b) **Bidders’ PQC:** The estimated cost for determination of PQC shall be the total estimated cost including ‘reimbursable items’ as well as ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ (excluding GST).
- c) **EMD value limit:** The estimated cost for determination of EMD shall be the total estimated cost including ‘reimbursable items’ as well as ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ (excluding GST).

- d) **TEC Approval:** TEC approval should be based on total financial outgo i.e., including any 'reimbursable items' and including all taxes.
- e) **Contract Value:** The contract value shall be the total awarded value of items, excluding any provision for 'reimbursement items'. Provision for 'reimbursement items' shall be separately mentioned. GST rate shall be separately mentioned.
- f) **Security Deposit / Performance Guarantee:** Security deposit shall be applicable on contract value excluding reimbursement items.
- g) **Job Completion Certificate:** The job completion certificate should be issued for total value of works executed, including any provision for 'reimbursement items'. Executed basic value and executed 'reimbursable items' shall be separately mentioned. (All values excluding GST).
- h) **Contract Variation:** The variation amount and percentage for the purpose of determining approving authority for variation of contract value would be based on the final executed value including any "reimbursement items" but excluding "changes due to inbuilt escalation/variation clause". The base amount shall be the awarded order value based on originally approved TEC. In case of clear original tender provisions for extension/enhancement in AMC/ARC (for 1+1 years, or 2+1 years etc.), the base value shall be the total awarded order value including extension/enhancement. However, all other variations such as extra item, additional qty., increase/decrease in man-days, etc. shall be treated as variation in contract value. Further, authority for approval for final executed contract value should be based on total financial outgo including all taxes as per DOA.
- i) **Liquidated Damages / Price reduction for delay:** LD / PRC shall be applicable on contract value excluding reimbursement items.

question_text: Why must emergency or distress‑sale prices be excluded from LPP comparisons for future procurement
answer:
Emergency or distress‑sale prices must be excluded from Last Purchase Price (LPP) comparisons because they do not provide accurate guidelines for future procurement. Such prices arise under abnormal conditions and can distort market‑based benchmarks, jeopardizing transparency and the achievement of value‑for‑money objectives. Consequently, procurement records should clearly note that these prices are not valid LPP for use in future contract evaluations.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 126)
cot:
First, I consider what the Last Purchase Price (LPP) is meant to do: it serves as a reference point for judging whether a new offer is reasonable, so it has to reflect a price that could be expected under ordinary market conditions.  

Looking at how emergency or distress‑sale prices come about, they are the result of abnormal pressures—either the buyer is forced to act quickly because of an urgent need, or the seller is eager to unload stock under duress. In either case the transaction does not represent the typical interplay of supply and demand that sets a normal market rate.  

If such an outlier were taken as the LPP, the benchmark would be distorted. A distress‑sale price, often markedly lower, would make future offers look expensive by comparison, while an emergency purchase price, often inflated, would make future offers seem too cheap. Either way the assessment of reasonableness would be skewed, leading to either unnecessary rejection of fair bids or unjustified acceptance of overpriced ones.  

This distortion undermines the core objectives of procurement: transparency and value‑for‑money. Decision‑makers would be basing their judgments on a price that does not reflect what the market would normally bear, which could erode confidence in the process and cause the organization to pay more—or less—than it should over time.  

Because of these risks, the guidance treats emergency and distress‑sale prices as invalid for LPP purposes. They must be flagged in the records and excluded from any future price‑reasonableness comparison, ensuring that the LPP used for benchmarking remains a genuine market‑based reference.  

Thus, emergency or distress‑sale prices are omitted from LPP comparisons to preserve the integrity, transparency, and value‑for‑money goals of the procurement process.

question_text: What is the purpose of the PQB/EOI stage in a two stage bidding process
answer: - The PQB/EOI stage evaluates bidders’ qualification and eligibility to shortlist qualified bidders for the second‑stage assessment of technical‑commercial and financial proposals. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 73)
cot:
First, I think about what distinguishes a two‑stage bidding process from a single‑stage one: the evaluation of bidders is split into two separate phases, with the first phase focusing only on whether a bidder is capable and eligible to undertake the contract.  

Looking at the description of the two‑stage approach, the first phase is labelled the PQB/EOI stage, which suggests it deals with pre‑qualification or an expression of interest rather than the detailed technical or price offers.  

This leads me to consider what information would be collected at that point—typically things like legal registration, financial strength, relevant past experience, and any mandatory eligibility documents—because those are the factors that determine if a bidder can even be considered for the work.  

If the procuring entity allowed all bidders to move forward regardless of these basic qualifications, the second stage would waste time evaluating technical and financial proposals from firms that are fundamentally unsuitable, so the logical purpose of the PQB/EOI stage is to filter out those that do not meet the minimum requirements.  

Therefore, the PQB/EOI stage serves to assess bidders’ qualification and eligibility, producing a shortlist of only those who satisfy the criteria, and this shortlisted group then proceeds to the second stage where their technical‑commercial and financial proposals are examined in detail.  

This reasoning directly matches the given answer: the PQB/EOI stage evaluates bidders’ qualification and eligibility to shortlist qualified bidders for the second‑stage assessment of technical‑commercial and financial proposals.
