### 5.5.3 Evaluation of Financial Bids and Ranking of Tenders
In case of two/multiple bid system, priced bid shall be opened only after the techno-commercial evaluation is complete, for evaluation of Financial Bids and ranking of tenders:-

- i) **Unresponsive Tenders:** Unresponsive tenders may again be identified after Financial Bid opening, as in case of Technical Bid opening. If the price bid is ambiguous so that it may very well lead to two equally valid total price amounts, then the bid should be treated as unresponsive.
- ii) **Non-conformities between Figures and Words:** Sometimes, non- conformities/ errors are also observed in responsive tenders between the quoted prices in figures and in words. This situation normally does not arise in case of e-Procurement. This should be taken care by defining the treatment of bids in the tender documents in the manner indicated below:
  - i) If, in the price structure quoted for the requirements, there is discrepancy between

the unit price and total price (which is obtained by multiplying the unit price by the quantity, or the total price is not worked out by bidder), the unit price shall prevail and the total price corrected accordingly;

- ii) If there is an error in a total corresponding to the addition or subtraction of sub-totals, the sub-totals shall prevail and the total shall be corrected; and
  - iii) If there is a discrepancy between words and figures, the amount in words shall prevail.
  - iv) Such a discrepancy in an offer should be conveyed to the tenderer asking him to respond by a target date and if the tenderer does not agree to Procuring Entity's observation, the tender is liable to be rejected.
- iii) **Correction of Bids:** Tender document should indicate that the evaluated bid prices will be adjusted after taking into account: (a) correction for errors; (b) adjustments for any acceptable variations, deviations; and (c) adjustments to reflect any discounts or other modifications offered. Unless announced beforehand explicitly in the tender documents, the quoted price should not be loaded on the basis of deviations in the commercial conditions. If it is decided to incorporate such clauses, these should be unambiguous and clear - and thereafter there should be no relaxation during evaluation. Variations, deviations, or alternative offers and other factors which are in excess of the bidding documents or otherwise result in unsolicited benefits for the contractor should not be taken into account in bid evaluation. All duties, taxes and other levies payable by the bidder under the contract or for any other cause shall be included in the rates, prices and total bid prices, and considered in evaluation of bids. Bids should be checked for any arithmetical errors. These corrections shall be done in accordance with the provisions of the bidding document. In cases other than e-Procurement, the quoted rates in the bids shall be protected with lamination by the committee, if not done by the bidders. In accordance with the corrections as approved by the Tender opening Committee, the amount stated in the bid will be adjusted with the concurrence of the bidder, and shall be binding on him. If the bidder does not accept the corrected amount, the bid will be rejected and the bid security forfeited. The arithmetical corrections will be done by the representatives of the Finance & Commercial department.
- iv) **Financial Evaluation:** All responsive bids are evaluated by the TEC with a view to select the lowest (L1) bidder - the lowest evaluated, substantially responsive, bid which meets the eligibility/ qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects.

question_text: Why should evaluation avoid hearsay information or undeclared conditions
answer: Evaluation must exclude hearsay information and undeclared conditions to ensure that every bidder is judged solely on verifiable, stated criteria. This preserves transparency, prevents any supplier from gaining an undue advantage, and upholds fairness in the selection process. By relying only on documented terms and conditions, the evaluation supports the process. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 116)
cot:
First, I consider what the evaluation process is fundamentally trying to achieve: selecting the supplier that best meets the stated requirements of the contract on an objective basis.  
Then, I ask what kinds of information can legitimately be used in that assessment—only facts that are explicitly recorded in the tender documents or that can be independently verified, because anything else rests on assumption rather than evidence.  
Next, I examine hearsay: it is second‑hand, unverified talk that may be inaccurate or biased, and relying on it would introduce criteria that bidders had no opportunity to address or contest.  
Similarly, undeclared conditions are requirements or preferences that were never communicated in the tender; bringing them in after the fact creates hidden standards that distort the level playing field.  
I see how this undermines transparency: if bidders cannot know what they are being judged against, they cannot tailor their offers fairly, and the process appears arbitrary.  
This opacity opens the door to inadvertent favoritism or perceived unfairness, which can lead to challenges, loss of trust, and potential legal or reputational risk for the procuring entity.  
Finally, I conclude that to preserve a fair, transparent, and risk‑aware selection—one that truly delivers value for money and aligns with organizational goals—evaluation must strictly avoid hearsay and any undeclared conditions, judging each bid solely on the verifiable, stated terms of the tender.

## 6.10 e-Payment
e-Banking and e-payments are now used by various banks by adopting Electronic Clearing System (ECS) and Electronic Fund Transfer (NEFT/ RTGS) procedure. Payments to suppliers may be made through such mechanism where such facilities are available. As per RBI guidelines, ECS mandate in RBI's format may be obtained at the time of registration of suppliers and in the bid document. The Format is available with all Banks.

All payments (including any advances) are to be routed through e-payment method (NEFT/RTGS/Online mode etc.), as per terms of the contract.

E-invoices / digitally signed invoices should be the preferred mode of invoicing to enable faster processing.

Payment through cheque, demand draft or such instruments may be made on exceptional cases following the prevailing guidelines issued by Finance Dept. from time to time.

## 6.11 Deduction of Income Tax, GST, and so on, at Source from Payments to Suppliers
This will be done as per the existing law in force during the currency of the contract.

## 6.12 Payment against Time Barred Claims
Ordinarily, all claims are time barred after a period of three years calculated from the date when the payment falls due unless the payment claim has been under correspondence. However, the limitation is saved if there is an admission of liability to pay, and fresh period of limitation starts from the time such admission is made. The paying authority is to ensure that no payment against such time barred claim is made till a decision has been taken in this regard by the CA.

# Chapter 7: Evaluation of Bids and Award of Contract


## 7.1 Tender Evaluation
7.1.1 The evaluation of tenders is one of the most significant areas of purchase management and the process must be transparent. All tenders are to be evaluated strictly on the basis of the terms and conditions incorporated in the tender document and those stipulated by the tenderers in their tenders. The Contracting Authority may include quality, price, technical merit, aesthetic and functional characteristics, environmental characteristics, running costs, cost-effectiveness, after-sales service and technical assistance, delivery date and delivery period or period of completion etc. No criteria shall be used for evaluation of tenders that cannot be verified. No hearsay information or hitherto undeclared condition should be brought in while evaluating the tenders. Care should be taken that preferences provided to any category of bidders on certain specified grounds should not result in single vendor selection. Similarly, no tender enquiry condition (especially the significant/essential ones) should be overlooked/ relaxed while evaluating the tenders. The aim should be ensure that no tenderer gets undue advantage at the cost of other tenderers and/or at the cost of Procuring Entity. Information relating to evaluation of tenders and the Tender Evaluation Committee's (TEC's) deliberations should be confidential and not be shared with persons not officially connected with the process. TEC should normally comprise of members including Finance and a representative of the user as per DOA in order to carry out evaluation of the tenders. TEC should not be very large as it may slow down the evaluation process. However, suitable domain/ technical experts may be included in the committee to render assistance in evaluation of the bids. The dealing officer of the proposal will work as a convenor of the TEC. No member of the tender committee should be reporting directly to any other member of such committee The process of tender evaluation is described in the subsequent paras.

question_text: What steps does the in‑house multidisciplinary team take to assure quality of work according to section 6.2.1
answer: The in‑house multidisciplinary team inspects the work, verifies that it meets the required standards, and controls the quality to achieve the desired level as set out in the contractual terms and specifications (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 91).
cot:
I start by clarifying what the question is really after: it wants the exact actions that the in‑house multidisciplinary team performs to guarantee quality, as spelled out in section 6.2.1.  
Turning my attention to that clause, I see a straightforward statement about the team’s role—it says they will inspect, verify and control the quality of work to the desired standard in line with the contractual terms and specifications.  
From that sentence I pull out the three core verbs that describe what the team does: first they inspect the work, then they verify that it meets the required standards, and finally they control the quality to keep it at that level.  
I note that the goal of these actions is to ensure the work conforms to the benchmark set by the contract and specifications, so each step is directed toward achieving that defined standard.  
Bringing the pieces together, I conclude that the in‑house multidisciplinary team assures quality by inspecting the work, verifying it meets the required standards, and controlling the quality to achieve the desired level as set out in the contractual terms and specifications.

## 6.2 Quality Assurance
**6.2.1** A multi-disciplinary in-house team of professionals/ engineers will inspect, verify and control the quality of work to the desired standard as per contractual terms & specifications.

**6.2.2** In case of non-availability of qualified professionals/ engineers in house for the purpose, then the approval of competent authority shall have to be taken for deploying professionals from outside agencies. The provision for third party quality check may also be considered for a work beyond a specified amount.

## 6.3 Design Approvals
In case of EPC contracts approval of the designs should be taken from the appropriate authority, as defined in the tender document, to ensure that the performance level are met by the design.

## 6.4 Time Monitoring


### 6.4.1 Time At Large
When the Procuring Entity does not explicitly express and reserve its rights and remedies under the contract for delays in execution, it legally forfeits his right to such remedies. Under such circumstances Time is said to become at large and the contractor gets freed from his obligation to complete within the specified time. To avoid such a situation, before the expiry of originally stipulated date of completion, the Procuring Entity should extend the currency of the contract/agreement and set a new time limit for completion and make the extended time as essence of the contract, stipulating that this is being done without prejudice to his right to recover damages and other remedies as per the contract.

### 6.4.2 Force Majeure (FM) Clause
A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

question_text: Before releasing the Performance Bank Guarantee in final settlement, what must be confirmed regarding any outstanding amounts from the contractor?
answer:
- Verify that the contractor has no outstanding payments, dues, or liabilities to the company before releasing the Performance Bank Guarantee.  
- This confirmation prevents unrecoverable amounts after the guarantee is released, safeguarding corporate financial resources and reinforcing transparent, value‑for‑money procurement practices.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 153)
cot:
To start with, releasing a Performance Bank Guarantee marks the point at which the contractor’s financial security instrument is withdrawn and the contract is considered closed.  
After that, any money the contractor still owes the company becomes much harder to reclaim because the guarantee that could be called upon is no longer in place.  
Building on this, it is essential to verify beforehand that the contractor has settled all payments, dues, and other liabilities to the company before the guarantee is released.  
Going deeper, this check includes looking for outstanding invoices, retention amounts, or any other claims that might remain unresolved; if such amounts exist and the guarantee is already gone, recovering them would be difficult and could lead to financial loss.  
In summary, confirming that no outstanding amounts remain protects the company’s funds, ensures that the settlement is truly final, and supports transparent, value‑for‑money procurement practices.

section: 10.2.3 Subsequent action after Identification and Categorization of asset as above
question_text: List three valuation methods that can be used to determine the reserve price for scrap or surplus materials.
answer:
Facilitator: Let’s look at three valuation approaches you can use to set the reserve price for scrap or surplus materials.

1. **Prevailing market price** – Check current market rates for comparable used items or the relevant metal index (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 167).  
2. **Book value** – Use the recorded book value of the materials (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 167).  
3. **Historical auction price with escalation** – Take the price obtained in a previous successful auction or sale with escalation (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 167).  

These three methods are the core options outlined for determining the reserve price before disposal. Feel free to discuss how each might work in your own projects or share a quick example from your experience.
cot: First, I think about what a reserve price really means – it’s the minimum amount we’d accept before we let the scrap or surplus go, so we need a basis that reflects what the material is actually worth in the current context. Looking at the situation, the material is no longer in service, so its value isn’t tied to original cost but to what someone would pay for it now or what we’ve historically gotten for similar items. That leads me to consider the most direct indicator: what the market is paying for comparable used scrap or the relevant metal index right now. That gives a real‑time floor that reflects supply and demand. Next, I wonder whether we have an internal record that could serve as a fallback when market data is thin or volatile; the book value carried in the fixed‑asset register represents what we’ve already expensed and can be a conservative baseline, especially for items that haven’t been traded recently. Then I recall that we often have our own auction history – if we’ve sold similar scrap before, that price, adjusted for inflation or market changes, provides a concrete reference point that’s grounded in our actual disposal experience. I weigh the three: market price for immediacy, book value for conservatism, and escalated historical auction price for a blend of realism and prudence. Each method addresses a different aspect of valuation, and together they cover the range of scenarios we might encounter when setting a reserve price. Concluding, these three approaches – prevailing market price, book value, and prior auction price with an escalation factor – are the core ways to determine the reserve price for scrap or surplus materials.

### 10.2.3 Subsequent action after Identification and Categorization of asset as above
- a) Assets / Material identified as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus shall be retired from the Fixed Asset Register and classified as “Assets held for Sale”, through Finance department. Finance shall accordingly intimate Warehouse after the write off of the asset for disposal action.
- b) The scrap/surplus shall be categorized and segregated based on MoC by the user department.
- c) Warehouse shall intimate the user department for handing over the scrap/surplus based on availability of space. If space is not available at warehouse disposal shall be done on as-is-where-is basis from the user’s place.
- d) Responsibility of handling and transportation during transfer to store shall lie with the user department.
- e) Warehouse Department shall initiate the process of disposal of such Condemned, Scrap and Surplus Assets in compliance with DOA.
- f) Scrap or surplus generated at NRL other location like SMT Siliguri, NRL Delhi, NRL Kolkata, NRL Paradip etc. shall be disposed directly from those location by respective location in-charge.

## 10.3 Valuation for Determining Reserve Price-
On accumulation of sufficient quantity of scrap / condemned / surplus materials, it needs to be disposed off. Valuation of the materials to be disposed off should be done based on one or more of the following options:

- On prevailing market price of such used items, metal index etc.
- Book value of the materials,
- Price from earlier successful auction / sale with escalation.
- If required, third party valuation may be done depending upon the cost of valuation as compared to the assumed worth of the items/materials.
- A multifunctional internal valuation team comprising of officers from Warehouse, Finance and User dept. Team to be constituted by Functional head of Commercial.
- Price from successful auction / sale of other PSUs as intimated by e-auction service provider.
- In case of sale of Surplus to PSUs, moving average cost or last purchase price of Non Hydro-Carbon (NHC) materials, whichever is higher plus 15 % administrative charges shall be applicable.

The Reserve Price so determined shall be the price excluding taxes & duties. However, Finance shall provide the applicable taxes & duties for calculation of estimated TFI.

## 10.4 Modes of Disposal
- A. By Public e-Auction through service provider.
- B. By open tendering

Minimum 15 to 21 days notice shall be given. In tendering mode, if sufficient bid is not received, extension may be allowed for maximum 02 (two) times of reasonable duration.

Disposal shall be on "**AS-IS-WHERE-IS**" and "**No COMPLAINT**" basis to the H-1 bidder to be calculated item-wise or on cumulative basis as specified in the bid. In case of tie between two or more parties (may happen in case of Open Tender mode of Disposal), it shall be resolved through Lottery / Divided equally among the H-1 bidders (provided that the quantity is divisible / economically viable).

question_text: How frequently should inspection reports be issued for a large shipment
answer: For a large shipment, inspection reports should be issued for each lot as it is inspected—normally every day or every two days—rather than waiting until the entire consignment is finished. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 160)

First, I need to figure out what the rule says about issuing inspection reports when dealing with a large shipment. The question is asking how often those reports should be produced, so I start by looking for any guidance that ties report frequency to the size of the consignment.  

I recall that the instructions require a separate inspection report for each consignment, but they also make an exception for large consignments: the report does not have to wait until the entire shipment is inspected. Instead, the guideline allows interim reports to be issued as inspection progresses.  

Next, I focus on the exact wording of that exception. It states that for large consignments the inspection report may be issued for lots inspected every day or every two days. This implies that the inspection process is broken down into daily or bi‑daily lots, and a report is produced after each lot is examined and accepted.  

I then consider why this approach makes sense. If we waited until the whole shipment was finished, the consignee would receive no feedback until the very end, which could delay acceptance, payment, or corrective action if problems were found early. Issuing reports frequently keeps the user informed and allows any issues to be addressed promptly.  

Putting these points together, the logical conclusion is that for a large shipment the inspection report should be prepared for each lot as it is inspected, with the frequency set to either daily or every two days, rather than holding back a single report until the entire consignment is completed.  

This matches the answer: inspection reports should be issued for each lot as it is inspected—normally every day or every two days—rather than waiting until the whole consignment is finished.

### 9.12.4 Issue of Inspection Report
After satisfactory inspection and tests, the acceptable goods shall be stamped, labelled, marked or sealed, in such a way as to make subsequent identification and tally with the inspection report of accepted lots easy for the consignee/user. The following guidelines should be used for inspection reports to be issued:

- i) Inspection reports should be prepared detailing the inspection done, samples examined, requirements as per the relevant specification/contract and the observations. Each inspection note copy issued should invariably bear the individual's name, stamp along with his designation.
- ii) A separate inspection report must be prepared for each consignment. In the case of large consignments, the issue of the inspection report may not be held up until the inspection of the full consignment is completed. These must be issued for lots inspected every day or every two days. If the contract is in terms of 'sets' or 'number' and materials are such that they comprise a number of components or accessories, the inspection report should be issued only when all parts, components and accessories forming a set are inspected and accepted. When plant and equipment are

ordered with spares, the inspection report for spares should not be issued before acceptance of the main equipment. In the case of contracts for imported materials that involve initial inspection in the country of origin and final inspection in India, the final inspection note should be issued giving reference of the certificate issued abroad;

- iii) In respect of materials which have been rejected by the inspecting officer, the rejection inspection report should be issued immediately following the completion of inspection. All the reasons for rejection and deviations against the governing specifications, drawings or other particulars should invariably be noted in detail in the "remarks" column of the rejection inspection note.

### 9.12.5 Approval of Acceptable Deviations
Under no circumstances will the inspecting officer have the authority to modify the governing specifications, approved drawings or samples during inspection without reference to the CA that approved the tender. For all cases of acceptance with deviation, the nature of deviation along with a justification for acceptance against such deviation should be duly documented. The CA that approved the tender should have the final decision on deviations.

Deviations from the contract specifications or requirements not affecting price, quality, performance and other terms of the contract may be allowed at the level of the CA in consultation with the user Department on merits or nature of deviations.

In all other cases, the goods should be rejected giving all reasons by issuing a rejection inspection report. Rejections should not be made in a piecemeal manner.

question_text: To which supplier must a repeat order be directed if the original order was issued to a specific party
answer: A repeat order must be placed with the same supplier or party to whom the original order was issued (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 88).
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question is really seeking: it wants to know who should receive a repeat order when the original order was already placed with a specific party.  

Then, I turn to the rules that govern repeat orders. The reference outlines six conditions that must be satisfied for a repeat order to be permissible, and the sixth condition makes it clear that repeat orders are to be placed only on the party that originally received the order.  

Next, I examine the other five conditions—time limit, cumulative value limit, cumulative quantity limit, market‑rate stability, and the L1 basis of the original order. These are prerequisites that determine whether a repeat order can be issued at all, but they do not change the identity of the supplier; they merely set the boundaries within which a repeat order may be made.  

Further, I note that because the sixth condition is phrased as an implication (“it is implied that Repeat Orders will be placed only on the party on whom the original order was placed”), any repeat order that meets the first five conditions automatically inherits the same supplier as the original order. There is no alternative party mentioned or allowed under these provisions.  

Finally, I synthesize the points: the repeat order can only be issued if the procedural conditions are satisfied, and when those conditions are met, the destination is fixed to the original party. Therefore, a repeat order must be directed to the same supplier or party to whom the original order was issued.
chunk_content:
Where the same material has been purchased or work contracted before, repeat order may be placed, provided the following conditions are satisfied and so recorded:

- I. The repeat order should be placed within 12 months of the issue of the original order.
- II. The total value of all repeat orders put together should not exceed the original order value.
- III. Similarly all repeat order/s quantity put together should not exceed the original ordered quantity.
- IV. There has been no reduction in the rates of similar materials / jobs in the market since the original order was placed.
- V. The original order was placed on “L1” basis as a result of a regular enquiry.
- VI. It is implied that Repeat Orders will be placed only on the party on whom the original order was placed.

Approval for placement of Repeat Order shall be given as per provisions of DOA.

question_text: Under what circumstance may a cancelled procurement process be subject to review through a bidder's representation
answer:
- A cancelled procurement process is reviewable only if the cancellation is made with the intention to subsequently re‑tender the same requirements; otherwise the decision to cancel is final and not subject to bidder representation. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 135)  
- This limitation prevents arbitrary cancellations, upholds transparency, and reinforces that procurement actions remain aligned with corporate goals of value‑for‑money and risk management.
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals say about when a cancelled procurement can be challenged by a bidder. The question is asking for the specific circumstance that allows a bidder to make a representation after a procurement process has been cancelled.

The manuals list several decisions of the procuring entity that are expressly excluded from review. Among those items, there is one that mentions cancellation of the procurement process, but it includes an important qualifier: the exclusion does not apply if the cancellation is made with the intention to subsequently re‑tender the same requirements.

This tells me that the general rule is that a cancellation is final and not open to bidder challenge. However, the exception carved out in the rule creates the only situation where a bidder can still raise a representation—namely, when the cancellation is not a final decision but rather a step toward issuing a new tender for the same work.

If the cancellation is made without any plan to re‑tender, then it falls squarely under the excluded decisions, meaning the procuring entity’s action is shielded from review and the bidder has no avenue to question it. Conversely, when the entity cancels with the clear intent to re‑issue the tender later, the exception kicks in, and the bidder may treat the cancellation as part of an ongoing process that can be scrutinized.

The rationale behind this distinction seems to be to prevent arbitrary or manipulative cancellations that could undermine competition, while still allowing a procuring entity to reset a tender when genuinely needed, provided the action is transparent and open to challenge.

Putting it together, a cancelled procurement process can be subject to bidder representation only when the cancellation is carried out with the intention to subsequently re‑tender the same requirements; in all other cases the cancellation is final and not reviewable. This limitation safeguards against arbitrary cancellations, promotes transparency, and ensures that procurement actions remain aligned with objectives of value‑for‑money and risk management.

question_text: How must a clarification request be delivered to the bidder, and what is stated as the consequence if the bidder does not respond by the specified date?
answer:
Clarification requests must be issued in writing, specifying a clear response deadline for the bidder. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 120)  
The written notice must state that if the bidder fails to comply or respond by the specified date, the tender will be liable to rejection. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 120)  

This formal, time‑bound process promotes transparency, prevents unilateral bid alterations, and safeguards the procurement cycle—key elements for managing risk and securing value for money in corporate purchasing.
cot: First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants to know how a clarification request must be sent to a bidder and what the notice must say about missing the deadline. Then I recall that the rule for bid clarifications specifies that the request shall be given in writing, which tells me the delivery method must be written. Next, the rule continues by saying the request should ask the tenderer to respond by a specified date, so the notice has to include a clear deadline for the bidder’s reply. Further, the rule adds that the notice must also mention that if the tenderer does not comply or respond by that date, his tender will be liable to be rejected, giving the consequence that failure to respond on time leads to the tender being liable to rejection. Combining these points, the clarification request must be issued in writing, it must state a specific response date, and it must warn that non‑response by that date will make the tender liable to rejection. This matches the answer required.
chunk_content:
### 7.3.4 Clarification of Bids/Shortfall Documents
During evaluation and comparison of bids, the purchaser may, at his discretion, ask the bidder for clarifications on the bid. The request for clarification shall be given in writing, asking the tenderer to respond by a specified date, and also mentioning therein that, if the tenderer does not comply or respond by the date, his tender will be liable to be rejected. Depending on the outcome, such tenders are to be ignored or considered further. No change in prices or substance of the bid shall be sought, offered or permitted. No post-bid clarification at the initiative of the bidder shall be entertained. The shortfall information/documents should be sought only in case of historical documents which pre-existed at the time of the tender opening and which have not undergone change since then. (Example: if the Permanent Account Number, registration with sales tax/ VAT has been asked to be submitted and the tenderer has not provided them, these documents may be asked for with a target date as above). So far as the submission of documents is concerned with regard to qualification criteria, after submission of the tender, only related shortfall documents should be asked for and considered. For example, if the bidder has submitted a supply order without its completion/performance certificate, the certificate can be asked for and

lakhs considered. However, no new supply order should be asked for so as to qualify the bidder.

If the bidder cites any reference of a job executed for NRL and the bidder is not able to furnish documentary evidence, the internal records of shall be considered.

## 7.4 Evaluation of Responsive Bids and Decision on Award of Contract
All responsive bids are evaluated with a view to select the lowest (L1) bidder who meets the qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects. In case of single stage single envelop bidding, the evaluation of qualification of bidders, technical, commercial and financial aspect is done simultaneously. In single stage multiple envelops, initially only the techno-commercial bids would be opened and evaluated for bids which successfully meet the qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects. Financial bids of such successful bidders only would be opened for selecting the L1 bidder. In two stage bids, the PQB/ Eol stage would have already been evaluated as detailed in Chapter 4 and this second stage is for evaluation of responses to the Second Stage multiple envelops from the shortlisted qualified bidders. Evaluation of techno-commercial and financial aspects are, however, discussed separately below.

question_text: How long does NRL normally keep a vendor or contractor on its empanelled list before reviewing it again
answer: NRL normally keeps a vendor or contractor on its empanelled list for a defined period of normally 2 years before reviewing it again (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 51).
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question really wants to know: the standard length of time NRL leaves a vendor or contractor on its empanelled list before it initiates a review.  
To answer that, I need to recall where the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals address the duration of empanelment and any review schedule attached to it.  
The manuals contain a section that deals specifically with empanelment of vendors and contractors. It explains that empanelment is intended for goods required regularly and that performance should be checked periodically.  
Crucially, the manuals state that empanelment should be for a defined period and then give the normal length of that period: two years.  
They also note that after this period the empanelment shall be reviewed subsequently, linking the two‑year span directly to the review cycle.  
Putting those pieces together, the logical inference is that NRL keeps a vendor or contractor empanelled for roughly two years before it conducts the next review.  
This matches the answer that specifies a defined period of normally 2 years before a review is required.

question_text: What prior approval is required before implementing a bonus clause in any tender?
answer: Prior to implementing a bonus clause in any tender, the indenting or user department must obtain prior administrative approval of the CFD. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 149)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know what must be secured beforehand if a bonus clause is to be included in any tender.
The core of the issue is the implementation of an incentive—specifically a bonus for early completion—so I should look for where the Procurement of Goods Manual discusses incentives or bonuses and any procedural safeguards attached to them.
In the relevant section, incentives and bonuses are treated together with liquidated damages, and the manual explicitly states that before a bonus clause can be put into a tender, a certain administrative step must be taken.
That step is described as obtaining prior administrative approval from the CFD, and it is made clear that the responsibility for securing this approval lies with the indenting or user department.
Putting these pieces together, the logical conclusion is that the required prior approval is the administrative sign‑off from the CFD, to be obtained by the indenting/user department before the bonus clause is incorporated into any tender.
chunk_content:
### 9.7.5 Force Majeure Clause
A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

### 9.7.6 Denial Clause
Since delay in delivery is a default by the seller. In such a case, the buyer should protect himself against extra expenditure during the extended period by stipulating a denial clause (over and above levy of LD) in the letter informing the supplier of extension of the delivery period. In the denial clause, any increase in statutory duties and/or upward rise in prices due to the PVC clause and/or any adverse fluctuation in foreign exchange are to be borne by the seller during the extended delivery period, while the purchaser reserves his right to get any benefit of a downward revisions in statutory duties, PVC and foreign exchange rate. Thus, PVC, other variations and foreign exchange clauses operate only during the original delivery period.

### 9.7.7 Liquidated Damages and Incentives/ Bonus
Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of supplies. Provision of incentives for completion of supplies before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear

monetary terms.

Incentives/ Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

question_text: What specific actions should auditors check to ensure that commercial dealing officer(s) have received opened bids and related documents and are maintaining their safe custody throughout the procurement process
answer:
- Verify that commercial dealing officer(s) have received the opened bids and related documents from the tender opening officials. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117)  
- Verify that commercial dealing officer(s) maintain safe custody of the received bids and documents throughout the procurement process. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117)  
- Verify that commercial dealing officer(s) process the bids and documents at all steps involved in finalising the procurement. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117)
cot:
First, I think about what the auditors need to verify regarding the commercial dealing officer’s handling of bids. The officer’s role starts the moment the tender opening officials hand over the opened bids and related paperwork, so the first check is whether that transfer actually took place – looking for a receipt, handover note, or signed acknowledgment that shows the officer received the documents.  

Then I consider the next responsibility: keeping those bids safe. Safe custody means the documents are stored securely, access is limited, and they remain unchanged from receipt through to the final award. To verify this, auditors would examine storage logs, access control records, and periodic reconciliations that demonstrate the bids stayed under the officer’s control without loss or tampering.  

Next, I reflect on the officer’s duty to process the bids at every stage of finalising the procurement. This includes preparing comparative statements, conducting evaluations, and forwarding the documents for approval. Auditors should trace the flow of the bids through these steps, confirm that the officer performed the required actions, and ensure no steps were skipped or altered.  

Finally, I combine these lines of thought: the audit must confirm that the commercial dealing officer(s) received the opened bids and documents, that they maintained safe custody of those items throughout the procurement process, and that they processed the bids at all steps involved in finalising the procurement. These three checks together satisfy the requirement to ensure proper handling of bids by the dealing officer.

question_text: How does the treatment of a withdrawal request received after the prescribed receipt deadline differ from one received before that deadline?
answer: A withdrawal request received on or before the prescribed receipt deadline is accepted and does not result in forfeiture of the bid security/EMD, provided it is duly sealed and marked like the original tender. In contrast, a withdrawal request received after that deadline is not considered by the procuring entity; if a bid is nevertheless withdrawn after the submission deadline but before the bid‑validity period expires, the bidder forfeits the EMD and may be subject to additional sanctions. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 61)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the rule actually says about when a withdrawal can be acted upon and what happens if it isn’t. The key factor is the timing of the request relative to the prescribed receipt deadline for tenders.  

Next, I recall the procedural requirements for a withdrawal to be effective: it must be submitted in writing, properly sealed, and marked exactly like the original tender, and it must reach the procuring entity no later than the deadline for receipt of tenders.  

Then I consider the scenario where the request satisfies that timing condition—arriving on or before the deadline. Because it meets the deadline and the sealing/marking rules, the procuring entity treats it as a valid withdrawal, returns the bid security or EMD without forfeiture, and the tender is removed from consideration.  

After that, I turn to the opposite case: a withdrawal request that arrives after the deadline. The provision explicitly states that any such request received after the prescribed date and time will not be considered, so the procuring entity ignores it and proceeds with the originally submitted tender as if no withdrawal had been made.  

Finally, I reflect on the consequence of attempting to withdraw after the submission deadline but before the bid‑validity period expires. Even though the after‑deadline request is ineffective, if the bidder nonetheless acts to withdraw the bid during that interval, the rules trigger forfeiture of the EMD and may attract additional sanctions, which explains why the treatment diverges so sharply between the two timing cases.  

Putting these points together, the difference is clear: a timely withdrawal is accepted and incurs no penalty, whereas a late withdrawal is disregarded and, if pursued, results in loss of the bid security and possible further penalties.

### 4.9.2 Sealing and Marking of Tenders
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (e.g., in duplicate or in triplicate etc) required to be submitted. In case bids are asked in a number of copies, the tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate" and so on and also marking these as mentioned above. In case of two envelope bidding system, the techno- commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate inner covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed inner covers are to be put in a bigger outer cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the Procuring Entity will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening etc. These details regarding the submission of bids should also form a part of the ITB and AITB in the tender documents; all the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

### 4.9.3 Withdrawal, Substitution and Modification of Tenders
The tenderer, after submitting the tender, is permitted to withdraw, substitute or modify the tenders in writing without forfeiture of Bid Security/ EMD, provided these are received duly sealed and marked like the original tender, up to the date and time of receipt of the tender. Any such request received after the prescribed date and time of receipt of tenders will not be considered. No bid may be withdrawn in the interval between the deadline for submission of bids and expiration of the period of bid validity. Withdrawal of a bid during this period will result in forfeiture of the bidder's bid security (EMD) and other sanctions.

question_text: Why is the inception phase considered critical in more complex consultancies
answer: It is critical because it covers the submission and review of the work plan with the Procuring Entity and the initiation of field work. This step establishes the scope, aligns expectations, and begins actual work, laying the groundwork for the rest of the assignment. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 61)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what makes the inception phase stand out in the context of complex consultancies. The question points to its critical nature, so I should look for what the inception phase actually involves and why that matters more when the assignment is intricate.

Looking at the description of how work is structured for more complex consultancies, it mentions that the effort is broken into phases and highlights one of those phases—the inception phase—as especially important. This tells me that the phase isn’t just a formality; it carries weight that can influence the whole effort.

Next, I examine what the inception phase consists of. It covers two main activities: the submission and review of the work plan with the procuring entity, and the kickoff of field work. The first part is about agreeing on what will be done, how it will be done, and confirming that both sides share the same understanding of objectives, deliverables, timelines, and responsibilities. The second part is about moving from planning to action, sending the team out to begin gathering information or performing the tasks outlined.

Now I think about why reviewing the work plan up front is so vital. In a complex consultancy, there are many moving parts—multiple stakeholders, technical details, interdependencies, and potential risks. If the plan is vague or misaligned, those complexities can quickly lead to misunderstandings, duplicated effort, or missed requirements. By formally submitting the plan and having it reviewed, the team can catch ambiguities, adjust scope, allocate the right experts, and set clear acceptance criteria before any substantial resources are expended.

Then I consider the significance of initiating field work at this stage. Starting actual data collection or on‑site activities early provides immediate feedback on whether the assumptions in the plan hold true. It allows the team to uncover practical constraints—access issues, data availability, environmental factors—that might not be apparent in a purely desk‑based review. Detecting these issues early means the approach can be tweaked while the effort is still flexible, rather than after significant work has already been done.

Putting these pieces together, I see that the inception phase serves as the foundation for the entire assignment. It locks in a shared, vetted roadmap and begins the real‑world validation of that roadmap. For a simple, straightforward consultancy, a less formal start might suffice because there are fewer variables to manage. But when the consultancy is complex, the cost of getting the foundation wrong—rework, delays, cost overruns, or unsatisfactory deliverables—is much higher. Therefore, ensuring that the inception phase is thorough and well‑executed becomes a critical success factor.

Finally, I synthesize this reasoning: the inception phase is critical because it establishes a clear, agreed‑upon work plan and launches the field work that tests that plan, thereby aligning expectations, identifying risks early, and setting the stage for controlled, effective execution—elements that are especially indispensable in more complex consultancies.

section: 5.2.6 Withdraw/ Amendments / Modifications to Bids by Bidders
question_text: What is the latest time by which a withdrawal, alteration, or modification to a tender must be received to be considered valid
answer: The withdrawal, alteration, or modification must be received on or before the date and time of receipt of the tender (the prescribed date & time); any receipt after that date and time is not considered valid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 103)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what makes a withdrawal, alteration, or modification valid according to the rules governing tenders. The core requirement is that any such change must arrive in the proper form—sealed and marked just like the original tender—and it must arrive within a specific time window.  

Next, I look at how that time window is defined. The reference makes it clear that the permissible period extends “up to the date & time of receipt of tender.” In other words, the cutoff point is exactly the moment when the tender itself is considered received; anything that arrives at that moment or earlier satisfies the condition, while anything arriving later does not.  

Then I consider the implication of the phrase “up to.” It sets an inclusive boundary: the latest permissible instant is the prescribed date and time itself. If a withdrawal arrives after that instant, the rule explicitly states it “are not to be considered,” meaning it is invalid.  

After that, I verify that no other qualifications affect the timing rule. The only additional stipulation is about the sealing and marking, which does not shift the deadline; it merely governs the format of the submission. Therefore, the timing condition stands independently as the decisive factor for validity.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the withdrawal, alteration, or modification must be received no later than the date and time the tender is due; any receipt after that moment fails to meet the requirement and is consequently invalid. This aligns directly with the answer that the latest acceptable time is the prescribed date and time of receipt, with no leeway beyond it.
chunk_content: The tenderer, after submitting its tender, is permitted to withdraw/ alter/modify its tender so long such withdrawal/ alterations/ modifications are received duly sealed and marked like original tender, up to the date & time of receipt of tender. Any withdrawal/ amendment/ modification received after the prescribed date & time of receipt of tenders are not to be considered.

question_text: What information must a bidder provide if they are involved in litigation or arbitration related to past contracts
answer:
If a tender contains a litigation/arbitration declaration clause (see clause 5.1.2.3), a bidder who states that they are involved in any litigation or arbitration must furnish detailed information about the status of litigation (including the arbitration) filed by or against the bidder during the past years with respect to contract(s) executed by the bidder.

This information is required solely for record‑keeping; the clause expressly states that such details have no bearing on the bidder’s eligibility nor on the awarding of the order (see clause 5.1.2.3). If the tender does not include this declaration, the bidder is not required to submit litigation/arbitration information.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 94)
cot:
First, I need to figure out when a bidder is actually asked to give any litigation or arbitration information. The reference mentions a specific clause—5.1.2.3—that some tenders include, which seeks a declaration from bidders about whether they are involved in any litigation or arbitration. If that clause is not present, there is no obligation to disclose anything at all.

Assuming the tender does contain that clause, the next step is to understand what the clause requires when a bidder answers that they are involved. It says the bidder must furnish detailed information about the status of the litigation or arbitration, including any arbitration, that was filed by or against the bidder during the past years and that relates to contracts the bidder has executed.

From there I can break down what “detailed information about the status” entails. The status itself is not just a simple yes/no; it needs to show where the matter stands in the legal process. So I would need to indicate whether the case is still in pleadings, moving to hearing, has an award, is settled, or is at some other stage.

Beyond the stage, the bidder should also identify the case concretely. That means providing the case or reference number, the specific forum or court where it is being heard, and the names of the opposing parties—whether the bidder is the claimant or the respondent.

Then there is the substance of the dispute. The bidder must give a brief description of what the litigation or arbitration is about, and crucially, explain how it connects to any contract(s) the bidder has carried out in the past years. This links the dispute to the procurement context the clause is meant to address.

Finally, the bidder should report any interim developments: orders, awards, or decisions that have already been issued, even if the case is not yet finished. This gives a full picture of the current state of the proceedings.

The reference also notes that this information is collected purely for record‑keeping; the clause explicitly states that the details do not affect the bidder’s eligibility nor influence the award decision. If the tender omits the litigation/arbitration declaration, the bidder is not required to submit any of this information at all.

Putting those pieces together—checking for the clause, then, if present, providing the case identifier, forum, parties, description with past‑contract link, current stage, and any interim rulings—matches exactly what the answer describes as the required disclosure.

question_text: What steps should a procuring entity take when it encounters an abnormally low bid?
answer: The procurement manuals outline different steps depending on the situation. If the entity seeks written clarifications, it may request detailed price analyses of the bid. If, after evaluating those analyses, the bidder substantially failed to demonstrate capability, the entity may reject the bid. If the entity wishes to request an additional security deposit or bank guarantee, it may do so only with approval of the next higher authority competent to finalise the tender and only when there are compelling circumstances. Please clarify which of these situations applies to your case.
chunk_content:
### 7.5.7 Consideration of Abnormally Low Bids
An Abnormally Low Bid is one in which the Bid price, in combination with other elements of the Bid, appears so low that it raises material concerns as to the capability of the Bidder to perform the contract at the offered price. Procuring Entity may in such cases seek written clarifications from the Bidder, including detailed price analyses of its Bid price in relation to scope, schedule, allocation of risks and responsibilities, and any other requirements of the bids document. If, after evaluating the price analyses, procuring entity determines that the Bidder has *substantially failed* to demonstrate its capability to deliver the contract at the offered price, the Procuring Entity may reject the Bid/Proposal. However it would not be advisable to fix a normative percentage below the estimated cost, which would be automatically be considered as an abnormally low bid. Due care should be taken while formulating the specifications at the time of preparation of bid document so as to have a safeguard against the submission of abnormally low bid from the

bidder.

In the case of predatory pricing as well, procuring entities may refer to the above consideration of Abnormally Low Bids to assist themselves in finalization of tenders.

No provisions should be kept in the Bid Documents regarding the Additional Security Deposit/ Bank Guarantee (BG) in case of Abnormally Low Bids. Wherever, there are compelling circumstances to ask for Additional Security Deposit/ Bank Guarantee (BG) in case of ALBs, the same should be taken only with the approval of the next higher authority competent to finalise the particular tender.

### 7.5.8 Cartel Formation/Pool Rates
It is possible that sometimes a group of bidders quote the same rate against a tender, where they were at liberty to quote any competitive price. Such pool/cartel formation is against the basic principle of competitive bidding and defeats the very purpose of an open and competitive tendering system. A warning clause may also be included in the bid documents to discourage the bidders from indulging in such practices.

# Chapter 10: Identification and Disposal of Scrap, Condemned & Surplus Assets
Disposal of Scrap, Condemned Goods & Surplus Assets is desirable considering the following benefits:-

- Monetary returns to the organization.
- Reduce cost of maintaining idle inventories.
- Reduce security hazard, enhance safety.
- Make space available for other purpose.
- Recycling for cleaner environment.
- Improvement of housekeeping.

Consequently, there accumulates, a large quantity of material which is neither usable for the purpose for which it was originally procured nor of any other operational value. section: 7.5.10 Consideration of Lack of Competition in OTE/ GTE and LTE
question_text: What three conditions must be satisfied for a single offer situation to be considered valid?
answer:
For a single‑offer situation to be treated as a valid single tender, the following three conditions must be met:

1. The procurement was satisfactorily advertised (e.g., on notice boards, websites) and sufficient time was allowed for bidders to submit their offers.  
2. The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive.  
3. The quoted price is reasonable when compared with prevailing market values.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 130)
cot:
First, I ask myself why a situation with only one responsive bid could still be considered legitimate instead of automatically triggering a re‑tender. The core issue is whether the lack of competition stems from a flaw in the procurement process or from genuine market conditions.  

Looking at the process, the first thing I check is whether the opportunity was properly publicized and whether bidders were given enough time to prepare and submit their offers; if the advertisement was inadequate or the deadline too short, the single offer would simply reflect a procedural shortcoming.  

Next, I turn to the eligibility rules: even with good notice, overly strict qualification criteria could have screened out otherwise capable suppliers, so I assess whether those criteria were proportionate to the work and did not unduly restrict participation.  

Then I examine the financial aspect. Assuming the process was open and the criteria fair, the remaining safeguard is the price itself—I compare the quoted amount with prevailing market rates to see if it is reasonable; an excessively high price would suggest that the lone bid is taking advantage of the lack of competition.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: only when the procurement was satisfactorily advertised with sufficient time, the qualification criteria were not unnecessarily restrictive, and the price aligns with market values can the single‑offer outcome be trusted as a valid single tender, making re‑tender unnecessary.
chunk_content:
Sometimes, against open/limited tender cases, the procuring entity may not receive a sufficient number of bids and/or after analysing the bids, ends up with only one responsive bid - a situation referred to as 'Single Offer'. **Such situation of 'Single Offer' is to be treated as Single Tender.** It is possible that there may be single offer situation against open tenders and there may be tendency to go for re-tender as a safe course of action. Re-bidding has costs: firstly the actual costs of retendering; secondly the delay in execution of the work with consequent delay in the attainment of the purpose for which the procurement is being done; and thirdly the possibility that the re-bid may result in a higher bid. Even when only one Bid is submitted, the process may be considered valid provided following conditions are satisfied:

- i) The procurement was satisfactorily advertised (publicized in notice boards, websites etc.) and sufficient time was given for submission of bids.
- ii) The qualification criteria were not unduly restrictive; and
- iii) Prices are reasonable in comparison to market values

However restricted powers of approval of award on Single tender basis of procurement would apply. In case of price not being reasonable, negotiations (with L1) or retender may be considered as justifiable.

Unsolicited offers against LTEs should be ignored.

question_text: Under what circumstance can a delivery date extension be granted without the supplier's specific request?
answer:
- **Clause Reference:** 9.7.3 Extension of Delivery  
- **Requirement:** No extension of the delivery date may be granted suo motu (i.e., on the procuring entity’s own initiative) unless the supplier has specifically requested the extension.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 148)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know when a delivery‑date extension can be given without the supplier having to ask for it explicitly.  

The section that deals with extensions of delivery makes clear that an extension amounts to a contract amendment and can only be done with the consent of both parties—the purchaser and the supplier. It states outright that no extension is to be granted suo motu, meaning on the purchaser’s own initiative, unless the supplier has specifically asked for it.  

That rule tells me the principle: an extension cannot be granted unilaterally by the purchaser; the supplier’s request is a prerequisite.  

To be thorough, I consider whether there are any exceptions mentioned elsewhere. The next subsection discusses delays for which the supplier is not responsible and says the delivery period may be re‑fixed without penalty in three specific cases. However, even there, the rule does not say the purchaser can impose the new date on its own; it only says the period needs to be re‑fixed to account for the lost time. The earlier rule about mutual consent still applies, so those cases do not override the requirement for a supplier request.  

Putting the pieces together, the only way an extension can be granted without the supplier’s specific request would be if the rule allowing suo motu action existed, but the reference explicitly denies that possibility. Therefore, there is no circumstance under the given rules where the purchaser can extend the delivery date on its own.  

The conclusion matches the answer: a delivery‑date extension may not be granted suo motu unless the supplier has specifically requested it; in other words, an extension without a supplier request is not permitted.

### 9.7.2 Terms of Delivery
Terms of delivery (FOR, FOB, CIF, and CFR, and so on), inter alia, determine the delivery point of the ordered goods from where the purchaser is to receive/collect the goods. It also decides the legally important issue of when the 'titles of the goods' have passed to the purchaser. The delivery period is to be read in conjunction with the terms of delivery, therefore the delivery is taken to have been made at the time when goods reach the delivery point as per the delivery terms. The delivery condition of FOR NRL (Location) may be adopted as far as possible.

### 9.7.3 Extension of Delivery
Suppliers shall be required to adhere to the delivery schedule specified in the purchase order and, if there is delay in supplies, LD shall be levied wherever there is failure by the party. Extension of the delivery date amounts to amendment of the contract. Such an extension can be only done with the consent of both parties (that is, the purchaser and supplier). No extension of the delivery date is to be granted suo motu unless the supplier specifically asks for it.

The confirmation of extension of delivery period (provisional / firm) should inter-alia contain the following:-

- (i) The time for delivery is extended from (CDD) to (extended CDD)
- (ii) Applicability & mention of LD clause beyond the original contract delivery date / the last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date.
- (iii) Requirement of extension of the validity period of the performance guarantee.
- (iv) That the above extension of delivery date will also be subject to the Denial Clause.

On receiving the supplier's communication, the procuring entity shall examine the proposal and, on approval from the CA, may agree to extend the delivery schedule, with or without LD

### 9.7.4 Delay in Supplies for which Supplier is not Responsible
Normally, in the following circumstances, the contractual delivery period needs to be re-fixed to take care of the lost period, without imposing any penalty to the supplier:

- i) Cases where the manufacture of stores is dependent on the approval of the advance sample and delay occurs in approving the sample though submitted by the supplier in time;

- ii) Where extension in the delivery period is granted on account of some omission on the part of the purchaser which affects the due performance of the contract by the supplier; and
- iii) Cases where the purchaser controls the entire production.

question_text: How frequently should the engineer update cash flow projections, cost estimates, and milestones for financial monitoring
answer:
- Engineer updates cash flow projections, cost estimates, and milestones on a monthly/quarterly basis (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 94).  
- Updates are performed more frequently when a significant number of variation orders occur or cost escalation is rapid (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 94).
cot:
First, I think about what the engineer’s financial monitoring duties involve: they must regularly check the project’s financial position and keep the procuring entity informed about cash flow, costs and schedule milestones.  
Next, I recall that the Procurement of Works Manual states that the engineer will update cash flow projections, cost estimates and the relevant milestones on a monthly or quarterly basis as part of routine financial control.  
Then I consider what might trigger a need for more frequent updates; the Procurement of Works Manual notes that when a significant number of variation orders arise or when cost escalation occurs unexpectedly quickly, the engineer should increase the update frequency to stay on top of the financial situation.  
Combining these points, the standard cadence is monthly/quarterly, with the possibility of more frequent revisions under volatile or change‑heavy conditions.  
This reasoning directly yields the answer: the engineer updates cash flow projections, cost estimates and milestones monthly/quarterly, and does so more often when there are many variation orders or rapid cost escalation.

### 6.4.5 Extension of Time (EOT)
- i) Extension of Time (EOT) / Provisional extension of time must not be left to the end; it should be dealt with promptly during the progress of the contract and for ongoing critical delay interim EOT may be awarded. The engineer shall, after due review with the contractor, determine the length of such extension and notify the contractor accordingly, with a copy to the procuring department. After the final stage of completion is reached (final taking-over certificate issued), EOT and LD may be reviewed, if required. Delay analysis should be supported by appropriate hindrance register / back-up records.
- ii) If a compensation event occurs during the execution of the contract, the same shall be dealt with in terms of the GCC. The Engineer will assess whether and by how much the intended completion date shall be extended.
- iii) Graded authority structure for extension of time for completion of contract as per DOA to be followed.
- iv) In case of contracts of regular nature (AMCs, ARCs etc.) where the works/services are required on continuous basis, action for renewal of such contracts or lining up of fresh contracts in its place must be taken by the user functions and PR should be forwarded to Commercial Dept. at least **four months** before the date of expiry/completion of contract.

As far as possible, extension of contract beyond provision of tender terms & conditions, should be avoided. Cases where action is not taken on time and extension of contract is necessary, prior approval from the competent authority must be taken before expiry of the contractual period.

## 6.5 Financial Monitoring
Besides administering the contract with regard to its quality and completion, the engineer will regularly assess the financial position and exercise financial control. He will update, on a monthly / quarterly basis, cash flow projections, cost estimates and yearly/ quarterly /monthly milestones, and submit them to the Procuring Entity. Variations should take place with a view to achieving economical completion of the work, and not to result in avoidable higher rates or costs. In case of a significant number of variation orders or unexpectedly rapid cost escalation, updation may be done more frequently. The financial statements should bring out comparisons of the initial estimated/ tendered cost with the actual cost -- component- and activity --wise -- both with respect of quantities and value. The Procuring Entity should examine these statements critically. If costs are likely to be exceeded, this should be anticipated, and a revised estimate of cost prepared, with complete explanations, for approval by the CA.

### (i) APPROVAL BY ENGINEER-in-CHARGE :
In circumstances where the situation warrants an immediate decision, the Engineer in charge can take a decision to go ahead with the extra work including increase in SOR quantities and seek post facto approval from the appropriate authority at the earliest possible time.

The detailed justification for not seeking prior approval duly approved by the HOD shall be forwarded along with the bill. Post facto approval shall be obtained immediately and in no case not more than three months from the date of the deviation. Further, in respect of tenders approved by Standing Committee/ Board, prior approval of functional director shall be obtained in such circumstances.

In case of change in the scope of work, prior approval should be obtained from Functional Head of executing department. However, in case of proposals approved by CFD/SCBT/Board, prior approval should be obtained from D(F) & D(T).

question_text: Who is eligible to bid in a global tender?
answer: In a global tender, all three types of suppliers can participate: Class‑I local suppliers, Class‑II local suppliers, and non‑local suppliers are all eligible to bid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 30)
cot:
First, I need to pin down what the question is really asking: it wants to know which kinds of suppliers are allowed to submit a bid when a tender is issued on a global basis.  

To answer that, I have to recall how the procurement rules distinguish suppliers. The definitions split them into three groups based on the local content of what they offer—Class‑I local suppliers with ≥ 50 % local content, Class‑II local suppliers with 20 % to < 50 %, and non‑local suppliers with < 20 % local content.  

Next, I look at the eligibility provisions. For tenders that are purely domestic, the rule says only Class‑I and Class‑II local suppliers may bid. But there is a separate clause that deals with tenders issued on a global tender basis, and it explicitly adds non‑local suppliers to the pool of eligible bidders, alongside the two local classes.  

Putting those pieces together, a global tender does not restrict participation to local firms only; it opens the door to any supplier regardless of their local content percentage. Therefore, the eligible bidders are precisely the three categories defined earlier: Class‑I local suppliers, Class‑II local suppliers, and non‑local suppliers.  

That matches the statement that in a global tender all three types of suppliers can participate.
