section: 1.9 The Basic Principles of undertaking works
question_text: Under what circumstances may a contract be awarded before acquiring the entire required land parcel
answer:
- Full land possession is not feasible due to prevailing circumstances. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 16)  
- Delaying contract award to await the remaining land would be imprudent and could impede project progress. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 16)  
- The minimum necessary encumbrance‑free land required to commence essential works is secured. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 16)  
- The balance land can be acquired in a targeted manner after award without affecting progress, as assessed by the public or project executing authority. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 16)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: when is it acceptable to award a contract before the whole piece of land needed for the project is actually in hand?  

Looking at the situation, the ideal would be to have 100 % of the site secured before any work begins, because that eliminates risk of delays or redesign later. But in practice, there are often obstacles—owners unwilling to sell, legal disputes, or simply the time it takes to complete every parcel—that make full possession unrealistic before the project schedule demands action.  

If we waited until every last bit of land was acquired, the project would sit idle, and that delay would not only waste time but could also increase costs and jeopardize funding timelines. The authority therefore has to weigh the cost of waiting against the risk of starting work without the full site.  

The next logical step is to identify what land is absolutely essential to get the project moving. Only the portions that host critical foundations, main structures, or indispensable utilities need to be free of encumbrances at the outset; the remaining parcels might be used later for ancillary facilities, landscaping, or phased expansion.  

Once that minimum necessary, encumbrance‑free area is confirmed as available, the authority can justify moving forward with the contract award, trusting that the outstanding parcels can be pursued in a focused, targeted manner after the contractor is on board.  

Finally, I verify that this approach satisfies all the conditions laid out: full possession isn’t feasible due to prevailing circumstances, delaying award would be imprudent and could stall progress, the essential land is already secured, and the balance can be acquired later without affecting the work, as judged by the executing authority. This reasoning naturally leads to the answer points.
chunk_content: xi) The process of land acquisition shall be started well ahead and completed entirely, or at least substantially, before the work is started. Availability of auxiliary services has been ensured - like roads/access, power, water, solid & liquid waste disposal system, street lighting and other civic services shall be ensured. It is desirable to have 100% of the required land in possession before award of contract; however, it may not always be possible to have the entire land due to prevailing circumstances. Also, it may not be prudent to put the entire process of award of contract on hold for want of the remaining portion of land, which in the assessment of public authority or the project executing authority, could possibly be acquired in a targeted manner after award of the contract, without affecting progress. Minimum necessary encumbrance free land should be available before award of contract. The minimum may be determined based on the circumstances of each case or general guidelines, issued by the concerned authorities. Such land, non-availability of which, will prevent essential components of work from execution, should be insisted upon. Project Executing Authorities should plan for acquiring balance land quickly and proper efforts be made for the same, which also should be duly recorded. The progress regarding land acquisition should be closely monitored.

question_text: How does the NRL manual define the Engineer-in-Charge’s role in issuing and forwarding the Defects Liability Certificate/SD/PBG release certificate to the payment section, and what implications does this have for compliance with the Department of Expenditure’s procedural timelines?
answer:
The NRL manual assigns the Engineer‑in‑Charge (EIC) the specific duty to issue a Defects Liability Certificate (DLC) or a Security Deposit/Performance Guarantee (SD/PBG) release certificate only after the contractor has satisfied all defect‑liability obligations under the contract. The EIC must then forward that certificate to the payment section without delay, and before releasing the SD/PBG must verify that no outstanding claims or recoveries remain against the contractor. Only one DLC is to be issued, and it is granted when the contractor has completed every contractual obligation (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 109‑110).

For compliance with the Department of Expenditure’s procedural timelines, this provision creates a direct linkage between the EIC’s action and the schedule for final payment. The Department’s guidelines require that defect‑liability clearance be obtained and the final bill processed within a prescribed period after work completion. By mandating that the EIC issue and forward the DLC/SD/PBG release certificate “as soon as” the defect‑liability obligations are fulfilled, the NRL manual ensures that the prerequisite for payment release is met promptly, thereby supporting adherence to the Department’s timelines. Conversely, any postponement in the EIC’s issuance or forwarding of the certificate would delay the payment reconciliation steps (material, works, and payment reconciliations) and risk breaching the Department’s stipulated deadline, potentially leading to audit findings of non‑compliance (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 111). Thus, the EIC’s timely execution of the certificate issuance and forwarding function is critical to maintaining alignment between the NRL manual’s internal procedures and the Department of Expenditure’s external procedural requirements.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the NRL manual actually says about the Engineer‑in‑Charge’s responsibility concerning the Defects Liability Certificate or the SD/PBG release certificate. The manual makes it clear that the EIC does not simply hand over a completion certificate and call it a day; instead, the defect‑liability phase must be closed formally. The EIC is the one who issues the DLC or the SD/PBG release certificate, and he does so only after confirming that the contractor has fulfilled every defect‑liability obligation set out in the contract. Moreover, the manual stresses that this certificate must be forwarded to the payment section without delay, and that before the SD/PBG is actually released the EIC must verify that there are no outstanding recoveries or claims against the contractor. It also notes that only a single DLC is to be issued, and it is granted when the contractor has satisfied all contractual duties, not just the works completion.

Next, I consider why the timing of that issuance and forwarding matters for the payment process. Once the DLC/SDPBG release certificate reaches the payment section, the subsequent steps—material reconciliation, works reconciliation, and payment reconciliation—can begin. Those reconciliations are prerequisites for releasing the final payment and for returning the security deposit or performance guarantee. If the EIC postpones issuing the certificate or fails to send it promptly, the payment section cannot start its reconciliation work, and the whole closure sequence stalls.

Then I think about the external requirement from the Department of Expenditure. The Department’s procedural timelines expect that, after the physical completion of the work, the defect‑liability clearance be obtained and the final bill processed within a prescribed window. The NRL manual’s directive that the EIC issue and forward the certificate “as soon as” the defect‑liability obligations are met is precisely the mechanism that aligns the internal workflow with that external deadline. By acting promptly, the EIC ensures that the prerequisite for payment release is satisfied early enough to keep the overall schedule on track.

Conversely, any delay on the EIC’s part would push back the start of the reconciliations, thereby extending the time needed to clear the final bill and release the SD/PBG. That extension would likely cause the project to exceed the Department of Expenditure’s stipulated period, exposing the organization to audit findings of non‑compliance and possible financial penalties.

Putting these pieces together, the EIC’s role is not merely administrative; it is a gate‑keeping function that directly controls whether the payment section can proceed and whether the project stays within the Department’s timing requirements. The manual’s emphasis on immediate issuance and forwarding, coupled with the need to verify no outstanding claims, is designed to guarantee that the defect‑liability phase is closed swiftly, thus supporting compliance with the Department of Expenditure’s procedural timelines. The EIC’s timely execution of this duty is therefore critical to maintaining alignment between internal NRL procedures and external governmental expectations.

question_text: What approval is needed for any bid due date extension beyond the two normally allowed extensions
answer: - Commercial HOD's prior consent is required for any bid due date extension beyond the two normally allowed extensions (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 55).
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know what kind of approval is required when someone tries to push a bid due date past the two extensions that are normally permitted.  

Looking at the policy, I see that the standard practice is to allow up to two extensions for any enquiry without any special sign‑off; those are considered routine adjustments that the purchase officer can handle on their own.  

The next piece of information tells me what happens when the situation goes beyond that limit: if a third or further extension is needed, the rule explicitly states that prior consent from the Commercial Head of Department must be obtained.  

Putting those two points together, the logical flow is clear—since the first two extensions are covered by the purchase officer’s authority, any request for an additional extension steps outside that authority and triggers the higher‑level approval requirement.  

Therefore, the approval that must be secured for any bid due date extension beyond the two normally allowed extensions is the prior consent of the Commercial HOD.
chunk_content:
### 4.4.1 (B) Minimum Response in Open/Limited Tenders:
1. **"Minimum Response"** shall be considered as under, and no separate approval note to be processed for un-priced bid opening:
  - i. Where the enquiry is issued on open tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids.
  - ii. Where the enquiry is issued on limited tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids. Wherever limited tender is issued to two parties only, minimum response shall be two.
2. Respective purchase officer shall suitably extend the bid due date in either of the following two situations:
  - i) Where Minimum response is not obtained, Purchase officer can give first extension of up to one week but subsequent extensions shall require Commercial HOD's consent. Indentor and HOD of user dept. is to be notified about such extensions.
  - ii) Where Minimum response is obtained but one or more of the vendors have requested for extension by the due date. In such a cases, user dept HOD's prior consent shall be obtained.
3. Normally two extensions shall be given to any enquiry. In case, even after two bid due date extension(s), minimum response is not obtained, whatever bids are received, may be opened. In the case of no response, refloating may be done only in consultation with user department.
4. Where extension is required for any reason(s) beyond two extensions, Commercial HOD's prior consent shall be obtained. Reason for such extensions should be recorded.

## 4.5 Eligibility and Qualifications of Bidders


### 4.5.1 Eligibility of Bidders
- i) All eligible bidders meeting the eligibility criteria as defined in ITB can participate in the

tender. The bidder should be a private or government-owned legal entity.

- ii) Bidder should have valid registration with Employees Provident Fund organization under 'EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952', wherever applicable.
- iii) Tenders where Joint Ventures / LLPs (limited liability partnerships) are allowed, all the partners shall be jointly and severally liable (as applicable) for the successful completion of the work.
- iv) A firm that has been engaged by the procuring entity to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, and any of its affiliates (associates, subsidiary, JV partner), shall not be eligible for subsequently providing goods or works (other than a continuation of the firm's earlier consultancy services) for the same project.
- v) A firm determined non-performing by the Procuring Entity shall not be eligible to bid during the period so determined.

### 4.5.2 Qualification of Bidders
Qualification of bidders is done on Pre-qualification Bidding basis (refer Para 3.3.6, PQB) or on post-qualification basis (refer Para 3.3.4, single stage multiple envelope system). In both cases Qualification criteria needs to be laid down in the Bid Document (refer para 3.3.6 iii). It is of utmost importance to develop new contractors and also to provide avenues to Sub-contractors executing NRL contracts, since they may not get opportunities to accumulate the required credentials to compete in normal tenders. question_text: What final measure may the Procuring Entity consider if the consultant fails to take corrective action for unsatisfactory performance?
answer: - Consider terminating the contract. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 61)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants the final action the Procuring Entity might take when a consultant does not correct unsatisfactory performance after being asked to do so.  

Next, the guidance on poor or unsatisfactory performance explains that when performance is lacking, the Procuring Entity first advises the consultant to take necessary measures to improve or replace staff.  

Then, it notes that if the consultant does not act on that advice, the Procuring Entity should escalate the matter—bringing it to the consultant’s top management and issuing a formal notice to rectify the situation.  

After that notice is given, the guidance indicates that the Procuring Entity still has a recourse if the consultant continues to fail to correct the problem. The logical next step, presented as the ultimate option, is to consider ending the contractual relationship.  

Putting those steps together—initial advice, escalation to top management with a notice to rectify, and finally the possibility of ending the agreement—leads to the conclusion that the final measure the Procuring Entity may consider is terminating the contract.  

Thus, the answer follows naturally from the sequence: unsatisfactory performance → advise correction → notice to rectify → consider contract termination.

## 8.5 Reporting of Progress
The timing, nature, and number of reports that the consultant/ service provider should provide are normally contained in the Consultancy and other services contract. If the assignment is of a routine nature over a long period (for example, implementation supervision), then monthly, quarterly, and annual progress reports may be required. On the other hand, if the assignment is to prepare a study or to implement a particular task, a more specific type of reporting may be required.

## 8.6 Monitoring a Time-based Contract
As indicated earlier, the performance of a time-based contract may depend on the progress in other contracts (for example, the progress of a construction supervision contract depends on the progress of a construction contract). In such situations, the mobilisation and demobilisation of resources/ key experts and time employed by them should be mobilised and monitored carefully as it is possible that the contract period and the total amount under the contract are spent fully and construction work being supervised is not even half complete. These situations could lead to claims and disputes.

## 8.7 Monitoring a Lump-sum Contract
As Lump-sum contract is based on output and deliverables, it is important that the quality of draft reports is checked carefully before release of stage payment as subsequent dispute after completion of the task could lead to disputes. In this form of contract, if there are extra additional services, there should be timely amendment to the contract to reflect these increases and to regulate payment. In general, in a lump-sum contract, the increase should not be more than 10-15 (ten to fifteen) per cent.

## 8.8 Unsatisfactory Performance
Poor performance may involve one or more particular staff from the consultant/ service provider's team, or the whole team or non-participation by the main qualifying JV member. Based on the provisions of the contract, the Procuring Entity will advise the consultant/ service provider to take the necessary measures to address the situation. Poor performance should not be tolerated; therefore, the consultant/ service provider should act quickly to comply with a reasonable request to improve the performance of the team or to replace any particular staff member who is not performing adequately. If the consultant/ service provider fails to take adequate corrective actions, the Procuring Entity may take up the issue with the top management of the consultant/ service provider and issue notice to rectify the situation and finally consider terminating the contract.

## 8.9 Delays
Consultancy and other services may be delayed for a variety of reasons. The consultant/ service

provider should notify the Procuring Entity and explain the causes of such delays. If corrective action requires extra work and the delay cannot be attributed to the consultant/ service provider, the extra work should be reimbursed in accordance with the contract.

## 8.10 Issuing Contract Variations
8.10.1 The formal method of making and documenting a change in the Consultancy and other services contract is through a contract variation.

Contract variations are issued when there are agreed-upon changes in the scope of work, personnel inputs, costs, timing of the submission of reports, or out-of-pocket expenditures. There are few Consultancy and other services contracts of any type that do not require a contract variation at one time or another. Normally, these relate to changes that have a cost implication, but when there is a significant change in the timing of an activity or a particular output, these should also be recorded through a contract variation. Normally, the request for contract variation is prepared by the consultant/ service provider or Consultancy/ service provider firm and submitted to the Procuring Entity.

## 4.8 Drawals against Rate Contract (RC)/Framework Contract (FC)
4.8.1 RC is essentially a price agreement with the vendors/contractors at a specified price and terms and conditions during the period covered by the RC. No quantity is mentioned nor is any minimum commitment guaranteed in the RC. RC is most frequently used in procurement of goods, but can as well be used *mutatis mutandis* in works, services and consultancy - where it is commonly known as a Framework Contract (FC). *For appropriate items (please see para 4.8.3 below), drawals against an existing RC exploits the power of collaboration/ clubbing of numerous small and frequent requirements and thus provides best VfM along with a simple and quick procedure.* However, entering into a new RC may have the same procedural complexity, prolonged timeframe and systemic cost as in OTE, which may not be viable for low volumes. In view of Government e Marketplace coming into operation, Rate Contract is not required to be executed for common use items like computers, printers, photocopiers, paper and stationary, other office items like furniture, bottled water etc., which are being placed on GeM and will now be applicable only for specialized and engineering items which are not available on GeM, and are identified as common use items and are needed on recurring basis. For any exceptions to the above, the reason for going for RC should be justified and recorded.

question_text: What formula is used to calculate the GST amount (Y) when the gross amount of work executed (Z) and the amount excluding GST (X) are known?
answer:
The source provides the following formulas for calculation:

Z = X + Y
Where Y = X · R / 100

(Z = Gross amount of work executed; X = Amount of work executed excluding GST amount; Y = GST amount; R = Percentage rate of GST for that HSN code).
cot: I start by recognizing that the gross amount of work executed (Z) represents the total paid to the contractor, which comprises the actual value of the work excluding tax plus the GST that has been added on top of that value. Since the amount of work executed excluding GST (X) is already known, the GST component must be whatever is left when that base amount is subtracted from the total. Therefore, the GST amount Y is obtained by taking the difference between Z and X, giving Y = Z – X. If one wishes to check the calculation, the applicable GST rate R can be applied to the base amount X, yielding Y = X × R / 100, which should match the previously derived difference. This confirms that the correct formula for determining the GST amount from the known gross and net figures is Y = Z – X.

question_text: What happens after the techno‑commercial bid evaluation is completed in a multiple‑envelope tender?
answer: After the techno‑commercial bid evaluation, the Technical Review Committee prepares a technical recommendation and the Commercial department examines the commercial terms and conditions of the techno‑commercial bid (Annexure 3) to declare the successful bidders. The evaluation results are then announced, including notification of any unsuccessful bidders. Subsequently, price bids are opened in the presence of the technically suitable bidders who wish to attend, at a pre‑publicised date, time and place, or via the e‑procurement portal if applicable. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 75)
cot:
First, I consider what the techno‑commercial bid evaluation actually entails in a multiple‑envelope setting: the technical and commercial aspects have already been examined together, and the next logical step is to turn that evaluation into a decision about which bidders move forward.  
Then I recall that the process splits the responsibility— the Technical Review Committee focuses on the technical side, while the Commercial department looks at the contractual and financial terms.  
So, after the evaluation, the TRC would draft a technical recommendation that captures whether each bidder meets the required specifications, quality, and performance criteria.  
At the same time, the Commercial team would scrutinize the commercial conditions laid out in Annexure 3, checking for any deviations, ensuring the bids are substantially responsive and that the tenderer's obligations align with the contract.  
Combining these two outputs, the committee and the department can jointly declare the successful bidders—those who are both technically compliant and commercially acceptable.  
Once that decision is made, the results need to be communicated: the evaluation outcome is announced, and any bidders who did not meet the criteria are formally notified of their unsuccessful status.  
Finally, because the price bids were kept in a separate envelope, they are opened next. This opening occurs in the presence of the technically suitable bidders who choose to attend, at a pre‑publicised date, time and place, or through the e‑procurement portal if the tender is conducted electronically.  

This sequence of steps naturally leads to the described post‑evaluation actions in a multiple‑envelope tender.

question_text: After an appeal is filed, what actions may the Appellate Authority take before issuing a decision?
answer:
The Appellate Authority may, before issuing a decision on an appeal, undertake the following actions:

- Request comments from the Competent Authority, if it considers such input useful.  
- Offer the appellant agency an opportunity for a personal hearing.  
- Examine the case facts, the documents on record, and the submissions made by the appellant agency.  

After completing these steps, the Authority may either uphold the Competent Authority’s decision (with or without variation or a lesser period of Holiday Listing) or annul the Competent Authority’s order. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 55)
cot:
First, I consider what happens once an appeal is lodged: the Appellate Authority now has a case to review before it can render a final decision.  
Next, I think about the authority’s discretion to gather additional information; it can ask the Competent Authority for its comments if it believes that perspective would help clarify the issues.  
Then, I reflect on the possibility of giving the appellant a chance to be heard directly—offering a personal hearing allows the agency to present its side in person.  
After those optional steps, the authority must look at what is already on file: the facts of the case, the documents that have been recorded, and any submissions the appellant has made.  
Only after reviewing that material can the Appellate Authority form a judgment, and at that point it has two clear paths: it may uphold the Competent Authority’s decision, possibly with some modification or a reduced Holiday Listing period, or it may overturn that decision entirely.  
Putting those pieces together, the actions the Appellate Authority may take before issuing a decision are to seek comments from the Competent Authority, to offer a personal hearing, and to examine the case facts, documents, and appellant’s submissions, after which it either upholds or annuls the original order.

question_text: How should the Order’s provisions be incorporated into tender conditions for procurements initiated after 23 July 2020
answer:
- For tenders issued after 23 July 2020, the Order’s provisions must be embedded directly into the tender conditions (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 19).  
- This requirement applies to all Central Public Sector Enterprises and should be implemented in accordance with any applicable Department of Public Enterprises notifications (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 20).  
- Incorporating these provisions ensures that bidders from land‑border countries meet registration and transitional rules, reinforcing transparency, mitigating compliance risk, and aligning procurement with national policy goals such as Make‑in‑India and Ease of Doing Business—thereby supporting corporate value creation and resilient supply‑chain management.
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know the method for embedding the Order’s requirements into the tender documents for any procurement that begins after the specified cut‑off date of 23 July 2020.  

The key point is that for tenders to be issued after the date of the order, the relevant provisions of the Order must be incorporated directly into the tender conditions. This indicates that the incorporation is not an optional add‑on but a mandatory step that belongs in the very fabric of the tender paperwork.  

Next, I consider who must follow this rule. The applicability extends to all Central Public Sector Enterprises and any notifications issued by the Department of Public Enterprises should also be observed. This means the incorporation step is uniform across the CPSE sector, with room for additional guidance from the DPE where relevant.  

Now I think about what those provisions actually entail. The Order sets out a registration requirement for bidders coming from countries that share a land border with India, and it defines transitional handling for tenders that are still open or have passed certain evaluation stages. By weaving these rules into the tender conditions, the procuring authority ensures that any bidder from a land‑border country can only participate if they are registered with the competent authority, and that tenders are either rejected outright or restarted de novo if the process has already moved past the initial qualification stage.  

From there, I can see the practical effects of doing this correctly. Embedding the registration and transitional clauses makes the procurement process transparent, because all parties know exactly what eligibility criteria apply up front. It also reduces compliance risk, since the tender documents themselves enforce the rules rather than relying on ad‑hoc checks later. Moreover, the Order is linked to broader governmental aims—such as promoting domestic manufacturing under Make‑in‑India, improving the ease of doing business, and fostering job creation—so adhering to its provisions helps align procurement outcomes with those national policy goals.  

Finally, when the tender conditions reflect the Order’s provisions, the resulting contracts are more likely to support corporate value creation and build resilient supply chains, because they exclude non‑compliant foreign bidders and encourage participation from registered, vetted sources that meet the stipulated standards.  

Putting it all together, the answer is clear: for any procurement initiated after 23 July 2020, the procuring authority must embed the Order’s registration, transitional, and related requirements directly into the tender conditions, apply this uniformly across all CPSEs while observing any DPE notifications, and thereby achieve transparency, risk mitigation, and alignment with wider economic and social objectives.

### iii) **Broader Obligations Principle**
Over and above transparency and professionalism, the procuring authorities have also the responsibility and accountability to conduct public procurement in a manner to facilitate achievement of the broader objectives of the Government - to the extent these are specifically included in the 'Procurement Guidelines':

- a) *Preferential* procurement from backward regions, weaker sections and MSEs, locally manufactured goods or services, to the extent specifically included in the 'Procurement Guidelines'; and
- b) *Reservation of procurement* of specified class of goods from or through certain nominated CPSEs or Government Organisations, to the extent specifically included in the 'Procurement Guidelines'.
- c) *Support* to broader social *policy* and programme objectives of the Government (for example, economic growth, strengthening of local industry - make-in-India, Ease of Doing Business, job and employment creation, and so on, to the extent specifically included in the 'Procurement Guidelines');
- d) Facilitating administrative goals of other Departments of Government (for example, *ensuring* tax or environmental compliance by participants, Energy Conservation, accessibility for People With *Disabilities* etc. to the extent specifically included in the 'Procurement Guidelines').
- e) **Procurement from a Bidder from a country which shares Land Border with India:** Procurement *policies* and procedures must comply with accessibility criteria which may be mandated by the Government from time to time, which are as follows:

#### 1. **Requirement of registration**
- a) Any bidder from a country which shares a land border with India will be eligible to bid in any procurement whether of goods, services (including consultancy services and non-consultancy services) or works (including turnkey projects) only if the bidder is registered with the Competent Authority, specified in Para 12(c) below.
- b) The Order shall not apply to (i) cases where orders have been placed or contract has been concluded or letter/notice of award/ acceptance (LoA) has been issued on or before the date of the order (23rd July 2020); and (ii) cases falling under para 13 below.

#### 2. **Transitional cases**
Tenders where no contract has been concluded or no LoA has been issued so far shall be handled in the following manner: -

- a) In tenders which are yet to be opened, or where evaluation of technical bid or the first exclusionary qualifying stage (i.e. the first stage at which the qualifications of tenderers are evaluated and unqualified bidders are excluded) has not been completed: No contracts shall be placed on bidders from such countries. Tenders received from bidders from such countries shall be dealt with as if they are non-

compliant with the tender conditions and the tender shall be processed accordingly.

- b) If the tendering process has crossed the first exclusionary qualificatory stage, if the qualified bidders include bidders from such countries, the entire process shall be scrapped and initiated *de nova*. The *de nova* process shall adhere to the conditions prescribed in the Order.
- c) As far as practicable, and in cases of doubt about whether a bidder falls under paragraph (1) above, a certificate shall be obtained from the bidder whose bid is proposed to be considered or accepted, in terms of paras 5(c), 5(d) and 6 read with para (1).

#### 3. Incorporation in tender conditions
In tenders to be issued after the date (23rd July 2020) of the order, the relevant provisions of the Order shall be incorporated in the tender conditions.

Applicable to all Central Public Sector Enterprises and as per notification(s) of Department of Public Enterprises.

question_text: What are the three terms used to describe the refined concept of cost that includes acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal costs?
answer: The refined concept of cost that includes acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal costs is described by the three terms: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), Life Cycle Cost (LCC), and Whole-of-Life (WOL). (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 16)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking for: it wants the three labels that are used for a more comprehensive cost idea—one that adds acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal to the basic purchase price.  

Next, I think about how cost is usually treated in procurement discussions. The plain “price” or “acquisition cost” only looks at what you pay up front, but decision‑makers often need to consider everything that will be spent over the item’s useful life. That broader view is what the question is hinting at.  

In the Procurement of Goods Manual, the simple price concept is refined to take into account not only the initial acquisition price but also the costs of operation, maintenance, and disposal during the lifetime of the procured resource.  

The manual gives the specific names that are used for this refined idea: it mentions Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), Life Cycle Cost (LCC), and Whole‑of‑Life (WOL) as the three interchangeable terms.  

I check that each of those terms indeed covers the four cost elements mentioned—acquisition (the upfront price), operation (running the item), maintenance (keeping it functional), and disposal (end‑of‑life handling)—because they are all described as life‑cycle or ownership‑wide cost measures.  

Putting it together, the three terms that describe the refined cost concept including acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal are Total Cost of Ownership, Life Cycle Cost, and Whole‑of‑Life.

### ii) Right Quantity
There are extra costs and systemic overheads involved with both procuring a requirement too frequently in small quantities or with buying large quantities for prolonged use. Hence, the right quantity should be procured (in appropriate size of contract) which balances extra costs associated with larger and smaller quantities.

### iii) Right Price
It is not correct to aim at the cheapest materials/ facilities/ Services available. The price should be just right for the quality, quantity and other factors involved (or should not be abnormally low for a facilities/works/ services which could lead to a situation of non-performance or failure of contract). The concept of price can be refined further to take into account not only the initial price paid for the requirement but also other costs such as maintenance costs, operational costs and disposal costs (Also termed as life cycle costing - please also refer to para 1.6 below)

### iv) Right Time and Place
If the material (or facility or services) is needed by an organisation in three months' time, it will be costly to procure it too late or too early. Similarly, if the vendor delivers the materials/ facilities/ services in another city, extra time and money would be involved in logistics. An unrealistic time schedule for completion of a facility may lead to delays, claims and disputes.

### v) Right Source
Similarly, the source of delivery of Goods, Works and Services of the requirement must have just right financial capacity and technical capability for our needs (demonstrated through satisfactory past performance of contracts of same or similar nature). Buying a few packets of printer paper directly from a large manufacturer may not be the right strategy. On the other

hand, if our requirements are very large, buying such requirements through dealers or middlemen may also not be right.

## 1.6 Refined Concepts of Cost and Value - Value for Money
The concept of price or cost has been further refined into Total Cost Of Ownership (TCO) or Life Cycle Cost (LCC) or Whole-of-Life (WOL) to take into account not only the initial acquisition cost but also cost of operation, maintenance and disposal during the lifetime of the external resource procured. Similarly, the concept of quality is linked to the need and is refined into the concept of utility/ value. These two, taken together, are used to develop the concept of Value for Money (VfM, also called Best Value for Money in certain contexts). VfM means the effective, efficient, and economic use of resources, which may involve the evaluation of relevant costs and benefits, along with an assessment of risks, non-price attributes (e.g. in goods and/or services that contain recyclable content, are recyclable, minimise waste and greenhouse gas emissions, conserve energy and water and minimize habitat destruction and environmental degradation, are non-toxic etc.) and/or life cycle costs, as appropriate. Price alone may not necessarily represent VfM. In public procurement, VfM is achieved by attracting the widest competition by way of optimal description of need; development of value-engineered specifications/ Terms of Reference (ToR); appropriate packaging/ slicing of requirement; selection of an appropriate mode of procurement and bidding system.

question_text: What stage ensures that the work is carried out according to quality standards after the award of work
answer: The stage that ensures the work is carried out according to quality standards after the award of work is Execution and Monitoring of works and Quality Assurance.
cot: I need to figure out which phase comes right after a contract is awarded and is responsible for making sure the work is done to the required quality. First, I think about the overall workflow: a project starts with ideas, moves through planning and approvals, then design, then the bidding process, and finally the award of work. Once the award is made, the focus shifts from paperwork to actually getting the work done on the ground. The next logical step in the sequence is where the contractor begins construction and the overseeing body keeps track of progress, checks materials, and verifies that everything meets the specifications. Looking at the list of stages, after the award of work there is a phase called “Execution and Monitoring of works and Quality Assurance.” This stage is explicitly about carrying out the work while continuously monitoring it and applying quality‑assurance measures to ensure compliance with standards. Therefore, the stage that guarantees the work is performed according to quality standards after the award is the Execution and Monitoring of works and Quality Assurance stage.

question_text: If the highest acceptable bidder cannot take the total quantity offered, how is the remaining quantity allocated?
answer:
- When the highest acceptable bidder cannot accept the full quantity, the remaining lot is offered to the next‑highest bidder(s) at the same price quoted by the top bidder.  
- The tender must specify the minimum quantity that will be accepted from those bidders, ensuring clarity and preventing fragmented allocations.  

This approach preserves the agreed‑upon value, limits exposure to unsold inventory, and supports risk‑managed disposal of surplus material. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 172)
cot:
First, I picture the situation: the auction has closed, the highest acceptable bidder has won the lot but, for whatever reason, can only take a portion of the quantity that was put up for sale. The question is what happens to the rest of the material that remains unclaimed.

Next, I think about the goals of the disposal process. The seller wants to realize the value that was agreed upon in the bid, avoid leaving unsold inventory that would have to be re‑advertised, and treat all bidders fairly without reopening price negotiations. Any solution should keep the transaction as close to the original award as possible while still clearing the remaining goods.

Then, I consider who would be the most natural counterpart to take the leftover. The other bidders have already submitted offers; they have demonstrated interest in buying the material at prices they deemed acceptable. The next‑highest bidder(s) are the logical candidates because they are already willing to pay at least as much as the price they quoted, and they have passed the qualification checks.

After that, I reason about the price at which the leftover should be sold. If we were to ask the next bidder to pay a different amount, we would either have to renegotiate—which defeats the purpose of a sealed‑bid process—or risk selling below the winning bid, which would undermine the seller’s expected return. Keeping the price identical to the winning bid preserves the agreed‑upon value and avoids any perception of unfairness or post‑auction haggling.

I also recall that tenders for such disposals usually include a safeguard to prevent the lot from being split into impractically small pieces. To make sure the allocation remains workable, the tender document states a minimum quantity that any bidder must accept if offered a portion of the lot. This clause ensures that the remaining quantity is only passed on in chunks that are economically viable for the next bidder to handle.

Putting these pieces together, the remaining quantity is offered to the next‑highest bidder(s) at exactly the same price the top bidder had quoted, and the transfer is only made if the offered lot meets the minimum quantity stipulated in the tender. This approach maintains the winning bid’s value, limits the seller’s exposure to unsold stock, and follows the pre‑agreed rules for allocating partial awards. 

Thus, the allocation rule is: when the highest acceptable bidder cannot take the full quantity, the balance goes to the next‑highest bidder(s) at the winning bidder’s price, subject to the minimum‑quantity condition set out in the tender.

question_text: How do I determine the base exchange rate to use for my bid
answer:
To determine the base exchange rate for your bid, you should use the TT (telegraphic transfer) selling rate that is quoted by any RBI‑authorised exchange banker on the **base date** specified in the tender.  

The base date is either the due date for opening of tenders or seven days before that date – the buying organisation will decide which one to apply and will state it in the tender documents.  

Once you know the base date, obtain the TT selling rate for each foreign currency involved in your import content from an authorised bank on that date. That rate becomes your base exchange rate, which you then use to convert the foreign‑currency value of your imported items into Indian Rupees for the total quoted price in your bid.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 112)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the tender is asking for when it mentions a base exchange rate – it’s the rate I’ll use to turn the foreign‑currency cost of any imported components into Indian rupees so that my overall bid price can be expressed in INR.  

Next, I look at what the tender documents usually specify about that rate. They will define a “base date,” which is either the day the tenders are due to be opened or a week before that day, and the buying organisation will state which of the two they are adopting.  

With the base date fixed, the next logical step is to find the actual exchange rate to apply on that day. The clause makes clear that the rate to use is the TT (telegraphic‑transfer) selling rate quoted by any bank that is authorised by the RBI to deal in foreign exchange.  

So I would contact one of those authorised banks, ask for the TT selling rate for each foreign currency I have in my import bill on the base date, and record those figures. Those rates become my base exchange rates for the respective currencies.  

Having obtained the rates, I then convert the foreign‑currency value of each imported item into rupees by multiplying the amount by the TT selling rate I just gathered, add up all the converted amounts together with any local‑cost elements, and arrive at the total quoted price in INR that I will put in my bid.  

Finally, I check that using the TT selling rate on the base date fits the exchange‑variation mechanism described – any later movement of the rate beyond the agreed band will be handled through the ERV clause, while the rate I locked in at the base date remains the reference for calculating those variations.  

Putting it all together, the base exchange rate for my bid is simply the TT selling rate from an RBI‑authorised exchange banker on the base date specified in the tender, applied to each foreign currency involved in my import content.

## 6.7 Exchange Rate Variation
**6.7.1** In case of a contract involving substantial import content(s) and having a long delivery period (exceeding one year from the date of contract), an appropriate Foreign Exchange Variation clause may be formulated by the procuring entity in consultation with its Finance, as needed, and incorporated in the tender enquiry document. In that clause, the tenderers are to be asked to indicate import content(s) and the currency (ies) used for calculating the value of import content(s) in their total quoted price, which (that is, the total quoted price) will be in Indian Rupees. The tenderers may be asked to indicate the Base Exchange rate for each such foreign currency used for converting the foreign exchange content into Indian Rupees and the extent of foreign Exchange Rate Variation (ERV) risk they are willing to bear.

To work out the variation due to changes (if any) in the exchange rate(s), the base date for this purpose will be the due date of opening of tenders/seven days prior to the due date of opening of tenders (the purchase organisation is to decide and adopt a suitable date). The variation may be allowed between the above base date and date of remittance to the foreign principal/mid-point of manufacture of the foreign component (the purchase organization is to choose the appropriate date). The applicable exchange rates as above will be according to the **TT** selling rates of exchange as quoted by authorised exchange bankers approved by RBI on the dates in question. No variation in price in this regard will be allowed if the variation in the rate of exchange remains within the limit of plus/minus \_\_\_\_per cent (the purchase organisation is to decide the limit, say plus/ minus band of 2.5% (Two point Five percent).

Any increase or decrease in the customs duty by reason of the variation in the rate of exchange in terms of the contract will be to the buyer's account. The following general principles should be observed while entering into contracts:

question_text: What declaration must the contractor provide on the final bill regarding any further claims and acceptance of payment?
answer: A certificate from the contractor shall be obtained on the final bill that he has no further claims than those given in the final bill and that he accepts the payment in full and final settlement of all his claims.
cot:
First, I focus on what the question is really asking: it wants the exact wording of the contractor’s statement that must appear on the final bill, specifically concerning any leftover claims and the acceptance of payment as settlement.  

Next, I recall the part of the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals that deals with final bill preparation, specifically regarding any mention of a contractor‑provided certificate or declaration.  

There is a requirement that a certificate be obtained from the contractor on the final bill, and the language is quite explicit: the contractor must state that he has no further claims beyond those already listed in the bill and that he accepts the payment as full and final settlement of all his claims.  

I note that this is the only clause that addresses both the renunciation of additional claims and the acknowledgment of payment completeness; the surrounding items—deviation statements, completion certificates, material appropriation, etc.—do not touch on this particular point.  

I then consider whether any other section adds a qualifier or alternative phrasing, but the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals consistently repeat that same declaration, confirming that it is the sole and complete statement required.  

Finally, I synthesize the finding: the contractor must attach a declaration to the final bill affirming that he has no further claims than those itemised in the bill and that he accepts the payment as full and final settlement of all his claims. This matches the answer’s description and satisfies the question’s demand.

### 6.7.6 Payment of Final Bill
When a final bill (bill summary; GST/tax invoice may be collected prior to final payment certification) of the contractor is submitted, the following requirements shall be compiled by the engineer-in-charge in addition to the requirements applicable to the running account bills:

- i) A Deviation Statement shall be prepared by the Engineer-in-charge showing the quantity and cost of each item of work executed as compared to the estimated quantities and amount of the contract giving reasons for excesses and savings, extra/substituted items, as applicable.
- ii) A time extension statement with reasons and details, if applicable
- iii) A completion certificate (**Annexure 11**) in the prescribed form stating that the work has been completed in all respects strictly according to the specifications given in the tender documents.
- iv) A final statement of recoveries / deductions / penalties / clearance of hold amount, if any (**Annexure 12 and Annexure 13**) along with a certificate that no other amount is recoverable from the contractor on any account.
- v) A certificate from the contractor shall be obtained on the final bill that he has no further claims than those given in the final bill and that he accepts the payment in full and final settlement of all his claims.

If the contractor has any claim still persisting at the time of preparation of final bill, it should be ensured that the contractor attaches a statement of claims to the final bill giving particulars of such claims, grounds on which it is based and the amount claimed duly supported with copies of notices sent to the Engineer-in- Charge.

- vi) A material appropriation statement (**Annexure 26**) shall be given by the Engineer-in-charge indicating the details of issue voucher reference numbers, quantity issued, quantify utilised in the work and the amount chargeable to the contractor for non-return / excess consumption of materials in accordance with the terms of the contract. The quantity of theoretical consumption as indicated by the Engineer-in-Charge in the material appropriation statement shall be accepted as final.
- vii) An undertaking from the contractor that he has discharged all his obligation under various laws and he would indemnify the owner if there is any demand against the Company on his account. A labour liability certificate (in case labour is involved)
- viii) Any special certificates, if required, from any statutory authorities
- ix) A contractor performance evaluation statement as per performance evaluation policy in vogue.

The Payments against final bills should be authorised only after the certification of Engineer-in-charge of contract execution (and User department, wherever applicable) for completeness of the job as per scope of work as well as regarding clearance of the work site.

Following additional test checks shall be exercised by Finance Department (payment section)

in respect of final bills:

- i) That the certificates and statements required to be submitted by the Engineer-in-charge along with the final bill have been submitted.
- ii) The material appropriation statement shall be checked to see whether the allowance allowed are in line with the provisions of contract only. No other checking in this regard need to be made.
- iii) It shall be seen that the work has been completed by the contractor within the stipulated period or within such extended time as may be given by the Engineer-in-charge.
- iv) If extension of time has been granted to the contractor, Finance Department shall see that order amendment or approval copy is made available.

After the bills have been checked, adjustment entries required, if any, shall be passed by Finance officials and final payment shall be authorized by finance officials.

All the payments related to WOs shall be made as per contract conditions.

question_text: What inputs and facilities does the purchasing organization indicate it will provide to the contractor in a turnkey arrangement
answer:
- The purchasing organization specifies the inputs and other facilities it will provide to the contractor, as detailed in the tender enquiry document (alongside the required performance and output specifications).  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 141)
cot:
I start by thinking about what a turnkey arrangement actually means in procurement: the contractor takes on the design, manufacture, supply, installation and commissioning of the plant, while the buyer sets out what the finished facility must do.  

From there I consider how the buyer communicates those expectations. In a turnkey tender the purchaser not only defines the required performance and output levels but also makes clear what it will contribute to the contractor’s effort.  

That contribution consists of the inputs—things like utilities, site access, or raw material supplies—and the other facilities, such as existing infrastructure or support services, that the buyer will make available at the site.  

I note that these details are deliberately spelled out in the tender enquiry document so the contractor can understand exactly what will be provided and price the work accordingly.  

Putting it together, the purchasing organization indicates the inputs and other facilities it will supply to the contractor, as laid out in the tender enquiry document alongside the performance and output specifications.
chunk_content: In the context of procurement of goods, a turnkey contract may include the manufacture, supply, assembly, installation/ commissioning of equipment (or a group of plant and machines working in tandem - even though some of the machines may not be manufactured by the supplier himself) and some incidental works or services. Generally, in the tender enquiry documents for a turn key contract, the purchase organization specifies the performance and output required from the plant proposed to be set up and broadly outlines the various parameters it visualizes for the desired plant. The inputs and other facilities, which the purchase organization will provide to the contractor, are also indicated in the tender enquiry document. The contractor is to design the plant and quote accordingly. The responsibility of the contractor will include supplying the required goods, machinery, equipment etc. needed for the plant; assembling, installing and erecting the same at site as needed; commissioning the plant to meet the required output etc., as specified in the tender enquiry documents.

question_text: What should bid documents clearly specify about whether joint ventures are allowed to bid on an assignment?
answer:
Bid documents should clearly state whether joint ventures (JVs) are allowed to bid on the assignment. If JVs are permitted, the documents must also specify the maximum number of partners allowed in a JV, the collective qualifications the JV must meet (such as relevant experience and financial turnover), the individual qualifications each partner must satisfy (such as financial soundness), and that each partner must meet at least 25 % of the qualifying criteria while the lead partner must meet at least 50 % of those criteria for experience and financial turnover.  

This clarification helps bidders understand the consortium rules and avoid disqualification due to unclear eligibility requirements. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 17)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the question is really asking: it wants to know what information bid documents must make explicit when it comes to the possibility of joint ventures submitting a bid for an assignment.  

Thinking about the context, large or complex assignments often lead consultants to team up, and the procurement rules have to make clear whether such teaming is permitted and, if it is, under what conditions.  

Looking at the guidance, it explains that after a shortlist is created, any joint‑venture or sub‑consultancy arrangement among the short‑listed firms is allowed only if the request for proposal spells it out. It also notes that one member must act as the lead and that the procuring entity deals solely with that lead.  

From that, I can see that the bid documents must first state outright whether joint ventures are allowed to bid at all—this is the baseline condition.  

If the answer is yes, the documents then need to set a ceiling on how many firms can join together in a single joint venture, because unlimited numbers would make evaluation unmanageable.  

Next, the documents have to describe what the joint venture as a whole must satisfy—collective requirements such as relevant project experience and overall financial turnover.  

At the same time, each individual partner must meet certain personal criteria, chiefly financial soundness, to ensure that no member is a weak link.  

Finally, the guidance specifies quantitative thresholds: every partner should fulfill at least 25 % of the qualifying thresholds for experience and turnover, while the lead partner must reach at least 50 % of those thresholds.  

Putting these pieces together, the bid documents should clearly state whether joint ventures are permitted, and if they are, they must define the maximum number of partners, the collective qualifications the joint venture must meet, the individual qualifications each partner must satisfy, and the minimum percentage contributions (25 % for each partner, 50 % for the lead) for experience and financial turnover.  

This chain of reasoning leads directly to the required answer.

### 2.1.1 Consortium of consultants/ service providers
In large and complex assignments consultants/ service providers may associate with each other to form a consortium to complement their respective areas of expertise, to increase the technical responsiveness of their proposal, and make larger pools of experts available or for other reasons. Such an association may be for the long term (independent of any particular assignment) or for a specific assignment. The consortium may take the form of a Joint Venture (JV) or a sub consultancy. In case of a JV, all members of the JV shall sign the contract and shall be jointly and severally liable for the entire assignment. After the short list is finalised, and the Request for Proposal (RfP) is issued, any association in the form of a JV or sub consultancy among the short-listed firms shall be permissible in accordance with provisions stated in the RfP. Under such circumstance, one of the shortlisted consultants/ service providers must become the lead member of the consortium. The Procuring Entity only deals with the lead member of consortiums for all the purposes. Bid documents should clearly specify whether JVs are allowed to bid (in case of complex and large assignments, say above certain values (say - Rupees five crore). Maximum number of partners in JV shall be limited (say - three). In case JVs are permitted to bid, it should be clarified what qualifications are to be collectively (clubbed together) met by the JV partners (say experience of particular consultancy, Financial Turnover etc) and what each partner has to individually and separately meet (financial soundness). In this case it should also be specified that each partner should meet at least 25% (and the lead partner at least 50%) out of the qualifying limit in case of experience of particular consultancy and financial turnover, if any.

**Conflicting Association:** A firm shall submit only one proposal, either individually or as a JV partner in another proposal. If a firm, including a JV partner, submits or participates in more than one proposal, all such proposals shall be disqualified. This does not, however, preclude a firm from participating as a sub-consultant or an individual consultant to participate as a team member in more than one proposal when circumstances justify but only if permitted by the RfP document.

### 2.1.2 Consultancy or Service Providing Firms
The main source of consultants and service providers is Consultancy or Service providing firms of diverse specializations that provide teams to Clients. These firms provide project preparation services, project implementation supervision services, training, advisory services, and policy guidance. Such firms are normally classified as either international - firms that have international experience and are capable of undertaking work at international level at international rates; or national - firms that may not have international exposure and normally undertake assignments only within that country, usually at significantly lower rates.

question_text: What financial data are required in the financial statement concerning running account payments?
answer: The financial statement for running account payments must disclose the gross value of work done, advances taken, recoveries effected, amounts withheld, net payments, and details of cheque payments received, among other broad particulars (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 91).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: which specific financial figures must be disclosed in the part of the report that deals with running account payments.  
Looking at the description of that section, it says the statement is meant to show the broad details of all running account payments received up to the current date.  
From that description, the elements that are explicitly called out are the gross value of work done, any advances that have been taken, recoveries that have been effected, amounts that have been withheld, the resulting net payments, and the details of cheque payments received, with a note that other broad particulars may also be included.  
Putting those pieces together, it becomes clear that the statement must capture both the inflows (work done value, advances, cheque receipts) and the outflows or adjustments (recoveries, amounts withheld) to arrive at the net amount actually paid.  
Therefore, the financial data required are precisely the gross value of work done, advances taken, recoveries effected, amounts withheld, net payments, and the details of cheque payments received, plus any additional broad particulars needed to give a complete picture of the running account payments.

question_text: What role do Specifications play in describing inputs, processes, tests, and mode of measurement for commonly executed work
answer: - Specifications describe the inputs, processes, tests, and mode of measurement for each kind of work commonly executed. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 20)
cot:
I start by asking what the question is really after: it wants to know what specifications do when it comes to the inputs, the way work is carried out, the tests that verify quality, and how those quantities are measured for the kinds of jobs that show up repeatedly.

Next I think about the setting in which specifications are used. The Procurement of Works Manual discusses preparing estimates and then actually executing work, and it lists several reference documents that are consulted for those purposes—plinth area rates, schedule of rates, analysis of rates, and specifications. This tells me that specifications are one of the core references that professionals rely on, alongside cost‑based tools.

The Procurement of Works Manual describes specifications as detailing the inputs, the processes, the tests, and the mode of measurement for each kind of work that is commonly executed. In other words, they spell out what materials go into the job, the steps to follow, the checks to confirm it meets standards, and the rule for measuring how much of each item is involved.

Putting those pieces together, the function of specifications becomes clear: they provide a complete, standardized description of those four elements so that estimators can price the work accurately, contractors can execute it uniformly, and inspectors can verify compliance using a common measurement basis.

Therefore, the role of specifications is precisely to describe the inputs, processes, tests, and mode of measurement for each kind of work commonly executed.

For preparation of estimates and during execution of work following reference documents are used. These may be separate for different regions, various types of works - Building, Electrical and Mechanical.

- i) **Plinth Area Rates** which provide a quick but fairly accurate method of estimation of cost of buildings (e.g. CPWD DPAR- Delhi Plinth Area Rates).
- ii) **Schedule of Rates** for each kind of work commonly executed to facilitate the preparation of **estimates**, as also to serve as a guide in settling rates in connection with contract agreements, maintained up-to-date (e.g. CPWD DSR - Delhi Schedule of Rates).

Endeavour may be made to enlarge the base of the 'Schedule of Rates' published by various organizations to bring a maximum number of items under its ambit. For non-scheduled items, rates may be finalized by a committee constituted for the purpose.

- iii) **Analysis of Rates** by taking market rates of labour, materials, cartage etc and their **quantities** for each kind of work commonly executed (e.g. CPWD Analysis of Rates)
- iv) **Specifications** describing inputs, processes, tests and mode of measurement for each kind of work commonly executed (e.g. CPWD Specifications)

Further relevant sections in the Manuals for Procurement of “Goods” and/or “Consultancy & Other Services” may be referred for preparation of estimates, wherever deemed relevant.

question_text: Which selection methods can be used for financial advisors undertaking preparation of studies and financial consultancy?
answer:
Financial advisors for the preparation of studies and financial Consultancy can be selected under any of the methods described in the chapter.

(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 58)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: which selection procedures are allowable when a financial advisor is hired to prepare studies and provide financial consultancy.  

Next, I recall that for the first type of assignment—preparation of studies and financial consultancy—the advisor can be chosen using any of the methods described in the chapter, with the choice depending on the scope of the work.  

Then I think about what methods are actually described elsewhere in that same chapter. I recall that the procurement agents and inspection agents sections both mention using Quality‑ and Cost‑Based Selection (QCBS). The NGO section shows that Single Source Selection (SSS) can be used when only one suitable organization is available. Finally, the auditor section notes that auditors are selected under Least Cost Selection (LCS).  

Putting these observations together, the chapter outlines QCBS, SSS, and LCS as the selection methods it covers. Since the financial‑advisor guidance says any of those methods may be applied to studies and financial consultancy, those three are precisely the options available.  

Therefore, the selection methods that can be used for financial advisors undertaking preparation of studies and financial consultancy are QCBS, SSS, and LCS.

## 7.4 Selection of Non-Governmental Organizations (NGO)
7.4.1 Procuring Entity may engage NGOs meeting qualifying for assignments typically attributable to NGOs. In this case, QCBS should be followed, and the evaluation criteria of proposals should reflect the NGO-unique qualifications, such as the following:

- i) History of work with grassroots communities and evidence of satisfactory performance;
- ii) Familiarity with participatory development approaches and low-cost technologies;

- iii) Experienced staff conversant with the cultural and socioeconomic dimensions of beneficiaries;
- iv) Committed leadership and adequate management;
- v) Capacity to co-opt beneficiary participation

7.4.2 Procuring Entities may select NGOs using SSS, provided the approvals and procedures laid down for the same are followed. For example, SSS may be adopted to hire a local NGO for a very small assignment in a remote area where only one NGO is available and competition is impractical.

## 7.5 Procurement Agents
Procurement agents (PAs) may be hired by the Procuring Entity to assist in carrying out procurement, to provide advice, or a combination of both. When PAs are specifically used as "agents" handling the procurement of specific items and generally working from their own offices, they are paid a percentage (either fixed or inversely proportional) of the value of the procurements handled or a fixed fee or a combination of a percentage and a fixed fee. In such cases, they are selected under QCBS, with cost being given a weight of up to 50 (fifty) percent. If the weight of the cost element adopted were as high as 50 (fifty) percent, financial considerations would dominate the selection, creating the risk of an unacceptably lower service quality. In such cases, it is essential to ensure that the quality threshold in the evaluation is set sufficiently high. When PAs provide only advisory services for procurement or act as "agents" for a whole project in a specific Unit of Procuring Entity, they are usually paid based on the staff-months of effort provided, and they shall be selected following the appropriate procedures for other Consultancy assignments using QCBS and time-based contracts, as specified for other Consultancy assignments.

## 7.6 Inspection Agents
Procuring Entities may hire inspection agents to inspect and certify goods before shipment or on arrival in the Procuring Entity country. The inspection by such agents usually covers the quality and quantity of the goods concerned and the reasonableness of the price. Inspection agents are selected using QCBS, with cost being allocated a weight of up to 50 (fifty) percent. Payment is usually based on a percentage of the value of goods inspected and certified.

## 7.7 Financial Advisors
7.7.1 Procuring Entities may hire financial institutions to implement two main types of assignment:

- i) in the preparation of studies and financial Consultancy; or
- ii) As advisers on financial restructuring, M&A or demerger etc.

7.7.2 In the first case, the advisers can be selected under any of the methods described in this chapter (that is, whichever is considered most suitable, depending on the scope of work of the assignment). In the second case, QCBS shall be adopted, whereby the RfP specifies technical evaluation criteria similar to those relevant to standard Consultancy assignments.

## 7.8 Auditors
Auditors typically carry out auditing tasks under well defined ToR and professional standards. They shall be selected according to LCS system, with cost as a selection factor.

question_text: What details must be included in the PRC generated by the consignee on the GeM portal?
answer:
- The PRC must specify the date of receipt of goods, milestone achievement, or service delivery as indicated in the certificate. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must bear the consignee’s digital signature or e‑sign. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be generated online on the GeM portal. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be a Provisional Receipt Certificate (PRC). (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be issued on a “said to contain basis”. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be issued within 48 hours of the seller’s entry of delivery, milestone achievement, or service delivery. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: it wants to know the mandatory elements that must appear in a Provisional Receipt Certificate (PRC) when the consignee creates it on the GeM portal.  
Then, I recall that upon delivery the consignee should receive the goods/services and issue an online Provisional Receipt Certificate, with his/her digital signature or e‑sign, mentioning the date of receipt, and that this is done on a “said to contain basis” within 48 hours of the seller’s entry.  
Next, I isolate each distinct requirement: the certificate must be provisional, it must be generated online on the GeM portal, it must bear the consignee’s digital or e‑signature, it must state the date of receipt of goods, milestone achievement, or service delivery, it must be based on a said to contain assessment, and it must be issued within the 48‑hour window after the seller’s logged delivery.  
Further, I note that none of these points are optional or implied elsewhere; the Procurement of Goods Manual repeatedly stresses that the consignee has to mandatorily acknowledge receipt through generation of the PRC, and that the timing, the digital signature, the said to contain basis, and the provisional nature are all explicit conditions for a valid PRC.  
Finally, I bring the pieces together and conclude that a PRC generated by the consignee on GeM must include the date of receipt, the consignee’s digital signature or e‑sign, be created online on the GeM portal, be a Provisional Receipt Certificate, be issued on a said to contain basis, and be issued within 48 hours of the seller’s entry of delivery, milestone achievement, or service delivery.
